The Author’s Apology For His Book

WHEN first of all I took my pen in hand

To write like this, I did not understand

That I would ever make a little book

In such a style; no, the work I undertook

Was quite another, which, when almost done,

Before I knew it, I had this begun.

And it was like this: writing of the way

And race of saints in this our gospel-day,

I suddenly fell into an allegory

About their journey, and the way to glory,

In more than twenty things I wrote, all told;

That done, my head had twenty more to hold,

And these in turn began to multiply,

Like sparks that from the coals of fire will fly.

No, then, I thought, if you+ breed so fast,

I’ll put you+ by yourselves+, lest you+ at last

Should run ad infinitum,1 and crowd out

The book that I have already set about.

Well, so I did; but still I did not think

Of showing all the world my pen and ink

In such a style; I only meant to make

I did not know what; nor did I undertake

By this to please my neighbor; no, not I;

It was myself I meant to gratify.

Nor did I more than my spare hours spend

On this, my scribbling; nor did I intend

Except to keep myself, by doing this,

From worse thoughts, which would make me act amiss.

So I set pen to paper with delight,

And quickly had my thoughts in black and white;

For now I had my method by the end,

And as I pulled, it came; and so I penned

It down, until it came at last to be,

In length and breadth, the size that you now see.

Well, when I had thus put my ends together,

I showed them to others, so I could see whether

They would condemn them, or would justify:

And some said, Let them live; some, Let them die;

Some said, John, print it; others said, Not so;

Some said, It might do good; others said, No.

Now I was in a bind, and could not see

Which was the best thing to be done by me:

At last I thought, Since you+ are so divided,

I’ll print it; and that the case decided.

For, I thought, some I see would have it done,

Though others in that channel do not run:

To find out, then, who advised for the best,

I thought it right to put it to the test.

I further thought, if I should now deny

Those who would have it, and not gratify,

For all I knew, I’d hinder them, and might

Withhold what would have been their great delight.

To those who were against its coming forth

I said, To give you+ offense I am loath;

Yet since your+ brethren like it, let it be,

And do not judge till you+ further see.

If you will not read it, leave it alone;

Some love the meat, some love to pick the bone.

Yes, so that I might calm them, I would state

My case to them like this, and so debate:

May I not write in such a style as this?

In such a manner too, and yet not miss

My aim—your good? Why can it not be done?

Dark clouds bring water, while the bright bring none.

Yes, dark or bright, if they let silver drops

Come down, the earth, by yielding up its crops,

Gives praise to both, and finds no fault with either,

But stores up all the fruit they yield together;

Yes, mixes both so well that in their fruit

No one can tell which one is which; they suit

Her well when hungry; but if she is full,

She spews out both, and makes their blessing null.

You see the ways the fisherman will take

To catch the fish; what devices he will make!

See how he puts to work all of his wits,

And also snares, lines, rods, hooks, and nets:

Yet there are fish no hook or line can land,

No snare, no net, no device bring to hand:

They must be groped for, and be tickled too,

Or they will not be caught, whatever you do.

How does the fowler try to catch his game

By many means, too many for one to name!

His guns, his nets, his lime-twigs, light and bell:

He creeps, he walks, he stands; yes, who can tell

All of his postures? Yet not one of these

Will make him master of the birds he’d seize.

Yes, he must pipe and whistle to catch this;

Yet if he does so, that bird he will miss.

If a pearl may within a toad’s head dwell,

And may be found too in an oyster-shell;

If things that promise nothing still contain

What is worth more than gold, who would disdain,

With an inkling of it, to go there and look,

So they may find it? Now, my little book,

(Though bare of all the ornaments that make

This man or that a fancy to it take,)

Is not without the things that far excel

What in fine-sounding, empty notions dwell.

“Well, still I am not fully satisfied

That this, your book, will stand when soundly tried.”

Why, what’s the matter? “It is dark.” And so?

“But it is fiction.” What of that? I know

Some men, by fictions just as dark as mine,

Make the truth sparkle, and its rays shine.

“But they lack solidity.” Speak, man, your mind.

“They drown the weak; metaphors make us blind.”

Solidity, indeed, befits the pen

Of him who writes of things divine to men:

But must I lack solidity because

I speak by metaphors? Were not God’s laws,

His gospel laws, in olden times set forth

By types, shadows, and metaphors? Yet loath

Would any sober man be to find fault

With them, for fear he’d be found to assault

The highest wisdom! No, he rather stoops,

And seeks to find out what, by pins and loops,

By calves and sheep, by heifers, and by rams,

By birds and herbs, and by the blood of lambs,

God speaks to him; happy the one who’s found

The light and grace with which they all abound.

So do not be too quick to conclude

That I lack solidity—that I am crude;

Things solid in their show aren’t always so;

Nor should we scorn all parables we know,

Lest we most harmful things too lightly take,

And good things, to our souls’ great loss, forsake.

My dark and cloudy words, they only hold

The truth, as cabinets enclose the gold.

The prophets often used metaphors

To set forth truth; yes, whoever considers

Christ, his apostles too, will plainly find

That truths today wear mantles of this kind.

Am I afraid to say that holy writ,

Which in its style and phrase outdoes all wit,

Is everywhere so full of all these things,

Dark figures, allegories? Yet there springs

From that same book that luster and those rays

Of light that turn our darkest nights to days.

Come, let my critic give his life a look,

And find there darker lines than in my book

He finds at all; yes, and let him know

That in his best things there are worse lines too.

If we could stand before impartial men,

To his poor one I’d dare to wager ten

That they will take my meaning in these lines

Far better than his lies in silver shrines.

Come, truth, although in swaddling clothes, I find

Informs the judgment, and sets right the mind;

Pleases the understanding, makes the will

Submit; the memory, too, it will fill

With things that please our imagination well;

It also helps our troubles to dispel.

Sound words, I know, Timothy is to use,

And old wives’ tales he is to refuse;

But nowhere does grave Paul at all forbid

His use of parables, in which lay hid

That gold, those pearls, and precious stones that were

Worth digging for, and that with the greatest care.

Let me add one word more. O man of God,

Are you offended? Do you wish I had

Put forth my matter in another dress,

Or put things plainly, using figures less?

Three things let me propose; then I submit

To those who are my betters, as is fit.

1. I do not find I am denied the use

Of this my method, if I don’t abuse

The words, things, readers, and am not crude

In handling figure or similitude,

In application, but, as best I may,

Seek to advance truth in this or that way.

Denied, did I say? No, I have leave

(Example too, and that from those who have

Pleased God better, by their words or ways,

Than any man alive in our own days)

Like this to express my mind, like this declare

To you the things most excellent there are.

2. I find that men as high as trees will write

In dialogue; yet no one thinks them slight

For writing so. Indeed, if they abuse

Truth, cursed are they, and the craft they use

To that end; but still let truth be free

To make her sallies upon you and me,

Which way it pleases God: for who knows how,

Better than he who taught us first to plow,

To guide our minds and pens for his designs?

And makes low things usher in the divine.

3. I find that holy writ, in many places,

Has likeness to this method, where the cases

Call for one thing to set forth another:

Then I may use it, and yet not smother

Truth’s golden beams; no, by this method I may

Make it cast forth its rays as light as day.

And now, before I put away my pen,

I’ll show the profit of my book; and then

Commit both you and it into that hand

That pulls the strong down, and makes weak ones stand.

This book sketches out before your eyes

The man who seeks the everlasting prize:

It shows you where he comes from, where he goes,

What he leaves undone, and also what he does;

It also shows you how he runs and runs,

Until he at the gate of glory comes.

It shows, too, some who set out with might and main

For life, as if the lasting crown they’d gain;

Here also you may see the reason why

They lose their labor, and like fools they die.

This book will make a traveler of you,

If you let its counsel tell you what to do;

It will direct you to the Holy Land,

If its directions you will understand:

Yes, it will make the lazy active; yes,

And make the blind see lovely things no less.

Do you want something rare and profitable?

Or would you see a truth within a fable?

Are you forgetful? Would you remember

From New Year’s Day to the last of December?

Then read my fancies; they will stick like burs,

And may, to the helpless, be comforters.

This book is written in a kind of speech

That even minds of listless men can reach:

It seems a novelty, and yet contains

Nothing but sound and honest gospel strains.

Would you distract yourself from melancholy?

Would you be cheerful, yet be far from folly?

Would you read riddles, and their explanation?

Or else be drowned in your contemplation?

Do you love picking meat? Or would you view

A man in the clouds, and hear him speak to you?

Would you be in a dream, and yet not sleep?

Or would you in a moment laugh and weep?

Would you lose yourself and come to no harm,

And find yourself again without a charm?

Would you read yourself, and read you don’t know what,

And yet know whether you are blessed or not,

By reading the same lines? Oh, then come, gather,

And lay my book, your head, and heart together.

JOHN BUNYAN.

1. Without end.

PART ONE

THE FIRST STAGE

As I walked through the wilderness of this world, I came upon a certain place where there was a den,2 and lay down in that place to sleep; and as I slept, I dreamed a dream. I dreamed, and behold, I saw a man clothed with rags, standing in a certain place, with his face turned from his own house, a book in his hand, and a great burden upon his back. Isa 64:6; Luke 14:33; Ps 38:4. I looked and saw him open the book and read in it; and as he read, he wept and trembled; and, no longer able to hold himself in, he broke out with a pitiful cry, saying, “What shall I do?” Acts 2:37; 16:30; Hab 1:2, 3.

In this plight he went home and held himself in as long as he could, so that his wife and children would not see his distress; but he could not keep quiet long, because his trouble grew. So at last he opened his mind to his wife and children, and began to talk to them like this: “O my dear wife,” he said, “and you+, my own children, I, your+ dear friend, am undone in myself because of a burden that lies heavy on me; what is more, I have been told for certain that this city of ours will be burned with fire from heaven; and in that terrible overthrow I myself, and you my wife, and you+ my sweet babes, will all miserably come to ruin, unless some way of escape can be found by which we may be delivered (and as yet I see none).” At this his family were deeply bewildered; not because they believed that what he had said to them was true, but because they thought some madness had got into his head; so, as night was coming on, and they hoped that sleep might settle his brains, they got him to bed as fast as they could. But the night was as troublesome to him as the day; so instead of sleeping, he spent it in sighs and tears. When morning came, they wanted to know how he was. He told them, “Worse and worse.” He also started talking to them again; but they began to be hardened. They also thought they could drive away his madness by treating him harshly and sullenly; sometimes they would mock him, sometimes they would scold him, and sometimes they would ignore him altogether. So he began to keep to his room, to pray for them and pity them, and also to grieve over his own misery; he would also walk alone in the fields, sometimes reading, and sometimes praying; and so he spent his time for some days.

Now I saw, one day when he was walking in the fields, that he was (as was his habit) reading in his book, and greatly distressed in his mind; and as he read, he burst out, as he had done before, crying, “What shall I do to be saved?” Acts 16:30, 31.

I saw also that he looked this way and that, as if he wanted to run; yet he stood still, because (as I could see) he could not tell which way to go. Then I looked, and saw a man named Evangelist coming to him, who asked, “Why are you crying?”

He answered, “Sir, I see by the book in my hand that I am condemned to die, and after that to come to judgment, Heb 9:27; and I find that I am not willing to do the first, Job 10:21, 22, nor able to do the second.” Ezek 22:14.

Then Evangelist said, “Why are you not willing to die, since this life is beset with so many evils?” The man answered, “Because I fear that this burden on my back will sink me lower than the grave, and I will fall into Tophet. Isa 30:33. And, sir, if I am not fit to go to prison, I am not fit to go to judgment, and from there to execution; and the thoughts of these things make me cry.”

Then Evangelist said, “If this is your condition, why are you standing still?” He answered, “Because I do not know where to go.” Then Evangelist gave him a parchment roll, and inside it was written, “Flee from the wrath to come.” Matt 3:7.

So the man read it, and looking at Evangelist very carefully, said, “Where must I flee?” Then Evangelist said (pointing with his finger over a very wide field), “Do you see that wicket-gate over there?” Matt 7:13, 14. The man said, “No.” Then the other said, “Do you see that shining light over there?” Ps 119:105; 2 Pet 1:19. He said, “I think I do.” Then Evangelist said, “Keep that light in your eye, and go straight up to it; so you will see the gate; and when you knock at it, you will be told what to do.” So I saw in my dream that the man began to run. Now he had not run far from his own door when his wife and children saw it and began to cry after him to come back; but the man put his fingers in his ears, and ran on crying, Life! life! eternal life! Luke 14:26. So he did not look behind him, Gen 19:17, but fled toward the middle of the plain.

The neighbors also came out to see him run, Jer 20:10; and as he ran, some mocked, others threatened, and some cried after him to come back; and among those who did, there were two who were determined to bring him back by force. The name of the one was Obstinate, and the name of the other Pliable. By now the man had got a good distance away from them; but they were determined to go after him all the same, which they did, and in a little while they overtook him. Then the man said, “Neighbors, why have you+ come?” They said, “To persuade you to go back with us.” But he said, “That can by no means be. You+ live,” he said, “in the city of Destruction, which is also the place where I was born: I see that it is so; and dying there, sooner or later, you+ will sink lower than the grave, into a place that burns with fire and brimstone. Be content, good neighbors, and come along with me.”

Obstinate: What! said Obstinate, and leave our friends and our comforts behind us?

Christian: Yes, said Christian (for that was his name), because all that you give up is not worth comparing with a little of what I am seeking to enjoy, 2 Cor 4:18; and if you will come along with me, and hold to it, you will fare as I will; for there, where I am going, is enough and to spare. Luke 15:17. Come away, and test my words.

Obstinate: What are these things you are seeking, since you are leaving all the world to find them?

Christian: I seek an inheritance incorruptible, undefiled, and that does not fade away, 1 Pet 1:4; and it is laid up in heaven, and safe there, Heb 11:16, to be given, at the appointed time, to those who diligently seek it. Read about it there in my book, if you like.

Obstinate: Nonsense! said Obstinate. Away with your book; are you going back with us or not?

Christian: No, not I, said the other, because I have put my hand to the plow. Luke 9:62.

Obstinate: Come then, neighbor Pliable, let us turn back and go home without him: there is a whole company of these crazy-headed fools who, when they get hold of a fancy, are wiser in their own eyes than seven men who can give a reason.

Pliable: Then Pliable said, Don’t mock him; if what the good Christian says is true, the things he looks for are better than ours: my heart is inclined to go with my neighbor.

Obstinate: What! more fools still? Listen to me, and go back; who knows where such a brain-sick fellow will lead you? Go back, go back, and be wise.

Christian: No, rather you come along with your neighbor Pliable; there are such things to be had as I spoke of, and many more glories besides. If you do not believe me, read here in this book; and for the truth of what it says, look, all of it is confirmed by the blood of Him who made it. Heb 9:17–21.

Pliable: Well, neighbor Obstinate, said Pliable, I am beginning to make up my mind; I intend to go along with this good man, and to cast in my lot with him. But, my good companion, do you know the way to this place we long for?

Christian: I have been directed by a man whose name is Evangelist to hurry on to a little gate that is ahead of us, where we will receive instructions about the way.

Pliable: Come then, good neighbor, let us be going. Then they both went on together.

Obstinate: And I will go back home, said Obstinate. I will be no companion to such misguided, fanciful fellows.

Now I saw in my dream that, when Obstinate had gone back, Christian and Pliable went talking over the plain; and this is how they began their conversation.

Christian: Come, neighbor Pliable, how are you? I am glad you were persuaded to come along with me. If even Obstinate himself had felt what I have felt of the powers and terrors of what is yet unseen, he would not have turned his back on us so lightly.

Pliable: Come, neighbor Christian, since there are only the two of us here, tell me more now: what are the things where we are going, and how are they to be enjoyed?

Christian: I can picture them better in my mind than speak of them with my tongue; but still, since you want to know, I will read about them in my book.

Pliable: And do you think that the words of your book are certainly true?

Christian: Yes, certainly; for it was made by Him who cannot lie. Titus 1:2.

Pliable: Well said; what are these things?

Christian: There is an endless kingdom for us to live in, and everlasting life to be given us, so that we may live in that kingdom forever. Isa 65:17; John 10:27–29.

Pliable: Well said; and what else?

Christian: There are crowns of glory to be given us, and garments that will make us shine like the sun in the firmament of heaven. 2 Tim 4:8; Rev 22:5; Matt 13:43.

Pliable: This is very pleasant; and what else?

Christian: There will be no more crying or sorrow; for he who owns the place will wipe all tears from our eyes. Isa 25:8; Rev 7:16, 17; 21:4.

Pliable: And what company will we have there?

Christian: There we will be with seraphim and cherubim, Isa 6:2; 1 Thess 4:16, 17; Rev 5:11; creatures that will dazzle your eyes when you look at them. There you will also meet thousands and ten thousands who have gone before us to that place; none of them harmful, but loving and holy; every one walking in the sight of God, and standing in his presence, accepted forever. In a word, there we will see the elders with their golden crowns, Rev 4:4; there we will see the holy virgins with their golden harps, Rev 14:1–5; there we will see men who were cut in pieces by the world, burned in flames, eaten by beasts, drowned in the seas, for the love they had for the Lord of the place, John 12:25; all well, and clothed with immortality as with a garment. 2 Cor 5:2.

Pliable: Just hearing this is enough to enrapture one’s heart. But are these things really to be enjoyed? How will we come to share in them?

Christian: The Lord, the ruler of the country, has recorded that in this book, Isa 55:1, 2; John 6:37; 7:37; Rev 21:6; 22:17; and the substance of it is that, if we are truly willing to have it, he will give it to us freely.

Pliable: Well, my good companion, I am glad to hear of these things: come on, let us quicken our pace.

Christian: I cannot go as fast as I would like, because of this burden on my back.

Now I saw in my dream that, just as they had finished this talk, they came near a very miry slough in the middle of the plain; and, not watching where they went, they both suddenly fell into the bog. The name of the slough was Despond. Here, then, they wallowed for a time, badly plastered with the mud; and Christian, because of the burden on his back, began to sink in the mire.

Pliable: Then Pliable said, Ah, neighbor Christian, where are you now?

Christian: Truly, said Christian, I do not know.

Pliable: At this Pliable began to be offended, and angrily said to his companion, Is this the happiness you have been telling me about all this while? If we have such bad luck at our first setting out, what may we expect between here and our journey’s end? If I can only get out again with my life, you shall possess the fine country alone, for all I care. And with that he gave a desperate struggle or two, and got out of the mire on the side of the slough that was nearest to his own house: so away he went, and Christian saw him no more.

So Christian was left to flounder in the Slough of Despond alone; but still he tried to struggle to the side of the slough that was farthest from his own house and nearest to the wicket-gate; and he got there, but could not get out, because of the burden on his back. But I saw in my dream that a man came to him whose name was Help, and asked him what he was doing there.

Christian: Sir, said Christian, I was told to go this way by a man called Evangelist, who also directed me to that gate over there, so that I might escape the wrath to come. And as I was going there, I fell in here.

Help: But why did you not look for the steps?

Christian: Fear followed me so hard that I fled the nearest way, and fell in.

Help: Then, he said, Give me your hand. So he gave him his hand, and Help drew him out, Ps 40:2, and set him on solid ground, and told him to go on his way.

Then I stepped up to the one who had pulled him out, and said, “Sir, since the way from the city of Destruction to that gate over there runs across this place, why is it that this patch is not mended, so that poor travelers might go there more safely?” And he said to me, “This miry slough is such a place as cannot be mended. It is the low place into which the scum and filth that come with conviction for sin continually run, and so it is called the Slough of Despond; for whenever the sinner is awakened to his lost condition, many fears and doubts and discouraging misgivings arise in his soul, and all of them get together and settle in this place: and this is why the ground is so bad.

“It is not the King’s wish that this place should remain so bad. Isa 35:3, 4. His laborers also, by the direction of his Majesty’s surveyors, have been at work on this patch of ground for more than these sixteen hundred years, to see if it might be mended. Yes, and to my knowledge,” he said, “at least twenty thousand cartloads have been swallowed up here, indeed millions of wholesome instructions, which have been brought at all seasons from every part of the King’s dominions (and those who know say they are the best materials for making good ground of the place), in the hope that it might be mended; but it is the Slough of Despond still, and so it will be when they have done all they can.

“True, there are, by the direction of the Lawgiver, certain good and solid steps placed right through the very middle of this slough; but at times when this place spews out a great deal of its filth, as it does before a change in the weather, these steps can hardly be seen; or if they are, men, through the dizziness of their heads, step off them, and then they are thoroughly mired, even though the steps are there. But the ground is good once they have got in at the gate.” 1 Sam 12:23.

Now I saw in my dream that by this time Pliable had got home to his house. So his neighbors came to visit him; and some of them called him a wise man for coming back, and some called him a fool for risking himself with Christian; others again mocked his cowardice, saying, “Surely, once you had begun to venture, I would not have been so base as to give up because of a few difficulties.” So Pliable sat cringing among them. But at last he grew more confident, and then they all changed their story, and began to ridicule poor Christian behind his back. And so much for Pliable.

Now as Christian was walking alone by himself, he caught sight of someone far off coming across the field to meet him; and as it happened, they met just as their paths crossed. The name of the gentleman who met him was Mr. Worldly Wiseman: he lived in the town of Carnal Policy, a very large town, and also close to the place Christian came from. So this man, meeting Christian, and having some inkling of who he was (for Christian’s setting out from the city of Destruction was much talked about, not only in the town where he lived, but it was also beginning to be the talk of the town in some other places)—Mr. Worldly Wiseman, then, having some guess who he was, from seeing his laborious going, and noticing his sighs and groans and the like, began to enter into some talk with Christian like this.

Mr. Worldly Wiseman: Well now, good fellow, where are you going in this burdened manner?

Christian: A burdened manner indeed, as much as I think any poor creature ever had! And since you ask me, Where are you going? I tell you, sir, I am going to that wicket-gate ahead of me; for there, as I have been told, I will be put into a way to be rid of my heavy burden.

Mr. Worldly Wiseman: Do you have a wife and children?

Christian: Yes; but I am so weighed down with this burden that I cannot take the pleasure in them that I used to: it is as if I had none. 1 Cor 7:29.

Mr. Worldly Wiseman: Will you listen to me, if I give you some advice?

Christian: If it is good, I will; for I am in need of good advice.

Mr. Worldly Wiseman: Then I would advise you to get rid of your burden as fast as you can; for you will never be settled in your mind till then, nor can you enjoy the benefits of the blessings God has given you till then.

Christian: That is just what I am seeking, to be rid of this heavy burden: but I cannot get it off by myself, nor is there any man in our country who can take it off my shoulders; that is why I am going this way, as I told you, so that I may be rid of my burden.

Mr. Worldly Wiseman: Who told you to go this way to be rid of your burden?

Christian: A man who seemed to me to be a very great and honorable person: his name, as I remember, is Evangelist.

Mr. Worldly Wiseman: A curse on him for his advice! There is not a more dangerous and troublesome way in the world than the one he has directed you into; and you will find that out, if you let yourself be ruled by his advice. You have met with something already, I see; for I see the dirt of the Slough of Despond on you: but that slough is the beginning of the sorrows that come to those who go on in that way. Listen to me; I am older than you: in the way you are going you are likely to meet with weariness, pain, hunger, perils, nakedness, sword, lions, dragons, darkness, and, in a word, death, and who knows what else. These things are certainly true, having been confirmed by many witnesses. And should a man so carelessly throw himself away by listening to a stranger?

Christian: Why, sir, this burden on my back is more terrible to me than all these things you have mentioned: indeed, I think I do not care what I meet with in the way, if only I can also meet with deliverance from my burden.

Mr. Worldly Wiseman: How did you come by your burden in the first place?

Christian: By reading this book in my hand.

Mr. Worldly Wiseman: I thought so; and it has happened to you as to other weak men, who, meddling with things too high for them, suddenly fall into frenzies like yours; and those frenzies not only unman men, as I see yours have done to you, but drive them into desperate ventures, to gain they do not know what.

Christian: I know what I want to gain; it is relief from my heavy burden.

Mr. Worldly Wiseman: But why will you seek relief this way, seeing that so many dangers come with it, especially since (if only you had the patience to listen to me) I could direct you to what you desire, without the dangers you will run yourself into this way? Yes, and the remedy is close at hand. Besides, I will add that instead of those dangers you will meet with much safety, friendship, and contentment.

Christian: Sir, please tell me this secret.

Mr. Worldly Wiseman: Why, in that village over there (the village is named Morality) there lives a gentleman whose name is Legality, a very sensible man, and a man of very good name, who has the skill to help men get such burdens as yours off their shoulders; indeed, to my knowledge, he has done a great deal of good this way; yes, and besides, he has the skill to cure those who are somewhat crazed in their wits by their burdens. To him, as I said, you may go, and be helped at once. His house is not quite a mile from this place; and if he should not be at home himself, he has a fine young man for a son, whose name is Civility, who can do it (so to speak) as well as the old gentleman himself. There, I say, you may be relieved of your burden; and if you have no mind to go back to your former home (as indeed I would not wish you to), you may send for your wife and children to this village, where there are houses standing empty now, one of which you may have at a reasonable rent; food there is also cheap and good; and what will make your life all the happier is that you will certainly live there among honest neighbors, in good repute and good standing.

Now Christian was somewhat at a loss; but he soon concluded, If what this gentleman has said is true, my wisest course is to take his advice; and with that he went on to say this.

Christian: Sir, which way do I go to this honest man’s house?

Mr. Worldly Wiseman: Do you see that high hill over there?

Christian: Yes, very well.

Mr. Worldly Wiseman: You must go by that hill, and the first house you come to is his.

So Christian turned out of his way to go to Mr. Legality’s house for help. But look, when he had now got close to the hill, it seemed so high, and the side of it next to the road hung over so far, that Christian was afraid to venture any further, for fear the hill would fall on his head; so he stood still there, and did not know what to do. His burden, too, now seemed heavier to him than it had while he was in the way. Flashes of fire also came, Exod 19:16, 18, out of the hill, which made Christian afraid that he would be burned: so here he sweated and shook with fear. Heb 12:21. And now he began to be sorry that he had taken Mr. Worldly Wiseman’s advice; and just then he saw Evangelist coming to meet him, and at the sight of him he began to blush for shame. So Evangelist drew nearer and nearer; and coming up to him, he looked at him with a stern and dreadful face, and began to reason with Christian like this.

Evangelist: What are you doing here, Christian? he said; at which words Christian did not know what to answer; so for the moment he stood speechless before him. Then Evangelist went on, Are you not the man I found crying outside the walls of the city of Destruction?

Christian: Yes, dear sir, I am the man.

Evangelist: Did I not show you the way to the little wicket-gate?

Christian: Yes, dear sir, said Christian.

Evangelist: How is it, then, that you have turned aside so quickly? For you are now out of the way.

Christian: I met a gentleman as soon as I had got over the Slough of Despond, who persuaded me that in the village ahead of me I might find a man who could take off my burden.

Evangelist: What sort of man was he?

Christian: He looked like a gentleman, and talked a great deal to me, and at last got me to give in; so I came here; but when I saw this hill, and how it hangs over the way, I stopped short, for fear it would fall on my head.

Evangelist: What did that gentleman say to you?

Christian: Why, he asked me where I was going; and I told him.

Evangelist: And what did he say then?

Christian: He asked me if I had a family; and I told him. But, I said, I am so weighed down with the burden on my back that I cannot take pleasure in them as I used to.

Evangelist: And what did he say then?

Christian: He told me to get rid of my burden quickly; and I told him it was relief that I was seeking. And, I said, that is why I am going to that gate over there, to receive further directions about how I may get to the place of deliverance. So he said that he would show me a better way, and a shorter one, not so beset with difficulties as the way, sir, that you set me on; and that way, he said, will lead you to the house of a gentleman who has the skill to take off these burdens. So I believed him, and turned out of that way into this one, hoping that I might soon be relieved of my burden. But when I came to this place, and saw how things are, I stopped, for fear (as I said) of danger: and now I do not know what to do.

Evangelist: Then Evangelist said, Stand still a little, so that I may show you the words of God. So he stood trembling. Then Evangelist said, “See that you+ do not refuse Him who speaks. For if they did not escape who refused Him who spoke on earth, much less will we escape if we turn away from Him who speaks from heaven.” Heb 12:25. He also said, “Now the just shall live by faith; but if anyone draws back, My soul shall have no pleasure in him.” Heb 10:38. And he applied them like this: You are the man who is running into this misery; you have begun to reject the counsel of the Most High, and to draw back your foot from the way of peace, even almost to the point of risking your perdition.

Then Christian fell down at his feet as if dead, crying, Woe is me, for I am undone! At the sight of this Evangelist caught him by the right hand, saying, “Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven men.” Matt 12:31. “Stop doubting and believe.” John 20:27. Then Christian revived a little again, and stood up trembling, as at first, before Evangelist.

Then Evangelist went on, saying, Listen more carefully to the things I am going to tell you. I will now show you who it was that deceived you, and also who it was he sent you to. The man who met you is one Worldly Wiseman, and he is rightly called so; partly because he has a taste only for the doctrine of this world, 1 John 4:5 (that is why he always goes to church in the town of Morality); and partly because he loves that doctrine best, for it best saves him from the cross, Gal 6:12. And because he is of this carnal disposition, he seeks to pervert my ways, though they are right. Now there are three things in this man’s advice that you must utterly abhor.

1. His turning you out of the way.

2. His efforts to make the cross hateful to you.

3. And his setting your feet on the way that leads to the ministry of death.

First, You must abhor his turning you out of the way; yes, and your own consenting to it; because this is to reject the counsel of God for the sake of the counsel of a Worldly Wiseman. The Lord says, “Strive to enter in at the narrow gate,” Luke 13:24, the gate to which I am sending you; “for narrow is the gate that leads to life, and few there are who find it.” Matt 7:13, 14. This wicked man has turned you away from this little wicket-gate, and from the way to it, and so has brought you almost to destruction. Hate, therefore, his turning you out of the way, and abhor yourself for listening to him.

Secondly, You must abhor his efforts to make the cross hateful to you; for you are to value it above the treasures of Egypt. Heb 11:25, 26. Besides, the King of glory has told you that he who would save his life will lose it. And he who comes after him, and does not hate his father, and mother, and wife, and children, and brethren, and sisters, yes, and his own life also, cannot be his disciple. Mark 8:34; John 12:25; Matt 10:39; Luke 14:26. I say, therefore, when a man works to persuade you that the very thing without which, as the truth has said, you cannot have eternal life will be your death, you must abhor this doctrine.

Thirdly, You must hate his setting your feet on the way that leads to the ministry of death. And for this you must consider whom he sent you to, and also how unable that person was to deliver you from your burden.

He to whom you were sent for relief, Legality by name, is the son of the bond-woman who now is, and is in bondage with her children, Gal 4:21–27, and is, in a mystery, this Mount Sinai, which you have feared will fall on your head. Now if she and her children are in bondage, how can you expect to be made free by them? This Legality, therefore, is not able to set you free from your burden. No man has ever yet been rid of his burden by him; no, nor is any man ever likely to be: you+ cannot be justified by the works of the law; for by the deeds of the law no man living can be rid of his burden. Therefore Mr. Worldly Wiseman is an alien, and Mr. Legality is a cheat; and as for his son Civility, for all his simpering looks, he is only a hypocrite, and cannot help you. Believe me, there is nothing in all this noise you have heard from these foolish men but a plot to cheat you of your salvation, by turning you from the way in which I had set you. After this, Evangelist called aloud to the heavens to confirm what he had said; and with that, words and fire came out of the mountain under which poor Christian stood, which made the hair of his flesh stand up. These were the words spoken: “All who rely on works of the law are under a curse. For it is written: ‘Cursed is everyone who does not continue to do everything written in the Book of the Law.’” Gal 3:10.

Now Christian expected nothing but death, and began to cry out pitifully, even cursing the time when he met Mr. Worldly Wiseman, and calling himself a thousand fools again and again for listening to his advice. He was also greatly ashamed to think that this gentleman’s arguments, coming only from the flesh, should have prevailed with him so far as to make him leave the right way. After this, he turned again to Evangelist, in words and sense as follows.

Christian: Sir, what do you think? Is there any hope? May I now go back and go up to the wicket-gate? Will I not be abandoned for this, and sent back from there ashamed? I am sorry I have listened to this man’s advice; but may my sin be forgiven?

Evangelist: Then Evangelist said to him, Your sin is very great, for by it you have committed two evils: you have forsaken the way that is good, to walk in forbidden paths. Yet the man at the gate will receive you, for he has good-will for men; only, he said, take care not to turn aside again, or you may “perish from the way, when His wrath is kindled but a little.” Ps 2:12.

2. Bedford jail, in which the author was imprisoned for conscience’ sake

THE SECOND STAGE

Then Christian got ready to go back; and Evangelist, after he had kissed him, gave him one smile and wished him God speed. So he went on in haste, and he spoke to no man on the way; and if anyone asked him anything, he would not give them an answer. He went like one who was treading on forbidden ground the whole time, and he could by no means feel safe until he had got back onto the way he had left to follow Mr. Worldly Wiseman’s advice. So in time Christian came up to the gate. Now over the gate was written, “Knock, and it will be opened to you.” Matt 7:7.

So he knocked, more than once or twice, saying,

““May I now enter here? Will he within

Open to sorry me, though I have been

An undeserving rebel? Then shall I

Not fail to sing his lasting praise on high.””

At last a grave person named Goodwill came to the gate, and asked who was there, where he came from, and what he wanted.

Christian: Here is a poor burdened sinner. I come from the city of Destruction, but I am going to Mount Zion, so that I may be delivered from the wrath to come. So, sir, since I am told that the way there lies through this gate, I would like to know whether you are willing to let me in.

Goodwill: I am willing with all my heart, he said; and with that he opened the gate.

So when Christian was stepping in, the other gave him a pull. Then Christian said, What does that mean? The other told him, A little way from this gate a strong castle has been built, and Beelzebub is its captain. From there both he and those who are with him shoot arrows at those who come up to this gate, in the hope that they may die before they can enter. Then Christian said, I rejoice and tremble. So when he had got in, the man of the Gate asked him who had directed him there.

Christian: Evangelist told me to come here and knock, as I did; and he said that you, sir, would tell me what I must do.

Goodwill: An open door is set before you, and no man can shut it.

Christian: Now I begin to reap the benefits of the risks I have run.

Goodwill: But how is it that you have come alone?

Christian: Because none of my neighbors saw their danger as I saw mine.

Goodwill: Did any of them know you were coming?

Christian: Yes, my wife and children saw me at the start, and called after me to turn back; and some of my neighbors also stood crying and calling after me to come back; but I put my fingers in my ears, and so came on my way.

Goodwill: But did none of them follow you, to persuade you to go back?

Christian: Yes, both Obstinate and Pliable; but when they saw that they could not succeed, Obstinate went back railing; but Pliable came with me a little way.

Goodwill: But why did he not come all the way?

Christian: We did indeed come together until we came to the Slough of Despond, into which we both suddenly fell. And then my neighbor Pliable lost heart, and would not risk going any farther. So, getting out again on the side nearest his own house, he told me I could have the fine country alone, for all he cared: so he went his way, and I came mine; he after Obstinate, and I to this gate.

Goodwill: Then Goodwill said, Alas, poor man! Is the celestial glory worth so little to him that he does not think it worth running the risk of a few difficulties to gain it?

Christian: Truly, said Christian, I have told the truth about Pliable; and if I were also to tell all the truth about myself, it would be clear that I am no better than he is. It is true he went back to his own house, but I also turned aside to go in the way of death, persuaded to it by the carnal arguments of one Mr. Worldly Wiseman.

Goodwill: Oh, did he come upon you? What! He wanted you to look for ease at the hands of Mr. Legality! They are both of them nothing but cheats. But did you take his advice?

Christian: Yes, as far as I dared. I went to find Mr. Legality, until I thought that the mountain that stands by his house would fall on my head; so there I was forced to stop.

Goodwill: That mountain has been the death of many, and will be the death of many more: it is good that you escaped being dashed to pieces by it.

Christian: Why, truly, I do not know what would have become of me there, if Evangelist had not fortunately met me again as I stood musing, down in the dumps; but it was God’s mercy that he came to me again, for otherwise I would never have come here. But now I have come, such as I am, more fit indeed to die by that mountain than to stand here talking with my Lord. But O, what a favor this is to me, that I am let in here after all!

Goodwill: We make no objection to anyone, whatever they have done before they come here; they are by no means cast out. John 6:37. And so, good Christian, come a little way with me, and I will teach you about the way you must go. Look ahead of you; do you see this narrow way? That is the way you must go. It was laid out by the patriarchs, prophets, Christ, and his apostles, and it is as straight as a rule can make it; this is the way you must go.

Christian: But, said Christian, are there no turnings or windings by which a stranger may lose his way?

Goodwill: Yes, there are many ways that run into this one, and they are crooked and wide; but this is how you can tell the right from the wrong: only the right one is straight and narrow. Matt 7:14.

Then I saw in my dream that Christian asked him further whether he could help him off with the burden that was upon his back. For as yet he had not got rid of it, and he could not by any means get it off without help.

He told him, “As for your burden, be content to bear it until you come to the place of deliverance; for there it will fall from your back by itself.”

Then Christian began to gird up his loins and get ready for his journey. So the other told him that when he had gone some distance from the gate, he would come to the house of the Interpreter, and he should knock at his door, and the Interpreter would show him excellent things. Then Christian took leave of his friend, and Goodwill again wished him God speed.

Then he went on till he came to the house of the Interpreter,3 where he knocked over and over. At last someone came to the door and asked who was there.

Christian: Sir, here is a traveler, who was told by an acquaintance of the head of this house to call here for my benefit; so I would like to speak with the master of the house.

So he called for the master of the house, who after a little while came to Christian and asked him what he wanted.

Christian: Sir, said Christian, I am a man who has come from the city of Destruction, and I am going to Mount Zion; and I was told by the man who stands at the gate at the head of this way that if I called here you would show me excellent things, such as would help me on my journey.

Interpreter: Then Interpreter said, Come in; I will show you what will do you good. So he told his servant to light the candle, and told Christian to follow him; so he took him into a private room, and told his servant to open a door. When the servant had done so, Christian saw the picture of a very grave person hanging on the wall; and this is what it looked like: It had its eyes lifted up to heaven, the best of books in its hand, the law of truth was written on its lips, the world was behind its back; it stood as if it were pleading with men, and a crown of gold hung over its head.

Christian: Then Christian said, What does this mean?

Interpreter: The man whose picture this is, is one in a thousand: he can father children, 1 Cor 4:15, labor in birth with children, Gal 4:19, and nurse them himself when they are born. And as you see him with his eyes lifted up to heaven, the best of books in his hand, and the law of truth written on his lips, it is to show you that his work is to know dark things and make them plain to sinners; just as you also see him standing as if he were pleading with men. And as you see the world cast behind him, and a crown hanging over his head, that is to show you that, as he slights and despises the things that are present for the love he has for his Master’s service, he is sure to have glory as his reward in the world that comes next. Now, said the Interpreter, I have shown you this picture first because the man whose picture this is, is the only man whom the Lord of the place where you are going has authorized to be your guide in all the difficult places you may meet on the way. So pay good attention to what I have shown you, and keep well in mind what you have seen, in case on your journey you meet some who pretend to lead you right, but their way goes down to death.

Then he took him by the hand and led him into a very large parlor that was full of dust, because it had never been swept. After the Interpreter had looked it over for a little while, he called for a man to sweep. Now when the man began to sweep, the dust flew about so thickly that Christian was almost choked by it. Then the Interpreter said to a maid who stood by, “Bring water here, and sprinkle the room”; and when she had done so, it was swept and cleansed with pleasure.

Christian: Then Christian said, What does this mean?

Interpreter: The Interpreter answered, This parlor is the heart of a man who was never sanctified by the sweet grace of the Gospel. The dust is his original sin and inward corruptions, which have defiled the whole man. He who began to sweep at first is the law; but she who brought water and sprinkled it is the Gospel. Now you saw that as soon as the first began to sweep, the dust flew about so much that he could not clean the room, and you were almost choked by it. This is to show you that the law, instead of cleansing the heart from sin (by its working), revives sin, Rom 7:9, puts strength into it, 1 Cor 15:56, and increases it in the soul, Rom 5:20, even as it reveals and forbids it; for it does not give power to subdue it. Again, you saw the maid sprinkle the room with water, and then it was cleansed with pleasure. This is to show you that when the Gospel comes into the heart with its sweet and precious influences, then, I say, just as you saw the maid lay the dust by sprinkling the floor with water, so sin is conquered and subdued, and the soul made clean, through faith in it, and so made fit for the King of glory to dwell in. John 15:3; Eph 5:26; Acts 15:9; Rom 16:25, 26.

I also saw in my dream that the Interpreter took him by the hand and led him into a little room, where two little children sat, each in his own chair. The name of the elder was Passion, and the name of the other Patience. Passion seemed very discontented, but Patience was very quiet. Then Christian asked, “Why is Passion so discontented?” The Interpreter answered, “Their guardian wants him to wait for his best things till the beginning of next year, but he must have everything now; Patience, though, is willing to wait.”

Then I saw that someone came to Passion, brought him a bag of treasure, and poured it out at his feet. He picked it up and rejoiced over it, and laughed at Patience in scorn as well. But I watched only a little while, and he had squandered it all, and had nothing left but rags.

Christian: Then Christian said to the Interpreter, Explain this matter to me more fully.

Interpreter: So he said, These two boys are pictures: Passion, of the men of this world, and Patience, of the men of the world to come. For, as you see here, passion must have everything now, this year, that is to say, in this world; and so it is with the men of this world. They must have all their good things now; they cannot wait till next year, that is, until the next world, for their share of good. That proverb, “A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush,” carries more weight with them than all the divine testimonies of the good of the world to come. But as you saw that he had quickly squandered everything, and soon had nothing left but rags, so it will be with all such men at the end of this world.

Christian: Then Christian said, Now I see that Patience has the best wisdom, and that on many counts. 1. Because he waits for the best things. 2. And also because he will have the glory of his when the other has nothing but rags.

Interpreter: Yes, and you may add another, namely, the glory of the next world will never wear out, but these are suddenly gone. So Passion did not have as much reason to laugh at Patience because he had his good things first, as Patience will have to laugh at Passion because he had his best things last; for first must give way to last, because last must have its time to come; but last gives way to nothing, for there is no other to follow it. So he who has his portion first must have a time when he spends it; but he who has his portion last will have it for ever. That is why it is said of Dives, “During your lifetime you received your good things, while Lazarus received bad things. But now he is comforted, while you are in agony.” Luke 16:25.

Christian: Then I see that it is not best to covet the things that are now, but to wait for things to come.

Interpreter: You speak the truth: for the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal. 2 Cor 4:18. But though this is so, yet because things present and our fleshly appetite are such close neighbors to each other, and again, because things to come and our carnal sense are such strangers to each other, that is why the first of these so quickly become friends, and the second are kept so far apart.

Then I saw in my dream that the Interpreter took Christian by the hand and led him into a place where a fire was burning against a wall, and someone was standing by it, always throwing a great deal of water on it to put it out; yet the fire burned higher and hotter.

Then Christian said, What does this mean?

The Interpreter answered, This fire is the work of grace that is done in the heart; the one who throws water on it, to extinguish it and put it out, is the devil. But as you see the fire burning higher and hotter in spite of it, you will also see the reason for that. So he took him around to the back of the wall, where he saw a man with a jar of oil in his hand, which he also kept pouring (but secretly) into the fire.

Then Christian said, What does this mean?

The Interpreter answered, This is Christ, who continually, with the oil of his grace, keeps up the work already begun in the heart; by which means, whatever the devil can do, the souls of his people remain full of grace. 2 Cor 12:9. And as you saw that the man stood behind the wall to keep the fire going, this is to teach you that it is hard for the tempted to see how this work of grace is kept up in the soul.

I also saw that the Interpreter took him by the hand again and led him into a pleasant place, where a stately palace had been built, beautiful to see; and Christian was greatly delighted at the sight of it. He also saw certain people walking on top of it, who were clothed all in gold.

Then Christian said, May we go in there?

Then the Interpreter took him and led him up toward the door of the palace; and there at the door stood a great company of men, wanting to go in, but they did not dare. A man also sat at a little distance from the door, at a table, with a book and his inkhorn in front of him, to take down the names of those who were to enter; and Christian saw that many men in armor stood in the doorway to guard it, resolved to do the men who wanted to enter whatever hurt and harm they could. Now Christian was somewhat bewildered. At last, when every man was shrinking back for fear of the armed men, Christian saw a man with a very resolute face come up to the man who sat there to write, saying, “Set down my name, sir”; and when the writer had done so, Christian saw the man draw his sword, put a helmet on his head, and rush toward the door at the armed men, who fell on him with deadly force; but the man, not at all discouraged, fell to cutting and hacking most fiercely. So after he had received and given many wounds to those who tried to keep him out, Matt 11:12; Acts 14:22; he cut his way through them all and pressed forward into the palace. At this a pleasant voice was heard from those who were inside, even from those who walked on top of the palace, saying,

““Come in, come in,

Eternal glory you will win.””

So he went in, and was clothed with garments like theirs. Then Christian smiled and said, I really think I know the meaning of this.

Now, said Christian, let me go on from here. No, stay, said the Interpreter, till I have shown you a little more, and after that you shall go on your way. So he took him by the hand again and led him into a very dark room, where a man sat in an iron cage.

Now the man looked very sad; he sat with his eyes cast down to the ground, his hands folded together, and he sighed as if his heart would break. Then Christian said, What does this mean? At this the Interpreter told him to talk with the man.

Then Christian said to the man, What are you? The man answered, I am what I once was not.

Christian: What were you once?

The Man: The man said, I was once a fair and flourishing professing Christian, Luke 8:13, both in my own eyes and in the eyes of others. I was once, as I thought, well on the way to the celestial city, and I even had joy then at the thought that I would get there.

Christian: Well, but what are you now?

The Man: I am now a man of despair, and am shut up in it, as in this iron cage. I cannot get out. Oh, now I cannot!

Christian: But how did you come into this condition?

The Man: I stopped watching and being sober; I gave my lusts free rein; I sinned against the light of the word and the goodness of God; I have grieved the Spirit, and he is gone; I tempted the devil, and he has come to me; I have provoked God to anger, and he has left me; I have so hardened my heart that I cannot repent.

Then Christian said to the Interpreter, But is there no hope for such a man as this? Ask him, said the Interpreter.

Christian: Then Christian said, Is there no hope? Must you be kept in the iron cage of despair?

The Man: No, none at all.

Christian: Why, the Son of the Blessed is full of compassion.

The Man: I have crucified him all over again to myself, Heb 6:6; I have despised his person, Luke 19:14; I have despised his righteousness; I have counted his blood an unholy thing; I have insulted the spirit of grace, Heb 10:29. So I have shut myself out of all the promises, and now nothing remains for me but threats, dreadful threats, faithful threats of certain judgment and fiery indignation, which will devour me as an adversary.

Christian: For what did you bring yourself into this condition?

The Man: For the lusts, pleasures, and profits of this world, in the enjoyment of which I then promised myself much delight; but now every one of those things also bites me and gnaws me like a burning worm.

Christian: But can you not repent and turn now?

The Man: God has denied me repentance. His word gives me no encouragement to believe; indeed, he himself has shut me up in this iron cage, and all the men in the world cannot let me out. Oh, eternity! eternity! How will I grapple with the misery that I must meet in eternity?

Interpreter: Then the Interpreter said to Christian, Remember this man’s misery, and let it be an everlasting warning to you.

Christian: Well, said Christian, this is fearful! God help me to watch and be sober, and to pray that I may avoid the cause of this man’s misery. Sir, is it not time for me to go on my way now?

Interpreter: Wait till I show you one thing more, and then you shall go on your way.

So he took Christian by the hand again and led him into a bedroom where someone was getting out of bed; and as he put on his clothes, he shook and trembled. Then Christian said, Why does this man tremble so? The Interpreter then told the man to tell Christian why he was doing so.

So he began, and said, “Last night, as I was sleeping, I dreamed, and behold, the heavens grew extremely black; it also thundered and lightning flashed in the most fearful way, so that it put me into an agony. So I looked up in my dream, and saw the clouds racing along at an unusual rate; at which I heard a great sound of a trumpet, and also saw a man sitting on a cloud, attended by the thousands of heaven: they were all in flaming fire, and the heavens too were in a burning flame. Then I heard a voice saying, ‘Arise, you+ dead, and come to judgment.’ And with that the rocks split, the graves opened, and the dead that were in them came out. Some of them were exceedingly glad, and looked upward; and some tried to hide themselves under the mountains. Then I saw the man who sat on the cloud open the book, and call the world to come near. Yet, because of a fierce flame that issued out and came from before him, there was a fitting distance between him and them, as between the judge and the prisoners at the bar. 1 Cor 15; 1 Thess 4:16; Jude 15; John 5:28, 29; 2 Thess 1:8–10; Rev 20:11–14; Isa 26:21; Mic 7:16, 17; Ps 5:4; 50:1–3; Mal 3:2, 3; Dan 7:9, 10. I also heard it proclaimed to those who attended the man who sat on the cloud, ‘Gather together the tares, the chaff, and stubble, and cast them into the burning lake.’ Matt 3:12; 13:30; 24:30; Mal 4:1. And with that the bottomless pit opened, just about where I stood; and out of its mouth came great quantities of smoke and coals of fire, with hideous noises. It was also said to the same persons, ‘Gather my wheat into the barn.’ Luke 3:17. And with that I saw many caught up and carried away into the clouds, but I was left behind. 1 Thess 4:16, 17. I also tried to hide myself, but I could not, for the man who sat on the cloud kept his eye on me all the time; my sins also came into my mind, and my conscience accused me on every side. Rom 2:14, 15. At this I woke from my sleep.”

Christian: But what was it that made you so afraid of this sight?

The Man: Why, I thought that the day of judgment had come, and that I was not ready for it; but what frightened me most was that the angels gathered up several, and left me behind. Also the pit of hell opened its mouth just where I stood. My conscience too afflicted me; and, as I thought, the Judge always had his eye on me, showing indignation in his face.

Then the Interpreter said to Christian, “Have you considered all these things?”

Christian: Yes, and they make me both hope and fear.

Interpreter: Well, keep all these things in your mind in such a way that they may be like a goad in your sides, to drive you forward in the way you must go. Then Christian began to gird up his loins and get ready for his journey. Then the Interpreter said, “May the Comforter be always with you, good Christian, to guide you in the way that leads to the city.” So Christian went on his way, saying,

““Here I have seen things rare and profitable,

Things pleasant, dreadful, things to make me stable

In what I have begun to take in hand:

Then let me think on them, and understand

Why they were shown to me, and let me too

Give thanks, O good Interpreter, to you.””

3. The Holy Spirit.

THE THIRD STAGE

Now I saw in my dream that the highway up which Christian was to go was fenced in on either side by a wall, and that wall was called Salvation. Isa 26:1. Up this way, then, burdened Christian ran, but not without great difficulty, because of the load on his back.

He ran like this till he came to a place where the ground rose a little; and on that place stood a cross, and a little below, at the bottom, a tomb. So I saw in my dream that just as Christian came up to the cross, his burden came loose from his shoulders and fell off his back, and began to tumble, and kept on tumbling till it came to the mouth of the tomb, where it fell in, and I saw it no more.

Then Christian was glad and light-hearted, and said with a merry heart, “He has given me rest by his sorrow, and life by his death.” Then he stood still a while, to look and wonder; for it was very surprising to him that the sight of the cross should ease him of his burden like this. So he looked, and looked again, until the springs that were in his head sent the waters down his cheeks. Zech 12:10. Now as he stood looking and weeping, behold, three Shining Ones came to him, and greeted him with, “Peace be to you.” Then the first said to him, “Your sins are forgiven,” Mark 2:5; the second stripped him of his rags, and clothed him with a change of clothes, Zech 3:4; the third set a mark on his forehead, Eph 1:13, and gave him a roll with a seal on it, which he told him to look at as he ran, and to hand in at the celestial gate; and so they went their way. Then Christian gave three leaps for joy, and went on singing,

““Thus far I have come laden with my sin,

And nothing eased the grief that I was in,

Till I came here. What a place is this!

Must this be the beginning of my bliss?

Must here the burden fall from off my back?

Must here the strings that bound it to me crack?

Blest cross! blest sepulchre! blest rather be

The Man that there was put to shame for me!””

Then I saw in my dream that he went on like this until he came to the bottom, where he saw, a little off the way, three men fast asleep, with fetters on their heels. One was named Simple, another Sloth, and the third Presumption.

Seeing them lying there like this, Christian went to them to see if he could wake them, and cried, You+ are like those who sleep on the top of a mast, Prov 23:34, for the Dead Sea is under you+, a gulf that has no bottom: so wake up and come away; be willing, too, and I will help you+ off with your+ irons. He also told them, If he who goes about like a roaring lion, 1 Pet 5:8, comes by, you+ will certainly become a prey to his teeth. At that they looked at him, and began to answer him like this: Simple said, I see no danger; Sloth said, Just a little more sleep; and Presumption said, Every tub must stand on its own bottom. And so they lay down to sleep again, and Christian went on his way.

Yet it troubled him to think that men in such danger should think so little of the kindness of one who so freely offered to help them, by waking them, by counseling them, and by offering to help them off with their irons. And while he was troubled about this, he saw two men come tumbling over the wall, on the left side of the narrow way; and they quickly caught up with him. The name of the one was Formalist, and the name of the other Hypocrisy. So, as I said, they came up to him, and he began to talk with them like this.

Christian: Gentlemen, where have you+ come from, and where are you+ going?

Formalist and Hypocrisy: We were born in the land of Vain-glory, and we are going to Mount Zion, for praise.

Christian: Why did you+ not come in at the gate that stands at the beginning of the way? Do you+ not know that it is written that “he who does not enter by the door, but climbs up some other way, is a thief and a robber”? John 10:1.

Formalist and Hypocrisy: They said that all their countrymen thought it too far around to go to the gate to get in; and so their usual way was to take a short cut, and climb over the wall, as they had done.

Christian: But will it not be counted a trespass against the Lord of the city we are bound for, to violate his revealed will like this?

Formalist and Hypocrisy: They told him that he need not trouble his head about that: they had custom on their side for what they did, and could produce, if need be, evidence that it had been done for more than a thousand years.

Christian: But, said Christian, will you stand up to a trial at law?

Formalist and Hypocrisy: They told him that custom, having stood for so long, more than a thousand years, would no doubt now be accepted as lawful by an impartial judge. And besides, they said, if we get into the way, what does it matter how we get in? If we are in, we are in. You are only on the way, you who, as we can see, came in at the gate; and we too are on the way, we who came tumbling over the wall. So how is your condition any better than ours?

Christian: I walk by the rule of my Master: you+ walk by the crude workings of your+ own fancies. You+ are already counted thieves by the Lord of the way: so I fear you+ will not be found honest men at the end of the way. You+ come in by yourselves+ without his direction, and you+ will go out by yourselves+ without his mercy.

They made little answer to this; they only told him to look out for himself. Then I saw that they went on, each man on his own way, without much talk with one another, except that these two men told Christian that, as for laws and ordinances, they had no doubt they would keep them as conscientiously as he did. So, they said, we do not see how you differ from us, except by the coat on your back, which, we suppose, was given you by some of your neighbors to hide the shame of your nakedness.

Christian: By laws and ordinances you+ will not be saved, since you+ did not come in by the door. Gal 2:16. And as for this coat on my back, it was given me by the Lord of the place where I am going; and, as you+ say, it was given to cover my nakedness. And I take it as a token of kindness to me; for I had nothing but rags before. Besides, I comfort myself with it as I go. Surely, I think, when I come to the gate of the city, its Lord will know me for one of his, since I have his coat on my back; a coat that he gave me freely on the day that he stripped me of my rags. Moreover, I have a mark on my forehead, which perhaps you+ have not noticed, which one of my Lord’s closest companions set there on the day my burden fell off my shoulders. I will tell you+, too, that I was then given a sealed roll, to comfort me as I read it on the way; I was also told to hand it in at the celestial gate, as a sign that I will surely go in after it. All these things, I suspect, you+ lack; and you+ lack them because you+ did not come in at the gate.

To these things they gave him no answer; they only looked at each other and laughed. Then I saw that they all went on, except that Christian kept ahead, and he talked no more except with himself, sometimes with sighs and sometimes with comfort; he would also often read in the roll that one of the Shining Ones had given him, and it refreshed him.

Then I saw that they all went on till they came to the foot of the hill Difficulty, at the bottom of which there was a spring. In the same place there were also two other ways besides the one that came straight from the gate: one turned to the left, and the other to the right, at the bottom of the hill; but the narrow way ran straight up the hill, and the climb up the side of the hill is called Difficulty. Christian now went to the spring, Isa 49:10, and drank from it to refresh himself, and then began to go up the hill, saying,

““The hill, though high, I’m eager to ascend;

The difficulty will not make me bend;

For I can see the way to life lies here:

Come, take heart now, let’s neither faint nor fear.

Better, though difficult, the right way to go,

Than wrong, though easy, where the end is woe.””

The other two also came to the foot of the hill. But when they saw that the hill was steep and high, and that there were two other ways to go; and supposing too that these two ways might meet up again with the one Christian went up, on the other side of the hill; they made up their minds to go by those ways. Now one of those ways was called Danger, and the other Destruction. So one of them took the way called Danger, which led him into a great wood; and the other went straight up the way to Destruction, which led him into a wide field full of dark mountains, where he stumbled and fell, and rose no more.

Then I looked after Christian, to see him go up the hill, and I saw that he dropped from running to walking, and from walking to clambering on his hands and knees, because the place was so steep. Now about halfway to the top of the hill was a pleasant Arbor, made by the Lord of the hill for the refreshment of weary travelers. So Christian made his way there, and sat down to rest. Then he pulled his roll from inside his coat and read it, to his comfort; he also now began to look over once more the coat or garment that had been given to him as he stood by the cross. Pleasing himself like this for a while, he at last fell into a doze, and from that into a deep sleep, which kept him in that place until it was almost night; and in his sleep his roll fell out of his hand. Now, as he was sleeping, someone came to him and woke him, saying, “Go to the ant, O sluggard; observe its ways and become wise.” Prov 6:6. And at that Christian started up, and hurried on his way, and went quickly till he came to the top of the hill.

Now when he had reached the top of the hill, two men came running at full speed; the name of the one was Timorous, and of the other Mistrust. Christian said to them, Sirs, what is the matter? You+ are running the wrong way. Timorous answered that they had been going to the city of Zion, and had got up that difficult place; but, he said, the farther we go, the more danger we meet; so we turned around, and we are going back again.

Yes, said Mistrust, for just ahead of us a couple of lions are lying in the way, whether asleep or awake we do not know; and we could only think that if we came within their reach they would tear us to pieces at once.

Christian: Then Christian said, You+ make me afraid; but where can I flee to be safe? If I go back to my own country, that is prepared for fire and brimstone, and I will certainly perish there; if I can get to the celestial city, I am sure to be safe there: I must risk it. To go back is nothing but death; to go forward is fear of death, and everlasting life beyond it: I will still go forward. So Mistrust and Timorous ran down the hill, and Christian went on his way. But thinking again of what he had heard from the men, he felt inside his coat for his roll, so that he might read it and be comforted; but he felt, and it was not there. Then Christian was in great distress, and did not know what to do; for he lacked the thing that used to relieve him, and that should have been his pass into the celestial city. Here, then, he began to be very perplexed, and did not know what to do. At last he remembered that he had slept in the arbor on the side of the hill; and falling down on his knees, he asked God to forgive him for that foolish act, and then went back to look for his roll. But all the way back, who can fully describe the sorrow of Christian’s heart? Sometimes he sighed, sometimes he wept, and often he scolded himself for being so foolish as to fall asleep in that place, which was built only for a little refreshment from his weariness. So he went back, looking carefully on this side and on that, all the way as he went, in the hope that he might find his roll, which had been his comfort so many times on his journey. He went on like this till he came in sight of the arbor again, where he had sat and slept; but that sight renewed his sorrow all the more, by bringing the wrong of his sleeping back to his mind again, as fresh as ever. Rev 2:4; 1 Thess 5:6–8. So now he went on, lamenting his sinful sleep, and saying, O wretched man that I am, that I should sleep in the daytime! that I should sleep in the midst of difficulty! that I should so indulge the flesh as to use for my flesh’s ease the rest that the Lord of the hill built only to revive the spirits of pilgrims! How many steps have I taken in vain! This is what happened to Israel; for their sin they were sent back again by the way of the Red Sea; and I am made to tread these steps with sorrow, which I might have trodden with delight, if it had not been for this sinful sleep. How far along my way I might have been by now! I am made to tread these steps three times over, when I need only have trodden them once: yes, and now I am likely to be overtaken by night, for the day is almost spent. Oh, if only I had not slept!

Now by this time he had come to the arbor again, where he sat down for a while and wept; but at last (as Providence would have it), looking sorrowfully down under the bench, he spotted his roll there; and trembling and in haste he snatched it up and put it inside his coat. But who can tell how joyful this man was when he had his roll again? For this roll was the assurance of his life, and of his acceptance at the haven he longed for. So he put it away safely inside his coat, thanked God for directing his eye to the place where it lay, and with joy and tears set out on his journey again. And oh, how nimbly he went up the rest of the hill! Yet before he got to the top, the sun went down on Christian; and this brought the folly of his sleeping back to his mind again; and so he began once more to lament to himself: Oh, you sinful sleep! Because of you I am likely to be overtaken by night on my journey! I must walk without the sun, darkness must cover the path of my feet, and I must hear the noise of the doleful creatures, because of my sinful sleep! Now he also remembered the story Mistrust and Timorous had told him, of how they were frightened by the sight of the lions. Then Christian said to himself again, These beasts roam in the night for their prey; and if they should meet me in the dark, how could I get away from them? How could I escape being torn to pieces by them? So he went on his way. But while he was lamenting his unhappy blunder, he looked up, and there before him was a very stately palace, whose name was Beautiful, and it stood beside the highway.

So I saw in my dream that he hurried on, so that if possible he might get lodging there. Now before he had gone far, he entered a very narrow passage, about a furlong from the Porter’s lodge; and looking very carefully ahead of him as he went, he spotted two lions in the way. Now, he thought, I see the dangers that drove Mistrust and Timorous back. (The lions were chained, but he did not see the chains.) Then he was afraid, and he too thought of going back after them; for he thought nothing but death was before him. But the Porter at the lodge, whose name is Watchful, seeing that Christian had stopped as if he would go back, called out to him, saying, Is your strength so small? Mark 4:40. Do not fear the lions, for they are chained, and they are placed there to test faith where there is any, and to expose those who have none. Keep to the middle of the path, and no harm shall come to you.

Then I saw that he went on, trembling for fear of the lions, but carefully following the Porter’s directions; he heard them roar, but they did him no harm. Then he clapped his hands, and went on till he came and stood before the gate where the Porter was. Then Christian said to the Porter, Sir, what house is this? And may I stay here tonight? The Porter answered, This house was built by the Lord of the hill, and he built it for the relief and safety of pilgrims. The Porter also asked where he was from, and where he was going.

Christian: I have come from the city of Destruction, and I am going to Mount Zion; but because the sun has now set, I would like, if I may, to stay here tonight.

The Porter: What is your name?

Christian: My name is now Christian, but my name at first was Graceless: I am of the race of Japheth, whom God will persuade to dwell in the tents of Shem. Gen 9:27.

The Porter: But how is it that you come so late? The sun has set.

Christian: I would have been here sooner, except that, wretched man that I am, I slept in the arbor that stands on the hillside!
