Indeed, even so, I would have been here much sooner, except that in my sleep I lost my evidence, and came without it to the brow of the hill; and then, feeling for it and not finding it, I was forced with sorrow of heart to go back to the place where I slept my sleep, and there I found it; and now here I am.

The Porter: Well, I will call out one of the young women of this place, who will, if she likes your talk, bring you in to the rest of the family, according to the rules of the house. So Watchful the Porter rang a bell, and at the sound of it a grave and beautiful young woman named Discretion came out of the door of the house, and asked why she had been called.

The Porter answered, This man is on a journey from the city of Destruction to Mount Zion; but being weary and overtaken by night, he asked me if he might stay here tonight. So I told him I would call for you, and after talking with him you may do as you think best, according to the law of the house.

Then she asked him where he was from, and where he was going; and he told her. She also asked him how he got into the way; and he told her. Then she asked him what he had seen and met with on the way; and he told her. And at last she asked his name. So he said, It is Christian; and I want to stay here tonight all the more because, from what I can see, this place was built by the Lord of the hill for the relief and safety of pilgrims. So she smiled, but tears stood in her eyes; and after a little pause she said, I will call out two or three more of the family. So she ran to the door, and called out Prudence, Piety, and Charity, who, after talking with him a little more, brought him into the family; and many of them, meeting him at the threshold of the house, said, Come in, you blessed of the Lord; this house was built by the Lord of the hill for the very purpose of lodging such pilgrims as you. Then he bowed his head, and followed them into the house. So when he had come in and sat down, they gave him something to drink, and agreed among themselves that, until supper was ready, some of them should have a particular conversation with Christian, to make the best use of the time; and they appointed Piety, Prudence, and Charity to talk with him. And so they began.

Piety: Come, good Christian, since we have been so loving to you as to receive you into our house tonight, let us talk with you, in the hope that we may better ourselves by it, about all the things that have happened to you on your pilgrimage.

Christian: Very willingly; and I am glad that you are so inclined.

Piety: What first moved you to take up a pilgrim’s life?

Christian: I was driven out of my native country by a dreadful sound that was in my ears: namely, that unavoidable destruction awaited me if I stayed in the place where I was.

Piety: But how did it happen that you came out of your country this way?

Christian: It was as God would have it; for when I was under the fear of destruction, I did not know where to go; but by chance a man came, right up to me, as I was trembling and weeping, whose name is Evangelist; and he directed me to the Wicket-gate, which I would never have found otherwise, and so set me on the way that has led me straight to this house.

Piety: But did you not come by the house of the Interpreter?

Christian: Yes, and I saw such things there that the memory of them will stay with me as long as I live; especially three things: namely, how Christ, in spite of Satan, keeps up his work of grace in the heart; how the man had sinned himself completely out of hope of God’s mercy; and also the dream of the man who thought in his sleep that the day of judgment had come.

Piety: Why, did you hear him tell his dream?

Christian: Yes, and a dreadful one it was, I thought; it made my heart ache as he was telling it, but still I am glad I heard it.

Piety: Was this all you saw at the house of the Interpreter?

Christian: No; he took me and brought me to where he showed me a stately palace, and how the people in it were dressed in gold; and how a daring man came and cut his way through the armed men who stood in the door to keep him out; and how he was told to come in and win eternal glory. Those things, I thought, enraptured my heart. I would have stayed at that good man’s house a whole year, except that I knew I had farther to go.

Piety: And what else did you see on the way?

Christian: Saw? Why, I went only a little farther, and I saw One, as I thought in my mind, hanging bleeding on a tree; and the very sight of him made my burden fall off my back; for I was groaning under a very heavy burden, but then it fell right off me. It was a strange thing to me, for I had never seen such a thing before. Yes, and while I stood looking up (for then I could not stop looking), three Shining Ones came to me. One of them declared that my sins were forgiven me; another stripped me of my rags, and gave me this embroidered coat which you see; and the third set the mark which you see on my forehead, and gave me this sealed roll (and with that he pulled it out from inside his coat).

Piety: But you saw more than this, did you not?

Christian: The things that I have told you were the best; yet I saw some other things. For instance, I saw three men, Simple, Sloth, and Presumption, lying asleep a little off the way as I came, with irons on their heels; but do you think I could wake them? I also saw Formalist and Hypocrisy come tumbling over the wall, to go, as they claimed, to Zion; but they were soon lost, just as I myself told them, but they would not believe me. But above all, I found it hard work to get up this hill, and just as hard to get past the lions’ mouths; and truly, if it had not been for the good man, the porter who stands at the gate, I might, for all I know, have gone back again after all; but I thank God I am here, and I thank you for receiving me.

Then Prudence thought it good to ask him a few questions, and asked him to answer them.

Prudence: Do you not sometimes think of the country you came from?

Christian: Yes, but with great shame and loathing. Truly, if I had been mindful of that country I came out of, I might have had the opportunity to return; but now I desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one. Heb 11:15, 16.

Prudence: Do you not still carry with you some of the things you were taken up with then?

Christian: Yes, but very much against my will; especially my inward and carnal thoughts, which all my countrymen, as well as I, delighted in. But now all those things are my grief; and if I could only choose for myself, I would choose never to think of those things again. But when I want to do what is best, what is worst is with me. Rom 7:15, 21.

Prudence: Do you not sometimes find those things seem to be defeated, which at other times are your distress?

Christian: Yes, but that is only seldom; but the hours when such things happen to me are golden hours to me.

Prudence: Can you remember what it is that makes you find your troubles at times as if they were defeated?

Christian: Yes: when I think of what I saw at the cross, that will do it; and when I look at my embroidered coat, that will do it; and when I look into the roll that I carry inside my coat, that will do it; and when my thoughts grow warm about where I am going, that will do it.

Prudence: And what is it that makes you so eager to go to Mount Zion?

Christian: Why, there I hope to see Him alive who hung dead on the cross; and there I hope to be rid of all those things that to this day are in me and trouble me. There, they say, there is no death, Isa 25:8; Rev 21:4; and there I will live with the kind of company I like best. For, to tell you the truth, I love Him because He eased me of my burden; and I am weary of my inward sickness. I long to be where I will die no more, and with the company that will continually cry, Holy, holy, holy.

Then Charity said to Christian, Do you have a family? Are you a married man?

Christian: I have a wife and four small children.

Charity: And why did you not bring them along with you?

Christian: Then Christian wept, and said, Oh, how gladly I would have done it! But every one of them was utterly against my going on pilgrimage.

Charity: But you should have talked to them, and tried to show them the danger of staying behind.

Christian: So I did; and I also told them what God had shown me of the destruction of our city; but they thought I was joking, and they did not believe me. Gen 19:14.

Charity: And did you pray to God that he would bless your advice to them?

Christian: Yes, and with deep feeling; for you can imagine that my wife and poor children were very dear to me.

Charity: But did you tell them of your own sorrow, and your fear of destruction? For I suppose the destruction was plain enough to you.

Christian: Yes, over, and over, and over. They could also see my fears in my face, in my tears, and in my trembling under the dread of the judgment that hung over our heads; but all of it was not enough to persuade them to come with me.

Charity: But what reason could they give for themselves for not coming?

Christian: Why, my wife was afraid of losing this world, and my children were given over to the foolish pleasures of youth; so, what with one thing and what with another, they left me to wander alone like this.

Charity: But did you not, by your vain life, dampen all the persuasion you used in words to bring them away with you?

Christian: Indeed, I cannot commend my life, for I know of many failings in it. I know too that a man, by his conduct, may soon overthrow what he labors, by argument or persuasion, to press on others for their good. Yet this I can say: I was very careful not to give them cause, by any unbecoming action, to turn them against going on pilgrimage. Yes, for this very thing they would tell me I was too strict, and that I denied myself things (for their sakes) in which they saw no harm. Indeed, I think I may say that if what they saw in me hindered them, it was my great tenderness about sinning against God, or about doing any wrong to my neighbor.

Charity: Indeed, Cain hated his brother, because his own works were evil, and his brother’s righteous, 1 John 3:12; and if your wife and children have been offended with you for this, they show by it that they are stubbornly hostile to good; you have delivered your soul from their blood. Ezek 3:19.

Now I saw in my dream that they sat talking together like this until supper was ready. So when everything was ready, they sat down to eat. Now the table was spread with rich food, and with wine that was well refined; and all their talk at the table was about the Lord of the hill: about what he had done, and why he did what he did, and why he had built that house. And from what they said, I understood that he had been a great warrior, and had fought with and killed him who had the power of death, Heb 2:14, 15; but not without great danger to himself, which made me love him all the more.

For, as they said, and as I believe, said Christian, he did it with the loss of much blood. But what put the glory of grace into all he did was that he did it out of pure love for his country. And besides, some of the household said they had been with him and spoken with him since he died on the cross; and they have declared that they heard it from his own lips, that he is such a lover of poor pilgrims that his like is not to be found from the east to the west. They also gave an example of what they affirmed; and it was this: he had stripped himself of his glory so that he might do this for the poor; and they had heard him say and affirm that he would not live on the mountain of Zion alone. They said, too, that he had made many pilgrims princes, though by nature they were born beggars, and had come from the dunghill. 1 Sam 2:8; Ps 113:7.

So they talked together till late at night; and after they had committed themselves to their Lord for protection, they went to bed. They put the pilgrim in a large upstairs room, whose window opened towards the sunrise. The name of the room was Peace; there he slept till daybreak, and then he woke and sang,

““Where am I now? Is this the love and care

Of Jesus, for the men who pilgrims are,

Thus to provide that I should be forgiven,

And dwell already right next door to heaven!””

So in the morning they all got up; and after some more talk, they told him that he must not leave till they had shown him the rare things of that place. And first they took him into the study, where they showed him records of the greatest age; in which, as I remember my dream, they showed him the family line of the Lord of the hill: that he was the Son of the Ancient of Days, and came by eternal generation. Here, too, the deeds he had done were recorded more fully, and the names of many hundreds whom he had taken into his service; and how he had placed them in such dwellings as could be destroyed neither by length of days nor by the decay of nature.

Then they read to him some of the noble deeds that some of his servants had done: how they had subdued kingdoms, worked righteousness, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, out of weakness were made strong, became valiant in battle, and turned to flight the armies of the aliens. Heb 11:33, 34.

Then they read another part of the records of the house, which showed how willing their Lord was to receive anyone into his favor, even anyone, though in the past they had greatly insulted his person and his dealings. Here also were various other histories of many other famous things, all of which Christian looked at: things both ancient and modern, together with prophecies and predictions of things that are certain to be fulfilled, both to the dread and dismay of enemies, and to the comfort and encouragement of pilgrims.

The next day they took him into the armory, where they showed him all kinds of equipment which their Lord had provided for pilgrims: sword, shield, helmet, breastplate, all-prayer, and shoes that would not wear out. And there was enough of this here to equip as many men for the service of their Lord as there are stars in the sky in all their multitude.

They also showed him some of the instruments with which some of his servants had done wonderful things. They showed him Moses’ rod; the hammer and nail with which Jael killed Sisera; and the pitchers, trumpets, and lamps too, with which Gideon put to flight the armies of Midian. Then they showed him the ox-goad with which Shamgar killed six hundred men. They also showed him the jawbone with which Samson did such mighty feats. They showed him, too, the sling and stone with which David killed Goliath of Gath; and also the sword with which their Lord will kill the man of sin, on the day that he rises up to the prey. Besides these they showed him many excellent things, which delighted Christian greatly. When this was done, they went to bed again.

Then I saw in my dream that the next morning he got up to go on, but they wanted him to stay till the following day as well; and then, they said, if the day is clear, we will show you the Delectable Mountains; which, they said, would add still more to his comfort, because they were nearer the haven he longed for than the place where he was now. So he agreed and stayed. When morning came, they took him up to the top of the house, and told him to look south. So he did, and there, at a great distance, he saw a most pleasant mountainous country, beautiful with woods, vineyards, fruits of all kinds, and flowers too, with springs and fountains, very delectable to look at. Isa 33:16, 17. Then he asked the name of the country. They said it was Immanuel’s land; and it is as open, they said, as this hill is, to all the pilgrims. And when you get there, you can see from there as far as the gate of the celestial city, as the shepherds who live there will show you.

Now he thought it was time to set out, and they were willing that he should. But first, they said, let us go into the armory again. So they did; and when he got there, they armed him from head to foot with proven armor, in case he should meet with attacks on the way. So, equipped like this, he walked out to the gate with his friends; and there he asked the Porter if he had seen any pilgrim go by. Then the Porter answered, Yes.

Christian: Tell me, did you know him? he said.

The Porter: I asked his name, and he told me it was Faithful.

Christian: Oh, said Christian, I know him; he is from my town, my close neighbor; he comes from the place where I was born. How far ahead do you think he may be?

The Porter: By now he has got below the hill.

Christian: Well, said Christian, good Porter, the Lord be with you, and add much increase to all your plain blessings, for the kindness that you have shown me.

THE FOURTH STAGE

Then he began to go forward; but Discretion, Piety, Charity, and Prudence were set on going with him down to the foot of the hill. So they went on together, going over their earlier conversations again, until they came to where the way went down the hill. Then Christian said, Just as it was hard coming up, so, as far as I can see, it is dangerous going down. Yes, said Prudence, so it is; for it is a hard thing for a man to go down into the valley of Humiliation, as you are doing now, and not slip on the way; that is why, they said, we have come out to go down the hill with you. So he began to go down, but very carefully; even so, he slipped once or twice.

Then I saw in my dream that these good companions, when Christian had got down to the bottom of the hill, gave him a loaf of bread, a bottle of wine, and a cluster of raisins; and then he went on his way,

““While Christian is among his godly friends,

Their golden mouths make him complete amends

For all his griefs; and when they let him go,

He’s clad in northern steel from top to toe.””

But now, in this valley of Humiliation, poor Christian was hard pressed; for he had gone only a little way when he caught sight of a foul fiend coming across the field to meet him: his name is Apollyon. Then Christian began to be afraid, and to turn over in his mind whether to go back or to stand his ground. But he considered again that he had no armor for his back, and so he thought that to turn his back on the fiend might give him all the greater advantage, and let him pierce him with his darts with ease. So he resolved to take the risk and stand his ground: for, he thought, even if I had nothing more in view than saving my life, it would be best to stand.

So he went on, and Apollyon met him. Now the monster was hideous to look at: he was clothed with scales like a fish, and they are his pride; he had wings like a dragon, and feet like a bear, and out of his belly came fire and smoke; and his mouth was like the mouth of a lion. When Apollyon had come up to Christian, he looked at him with a scornful face, and began to question him like this.

Apollyon: Where have you come from, and where are you bound?

Christian: I have come from the city of Destruction, which is the place of all evil, and I am going to the city of Zion.

Apollyon: From this I see that you are one of my subjects; for all that country is mine, and I am its prince and god. How is it, then, that you have run away from your king? If I did not hope that you may yet do me more service, I would strike you to the ground with one blow right now.

Christian: It is true that I was born in your dominions, but your service was hard, and your wages were such as a man could not live on; for the wages of sin is death, Rom 6:23. So when I came of age, I did as other thoughtful people do, and looked around to see if I could perhaps better myself.

Apollyon: No prince will lose his subjects so lightly, and I will not lose you yet either; but since you complain of your service and wages, be content to go back, and whatever our country can offer, I promise here and now to give you.

Christian: But I have hired myself out to another, to the King of princes himself; and how can I in fairness go back with you?

Apollyon: In this you have done what the proverb says, “changed a bad for a worse”; but it is common for those who have professed themselves his servants to give him the slip after a while and come back to me. You do the same, and all will be well.

Christian: I have pledged my faith to him, and sworn my allegiance to him; how then can I go back on this and not be hanged as a traitor?

Apollyon: You did the same to me, and yet I am willing to overlook it all, if you will even now turn around and go back.

Christian: What I promised you was when I was under age; and besides, I believe that the Prince under whose banner I now stand is able to absolve me, yes, and to pardon also what I did in going along with you. And besides, O you destroying Apollyon, to tell the truth, I like his service, his wages, his servants, his government, his company, and his country better than yours. So stop trying to persuade me: I am his servant, and I will follow him.

Apollyon: Think again, when you have cooled down, about what you are likely to meet with on the way you are going. You know that most of his servants come to a bad end, because they are transgressors against me and my ways. How many of them have been put to shameful deaths! And besides, you count his service better than mine; and yet he has never once come from the place where he is to deliver any who served him out of their enemies’ hands. But as for me, how many times, as all the world very well knows, have I delivered those who have served me faithfully from him and his, either by force or by fraud, even when they had been taken by them! And so I will deliver you.

Christian: If he holds back from delivering them for now, it is on purpose to test their love, to see whether they will hold fast to him to the end. And as for the bad end you say they come to, they count that most glorious. For they do not much expect to be delivered now; they are waiting for their glory, and they will have it when their Prince comes in his own glory and the glory of the angels.

Apollyon: You have already been unfaithful in your service to him; how do you expect to get wages from him?

Christian: In what way, O Apollyon, have I been unfaithful to him?

Apollyon: You lost heart as soon as you set out, when you were almost choked in the gulf of Despond. You tried wrong ways to get rid of your burden, when you should have waited until your Prince had taken it off. You sinfully fell asleep, and lost your precious things. You were also almost persuaded to go back at the sight of the lions. And when you talk about your journey, and about what you have seen and heard, inwardly you crave vainglory in all that you say or do.

Christian: All this is true, and much more that you have left out; but the Prince whom I serve and honor is merciful, and ready to forgive. And besides, these weaknesses took hold of me in your country, for that is where I sucked them in; and I have groaned under them, been sorry for them, and obtained pardon from my Prince.

Apollyon: Then Apollyon broke out into a terrible rage, saying, I am an enemy to this Prince; I hate his person, his laws, and his people: I have come out on purpose to oppose you.

Christian: Apollyon, be careful what you do, for I am on the King’s highway, the way of holiness; so watch yourself.

Apollyon: Then Apollyon straddled right across the whole width of the way, and said, I have no fear in this matter. Prepare to die; for I swear by my infernal den that you will go no further: here I will spill your soul. And with that he threw a flaming dart at Christian’s chest; but Christian had a shield in his hand, and he caught the dart with it, and so warded off that danger.

Then Christian drew his sword, for he saw it was time to act; and Apollyon came at him just as fast, throwing darts as thick as hail; and with them, in spite of all that Christian could do to avoid it, Apollyon wounded him in his head, his hand, and his foot. This made Christian fall back a little. So Apollyon pressed his attack with all his might, and Christian again took courage, and resisted as bravely as he could. This fierce combat lasted for more than half a day, until Christian was almost completely worn out: for you must understand that Christian, because of his wounds, was bound to grow weaker and weaker.

Then Apollyon, seeing his opportunity, began to close in on Christian, and wrestling with him, gave him a terrible fall; and with that Christian’s sword flew out of his hand. Then Apollyon said, I have you now: and with that he had almost crushed him to death, so that Christian began to despair of his life. But, as God would have it, while Apollyon was drawing back for his last blow, to finish off this good man with it, Christian quickly reached out his hand for his sword, and caught it, saying, Do not rejoice against me, O my enemy; when I fall, I shall arise, Mic 7:8; and with that he gave him a deadly thrust, which made him fall back, like one who had received his death wound. Seeing that, Christian came at him again, saying, No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through Him who loved us. Rom 8:37. And with that Apollyon spread out his dragon wings and sped away, so that Christian saw him no more. Jas 4:7.

No man can imagine, unless he had seen and heard it as I did, what yelling and hideous roaring Apollyon made all through the fight (he spoke like a dragon), and on the other side, what sighs and groans burst from Christian’s heart. In all that time I never once saw him give so much as one cheerful look, until he saw that he had wounded Apollyon with his two-edged sword; then, indeed, he did smile, and look upward! But it was the most dreadful sight I have ever seen.

So when the battle was over, Christian said, I will give thanks here to him who has delivered me out of the mouth of the lion, to him who helped me against Apollyon. And so he did, saying,

““Great Beelzebub, the captain of this fiend,

Designed my ruin; therefore to this end

He sent him out in armor; and with rage

From hell he came at me, fierce to engage:

But blessed Michael helped me, and I,

By dint of sword, was quick to make him fly:

Therefore to Him let me give lasting praise,

And thank and bless his holy name always.””

Then a hand came to him with some of the leaves of the tree of life, which Christian took and laid on the wounds he had received in the battle, and he was healed at once. He also sat down in that place to eat bread, and to drink from the bottle that had been given him a little before. So, being refreshed, he set out on his journey with his sword drawn in his hand; for he said, For all I know, some other enemy may be close by. But he met with no other attack from Apollyon all the way through this valley.

Now at the end of this valley was another, called the Valley of the Shadow of Death; and Christian had to go through it, because the way to the Celestial City lay through the middle of it. Now, this valley is a very lonely place. The prophet Jeremiah describes it like this: “A wilderness, a land of deserts and pits, a land of drought and of the Shadow of Death, a land where no man” (but a Christian) “travels, and where no man lives.” Jer 2:6.

Now here Christian was harder pressed than in his fight with Apollyon, as you will see from what follows.

I saw then in my dream that when Christian had reached the borders of the Shadow of Death, two men met him, children of those who brought back an evil report of the good land, Num 13:32, hurrying to go back; and Christian spoke to them as follows.

Christian: Where are you going?

The Two Men: They said, Back, back! And we would advise you to do the same, if you value either life or peace.

Christian: Why, what is the matter? said Christian.

The Two Men: Matter! they said. We were going that way, as you are, and went as far as we dared; and in fact we very nearly never came back; for if we had gone a little further, we would not be here to bring you the news.

Christian: But what have you met with? said Christian.

The Two Men: Why, we were almost in the Valley of the Shadow of Death, but by good luck we looked ahead of us, and saw the danger before we came to it. Ps 44:19; 107:19.

Christian: But what have you seen? said Christian.

The Two Men: Seen! Why, the valley itself, which is as dark as pitch. We also saw the hobgoblins, satyrs, and dragons of the pit there; and in that valley we heard a continual howling and yelling, as of a people in unspeakable misery, who sat there bound in affliction and irons. And over that valley hang the discouraging clouds of confusion; Death also always spreads his wings over it. In a word, it is dreadful through and through, being utterly without order. Job 3:5; 10:22.

Christian: Then, said Christian, nothing you have said so far shows me that this is not my way to the desired haven. Ps 44:18, 19; Jer 2:6.

The Two Men: Let it be your way; we will not choose it for ours.

So they parted, and Christian went on his way, but still with his sword drawn in his hand, for fear that he might be attacked.

I saw then in my dream that, as far as this valley reached, there was a very deep ditch on the right hand; that is the ditch into which the blind have led the blind in every age, and both have miserably perished there. Again, look, on the left hand there was a very dangerous quagmire, into which, if even a good man falls, he finds no bottom for his foot to stand on. King David once fell into that quagmire, and would no doubt have been smothered in it, if He who is able had not pulled him out. Ps 69:14.

The path here was also extremely narrow, and so good Christian was all the harder pressed; for when he tried, in the dark, to avoid the ditch on the one side, he was ready to tip over into the mire on the other; and when he tried to escape the mire, he would be ready to fall into the ditch unless he took great care. So he went on, and I heard him sigh bitterly here; for besides the danger mentioned above, the path here was so dark that often, when he lifted his foot to go forward, he did not know where, or on what, he would set it next.

About the middle of this valley, I saw, was the mouth of hell, and it stood right beside the way. Now, thought Christian, what shall I do? And every now and then the flame and smoke would pour out in such abundance, with sparks and hideous noises (things that cared nothing for Christian’s sword, as Apollyon had before), that he was forced to put away his sword, and turn to another weapon, called All-prayer, Eph 6:18. So he cried, in my hearing, O Lord, I beg you, deliver my soul. Ps 116:4. He went on like this for a long time, yet the flames kept reaching towards him; he also heard doleful voices, and rushing to and fro, so that at times he thought he would be torn in pieces, or trampled down like mire in the streets. He saw this frightful sight and heard these dreadful noises for several miles on end; and coming to a place where he thought he heard a company of fiends coming forward to meet him, he stopped, and began to think over what he had better do. At times he had half a mind to go back; then again he thought he might be halfway through the valley. He also remembered how he had already overcome many a danger, and that the danger of going back might be much greater than the danger of going forward. So he resolved to go on; yet the fiends seemed to come nearer and nearer. But when they had come almost up to him, he cried out with a most vehement voice, I will walk in the strength of the Lord God. So they drew back, and came no further.

One thing I must not pass over. I noticed that poor Christian was now so confused that he did not know his own voice; and this is how I saw it. Just as he came opposite the mouth of the burning pit, one of the wicked ones got behind him, stepped up softly to him, and whispered many grievous blasphemies to him, which Christian truly believed had come from his own mind. This troubled Christian more than anything he had met with before, even to think that he should now blaspheme Him whom he had loved so much before. Yet if he could have helped it, he would not have done it; but he did not have the presence of mind either to stop his ears, or to know where these blasphemies came from.

When Christian had traveled in this forlorn condition for quite some time, he thought he heard the voice of a man going ahead of him, saying, Though I walk through the Valley of the Shadow of Death, I will fear no evil, for You are with me. Ps 23:4.

Then he was glad, and for these reasons:

First, because he concluded from this that some who feared God were in this valley as well as himself.

Secondly, because he saw that God was with them, even in that dark and dismal state. And why not with me, he thought, though because of the hindrance that belongs to this place I cannot see it? Job 9:11.

Thirdly, because he hoped (if he could overtake them) to have company soon.

So he went on, and called to the man who was ahead; but that man did not know what to answer, because he too thought he was alone. And soon the day broke: then Christian said, “He has turned the shadow of death into the morning.” Amos 5:8.

Now that morning had come, he looked back, not because he wanted to return, but to see, by the light of day, what dangers he had gone through in the dark. So he saw more clearly the ditch that was on the one side, and the quagmire that was on the other; and also how narrow the way was that led between them both. He also saw the hobgoblins, and satyrs, and dragons of the pit now, but all far off; for after daybreak they did not come near; yet they were revealed to him, as it is written, “He reveals deep things out of darkness, and brings the shadow of death to light.” Job 12:22.

Now Christian was deeply moved by this deliverance from all the dangers of his lonely way; though he had feared those dangers greatly before, he saw them more clearly now, because the light of day made them plain to him. And about this time the sun was rising, and this was another mercy to Christian; for you must note that though the first part of the Valley of the Shadow of Death was dangerous, this second part, which he still had to go, was, if possible, far more dangerous. For from the place where he now stood, right to the end of the valley, the way was so full of snares, traps, nooses, and nets on this side, and so full of pits, pitfalls, deep holes, and steep drops on that side, that if it had been dark now, as it was when he came through the first part of the way, then even if he had had a thousand souls, they would by any reckoning have been lost. But, as I said, just now the sun was rising. Then he said, “His lamp shines upon my head, and by His light I go through darkness.” Job 29:3.

In this light, then, he came to the end of the valley. Now I saw in my dream that at the end of the valley lay blood, bones, ashes, and mangled bodies of men, even of pilgrims who had gone this way before; and while I was wondering what the reason could be, I noticed a cave a little ahead of me, where two giants, Pope and Pagan, lived in old times; by their power and tyranny the men whose bones, blood, ashes, etc., lay there had been cruelly put to death. But Christian went past this place without much danger, which rather surprised me; but I have learned since that Pagan has been dead many a day; and as for the other, though he is still alive, he has grown so frail and stiff in his joints, because of his age and also the many hard knocks he took in his younger days, that he can now do little more than sit in the mouth of his cave, grinning at pilgrims as they go by, and biting his nails because he cannot get at them.

So I saw that Christian went on his way; yet, at the sight of the old man who sat at the mouth of the cave, he could not tell what to think, especially because the old man spoke to him, though he could not go after him, saying, You people will never mend your ways till more of you are burned. But Christian held his tongue, and put a good face on it; and so he went by, and came to no harm. Then Christian sang,

““O world of wonders, (I can say no less,)

That I should be preserved in that distress

That I have met with here! O blessed be

That hand that from it has delivered me!

Dangers in darkness, devils, hell, and sin,

Surrounded me, while I this vale was in;

Yes, snares, and pits, and traps, and nets would lie

Around my path, that worthless, helpless I

Might have been caught, entangled, and cast down;

But since I live, let Jesus wear the crown.””

THE FIFTH STAGE

Now, as Christian went on his way, he came to a little rise, which had been thrown up on purpose so that pilgrims could see the way ahead of them. So Christian went up there; and looking forward, he saw Faithful ahead of him on his journey. Then Christian called out loud, Ho, ho! Hello there! Wait, and I will be your companion. At that Faithful looked back, and Christian called to him again, Wait, wait, till I catch up with you. But Faithful answered, No, I am running for my life, and the avenger of blood is behind me.

At this Christian was somewhat stung, and putting out all his strength, he quickly caught up with Faithful, and even ran past him; so the last was first. Then Christian smiled vaingloriously, because he had got ahead of his brother; but not watching his feet carefully, he suddenly stumbled and fell, and could not get up again until Faithful came up to help him.

Then I saw in my dream that they went on together very lovingly, and talked sweetly of all the things that had happened to them on their pilgrimage; and Christian began like this.

Christian: My honored and dearly loved brother Faithful, I am glad that I have caught up with you, and that God has so attuned our spirits that we can walk as companions on so pleasant a path.

Faithful: I had expected, my dear friend, to have your company all the way from our town, but you got a head start on me; so I was forced to come this much of the way alone.

Christian: How long did you stay in the city of Destruction before you set out after me on your pilgrimage?

Faithful: Until I could stay no longer; for soon after you left there was a great deal of talk that our city would shortly be burned to the ground with fire from heaven.

Christian: What, did your neighbors talk like that?

Faithful: Yes, for a while it was on everybody’s lips.

Christian: What, and did nobody but you come out to escape the danger?

Faithful: Though there was, as I said, a great deal of talk about it, I do not think they firmly believed it; for in the heat of the talk I heard some of them speak mockingly of you and of your desperate journey, which is what they called this pilgrimage of yours. But I believed, and still do, that our city will come to its end by fire and brimstone from above; and so I have made my escape.

Christian: Did you not hear any talk of neighbor Pliable?

Faithful: Yes, Christian, I heard that he followed you until he came to the Slough of Despond, where, as some said, he fell in; but he did not want it known that he had done so. Still, I am sure he was thoroughly spattered with that kind of dirt.

Christian: And what did the neighbors say to him?

Faithful: Since he went back he has been held in great scorn, and that among all sorts of people: some mock and despise him, and hardly anyone will give him work. He is now seven times worse than if he had never gone out of the city.

Christian: But why should they be so set against him, since they despise the way that he abandoned as well?

Faithful: Oh, they say, Hang him; he is a turncoat; he was not true to his profession of faith! I think God has stirred up even His enemies to hiss at him and make him a byword, because he has abandoned the way. Jer 29:18, 19.

Christian: Did you not talk with him before you came out?

Faithful: I met him once in the streets, but he slunk away on the other side, like a man ashamed of what he had done; so I did not speak to him.

Christian: Well, when I first set out I had hopes of that man; but now I fear he will perish when the city is overthrown. For it has happened to him just as the true proverb says, The dog has turned to his own vomit again, and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire. 2 Pet 2:22.

Faithful: Those are my fears for him too; but who can stop what will be?

Christian: Well, neighbor Faithful, Christian said, let us leave him, and talk of things that concern ourselves more closely. Tell me now what you have met with on the way as you came; for I know you have met with some things, or else it should be written down as a wonder.

Faithful: I escaped the slough that I see you fell into, and got up to the gate without that danger; only I met one whose name was Wanton, who nearly did me harm.

Christian: It was a good thing you escaped her net. Joseph was hard pressed by her, and he escaped her as you did; but it nearly cost him his life. Gen 39:11–13. But what did she do to you?

Faithful: You cannot imagine (unless you know something of it already) what a flattering tongue she had; she pressed me hard to turn aside with her, promising me every kind of satisfaction.

Christian: No, she did not promise you the satisfaction of a good conscience.

Faithful: You know what I mean; all carnal and fleshly satisfaction.

Christian: Thank God you escaped her: the abhorred of the Lord shall fall into her pit. Prov 22:14.

Faithful: Well, I do not know whether I escaped her completely or not.

Christian: Why, surely you did not consent to her desires?

Faithful: No, not to defile myself; for I remembered an old writing that I had seen, which said, “Her steps lead straight to Hell.” Prov 5:5. So I shut my eyes, so that I would not be bewitched by her looks. Job 31:1. Then she shouted abuse at me, and I went my way.

Christian: Did you meet no other attack as you came?

Faithful: When I came to the foot of the hill called Difficulty, I met a very old man, who asked me who I was and where I was going. I told him that I was a pilgrim, going to the Celestial City. Then the old man said, You look like an honest fellow; would you be willing to live with me for the wages that I will give you? Then I asked his name, and where he lived. He said his name was Adam the First, and that he lived in the town of Deceit. Eph 4:22. I asked him then what his work was, and what wages he would give. He told me that his work was many delights; and his wages, that I would be his heir at last. I further asked him what sort of house he kept, and what other servants he had. So he told me that his house was stocked with all the delicacies of the world, and that his servants were those he had fathered himself. Then I asked how many children he had. He said that he had only three daughters, the Lust of the Flesh, the Lust of the Eyes, and the Pride of Life, 1 John 2:16; and that I could marry them if I wanted to. Then I asked how long he wanted me to live with him. And he told me, as long as he lived himself.

Christian: Well, and what conclusion did you and the old man come to in the end?

Faithful: Why, at first I found myself somewhat inclined to go with the man, for I thought he spoke very persuasively; but looking at his forehead as I talked with him, I saw written there, “Put off the old man with his deeds.”

Christian: And what then?

Faithful: Then it came burning hot into my mind that, whatever he said and however he flattered, once he got me home to his house he would sell me as a slave. So I told him to stop talking, for I would not come near the door of his house. Then he heaped insults on me, and told me that he would send someone after me who would make my way bitter to my soul. So I turned to go away from him; but just as I turned to leave, I felt him take hold of my flesh and give me such a deadly wrench backward that I thought he had pulled part of me away with him. This made me cry, “O wretched man.” Rom 7:24. So I went on my way up the hill.

Now, when I had got more than halfway up, I looked back and saw someone coming after me, as swift as the wind; and he overtook me just about where the bench stands.

Christian: Just there, Christian said, I sat down to rest; but I was overcome with sleep, and there I lost this roll out of my bosom.

Faithful: But, good brother, hear me out. As soon as the man overtook me, it was only a word and a blow; for he knocked me down and left me for dead. But when I had come to myself a little, I asked him why he treated me like that. He said it was because of my secret leaning toward Adam the First. And with that he struck me another deadly blow on the chest, and beat me down backward; so I lay at his feet as dead as before. So when I came to myself again I begged him for mercy; but he said, I do not know how to show mercy; and with that he knocked me down again. He would certainly have finished me off, if someone had not come by and told him to stop.

Christian: Who was it that told him to stop?

Faithful: I did not know him at first; but as he went by, I saw the holes in his hands and in his side, and then I concluded that he was our Lord. So I went up the hill.

Christian: That man who overtook you was Moses. He spares no one, nor does he know how to show mercy to those who transgress the law.

Faithful: I know it very well; it was not the first time he has met me. It was he who came to me when I lived complacently at home, and who told me he would burn my house down over my head if I stayed there.

Christian: But did you not see the house that stood at the top of that hill, where Moses met you on the slope?

Faithful: Yes, and the lions too, before I reached it. But as for the lions, I think they were asleep, for it was about noon; and because I had so much of the day still ahead of me, I passed by the Porter, and came down the hill.

Christian: He did tell me that he saw you go by; but I wish you had called at the house, for they would have shown you so many rare things that you would hardly have forgotten them to your dying day. But please tell me, did you meet nobody in the Valley of Humility?

Faithful: Yes, I met one Discontent, who would gladly have persuaded me to go back with him. His reason was that the valley was altogether without honor. He told me, moreover, that going there was the way to alienate all my friends, such as Pride, Arrogancy, Self-Conceit, Worldly Glory, and others, who, he said, he knew would be very much offended if I made such a fool of myself as to wade through this valley.

Christian: Well, and how did you answer him?

Faithful: I told him that although all these he named might claim to be my kin, and rightly so (for indeed they were my relatives according to the flesh), yet since I became a pilgrim they have disowned me, and I have rejected them too; and so they were now no more to me than if they had never been of my family line. I told him, moreover, that as for this valley, he had quite misrepresented it; for before honor is humility, and a haughty spirit before a fall. Therefore, I said, I would rather go through this valley to what the wisest counted honor, than choose what he valued as most worthy of our affections.

Christian: Did you meet nothing else in that valley?

Faithful: Yes, I met Shame; but of all the men I met on my pilgrimage, he, I think, bears the wrong name. The others would take no for an answer after a little argument and one thing or another; but this bold-faced Shame would never give up.

Christian: Why, what did he say to you?

Faithful: What? Why, he objected to religion itself. He said it was a pitiful, low, cringing business for a man to care about religion. He said that a tender conscience was an unmanly thing; and that for a man to watch over his words and ways, so as to tie himself down from the swaggering liberty that the brave spirits of the times were used to, would make him the laughingstock of the age. He also objected that only a few of the mighty, rich, or wise were ever of my opinion; nor any of them either, until they had been persuaded to be fools, and to be so willingly foolish as to risk the loss of all for nobody knows what. 1 Cor 1:26; 3:18; Phil 3:7–9; John 7:48. He objected, moreover, to the poor and low estate and condition of those who were, for the most part, the pilgrims of the times in which they lived; and also to their ignorance and lack of understanding in all natural science. Yes, he pressed me hard in that way about a great many more things than I relate here: such as, that it was a shame to sit whining and mourning under a sermon, and a shame to come home sighing and groaning; that it was a shame to ask my neighbor’s forgiveness for petty faults, or to make restitution where I have taken from anyone. He said also that religion made a man grow distant from the great, because of a few vices (which he called by finer names), and made him acknowledge and respect the lowly, because they were of the same religious brotherhood. And is this not, he said, a shame?

Christian: And what did you say to him?

Faithful: Say? I could not tell what to say at first. Indeed, he pressed me so hard that my blood rushed up into my face; it was this Shame that brought it up, and he had almost beaten me off altogether. But at last I began to consider that what is highly valued among men is held in abomination by God. Luke 16:15. And I thought again, this Shame tells me what men are; but he tells me nothing about what God, or the word of God, is. And I thought, moreover, that at the day of doom we shall not be doomed to death or life according to the swaggering spirits of the world, but according to the wisdom and law of the Highest. Therefore, I thought, what God says is best is indeed best, though all the men in the world are against it. Seeing, then, that God prefers his religion; seeing God prefers a tender conscience; seeing those who make themselves fools for the kingdom of heaven are wisest, and that the poor man who loves Christ is richer than the greatest man in the world who hates him: Shame, depart; you are an enemy to my salvation. Shall I welcome you against my sovereign Lord? How then could I look him in the face at his coming? Mark 8:38. If I were ashamed of his ways and servants now, how could I expect the blessing? But indeed this Shame was a bold villain; I could hardly shake him out of my company; he kept on haunting me, and continually whispering in my ear about one or another of the weaknesses that go with religion. But at last I told him that it was useless to try any further in this business; for the very things he despised were the things in which I saw the most glory. And so at last I got past this persistent fellow. And when I had shaken him off, I began to sing,

““The trials those men meet with, one and all,

Who are obedient to the heavenly call,

Are manifold, and suited to the flesh,

And come, and come, and come again afresh;

That, now or later on, by them we may

Be taken, overcome, and cast away.

O let the pilgrims, let the pilgrims then,

Be watchful, and acquit themselves like men.””

Christian: I am glad, my brother, that you stood up to this villain so bravely; for of them all, as you say, I think he has the wrong name; for he is so bold as to follow us in the streets, and to try to put us to shame before all men; that is, to make us ashamed of what is good. But if he were not so audacious himself, he would never attempt to do what he does. But let us go on resisting him; for, in spite of all his bravado, he promotes the fool, and no one else. “The wise will inherit glory,” said Solomon, “but shame will be the promotion of fools.” Prov 3:35.

Faithful: I think we must cry for help against Shame to Him who would have us be valiant for truth on the earth.

Christian: You are right; but did you meet nobody else in that valley?

Faithful: No, I did not; for I had sunshine all the rest of the way through that valley, and through the Valley of the Shadow of Death as well.

Christian: You were fortunate; I am sure it went very differently with me. For a long time, almost as soon as I entered that valley, I had a dreadful fight with that foul fiend Apollyon; indeed, I truly thought he would kill me, especially when he got me down and crushed me under him, as if he would crush me to pieces; for as he threw me, my sword flew out of my hand. He even told me he was sure of me; but I cried to God, and he heard me, and delivered me out of all my troubles. Then I entered the Valley of the Shadow of Death, and had no light for almost half the way through it. I thought I would be killed there over and over; but at last day broke, and the sun rose, and I went through the rest with far more ease and quiet.

Moreover, I saw in my dream that as they went on, Faithful, happening to look to one side, saw a man whose name was Talkative, walking at a distance beside them; for in this place there was room enough for them all to walk. He was a tall man, and rather better-looking at a distance than close up. Faithful turned to this man and spoke to him like this.

Faithful: Friend, where are you headed? Are you going to the heavenly country?

Talkative: I am going to the same place.

Faithful: That is good; then I hope we will have your good company?

Talkative: I will be your companion very gladly.

Faithful: Come on, then, let us go together, and let us spend our time talking about things that are profitable.

Talkative: To talk of things that are good is very welcome to me, with you or with anyone else; and I am glad that I have met people who are inclined to so good a work; for, to tell the truth, there are only a few who care to spend their time like this as they travel; most would much rather talk of things of no profit; and this has troubled me.

Faithful: That is indeed something to be lamented; for what is so worthy of the use of men’s tongues and mouths on earth as the things of the God of heaven?

Talkative: I like you wonderfully well, for what you say is very convincing; and I will add, What is so pleasant, and what so profitable, as to talk of the things of God? What things are so pleasant? That is, if a man has any delight in things that are wonderful. For instance, if a man delights to talk of the history or the mystery of things; or if a man loves to talk of miracles, wonders, or signs, where will he find things recorded so delightfully, and so sweetly written, as in the holy Scripture?

Faithful: That is true; but our chief aim in our talk should be to profit from such things.

Talkative: That is just what I said; for to talk of such things is most profitable; for by doing so a man may gain knowledge of many things, such as the vanity of earthly things and the benefit of things above. That is in general; but more particularly, by this a man may learn the necessity of the new birth, the insufficiency of our works, the need of Christ’s righteousness, etc. Besides, by this a man may learn what it is to repent, to believe, to pray, to suffer, and the like; by this, also, a man may learn what the great promises and consolations of the Gospel are, to his own comfort. Further, by this a man may learn to refute false opinions, to defend the truth, and also to instruct the ignorant.

Faithful: All this is true; and I am glad to hear these things from you.

Talkative: Alas! the lack of this is the reason why so few understand the need of faith, and the necessity of a work of grace in their soul in order to have eternal life; instead they ignorantly live in the works of the law, by which a man can by no means obtain the kingdom of heaven.

Faithful: But, if I may say so, heavenly knowledge of these things is the gift of God; no man attains it by human effort, or only by talking about them.

Talkative: All this I know very well; for a man can receive nothing unless it is given him from heaven: all is of grace, not of works. I could give you a hundred scriptures to confirm this.

Faithful: Well, then, Faithful said, what is the one thing that we should base our talk on at this time?

Talkative: Whatever you like. I will talk of things heavenly or things earthly; things moral or things evangelical; things sacred or things profane; things past or things to come; things foreign or things at home; things more essential or things incidental: provided that it is all done to our profit.

Faithful: Now Faithful began to marvel; and stepping over to Christian (for Christian had been walking by himself all this while), he said to him, but softly, What a fine companion we have got! Surely this man will make a very excellent pilgrim.

Christian: At this Christian smiled modestly, and said, This man you are so taken with will deceive, with this tongue of his, twenty people who do not know him.

Faithful: Do you know him, then?

Christian: Know him? Yes, better than he knows himself.

Faithful: Then tell me, who is he?

Christian: His name is Talkative; he lives in our town. I am surprised that you should be a stranger to him, except that I remember that our town is large.

Faithful: Whose son is he? And whereabouts does he live?

Christian: He is the son of one Say-well. He lived in Prating-Row; and he is known to all who are acquainted with him as Talkative of Prating-Row; and in spite of his fine tongue, he is nothing but a sorry fellow.

Faithful: Well, he seems to be a very fine man.

Christian: That is, to those who do not know him thoroughly, for he is best away from home; near home he is ugly enough. Your saying that he is a fine man brings to mind what I have noticed in the work of a painter, whose pictures look best at a distance, but close up are less pleasing.

Faithful: But I am inclined to think you are only joking, because you smiled.

Christian: God forbid that I should joke (though I smiled) about this matter, or that I should accuse anyone falsely. I will show you more of what he is. This man is for any company and any talk; as he talks now with you, so he will talk when he is on the ale-bench; and the more drink he has in his head, the more of these things he has in his mouth. Religion has no place in his heart, or house, or life; all he has lies in his tongue, and his religion is to make a noise with it.

Faithful: Is that so? Then I have been badly deceived in this man.

Christian: Deceived! You may be sure of it. Remember the proverb, “They say, and do not”; but the kingdom of God is not in word, but in power. Matt 23:3; 1 Cor 4:20. He talks of prayer, of repentance, of faith, and of the new birth; but he only knows how to talk of them. I have been in his family, and have watched him both at home and away from home; and I know that what I say of him is the truth. His house is as empty of religion as the white of an egg is of taste. There is neither prayer there nor any sign of repentance for sin; indeed, the brute, in its own way, serves God far better than he does. He is the very stain, reproach, and shame of religion to all who know him, Rom 2:24, 25; because of him, religion can hardly get a good word in all that end of the town where he lives. So the common people who know him say, “A saint abroad, and a devil at home.” His poor family finds it so; he is such a boor, so abusive to his servants, and so unreasonable with them, that they neither know how to work for him nor how to speak to him. Men who have any dealings with him say, It is better to deal with a Turk than with him, for they will get fairer dealing at the Turks’ hands. This Talkative (if it is possible) will outwit them, defraud, deceive, and overreach them. Besides, he brings up his sons to follow in his steps; and if he finds in any of them a foolish timidity (for so he calls the first sign of a tender conscience), he calls them fools and blockheads, and will by no means trust them with much, or speak well of them before others. For my part, I am of the opinion that he has, by his wicked life, caused many to stumble and fall; and he will be, unless God prevents it, the ruin of many more.

Faithful: Well, my brother, I am bound to believe you, not only because you say you know him, but also because you report on men as a Christian should. For I cannot think that you say these things out of ill will, but because it is just as you say.

Christian: If I had known him no better than you, I might perhaps have thought of him as you did at first; yes, and if I had heard this report only from those who are enemies of religion, I would have thought it was a slander—a fate that often falls from bad men’s mouths on good men’s names and professions of faith. But all these things, yes, and a great many more just as bad, I can prove him guilty of from my own knowledge. Besides, good men are ashamed of him; they can call him neither brother nor friend; the very mention of his name among them makes them blush, if they know him.

Faithful: Well, I see that saying and doing are two things, and from now on I will mark this distinction better.

Christian: They are two things indeed, and are as different as the soul and the body; for as the body without the soul is only a dead carcass, so saying, if it is alone, is only a dead carcass too. The soul of religion is the practical part. “Pure and undefiled religion before our God and Father is this: to care for orphans and widows in their distress, and to keep oneself from being polluted by the world.” Jas 1:27; see also verses 22-26. Talkative is not aware of this; he thinks that hearing and saying will make a good Christian, and so he deceives his own soul. Hearing is only the sowing of the seed; talking is not enough to prove that fruit is really in the heart and life. And let us be sure that at the day of doom men will be judged according to their fruits. Matt 13:23. It will not be said then, Did you believe? but, Were you doers, or only talkers? and they will be judged accordingly. The end of the world is compared to our harvest, Matt 13:30, and you know that at harvest men care about nothing but fruit. Not that anything can be accepted that is not of faith; but I say this to show you how insignificant Talkative’s profession of faith will be on that day.

Faithful: This brings to mind what Moses says when he describes the beast that is clean. Lev 11; Deut 14. It is one that parts the hoof and chews the cud; not one that parts the hoof only, or that chews the cud only. The hare chews the cud, but is still unclean, because he does not part the hoof. And this is a true likeness of Talkative: he chews the cud, he seeks knowledge; he chews on the word, but he does not divide the hoof. He does not part with the way of sinners; but, like the hare, he keeps the foot of the dog or bear, and therefore he is unclean.

Christian: You have given, as far as I know, the true gospel sense of these texts. And I will add another thing: Paul calls some men, yes, and great talkers at that, sounding brass and tinkling cymbals, 1 Cor 13:1, 3; that is, as he explains them in another place, things without life that give a sound. 1 Cor 14:7. Things without life; that is, without the true faith and grace of the gospel; and so, things that will never be placed in the kingdom of heaven among those who are the children of life, even though their sound, by their talk, is like the tongue or voice of an angel.

Faithful: Well, I was no fonder of his company at first than I am sick of it now. What can we do to get rid of him?

Christian: Take my advice, and do as I tell you, and you will find that he will soon be sick of your company too, unless God touches his heart and turns it.

Faithful: What do you want me to do?

Christian: Why, go to him, and start a serious discussion about the power of religion; and ask him plainly (once he has approved of it, as he will) whether this thing is set up in his heart, house, or life.

Faithful: Then Faithful stepped forward again, and said to Talkative, Come, how are you doing? How is it going now?

Talkative: Fine, thank you. I thought we would have had a great deal of talk by now.

Faithful: Well, if you like, we will get down to it now; and since you left it to me to set the question, let it be this: How does the saving grace of God show itself when it is in the heart of man?

Talkative: I see, then, that our talk must be about the power of things. Well, it is a very good question, and I will gladly answer you. Here is my answer in brief: First, where the grace of God is in the heart, it causes a great outcry there against sin. Secondly—

Faithful: No, wait; let us consider one at a time. I think you should rather say, it shows itself by inclining the soul to abhor its sin.

Talkative: Why, what difference is there between crying out against sin and abhorring it?

Faithful: Oh! a great deal. A man may cry out against sin out of self-interest; but he cannot abhor it except through a godly hatred of it. I have heard many cry out against sin in the pulpit who can still put up with it well enough in the heart, house, and life. Gen 39:15. Joseph’s mistress cried out with a loud voice, as if she had been very holy; but in spite of that she would gladly have committed uncleanness with him. Some cry out against sin just as a mother cries out against the child in her lap, when she calls it little rascal and naughty girl, and then starts hugging and kissing it.

Talkative: You are trying to catch me out, I see.

Faithful: No, not I; I am only for setting things right. But what is the second thing by which you would prove that there is a work of grace in the heart?

Talkative: Great knowledge of gospel mysteries.

Faithful: This sign should have come first; but first or last, it is also false; for knowledge, great knowledge, may be gained in the mysteries of the Gospel, and yet there may be no work of grace in the soul. Even if a man has all knowledge, he may still be nothing, and so, consequently, be no child of God. 1 Cor 13:2. When Christ said, “Do you+ know all these things?” and the disciples answered, Yes, he added, “You+ will be blessed if you+ do them.” He does not place the blessing in knowing them, but in doing them. For there is a knowledge that is not followed by doing: “He who knows his Master’s will, and does not do it.” A man may know like an angel, and still be no Christian; so your sign is not true. Indeed, to know is a thing that pleases talkers and boasters; but to do is what pleases God. Not that the heart can be good without knowledge, for without that the heart is worthless. So there are two sorts of knowledge: knowledge that rests in the bare theory of things, and knowledge that is accompanied by the grace of faith and love, which sets a man to doing even the will of God from the heart. The first of these will serve the talker; but without the other, the true Christian is not content. “Give me understanding that I may obey Your law, and follow it with all my heart.” Ps 119:34.

Talkative: You are trying to catch me out again: this is not for edification.

Faithful: Well, if you please, put forward another sign of how this work of grace shows itself where it is.

Talkative: Not I, for I see we will not agree.

Faithful: Well, if you will not, will you allow me to do it?

Talkative: You are at liberty to.

Faithful: A work of grace in the soul shows itself either to the man who has it, or to those standing by.

To the man who has it, it shows itself like this: It gives him conviction of sin, especially of the defilement of his nature and of the sin of unbelief, for which he is sure to be damned if he does not find mercy at God’s hand by faith in Jesus Christ. This sight and sense of things works sorrow and shame for sin in him. Ps 38:18; Jer 31:19; John 16:8; Rom 7:24; Mark 16:16; Gal 2:16; Rev 1:6. He finds, moreover, the Savior of the world revealed in him, and the absolute necessity of embracing him for life; and at this he finds hungerings and thirstings after him; and it is to such hungerings, etc., that the promise is made. Now, according to the strength or weakness of his faith in his Savior, so is his joy and peace, so is his love of holiness, so are his desires to know him more, and also to serve him in this world. But though, I say, it shows itself to him in this way, yet he is only seldom able to conclude that this is a work of grace; because his corruptions now, and his abused reason, make his mind misjudge in this matter. So in the man who has this work, a very sound judgment is required before he can firmly conclude that this is a work of grace. John 16:9; Gal 2:15, 16; Acts 4:12; Matt 5:6; Rev 21:6.

To others it is shown like this:

1. By a confession of his faith in Christ from experience. 2. By a life matching that confession; that is, a life of holiness—heart-holiness, family-holiness (if he has a family), and holiness of conduct in the world; which in general teaches him inwardly to abhor his sin, and himself for it, in secret; to suppress it in his family, and to promote holiness in the world: not by talk only, as a hypocrite or talkative person may do, but by a practical submission in faith and love to the power of the word. Job 42:5, 6; Ps 50:23; Ezek 20:43; Matt 5:8; John 14:15; Rom 10:10; Ezek 36:25; Phil 1:27; 3:17–20. And now, sir, as to this brief description of the work of grace, and also of how it is shown, if you have any objection, make it; if not, then allow me to put a second question to you.

Talkative: No, my part now is not to object but to listen; so let me have your second question.

Faithful: It is this: Do you experience this first part of the description; and do your life and conduct bear witness to the same? Or does your religion stand in word or tongue, and not in deed and truth? Please, if you are inclined to answer me on this, say no more than you know the God above will say Amen to, and nothing but what your conscience can justify you in; for it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends. Besides, to say I am such and such, when my conduct and all my neighbors tell me I lie, is great wickedness.

Then Talkative at first began to blush; but, recovering himself, he replied like this: You come now to experience, to conscience, and to God, and appeal to him to justify what is spoken. I did not expect this kind of talk; nor am I disposed to answer such questions, because I do not count myself bound to, unless you take it upon yourself to catechize me; and even if you did, I may still refuse to make you my judge. But please, will you tell me why you ask me such questions?

Faithful: Because I saw you were eager to talk, and because I did not know that you had anything more than notions. Besides, to tell you the whole truth, I have heard of you that you are a man whose religion lies in talk, and that your conduct gives the lie to this profession of your mouth. They say you are a stain among Christians, and that religion fares the worse for your ungodly conduct; that some have already stumbled at your wicked ways, and that more are in danger of being destroyed by them: your religion, and an ale-house, and covetousness, and uncleanness, and swearing, and lying, and keeping vain company, etc., will all stand together. The proverb that is said of a harlot is true of you, namely, “That she is a shame to all women”: so you are a shame to all professing Christians.

Talkative: Since you are so ready to take up reports and to judge as rashly as you do, I can only conclude that you are some peevish or melancholy man, not fit to talk with; and so, goodbye.

Then Christian came up and said to his brother, I told you how it would turn out; your words and his lusts could not agree. He would rather leave your company than reform his life. But he is gone, as I said: let him go; the loss is no man’s but his own. He has saved us the trouble of leaving him; for if he went on as he is (as I suppose he will), he would have been nothing but a blot in our company. Besides, the apostle says, “From such withdraw yourself.”

Faithful: But I am glad we had this little talk with him; perhaps he will think about it again. In any case, I have dealt plainly with him, and so I am clear of his blood if he perishes.

Christian: You did well to talk to him as plainly as you did. There is very little of this faithful dealing with men nowadays, and that is what makes religion stink so in the nostrils of many; for it is these talkative fools, whose religion is only in word, and who are debauched and vain in their conduct, who (being admitted so much into the fellowship of the godly) confuse the world, blemish Christianity, and grieve the sincere. I wish that all men would deal with such people as you have done; then they would either be brought more into line with religion, or the company of saints would be too hot for them. Then Faithful said,

““How Talkative at first lifts up his plumes!

How grandly he can speak! How he presumes

To drive down all before him! But as soon

As Faithful talks of heart-work, like the moon

That’s past the full, into the wane he goes;

And so will all but he that heart-work knows.””

So they went on, talking of what they had seen on the way, and in this way made easy a way that would no doubt otherwise have been tedious to them, for now they were going through a wilderness.

THE SIXTH STAGE

Now when they had got almost all the way out of this wilderness, Faithful happened to glance back, and saw someone coming after them, and he knew him. Oh! Faithful said to his brother, who is that coming over there? Then Christian looked, and said, It is my good friend Evangelist. Yes, and my good friend too, said Faithful, for it was he who set me on the way to the gate. By now Evangelist had come up to them, and he greeted them like this.

Evangelist: Peace be with you+, dearly beloved, and peace be to your+ helpers.

Christian: Welcome, welcome, my good Evangelist! The sight of your face brings back to me your kindness of long ago and your tireless labors for my eternal good.

Faithful: And a thousand times welcome, said good Faithful. Your company, O sweet Evangelist, how dear it is to us poor pilgrims!

Evangelist: Then Evangelist said, How have things gone with you+, my friends, since we last parted? What have you+ met with, and how have you+ behaved yourselves+?

Then Christian and Faithful told him everything that had happened to them on the way, and how, and with what difficulty, they had reached that place.

I am very glad, said Evangelist, not that you+ have met with trials, but that you+ have been victors, and that, in spite of many weaknesses, you+ have kept on in the way to this very day.

I say, I am very glad of this, and that for my own sake and for yours+: I have sown, and you+ have reaped; and the day is coming when “both he who sows and they who reap will rejoice together,” John 4:36; that is, if you+ hold out: “for in due time you+ will reap a harvest if you+ do not give up.” Gal 6:9. The crown is before you+, and it is an incorruptible one; “run in such a way as to obtain it.” 1 Cor 9:24–27. There are some who set out for this crown, and after they have gone a long way for it, another comes in and takes it from them: “hold fast, therefore, to what you+ have, so that no one will take your+ crown.” Rev 3:11. You+ are not yet out of the devil’s gunshot; “you+ have not yet resisted to the point of shedding your+ blood, in your+ struggle against sin.” Let the kingdom be always before you+, and believe steadfastly in the things that are invisible. Let nothing on this side of the other world get inside you+. And above all, look well to your+ own hearts and to their lusts; for they are “deceitful above all things and desperately wicked.” Set your+ faces like a flint; you+ have all power in heaven and earth on your+ side.

Christian: Then Christian thanked him for his exhortations, but told him also that they wanted him to speak further to them, to help them for the rest of the way; and all the more because they knew well that he was a prophet, and could tell them of things that might happen to them, and also how they might resist and overcome them. Faithful also agreed to this request. So Evangelist began as follows.

Evangelist: My sons, you+ have heard in the word of the truth of the Gospel that you+ must “endure many hardships to enter the kingdom of God”; and again, that “in town after town chains and afflictions await you+”; and so you+ cannot expect to go long on your+ pilgrimage without them, of one kind or another. You+ have already found something of the truth of these testimonies for yourselves+, and more will follow immediately. For now, as you+ see, you+ are almost out of this wilderness, and so you+ will soon come into a town that you+ will shortly see ahead of you+; and in that town you+ will be hard pressed by enemies, who will strain hard to kill you+. And you+ can be sure that one or both of you+ must seal the testimony you+ hold with blood; but “be faithful even unto death, and the King will give you+ a crown of life.” He who dies there, although his death will be violent and his pain perhaps great, will still have the better of his companion; not only because he will have arrived at the Celestial City sooner, but because he will escape many miseries that the other will meet with in the rest of his journey. But when you+ have come to the town, and find fulfilled what I have told you+ here, then remember your+ friend, and acquit yourselves+ like men, and “entrust your+ souls to your+ faithful Creator and continue to do good.”

Then I saw in my dream that when they had got out of the wilderness, they at once saw a town before them, and the name of that town is Vanity; and at the town a fair is held, called Vanity Fair. It is held all year long. It bears the name of Vanity Fair because the town where it is held is lighter than vanity, Ps 62:9; and also because all that is sold there, or that comes there, is vanity; in the words of the wise, “All that comes is vanity.” Eccl 11:8; see also 1:2-14; 2:11-17; Isa 40:17.

This fair is no newly founded affair, but a thing of ancient standing. I will show you how it began.

Almost five thousand years ago there were pilgrims walking to the Celestial City, as these two honest men are; and Beelzebub, Apollyon, and Legion, with their companions, seeing by the path the pilgrims made that their way to the city lay through this town of Vanity, schemed to set up a fair here: a fair in which all sorts of vanity would be sold, and which would last all year long. So at this fair all such merchandise is sold as houses, lands, trades, positions, honors, preferments, titles, countries, kingdoms, lusts, pleasures; and delights of all sorts, such as harlots, wives, husbands, children, masters, servants, lives, blood, bodies, souls, silver, gold, pearls, precious stones, and what not.

And besides, at this fair there are at all times conjuring tricks, cheats, games, plays, fools, apes, rascals, and rogues to be seen, and of every kind.

Here too, and for nothing, can be seen thefts, murders, adulteries, perjurers, and all of a blood-red color.

And as in other fairs of less importance there are separate rows and streets under their own names, where such and such wares are sold, so here likewise you have particular places, rows, and streets (namely, countries and kingdoms), where the wares of this fair are most readily found. Here is the Britain Row, the French Row, the Italian Row, the Spanish Row, the German Row, where various sorts of vanities are to be sold.
