But as in other fairs one particular commodity is the chief of the whole fair, so the ware of Rome and her merchandise is greatly promoted in this fair; only our English nation, with some others, has taken a dislike to it.

Now, as I said, the way to the Celestial City lies right through this town, where this lively fair is held; and he who wants to go to the city, and yet not go through this town, “would have to leave this world.” 1 Cor 5:10. The Prince of princes himself, when he was here, went through this town to his own country, and on a fair-day too; yes, and I think it was Beelzebub, the chief lord of this fair, who invited him to buy some of his vanities; indeed, he would have made him lord of the fair, if only he would have paid him homage as he went through the town. Indeed, because he was such a person of honor, Beelzebub took him from street to street, and showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a short time, so that he might, if possible, lure that blessed One into bargaining for and buying some of his vanities; but he had no interest in the merchandise, and so he left the town without spending so much as one farthing on these vanities. Matt 4:8, 9; Luke 4:5–7. This fair, therefore, is an ancient thing, of long standing, and a very great fair.

Now these pilgrims, as I said, had to go through this fair. Well, so they did; but look, even as they entered the fair, all the people in the fair were stirred, and the town itself was, as it were, in a hubbub about them; and that for several reasons: for,

First, The Pilgrims were dressed in a kind of clothing different from the clothing of anyone who traded in that fair. So the people of the fair stared hard at them: some said they were fools, 1 Cor 4:9, 10; some, that they were madmen; and some, that they were foreigners.

Secondly, And as they wondered at their clothes, so they wondered at their speech too; for few could understand what they said. They naturally spoke the language of Canaan, but those who ran the fair were the men of this world; so that from one end of the fair to the other, they seemed like barbarians to each other. 1 Cor 2:7, 8.

Thirdly, But what puzzled the merchants not a little was that these pilgrims thought very little of all their wares. They did not even care to look at them; and if the merchants called on them to buy, they would put their fingers in their ears, and cry, “Turn away my eyes from beholding vanity,” Ps 119:37, and look upward, signifying that their trade and commerce was in heaven. Phil 3:20, 21.

One man, seeing how the men carried themselves, happened to say to them mockingly, “What will you+ buy?” But they looked at him gravely and said, “We buy the truth.” Prov 23:23. That gave the people an occasion to despise the men all the more; some mocked, some taunted, some spoke insultingly, and some called on others to strike them. At last things came to an uproar and a great stir in the fair, so that all order broke down. Now word was brought at once to the great one of the fair, who quickly came down, and appointed some of his most trusted friends to question the men over whom the fair had almost been turned upside down. So the men were brought in to be questioned; and those who sat in judgment on them asked them where they came from, where they were going, and what they were doing there in such unusual dress. The men told them that they were pilgrims and strangers in the world, and that they were going to their own country, which was the heavenly Jerusalem, Heb 11:13–16; and that they had given the men of the town no cause, nor the merchants either, to abuse them like this and to hinder them on their journey, unless it was that, when one asked them what they would buy, they said they would buy the truth. But those who were appointed to question them believed they were nothing other than lunatics and madmen, or else people who had come to throw everything in the fair into confusion. So they took them and beat them, and smeared them with dirt, and then put them into the cage, so that they might be made a spectacle to all the men of the fair. There they lay for some time, and were made the objects of any man’s sport, or malice, or revenge, while the great one of the fair laughed all the while at everything that happened to them. But the men were patient, “not repaying insult with insult, but with blessing,” and giving good words for bad, and kindness for injuries done; and some men in the fair, who were more observant and less prejudiced than the rest, began to rebuke and blame the baser sort for the continual abuse they were heaping on the men. The baser sort, in turn, lashed out at them angrily, counting them as bad as the men in the cage, and telling them that they seemed to be in league with them, and should be made to share their misfortunes. The others replied that, for all they could see, the men were quiet and sober, and meant nobody any harm; and that there were many who traded in their fair who deserved to be put into the cage, yes, and the pillory too, more than the men they had abused. So, after many words had passed on both sides (the men behaving very wisely and soberly before them all the while), they came to blows among themselves, and did one another harm. Then these two poor men were brought before their examiners again, and were charged with being guilty of the recent hubbub in the fair. So they beat them pitifully, and loaded them with irons, and led them in chains up and down the fair, as an example and a terror to others, so that no one would speak on their behalf or join them. But Christian and Faithful behaved yet more wisely, and took the disgrace and shame heaped on them with so much meekness and patience that it won several of the men in the fair to their side (though only a few compared with the rest). This put the other party into a still greater rage, so that they resolved on the death of these two men. So they threatened that neither cage nor irons would be enough for them, but that the two should die for the harm they had done, and for deceiving the men of the fair.

Then they were sent back to the cage again, until further orders should be given about them. So they put them in, and fastened their feet in the stocks.

Here also they called to mind again what they had heard from their faithful friend Evangelist, and were all the more strengthened in their way and their sufferings by what he had told them would happen to them. They also now comforted each other with this: that whichever of them it fell to suffer, he would have the best of it; so each man secretly wished that he might have that honor. But committing themselves to the all-wise ordering of Him who rules all things, they remained very contentedly in the condition they were in, until something else should be done with them.

Then, when a suitable time had been set, they brought them out for their trial, with a view to condemning them. When the time had come, they were brought before their enemies and formally charged. The judge’s name was Lord Hate-good. Their indictment was one and the same in substance, though it varied somewhat in form; and its contents were these: “That they were enemies to, and disturbers of, the trade; that they had made commotions and divisions in the town, and had won a party to their own most dangerous opinions, in contempt of the law of their prince.”

Then Faithful began to answer that he had only set himself against what had set itself against Him who is higher than the highest. And, he said, as for disturbance, I make none, since I am a man of peace myself; the people who were won to us were won by seeing our truth and innocence, and they have only been turned from the worse to the better. And as for the king you talk of, since he is Beelzebub, the enemy of our Lord, I defy him and all his angels.

Then a proclamation was made that those who had anything to say for their lord the king against the prisoner at the bar should appear at once and give their evidence. So three witnesses came in, namely, Envy, Superstition, and Pickthank. They were then asked if they knew the prisoner at the bar, and what they had to say against him for their lord the king.

Then Envy stepped forward and spoke to this effect: My lord, I have known this man a long time, and will testify on oath before this honorable bench that he is—

Judge: Wait; swear him in.

So they swore him in. Then he said, My lord, this man, in spite of his fair-sounding name, is one of the vilest men in our country. He respects neither prince nor people, law nor custom, but does all he can to fill all men’s heads with certain disloyal notions of his, which in general he calls principles of faith and holiness. And in particular, I once heard him myself declare that Christianity and the customs of our town of Vanity were diametrically opposed, and could not be reconciled. By that saying, my lord, he condemns at one stroke not only all our praiseworthy doings, but us for doing them.

Then the judge said to him, Do you have anything more to say?

Envy: My lord, I could say much more, only I do not wish to be tedious to the court. Yet if need be, when the other gentlemen have given their evidence, rather than let anything be lacking that will finish him off, I will add to my testimony against him. So he was told to stand aside.

Then they called Superstition, and told him to look at the prisoner. They also asked what he could say against him for their lord the king. Then they swore him in, and he began.

Superstition: My lord, I am not well acquainted with this man, nor do I want to know him any better. However, this I know, that he is a very pestilent fellow, from some talk I had with him the other day in this town; for then, talking with him, I heard him say that our religion was worthless, and such that a man could by no means please God by it. Your lordship knows very well, my lord, what must necessarily follow from that saying of his, namely, that we always worship in vain, are still in our sins, and in the end will be damned; and that is what I have to say.

Then Pickthank was sworn in, and told to say what he knew against the prisoner at the bar on behalf of their lord the king.

Pickthank: My lord, and all you gentlemen, I have known this fellow a long time, and have heard him say things that ought not to be said; for he has railed against our noble prince Beelzebub, and has spoken with contempt of his honorable friends, whose names are the Lord Old Man, the Lord Carnal Delight, the Lord Luxurious, the Lord Desire of Vain Glory, my old Lord Lechery, Sir Having Greedy, with all the rest of our nobility. And he has said, moreover, that if all men were of his mind, then, if possible, not one of these noblemen would be allowed to exist in this town any longer. Besides that, he has not been afraid to rail against you, my lord, who are now appointed to be his judge, calling you an ungodly villain, with many other such slanderous names, with which he has spattered most of the gentry of our town.

When this Pickthank had told his tale, the judge turned to the prisoner at the bar and said, You renegade, heretic, and traitor, have you heard what these honest gentlemen have testified against you?

Faithful: May I say a few words in my own defense?

Judge: Sirrah, sirrah, you deserve to live no longer, but to be put to death on the spot; yet, so that all men may see how gentle we are toward you, let us hear what you, vile renegade, have to say.

Faithful: 1. I say, then, in answer to what Mr. Envy has said, I never said anything but this: that whatever rules, or laws, or customs, or people are flatly against the word of God are diametrically opposed to Christianity. If I have said anything wrong in this, show me my error, and I am ready here before you to take it back.

2. As to the second, namely Mr. Superstition and his charge against me, I said only this: that in the worship of God a divine faith is required; but there can be no divine faith without a divine revelation of the will of God. Therefore whatever is thrust into the worship of God that does not agree with divine revelation can only be done by a human faith; and that faith will be of no benefit for eternal life.

3. As to what Mr. Pickthank has said, I say (leaving aside such charges as that I am said to rail, and the like) that the prince of this town, with all the rabble, his attendants, named by this gentleman, are more fit to live in hell than in this town and country. And so may the Lord have mercy on me.

Then the judge called to the jury (who had stood by all this while to hear and observe), Gentlemen of the jury, you+ see this man about whom so great an uproar has been made in this town; you+ have also heard what these worthy gentlemen have testified against him; and you+ have heard his reply and confession. It now rests with you+ to hang him or to save his life; but I think it right to instruct you+ in our law.

A law was passed in the days of Pharaoh the Great, servant to our prince, that, for fear those of a contrary religion should multiply and grow too strong for him, their males should be thrown into the river. Exod 1:22. A law was also passed in the days of Nebuchadnezzar the Great, another of his servants, that whoever would not fall down and worship his golden image should be thrown into a fiery furnace. Dan 3:6. A law was also passed in the days of Darius, that whoever for a certain time called upon any god but him should be cast into the lions’ den. Dan 6:7. Now this rebel has broken the substance of these laws, not only in thought (which is not to be endured), but also in word and deed; and that must therefore be utterly intolerable.

As for Pharaoh’s law, it was made on a supposition, to prevent harm, when no crime was yet apparent; but here a crime is apparent. As for the second and third, you+ see he argues against our religion; and for the treason he has already confessed, he deserves to be put to death.

Then the jury went out. Their names were Mr. Blindman, Mr. No-good, Mr. Malice, Mr. Love-lust, Mr. Live-loose, Mr. Heady, Mr. High-mind, Mr. Enmity, Mr. Liar, Mr. Cruelty, Mr. Hate-light, and Mr. Implacable; each one of them gave his own verdict against him in private among themselves, and afterward they unanimously agreed to find him guilty before the judge. And first among themselves, Mr. Blindman, the foreman, said, I see clearly that this man is a heretic. Then Mr. No-good said, Away with such a fellow from the earth. Yes, said Mr. Malice, for I hate the very look of him. Then Mr. Love-lust said, I could never stand him. Nor I, said Mr. Live-loose, for he was forever condemning my way of life. Hang him, hang him, said Mr. Heady. A miserable wretch, said Mr. High-mind. My heart rises against him, said Mr. Enmity. He is a rogue, said Mr. Liar. Hanging is too good for him, said Mr. Cruelty. Let us get him out of the way, said Mr. Hate-light. Then Mr. Implacable said, If I were given the whole world, I could not be reconciled to him; so let us at once bring in a verdict of guilty, and of death.

And so they did; so he was at once condemned to be taken from the place where he was to the place he had come from, and there to be put to the most cruel death that could be devised.

So they brought him out, to deal with him according to their law; and first they scourged him, then they struck him with their fists, then they slashed his flesh with knives; after that they stoned him with stones, then jabbed him with their swords; and last of all they burned him to ashes at the stake. So Faithful came to his end.

Now I saw that there stood behind the crowd a chariot and a pair of horses waiting for Faithful, who (as soon as his adversaries had put him to death) was taken up into it, and at once was carried up through the clouds with the sound of a trumpet, the nearest way to the celestial gate. But as for Christian, he had some respite, and was sent back to prison; so he stayed there for a while. But he who overrules all things, having the power of their rage in his own hand, so brought it about that Christian escaped them for that time, and went his way.

And as he went, he sang these words,

““Well, Faithful, you have faithfully professed

Unto your Lord, with whom you will be blessed,

When faithless ones, with all their vain delights,

Are crying out under their hellish plights:

Sing, Faithful, sing, and let your name survive;

For though they killed you, you are still alive.””

THE SEVENTH STAGE

Now I saw in my dream that Christian did not go on alone; for there was one whose name was Hopeful (made so by seeing Christian and Faithful in their words and behavior, and in their sufferings at the fair), who joined himself to him, and, entering into a brotherly covenant with him, told him that he would be his companion. So one died to bear witness to the truth, and another rises out of his ashes to be Christian’s companion on his pilgrimage. This Hopeful also told Christian that there were many more of the men in the fair who would follow after in their own time.

So I saw that soon after they had got out of the fair, they overtook a man who was going on ahead of them, whose name was By-ends; so they said to him, Where are you from, sir? and how far are you going this way? He told them that he came from the town of Fair-speech, and that he was going to the Celestial City; but he did not tell them his name.

From Fair-speech? said Christian; is there anyone good living there? Prov 26:25.

By-Ends: Yes, said By-ends, I hope so.

Christian: Please, sir, what should I call you? said Christian.

By-Ends: I am a stranger to you, and you to me: if you are going this way, I will be glad of your company; if not, I must be content.

Christian: This town of Fair-speech, said Christian, I have heard of; and, as I remember, they say it is a wealthy place.

By-Ends: Yes, I can assure you that it is; and I have a great many rich relatives there.

Christian: May I ask who your relatives there are, if a man may be so bold?

By-Ends: Almost the whole town; and in particular my Lord Turn-about, my Lord Time-server, and my Lord Fair-speech, from whose ancestors the town first took its name; also Mr. Smooth-man, Mr. Facing-both-ways, and Mr. Any-thing; and the parson of our parish, Mr. Two-tongues, was my mother’s own brother, on her father’s side. To tell you the truth, I have become a gentleman of good standing; yet my great-grandfather was only a waterman, looking one way and rowing another, and I made most of my fortune by the same trade.

Christian: Are you a married man?

By-Ends: Yes, and my wife is a very virtuous woman, the daughter of a virtuous woman; she was my Lady Feigning’s daughter, so she comes from a very honorable family, and she has reached such a height of good breeding that she knows how to behave toward everyone, prince and peasant alike. It is true that we differ somewhat in religion from those of the stricter sort, yet only on two small points: First, we never strive against wind and tide. Secondly, we are always most zealous when religion goes about in his silver slippers; we love to walk with him in the street, if the sun is shining and the people are applauding him.

Then Christian stepped a little aside to his fellow Hopeful and said, It runs in my mind that this is a certain By-ends, of Fair-speech; and if it is he, we have as thorough a scoundrel in our company as lives anywhere in these parts. Then Hopeful said, Ask him; surely he should not be ashamed of his name. So Christian came up with him again and said, Sir, you talk as if you knew something more than all the world knows; and, if I have not missed my mark, I think I can half guess who you are. Is your name not Mr. By-ends of Fair-speech?

By-Ends: That is not my name; it is only a nickname given me by some who cannot stand me, and I must be content to bear it as a reproach, as other good men have borne theirs before me.

Christian: But did you never give men any reason to call you by this name?

By-Ends: Never, never! The worst I ever did to give them reason to call me this was that I always had the luck to find my judgment falling in with the present way of the times, whatever it was, and it was my good chance to gain by it. But if things come my way like this, let me count them a blessing; and do not let the malicious heap reproach on me for it.

Christian: I thought, indeed, that you were the man I had heard of; and to tell you what I think, I fear this name belongs to you more truly than you would like us to think it does.

By-Ends: Well, if you choose to imagine so, I cannot help it; you will find me good company, if you will still have me as your companion.

Christian: If you will go with us, you must go against wind and tide, which, I can see, is against your opinion. You must also acknowledge Religion in his rags as well as in his silver slippers, and stand by him, too, when he is bound in irons, as well as when he walks the streets to applause.

By-Ends: You must not force your views on me, nor lord it over my faith; leave me my liberty, and let me go with you.

Christian: Not a step farther, unless you will do as we do in what I am proposing.

Then By-ends said, I will never desert my old principles, since they are harmless and profitable. If I may not go with you, I must do as I did before you overtook me, and go by myself, until someone overtakes me who will be glad of my company.

Now I saw in my dream that Christian and Hopeful left him, and kept their distance ahead of him; but one of them, looking back, saw three men following Mr. By-ends; and look, as they came up with him, he made them a very low bow, and they also bowed to him in return. The men’s names were Mr. Hold-the-world, Mr. Money-love, and Mr. Save-all, men whom Mr. By-ends had known in the past; for as boys they had been schoolfellows, taught by a Mr. Gripeman, a schoolmaster in Lovegain, which is a market-town in the county of Coveting, in the North. This schoolmaster taught them the art of getting, whether by violence, cheating, flattery, lying, or by putting on a show of religion; and these four gentlemen had learned so much of their master’s art that each of them could have kept such a school himself.

Well, when they had greeted each other in this way, as I said, Mr. Money-love said to Mr. By-ends, Who are those on the road ahead of us? For Christian and Hopeful were still in view.

By-Ends: They are a couple of men from a far country who, in their own fashion, are going on pilgrimage.

Mr. Money-Love: Alas! Why did they not wait, so that we could have had their good company? For they, and we, and you too, sir, I hope, are all going on pilgrimage.

By-Ends: We are indeed; but the men ahead of us are so rigid, and so much in love with their own notions, and think so little of other people’s opinions, that however godly a man may be, if he does not agree with them in everything, they throw him right out of their company.

Mr. Save-All: That is bad; but we read of some who are too righteous, and their rigidness leads such men to judge and condemn everyone but themselves. But tell me, what were the things on which you differed, and how many were there?

By-Ends: Why, in their headstrong way they conclude that it is their duty to rush on with their journey in all weathers, while I am for waiting for wind and tide. They are for risking everything for God at one stroke; I am for taking every advantage to keep my life and property safe. They are for holding to their notions, though all other men are against them; but I am for religion as far as, and in whatever way, the times and my safety will allow. They are for religion when he is in rags and contempt; but I am for him when he walks in his silver slippers, in the sunshine, and to applause.

Mr. Hold-the-World: Yes, and stick to that, good Mr. By-ends; for, for my part, I can only count a man a fool who, having the freedom to keep what he has, is so unwise as to lose it. Let us be wise as serpents. It is best to make hay while the sun shines. You see how the bee lies still in winter, and stirs herself only when she can have profit with pleasure. God sends rain at times, and sunshine at times: if they are such fools as to go through the first, let us still be content to take fair weather along with us. For my part, I like best the religion that goes along with keeping God’s good blessings safe in our hands; for who, if he is ruled by his reason, can imagine, since God has given us the good things of this life, that he would not have us keep them for his sake? Abraham and Solomon grew rich in religion; and Job says that a good man will lay up gold like dust; but he must not be like the men ahead of us, if they are as you have described them.

Mr. Save-All: I think that we are all agreed on this matter, so there is no need for more words about it.

Mr. Money-Love: No, there is no need for more words about this matter, indeed; for a man who believes neither Scripture nor reason (and you see we have both on our side) neither knows his own liberty nor looks after his own safety.

By-Ends: My brethren, as you see, we are all going on pilgrimage; and to keep our minds better turned away from things that are bad, allow me to put this question to you.

Suppose a man, a minister or a tradesman, etc., should have an opportunity in front of him to get the good blessings of this life, yet in such a way that he can by no means come by them unless, in appearance at least, he becomes extraordinarily zealous on some points of religion that he had nothing to do with before: may he not use this means to reach his end, and still be a thoroughly honest man?

Mr. Money-Love: I see what lies at the bottom of your question; and with these gentlemen’s kind permission, I will try to shape an answer for you. And first, to speak to your question as it concerns a minister himself: suppose a minister, a worthy man, has only a very small benefice, and has his eye on a greater one, far fatter and plumper; and he now has an opportunity of getting it, but only by being more studious, by preaching more often and more zealously, and, because the mood of the people requires it, by changing some of his principles. For my part, I see no reason why a man may not do this, provided he has a call (yes, and a great deal more besides), and still be an honest man. Here is why:

1. His desire for a greater benefice is lawful (this cannot be denied), since Providence has set it before him; so then he may get it if he can, without raising any question of conscience.

2. Besides, his desire for that benefice makes him more studious, a more zealous preacher, etc., and so makes him a better man; indeed, it makes him make better use of his gifts, which is according to the mind of God.

3. Now, as for his going along with the mood of his people, by giving up some of his principles to serve them, this shows, 1. That he has a self-denying disposition. 2. A sweet and winning manner. And, 3. That he is therefore more fit for the work of the ministry.

4. I conclude, then, that a minister who exchanges a small benefice for a great one should not be judged covetous for doing so; rather, since he has grown in his gifts and his diligence by it, he should be counted as one who is following his call, and using the opportunity put into his hand to do good.

And now to the second part of the question, which concerns the tradesman you mentioned. Suppose such a man has only a poor trade in the world, but by becoming religious he may improve his market, perhaps get a rich wife, or more and far better customers for his shop. For my part, I see no reason why this may not be done lawfully. Here is why:

1. To become religious is a virtue, by whatever means a man becomes so.

2. Nor is it unlawful to get a rich wife, or more customers for my shop.

3. Besides, the man who gets these by becoming religious gets what is good from those who are good, by becoming good himself; so here is a good wife, and good customers, and good gain, and all of it by becoming religious, which is good. Therefore to become religious to get all these is a good and profitable plan.

This answer that Mr. Money-love gave to Mr. By-ends’ question was highly applauded by them all; so they concluded, on the whole, that it was most wholesome and advantageous. And because, as they thought, no man could contradict it, and because Christian and Hopeful were still within call, they agreed together to set upon them with the question as soon as they overtook them; all the more because the two had opposed Mr. By-ends before. So they called after them, and Christian and Hopeful stopped and stood still until the others came up to them; but as they went, the four decided that old Mr. Hold-the-world, not Mr. By-ends, should put the question to them, because, as they supposed, the pilgrims’ answer to him would be free of what was left of the heat that had flared up between Mr. By-ends and them when they parted a little before.

So they came up to each other, and after a short greeting, Mr. Hold-the-world put the question to Christian and his fellow, and then told them to answer it if they could.

Then Christian said, Even a babe in religion can answer ten thousand questions like that. For if it is unlawful to follow Christ for loaves, as it is, John 6:26, how much more abominable is it to make him and religion a stalking-horse to get and enjoy the world! And we find no one but heathens, hypocrites, devils, and wizards who hold this opinion.

1. Heathens: for when Hamor and Shechem wanted Jacob’s daughter and cattle, and saw that there was no way for them to get at them except by being circumcised, they said to their companions, If every male of us is circumcised, as they are circumcised, will not their cattle, and their goods, and every beast of theirs be ours? Their daughters and their cattle were what they were after, and their religion was the stalking-horse they used to get at them. Read the whole story, Gen 34:20–24.

2. The hypocritical Pharisees were also of this religion: long prayers were their pretense, but getting widows’ houses was their aim; and greater damnation was God’s judgment on them. Luke 20:46, 47.

3. Judas the devil was also of this religion: he was religious for the money bag, so that he could have what was put in it; but he was lost, cast away, and the very son of perdition.

4. Simon the wizard was of this religion too; for he wanted the Holy Spirit so that he could make money by it; and the sentence Peter passed on him was to match. Acts 8:19–22.

5. Nor can I get it out of my mind that the man who takes up religion for the world will throw religion away for the world; for just as surely as Judas had his eye on the world in becoming religious, so surely did he also sell religion and his Master for the same. So to answer the question yes, as I see you+ have done, and to accept such an answer as sound, is heathenish, hypocritical, and devilish; and your+ reward will be according to your+ works.

Then they stood staring at one another, but had nothing to answer Christian with. Hopeful also agreed that Christian’s answer was sound; so there was a great silence among them. Mr. By-ends and his company also faltered and hung back, so that Christian and Hopeful could get ahead of them. Then Christian said to his fellow, If these men cannot stand before the sentence of men, what will they do with the sentence of God? And if they are struck dumb when dealt with by vessels of clay, what will they do when they are rebuked by the flames of a devouring fire?

Then Christian and Hopeful got ahead of them again, and went on until they came to a delightful plain called Ease, where they walked with great contentment; but that plain was only narrow, so they were soon across it. Now on the far side of that plain was a little hill called Lucre, and in that hill a silver-mine, which some who had gone that way before had turned aside to see, because it was such a rare thing; but going too near the edge of the pit, the ground, being treacherous under them, gave way, and they were killed. Some had also been maimed there, and to their dying day could never be their own men again.

Then I saw in my dream that a little off the road, opposite the silver-mine, stood Demas, like a gentleman, calling to passers-by to come and see; and he said to Christian and his fellow, Hello there! Turn aside here, and I will show you something.

Christian: What is so worth seeing that we should turn out of the way to see it?

Demas: Here is a silver-mine, and some are digging in it for treasure; if you will come, with a little effort you can provide richly for yourselves.

Hopeful: Then Hopeful said, Let us go and see.

Christian: Not I, said Christian. I have heard of this place before now, and of how many have been killed there; and besides, that treasure is a snare to those who seek it, for it hinders them in their pilgrimage.

Then Christian called to Demas and said, Is the place not dangerous? Has it not hindered many in their pilgrimage? Hos 9:6.

Demas: Not very dangerous, except to those who are careless. But he blushed as he said it.

Christian: Then Christian said to Hopeful, Let us not stir a step, but keep steadily on our way.

Hopeful: I promise you, when By-ends comes up, if he gets the same invitation as we did, he will turn in there to see.

Christian: No doubt about it, for his principles lead him that way, and it is a hundred to one that he dies there.

Demas: Then Demas called again, But will you not come over and see?

Christian: Then Christian answered him bluntly: Demas, you are an enemy to the right ways of the Lord of this way, and you have already been condemned for your own turning aside by one of his Majesty’s judges, 2 Tim 4:10; so why do you try to bring us into the same condemnation? Besides, if we turn aside at all, our Lord the King will certainly hear of it, and will put us to shame in the very place where we would want to stand before him with boldness.

Demas called out again that he too was one of their brotherhood, and that if they would wait a little, he would walk with them himself.

Christian: Then Christian said, What is your name? Is it not the name I have called you by?

Demas: Yes, my name is Demas; I am the son of Abraham.

Christian: I know you; Gehazi was your great-grandfather, and Judas your father, and you have walked in their steps. It is nothing but a devilish trick you are playing: your father was hanged for a traitor, and you deserve no better reward. 2 Kgs 5:20–27; Matt 26:14, 15; 27:3–5. You can be sure that when we come to the King, we will tell him about this behavior of yours. And so they went on their way.

By this time By-ends and his companions had come into sight again, and at the first beckoning they went over to Demas. Now, whether they fell into the pit by looking over its edge, or went down to dig, or were smothered at the bottom by the foul vapors that commonly rise there, I am not certain; but this I noticed: they were never seen again in the way. Then Christian sang,

““By-ends and silver Demas both agree;

One calls, the other runs, that he may be

A sharer in his lucre: so these two

Settle in this world, and no farther go.””

Now I saw that, just on the other side of this plain, the pilgrims came to a place where an old monument stood close beside the highway, and the sight of it troubled them both, because its form was so strange; for it seemed to them as if it were a woman changed into the shape of a pillar. So they stood here looking and looking at it, but for a while could not tell what to make of it. At last Hopeful noticed some writing in an unusual hand, high up on its head; but as he was no scholar, he called to Christian (for he was learned) to see if he could make out the meaning. So Christian came, and after piecing the letters together a little, he found it to say this, “Remember Lot’s wife.” So he read it to his fellow, and then they both concluded that this was the pillar of salt that Lot’s wife was turned into for looking back with a covetous heart as she was fleeing from Sodom for safety. Gen 19:26. And this sudden and astonishing sight led them to talk as follows.

Christian: Ah, my brother, this is a timely sight: it came to us at just the right moment, after Demas’s invitation to come over and look at the hill Lucre; and if we had gone over, as he wanted us to, and as you were inclined to do, my brother, we might, for all I know, have been made a spectacle like this woman, for those who come after us to gaze at.

Hopeful: I am sorry that I was so foolish, and I am left wondering that I am not now like Lot’s wife; for what was the difference between her sin and mine? She only looked back, and I wanted to go and see. Let grace be praised; and let me be ashamed that such a thing should ever have been in my heart.

Christian: Let us take note of what we see here, to help us in time to come. This woman escaped one judgment, for she did not fall in the destruction of Sodom; yet she was destroyed by another, as we see: she is turned into a pillar of salt.

Hopeful: True, and she may be both a caution and an example to us: a caution, that we should shun her sin; or a sign of what judgment will overtake those who will not be stopped by this caution. In the same way Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, with the two hundred and fifty men who perished in their sin, also became a sign or example to others to beware. Num 16:31, 32; 26:9, 10. But above all, I wonder at one thing: how Demas and his fellows can stand over there so confidently looking for that treasure, when this woman, only for looking back after it (for we do not read that she stepped one foot out of the way), was turned into a pillar of salt; especially since the judgment that overtook her made her an example within sight of where they are; for they cannot help seeing her, if they would only lift up their eyes.

Christian: It is something to wonder at, and it shows that their hearts have grown desperate in this matter; and I cannot think of anyone to compare them to so fitly as those who pick pockets in front of the judge, or who will cut purses under the gallows. It is said of the men of Sodom that they were “sinning greatly,” because they were sinning “before the Lord,” that is, in his sight, and in spite of the kindnesses he had shown them; for the land of Sodom was then like the garden of Eden of old. Gen 13:10–13. So this provoked him all the more to jealousy, and made their plague as hot as the fire of the Lord out of heaven could make it. And it is only reasonable to conclude that such people, even such as these, who sin in his sight, yes, and that in spite of such examples set continually before them to warn them against it, must share in the severest judgments.

Hopeful: You have certainly spoken the truth; but what a mercy it is that neither you, nor especially I myself, have been made this example! This gives us cause to thank God, to fear before him, and always to remember Lot’s wife.

I saw then that they went on their way to a pleasant river, which David the king called “the river of God,” and John “the river of the water of life.” Ps 65:9; Rev 22:1; Ezek 47:1–9. Now their way ran right along the bank of this river, so Christian and his companion walked here with great delight; they also drank of the water of the river, which was pleasant and refreshing to their weary spirits. Besides this, on the banks of this river, on either side, were green trees bearing all kinds of fruit; and they ate the leaves to prevent sickness from overeating and other illnesses that come on those who heat their blood by travel. On either side of the river there was also a meadow, beautifully adorned with lilies, and it was green all year round. In this meadow they lay down and slept, for here they could lie down safely. Ps 23:2; Isa 14:30. When they woke up they gathered of the fruit of the trees again, and drank of the water of the river again, and then lay down to sleep again. They did this for several days and nights. Then they sang:

““Behold, you+, how these Crystal Streams glide,

To comfort pilgrims by the highway-side.

The meadows green, besides their fragrant smell,

Yield dainties for them; And he that can tell

What pleasant fruit, yes, leaves these trees can yield,

Will soon sell all, that he may buy this field.””

So when they were ready to go on (for they were not yet at their journey’s end), they ate, and drank, and set off.

Now I saw in my dream that they had not gone far when the river and the way parted for a time, which made them more than a little sorry; yet they did not dare go out of the way. Now the way from the river was rough, and their feet were tender from their travels; so the souls of the pilgrims were much discouraged because of the way. Num 21:4. So as they went on, they kept wishing for a better way. Now a little ahead of them, on the left side of the road, there was a meadow, with a stile to climb over into it, and that meadow is called By-path meadow. Then Christian said to his fellow, If this meadow runs along beside our way, let us go over into it. Then he went to the stile to see, and sure enough, a path ran along beside the way on the other side of the fence. It is just what I wished for, said Christian; here is the easiest going; come, good Hopeful, let us go over.

Hopeful: But what if this path should lead us out of the way?

Christian: That is not likely, said the other. Look, does it not run along beside the way? So Hopeful, persuaded by his fellow, followed him over the stile. When they had gone over and got onto the path, they found it very easy on their feet; and also, looking ahead, they saw a man walking as they were, and his name was Vain-Confidence. So they called after him and asked him where that way led. He said, To the Celestial Gate. Look, said Christian, did I not tell you so? This shows you we are right. So they followed, and he went ahead of them. But then night came on, and it grew very dark, so that those who were behind lost sight of the one who went ahead.

So the one who went ahead (Vain-Confidence by name), not seeing the way in front of him, fell into a deep pit, which the prince of those grounds had made there on purpose to catch vainglorious fools in, and he was dashed to pieces by his fall. Isa 9:16.

Now Christian and his fellow heard him fall. So they called out to know what was the matter, but there was no one to answer; they only heard a groaning. Then Hopeful said, Where are we now? Then his fellow was silent, suspecting that he had led him out of the way; and now it began to rain, and thunder, and lighten in a most dreadful way, and the water rose fast.

Then Hopeful groaned to himself, saying, Oh, if only I had kept on my way!

Christian: Who would have thought that this path would lead us out of the way?

Hopeful: I was afraid of it from the very first, and that is why I gave you that gentle warning. I would have spoken more plainly, but you are older than I am.

Christian: Good brother, do not be offended; I am sorry I have brought you out of the way, and that I have put you in such imminent danger. Please, my brother, forgive me; I did not do it with any evil intent.

Hopeful: Take comfort, my brother, for I forgive you; and believe, too, that this will be for our good.

Christian: I am glad I have a merciful brother with me; but we must not stand here; let us try to go back again.

Hopeful: But, good brother, let me go in front.

Christian: No, if you please, let me go first, so that if there is any danger, I may be the first to meet it, because it is my fault that we have both gone out of the way.

Hopeful: No, said Hopeful, you shall not go first, for your mind is troubled, and it may lead you out of the way again. Then, to encourage them, they heard the voice of someone saying, “Keep the highway in mind, the road you have traveled. Return.” Jer 31:21. But by this time the waters had risen high, which made going back very dangerous. (Then I thought that it is easier to go out of the way when we are in it than to get into it when we are out.) Still they ventured to go back; but it was so dark, and the flood was so high, that on their way back they nearly drowned nine or ten times.

Nor could they, with all the skill they had, get back to the stile that night. So at last, coming on a little shelter, they sat down there until daybreak; but being weary, they fell asleep. Now not far from the place where they lay there was a castle called Doubting Castle, whose owner was Giant Despair, and it was on his grounds that they were now sleeping. So the giant, getting up early in the morning and walking up and down in his fields, caught Christian and Hopeful asleep on his grounds. Then in a grim and surly voice he told them to wake up, and asked them where they came from and what they were doing on his grounds. They told him they were pilgrims, and that they had lost their way. Then the giant said, You have trespassed on me this night by trampling over and lying on my grounds, and so you must come along with me. So they were forced to go, because he was stronger than they were. They also had little to say, for they knew they were in the wrong. So the giant drove them before him and put them into his castle, into a very dark dungeon, filthy and stinking to the spirits of these two men. Here, then, they lay from Wednesday morning until Saturday night, without one bit of bread or drop of drink, or light, or anyone to ask how they were doing; so they were in a bad way here, and far from friends and acquaintances. Ps 88:18. Now in this place Christian had double sorrow, because it was through his rash advice that they had been brought into this distress.

Now Giant Despair had a wife, and her name was Diffidence. So when he had gone to bed, he told his wife what he had done, namely, that he had taken a couple of prisoners and thrown them into his dungeon for trespassing on his grounds. Then he also asked her what he had better do to them next. So she asked him who they were, where they came from, and where they were going, and he told her. Then she advised him that when he got up in the morning he should beat them without mercy. So when he gets up, he takes a brutal crab-tree cudgel and goes down into the dungeon to them, and there he first starts berating them as if they were dogs, although they never gave him one offensive word. Then he falls on them and beats them fearfully, so badly that they could not help themselves, or even turn over on the floor. This done, he withdraws and leaves them there to lament their misery and to mourn under their distress; so all that day they spent their time in nothing but sighs and bitter lamentations. The next night she, talking further with her husband about them, and learning that they were still alive, advised him to urge them to do away with themselves. So when morning had come, he goes to them in a surly manner, as before, and seeing that they were very sore from the beating he had given them the day before, he told them that since they were never likely to get out of that place, their only way would be to make an end of themselves at once, with a knife, a noose, or poison. Why, he said, should you choose to live, when living brings so much bitterness? But they begged him to let them go. At that he gave them an ugly look, and rushing at them, would no doubt have made an end of them himself, except that he fell into one of his fits (for in sunny weather he sometimes fell into fits) and lost the use of his hands for a while; so he withdrew, and left them as before to think over what to do. Then the prisoners talked it over between themselves, whether it was best to take his advice or not; and this is how they began to talk:

Christian: Brother, said Christian, what shall we do? The life we are living now is miserable. For my part, I do not know whether it is better to live like this or to die at once. My soul chooses strangling rather than life, and the grave would be easier for me than this dungeon. Job 7:15. Shall we do as the giant says?

Hopeful: Our present condition is indeed dreadful, and death would be far more welcome to me than to stay like this forever; but still, let us consider: the Lord of the country we are going to has said, “You shall not murder,” no, not even another man’s person; much more, then, are we forbidden to take the giant’s advice and kill ourselves. Besides, a man who kills another can only commit murder on his body; but for a man to kill himself is to kill body and soul at once. And what is more, my brother, you talk of ease in the grave; but have you forgotten the hell where murderers certainly go? For “eternal life does not reside in a murderer,” etc. And let us consider again that all the law is not in Giant Despair’s hand: others, as far as I can understand, have been taken by him as well as we have, and yet have escaped out of his hands. Who knows whether God, who made the world, may cause Giant Despair to die; or whether at some time or other he may forget to lock us in; or whether he may soon have another of his fits in front of us and lose the use of his limbs? And if that should ever happen again, for my part, I am resolved to pluck up the heart of a man and try my utmost to get out from under his hand. I was a fool not to try to do it before. But all the same, my brother, let us be patient and endure a while: the time may come that brings us a happy release; but let us not be our own murderers. With these words Hopeful calmed his brother’s mind for the present; so they stayed together in the dark that day, in their sad and miserable condition.

Well, toward evening the giant goes down into the dungeon again, to see if his prisoners had taken his advice. But when he got there he found them alive; and truly, alive was all they were; for now, what with the lack of bread and water, and the wounds they had received when he beat them, they could do little but breathe. But, as I say, he found them alive; at which he flew into a terrible rage, and told them that, since they had disobeyed his advice, it would be worse for them than if they had never been born.

At this they trembled greatly, and I think that Christian fainted; but when he had come to himself a little, they took up their talk again about the giant’s advice, and whether they had better take it after all. Now Christian again seemed to be for doing it; but Hopeful made his second reply as follows:

Hopeful: My brother, he said, do you not remember how brave you have been before now? Apollyon could not crush you, nor could all that you heard, or saw, or felt in the Valley of the Shadow of Death. What hardship, terror, and bewilderment you have already gone through! And are you now nothing but fears? You see that I am in the dungeon with you, a far weaker man by nature than you are. This giant has also wounded me as well as you, and has cut off the bread and water from my mouth too, and with you I mourn without the light. But let us show a little more patience. Remember how you stood like a man at Vanity Fair, and were not afraid of the chain or the cage, or even of a bloody death. So let us (if only to avoid the shame that a Christian should never be found in) bear up with patience as well as we can.

Now when night had come again, and the giant and his wife were in bed, she asked him about the prisoners, and whether they had taken his advice. To this he replied, They are sturdy rogues; they would rather bear every hardship than do away with themselves. Then she said, Take them into the castle-yard tomorrow, and show them the bones and skulls of those you have already killed, and make them believe that before the week is out you will tear them in pieces, as you have done to their fellows before them.

So when morning had come, the giant goes to them again and takes them into the castle-yard, and shows them what his wife had told him to. These, he said, were pilgrims once, as you are, and they trespassed on my grounds, as you have done; and when I saw fit, I tore them in pieces; and within ten days I will do the same to you. Get down to your den again! And with that he beat them all the way there. So they lay there all day on Saturday in a pitiful state, as before. Now when night had come, and Mrs. Diffidence and her husband the giant had gone to bed, they began to talk about their prisoners again; and the old giant also wondered that he could not bring them to their end either by his blows or by his advice. And at that his wife replied, I fear, she said, that they are living in hope that someone will come to rescue them, or that they have lock picks on them, by which they hope to escape. Do you think so, my dear? said the giant; then I will search them in the morning.

Well, on Saturday, about midnight, they began to pray, and went on praying until almost daybreak.

Now, a little before it was day, good Christian, like a man half dazed, burst out with this passionate speech: What a fool I am, he said, to lie like this in a stinking dungeon, when I could just as well be walking free! I have a key in my bosom, called Promise, that will, I am persuaded, open any lock in Doubting Castle. Then Hopeful said, That is good news; good brother, pull it out of your bosom and try it.

Then Christian pulled it out of his bosom and began to try it on the dungeon door, and as he turned the key, the bolt slid back, and the door flew open with ease, and Christian and Hopeful both came out. Then he went to the outer door that leads into the castle-yard, and opened that door too with his key. After that he went to the iron gate, for that had to be opened too; and that lock was terribly hard to turn, yet the key did open it. Then they pushed the gate open to make their escape quickly; but as that gate opened, it creaked so loudly that it woke Giant Despair, who got up in haste to chase his prisoners, but felt his limbs fail him, for his fits came on him again, so that he could by no means go after them. Then they went on and came to the King’s highway, and so were safe, because they were out of his jurisdiction.

Now when they had gone over the stile, they began to work out between themselves what they should do at that stile to keep those who would come after them from falling into the hands of Giant Despair. So they agreed to put up a pillar there, and to engrave on its side these words: “Over this stile is the way to Doubting Castle, which is kept by Giant Despair, who despises the King of the Celestial country, and seeks to destroy his holy pilgrims.” Many who followed after therefore read what was written there, and escaped the danger. When this was done, they sang as follows:

““Out of the way we went, and then we found

What it was to tread upon forbidden ground:

And let those coming after us take care,

Lest heedlessness should make them, like us, fare;

Lest they, for trespassing, his prisoners are,

Whose castle’s Doubting, and whose name’s Despair.””

THE EIGHTH STAGE

Then they went on until they came to the Delectable Mountains, which belong to the Lord of the hill we spoke of before. So they went up into the mountains to see the gardens and orchards, the vineyards and fountains of water; and there they also drank and washed themselves, and ate freely of the vineyards. Now on the tops of these mountains there were shepherds feeding their flocks, and they were standing beside the highway. So the pilgrims went to them, and, leaning on their staffs (as weary pilgrims commonly do when they stop to talk with anyone by the way), they asked, Whose Delectable Mountains are these, and whose are the sheep that feed on them?

The Shepherds: These mountains are Immanuel’s land, and they are within sight of his city; and the sheep also are his, and he laid down his life for them. John 10:11, 15.

Christian: Is this the way to the Celestial City?

The Shepherds: You are right on your way.

Christian: How far is it from here?

The Shepherds: Too far for anyone but those who will truly get there.

Christian: Is the way safe or dangerous?

The Shepherds: Safe for those for whom it is meant to be safe; but transgressors shall fall in it. Hos 14:9.

Christian: Is there any relief in this place for pilgrims who are weary and faint on the way?

The Shepherds: The Lord of these mountains has given us a charge not to forget to show hospitality to strangers, Heb 13:2; so the good things of the place are yours.

I saw also in my dream that when the shepherds saw that they were travelers, they also put questions to them (which they answered as they had in other places), such as, Where have you come from? and, How did you get into the way? and, By what means have you persevered in it so far? For only a few of those who set out for this place ever show their faces on these mountains. But when the shepherds heard their answers, they were pleased with them, and they looked on them very lovingly and said, Welcome to the Delectable Mountains.

The shepherds, I say, whose names were Knowledge, Experience, Watchful, and Sincere, took them by the hand and led them to their tents, and had them share what was ready at the time. They also said, We would like you to stay here a while, to get to know us, and still more to refresh yourselves with the good things of these Delectable Mountains. Then the pilgrims told them that they were glad to stay. So they went to bed that night, because it was very late.

Then I saw in my dream that in the morning the shepherds called Christian and Hopeful to walk with them on the mountains. So they went out with them and walked a while, with a pleasant view on every side. Then the shepherds said to one another, Shall we show these pilgrims some wonders? So when they had decided to do it, they took them first to the top of a hill called Error, which was very steep on the far side, and told them to look down to the bottom. So Christian and Hopeful looked down, and at the bottom they saw several men dashed all to pieces by a fall they had had from the top. Then Christian said, What does this mean? The shepherds answered, Have you not heard of those who were led into error by listening to Hymenaeus and Philetus about the faith of the resurrection of the body? 2 Tim 2:17, 18. They answered, Yes. Then the shepherds said, Those you see lying dashed to pieces at the bottom of this mountain are the very men; and, as you see, they have lain unburied to this day, as an example to others to take care how they climb too high, or how they come too near the edge of this mountain.

Then I saw that they took them to the top of another mountain, whose name is Caution, and told them to look far off; and when they did, they saw, as they thought, several men walking up and down among the tombs that were there; and they could tell that the men were blind, because they sometimes stumbled over the tombs, and because they could not find their way out from among them. Then Christian said, What does this mean?

The shepherds then answered, Did you not see, a little below these mountains, a stile that led into a meadow, on the left side of this way? They answered, Yes. Then the shepherds said, From that stile a path runs that leads straight to Doubting Castle, which is kept by Giant Despair; and these men (pointing to them among the tombs) once came on pilgrimage, as you are doing now, until they came to that same stile. And because the right way was rough in that place, they chose to leave it for that meadow, and there they were taken by Giant Despair and thrown into Doubting Castle; and after they had been kept in the dungeon a while, he at last put out their eyes and led them among those tombs, where he has left them to wander to this very day, so that the saying of the wise man might be fulfilled, “The man who wanders from the way of understanding will remain in the assembly of the dead.” Prov 21:16. Then Christian and Hopeful looked at one another, with tears streaming down, but still said nothing to the shepherds.

Then I saw in my dream that the shepherds took them to another place, down in a hollow, where there was a door in the side of a hill; and they opened the door and told them to look in. So they looked in, and saw that inside it was very dark and smoky; they also thought they heard a rumbling noise there, as of fire, and the cry of some who were in torment, and that they smelled the smell of brimstone. Then Christian said, What does this mean? The shepherds told them, This is a by-way to hell, a way that hypocrites go in by; namely, those who sell their birthright, like Esau; those who sell their Master, like Judas; those who blaspheme the Gospel, like Alexander; and those who lie and deceive, like Ananias and his wife Sapphira.

Then Hopeful said to the shepherds, I take it that every one of these had a show of pilgrimage about them, as we have now; did they not?

The Shepherds: Yes, and kept it up a long time, too.

Hopeful: How far might they have gone on pilgrimage in their day, since they were, for all that, miserably cast away?

The Shepherds: Some farther, and some not as far as these mountains.

Then the pilgrims said to one another, We need to cry to the Strong for strength.

The Shepherds: Yes, and you will need to use it when you have it, too.

By this time the pilgrims wanted to go on, and the shepherds wanted them to; so they walked together toward the end of the mountains. Then the shepherds said to one another, Let us show the pilgrims the gates of the Celestial City here, if they have the skill to look through our spyglass. The pilgrims lovingly accepted the offer; so the shepherds took them to the top of a high hill called Clear, and gave them the spyglass to look through.

Then they tried to look; but the memory of that last thing the shepherds had shown them made their hands shake, and because of this they could not hold the spyglass steady to look through it; yet they thought they saw something like the gate, and also some of the glory of the place. Then they went away and sang,

““Thus by the shepherds secrets are revealed,

Which from all other men are kept concealed:

Come to the shepherds then, if you would see

Things deep, things hidden, things of mystery.””

When they were about to leave, one of the shepherds gave them directions for the way. Another of them told them to beware of the Flatterer. The third told them to take care not to sleep on Enchanted Ground. And the fourth wished them Godspeed. So I awoke from my dream.

THE NINTH STAGE

And I slept, and dreamed again, and saw the same two pilgrims going down the mountains along the highway towards the city. Now a little below these mountains, on the left, lies the country of Conceit; and from that country a little crooked lane comes into the way in which the pilgrims walked. Here, then, they met a very brisk lad who came out of that country, and his name was Ignorance. So Christian asked him what parts he came from, and where he was going.

Ignorance: Sir, I was born in the country that lies over there, a little to the left, and I am going to the Celestial City.

Christian: But how do you expect to get in at the gate? You may find some difficulty there.

Ignorance: As other good people do, he said.

Christian: But what do you have to show at that gate, so that the gate will be opened to you?

Ignorance: I know my Lord’s will, and have lived a good life; I pay every man what is his; I pray, fast, pay tithes, and give alms, and I have left my country for the place I am going to.

Christian: But you did not come in at the wicket-gate that is at the head of this way; you came in here through that same crooked lane. And so I fear that, whatever you may think of yourself, when the day of reckoning comes, you will have it laid to your charge that you are a thief and a robber, instead of being let into the city.

Ignorance: Gentlemen, you+ are complete strangers to me; I do not know you+. Be content to follow the religion of your+ country, and I will follow the religion of mine. I hope all will be well. And as for the gate you+ talk of, all the world knows that it is a long way from our country. I cannot think that any man in all our parts so much as knows the way to it; nor do they need to care whether they do or not, since we have, as you+ see, a fine, pleasant, green lane that comes down from our country, the shortest way into the way.

When Christian saw that the man was wise in his own conceit, he whispered to Hopeful, “There is more hope for a fool than for him.” Prov 26:12. And he went on, “Even as the fool walks along the way, his sense is lacking, and he shows everyone that he is a fool.” Eccl 10:3. What, shall we talk with him further, or go on ahead of him for now, and leave him to think over what he has already heard, and then stop and wait for him later, and see if little by little we can do him any good? Then Hopeful said,

““Let Ignorance a little while now muse

On what is said, and let him not refuse

Good counsel to embrace, lest he remain

Still ignorant of what’s the greatest gain.

God says, those who no understanding have,

(Although he made them,) them he will not save.””

Hopeful: He added further, I do not think it is good to tell him everything at once; let us pass him by, if you are willing, and talk to him later, as far as he is able to bear it.

So they both went on, and Ignorance came after them. Now when they had passed him a little way, they entered a very dark lane, where they met a man whom seven devils had bound with seven strong cords, and they were carrying him back to the door that they saw on the side of the hill. Matt 12:45; Prov 5:22. Now good Christian began to tremble, and so did Hopeful, his companion; yet, as the devils led the man away, Christian looked to see if he knew him, and he thought it might be one Turn-away, who lived in the town of Apostasy. But he did not see his face clearly, for the man hung his head like a thief who has been caught. When he had gone past, Hopeful looked after him and saw on his back a paper with this inscription: “Wanton professing Christian, and damnable apostate.”

Then Christian said to his companion, Now I remember something I was told about a thing that happened to a good man around here. The man’s name was Little-Faith, but he was a good man, and he lived in the town of Sincere. This is what happened. At the entrance of this passage, a lane comes down from Broadway-gate called Dead-Man’s lane, so called because of the murders that are commonly done there; and this Little-Faith, going on pilgrimage as we are now, happened to sit down there and sleep. Now at that time three sturdy rogues happened to come down the lane from Broadway-gate, and their names were Faint-Heart, Mistrust, and Guilt, three brothers; and when they spotted Little-Faith where he was, they came galloping up at full speed. Now the good man had just woken from his sleep, and was getting up to go on his journey. So they all came up to him, and with threatening words ordered him to stand still. At this Little-Faith turned as white as a sheet, and had no strength either to fight or to flee. Then Faint-Heart said, Hand over your purse. But as he made no haste to do it (for he was unwilling to lose his money), Mistrust ran up to him, thrust his hand into his pocket, and pulled out a bag of silver. Then Little-Faith cried out, Thieves, thieves! At that, Guilt, with a great club that was in his hand, struck Little-Faith on the head, and with that blow knocked him flat to the ground, where he lay bleeding like one who would bleed to death. All this while the thieves stood by. But at last, hearing that some people were coming along the road, and fearing that it might be one Great-Grace, who lives in the town of Good-Confidence, they took to their heels and left this good man to fend for himself. Now after a while Little-Faith came to himself, and getting up, managed to scramble on his way. That was the story.

Hopeful: But did they take from him everything he had?

Christian: No; they never ransacked the place where his jewels were, so he still kept those. But, as I was told, the good man was much distressed by his loss, for the thieves got most of his spending-money. What they did not get, as I said, were his jewels; he also had a little loose change left, but hardly enough to bring him to his journey’s end. Indeed (if I was not misinformed), he was forced to beg as he went, to keep himself alive, for he was not allowed to sell his jewels; but beg and do what he could, he went, as we say, with many a hungry belly for most of the rest of the way. 1 Pet 4:18.

Hopeful: But is it not a wonder that they did not get his certificate from him, by which he was to be admitted at the Celestial Gate?

Christian: It is a wonder; but they did not get that, though it was not through any skill of his that they missed it; for he was so dismayed by their attack that he had neither the strength nor the skill to hide anything. So it was more by good providence than by his own effort that they missed that good thing. 2 Tim 1:12–14; 2 Pet 2:9.

Hopeful: But it must surely be a comfort to him that they did not get this jewel from him.

Christian: It might have been a great comfort to him, had he used it as he should; but those who told me the story said that he made very little use of it all the rest of the way, and that because of the dismay he felt at their taking away his money. In fact, he forgot it for a great part of the rest of his journey; and besides, whenever it came into his mind and he began to be comforted by it, fresh thoughts of his loss would come over him again, and these thoughts would swallow up everything.

Hopeful: Alas, poor man, this must have been a great grief to him.

Christian: Grief? Yes, a grief indeed! Would it not have been so to any of us, had we been treated as he was, robbed and wounded too, and that in a strange place, as he was? It is a wonder he did not die of grief, poor soul. I was told that he scattered almost all the rest of the way with nothing but sad and bitter complaints; telling everyone who overtook him, or whom he overtook on the way as he went, where he was robbed, and how; who it was that did it, and what he had lost; how he was wounded, and that he barely escaped with his life.

Hopeful: But it is a wonder that his need did not drive him to sell or pawn some of his jewels, so that he might have something to sustain himself with on his journey.

Christian: You talk like one who still has the shell on his head to this very day. Why should he pawn them? Or to whom should he sell them? In all that country where he was robbed, his jewels were thought nothing of; nor did he need the relief that could be given him from there. Besides, had his jewels been missing at the gate of the Celestial City, he would have been (and he knew this well enough) shut out from an inheritance there, and that would have been worse to him than the appearance and villainy of ten thousand thieves.

Hopeful: Why are you so sharp, my brother? Esau sold his birthright, and that for a mess of pottage, Heb 12:16; and that birthright was his greatest jewel. And if he did, why might not Little-Faith do so too?

Christian: Esau did indeed sell his birthright, and so do many others, and by doing so they shut themselves out from the chief blessing, as that wretch did too. But you must make a distinction between Esau and Little-Faith, and also between their states. Esau’s birthright was a type; but Little-Faith’s jewels were not. Esau’s belly was his god; but Little-Faith’s belly was not. Esau’s need lay in his fleshly appetite; Little-Faith’s did not. Besides, Esau could see no further than the fulfilling of his lusts: For I am about to die, he said, and what good will this birthright do me? Gen 25:32. But Little-Faith, though it was his lot to have only a little faith, was kept by his little faith from such extravagances, and made to see and prize his jewels too much to sell them, as Esau did his birthright. You do not read anywhere that Esau had faith, no, not even a little; so it is no wonder, where the flesh alone holds sway (as it will in the man who has no faith to resist it), if he sells his birthright and his soul and all, and that to the devil of hell; for it is with such men as it is with the donkey, who in her heat cannot be turned away, Jer 2:24: when their minds are set on their lusts, they will have them, whatever they cost. But Little-Faith was of another disposition; his mind was on things divine; his livelihood was in things that were spiritual, and from above. So to what end should a man of such a disposition sell his jewels (had there been anyone who would have bought them) to fill his mind with empty things? Will a man give a penny to fill his belly with hay? Or can you persuade the turtle-dove to live on carrion, like the crow? Though faithless people can, for carnal lusts, pawn, or mortgage, or sell what they have, and themselves outright into the bargain, yet those who have faith, saving faith, though only a little of it, cannot do so. Here, then, my brother, is your mistake.

Hopeful: I admit it; but still, your severe rebuke had almost made me angry.

Christian: Why, I only compared you to some of the birds of the brisker sort, which will run to and fro on untrodden paths with the shell still on their heads. But let that pass, and consider the matter we are discussing, and all will be well between you and me.

Hopeful: But, Christian, I am persuaded in my heart that these three fellows are nothing but a pack of cowards. Would they otherwise have run as they did, do you think, at the noise of someone coming along the road? Why did Little-Faith not pluck up a greater heart? I think he might have stood one brush with them, and given in when there was no help for it.

Christian: That they are cowards many have said, but few have found it so in the time of trial. As for a great heart, Little-Faith had none; and I can see from what you say, my brother, that had you been the man concerned, you would stand only one brush, and then give in. And truly, since this is how high your courage runs now that they are far away from us, should they appear to you as they did to him, they might give you second thoughts.

But consider again that they are only journeymen thieves; they serve under the king of the bottomless pit, who, if need be, will come to their aid himself, and his voice is like the roaring of a lion. 1 Pet 5:8. I myself have been attacked as this Little-Faith was, and I found it a terrible thing. These three villains set on me, and as I began like a Christian to resist, they gave just one call, and in came their master. I would, as the saying goes, have given my life for a penny, but, as God would have it, I was clothed in tested armor. Yes, and even so, though I was armed like that, I found it hard work to acquit myself like a man. No man can tell what we face in that combat but he who has been in the battle himself.

Hopeful: Well, but they ran, you see, when they merely supposed that one Great-Grace was on the road.

Christian: True, they have often fled, both they and their master, when Great-Grace has merely appeared; and no wonder, for he is the King’s champion. But I suppose you will make some distinction between Little-Faith and the King’s champion. Not all the King’s subjects are his champions; nor can they, when tested, do such feats of war as he does. Is it right to think that a little child could handle Goliath as David did? Or that there should be the strength of an ox in a wren? Some are strong, some are weak; some have great faith, some have little. This man was one of the weak, and so he went to the wall.

Hopeful: I wish it had been Great-Grace, for their sakes.

Christian: If it had been he, he might have had his hands full. For I must tell you that, though Great-Grace is excellent with his weapons, and has done and can do well enough with them so long as he keeps them at sword’s point, yet if they get within his guard, even Faint-Heart, Mistrust, or the other, they will almost certainly knock him off his feet. And when a man is down, you know, what can he do?

Whoever looks closely at Great-Grace’s face will see scars and cuts there that will easily prove what I say. Indeed, I once heard that he said (and that when he was in the combat), We despaired even of life. How these sturdy rogues and their fellows made David groan, mourn, and roar! Yes, Heman, Ps 88, and Hezekiah too, though champions in their day, were forced to rouse themselves when these attacked them; and even so, they had their coats soundly dusted by them. Peter once wanted to go and try what he could do; but though some say of him that he is the prince of the apostles, they handled him so that in the end they made him afraid of a mere girl.

Besides, their king comes at their whistle; he is never out of hearing; and if at any time they are getting the worst of it, he comes in to help them if he can; and of him it is said, “The sword that reaches him has no effect, nor does the spear or dart or arrow. He regards iron as straw and bronze as rotten wood. No arrow can make him flee; slingstones become like chaff to him. A club is regarded as straw, and he laughs at the sound of the lance.” Job 41:26–29. What can a man do in such a case? It is true, if a man could have Job’s horse at every turn, and had the skill and courage to ride him, he might do notable things. “For his neck is adorned with a mane; he leaps like a locust, striking terror with his proud snorting. He paws in the valley and rejoices in his strength; he charges into battle. He laughs at fear, frightened of nothing; he does not turn back from the sword. A quiver rattles at his side, along with a flashing spear and lance. Trembling with excitement, he devours the distance; he cannot stand still when the ram’s horn sounds. At the blast of the horn, he snorts with fervor. He catches the scent of battle from afar—the shouts of captains and the cry of war.” Job 39:19–25.

But as for foot soldiers such as you and I are, let us never wish to meet an enemy, nor boast as if we could do better when we hear of others who have been beaten, nor be tickled by the thought of our own manhood; for such people commonly come off worst when tested. Witness Peter, whom I mentioned before: he would swagger, yes, he would; he would, as his vain mind prompted him to say, do better and stand up more for his Master than all men; but who was so beaten and run down by those villains as he?

So when we hear that such robberies are done on the King’s highway, there are two things we ought to do.

1. To go out armed, and be sure to take a shield with us; for it was for lack of a shield that he who laid on so vigorously at Leviathan could not make him yield; for indeed, if that is lacking, he does not fear us at all. That is why he who had skill in this has said, “Above all, take up the shield of faith, with which you+ can quench all the fiery darts of the evil one.” Eph 6:16.

2. It is good also that we ask the King for an escort, yes, that he will go with us himself. This made David rejoice when he was in the Valley of the Shadow of Death; and Moses would rather have died where he stood than go one step without his God. Exod 33:15.

O my brother, if he will only go along with us, why should we be afraid of tens of thousands who set themselves against us? Ps 3:5–8; 27:1–3. But without him, the proud helpers fall under the slain. Isa 10:4.

For my part, I have been in the fray before now; and though (through the goodness of Him who is best) I am alive, as you see, yet I cannot boast of any manhood.
