I will be glad if I meet no more such onslaughts; though I fear we are not yet past all danger. However, since the lion and the bear have not yet devoured me, I hope God will also deliver us from the next uncircumcised Philistine. Then Christian sang,

““Poor Little-Faith! Have you been among the thieves?

And robbed? Remember this, whoever believes,

And get more faith; then you will victors be

Over ten thousand—else hardly over three.””

So they went on, and Ignorance followed. They went on until they came to a place where they saw another way join their way, and it seemed to lie as straight as the way they ought to go; and here they did not know which of the two to take, for both seemed straight before them. So here they stood still to think it over. And as they were thinking about the way, a man black of flesh, but covered with a very light robe, came up to them and asked them why they were standing there. They answered that they were going to the Celestial City, but did not know which of these ways to take. “Follow me,” said the man, “that is where I am going.” So they followed him in the way that had just come into the road, which little by little turned, and turned them so far from the city they wanted to go to that in a short time their faces were turned away from it; yet they followed him. But soon, before they were aware of it, he led them both into the middle of a net, in which they were both so entangled that they did not know what to do; and with that the white robe fell off the black man’s back. Then they saw where they were. So there they lay crying for some time, for they could not get themselves out.

Christian: Then Christian said to his companion, Now I see that I was mistaken. Did the shepherds not tell us to beware of the Flatterer? As the wise man says, so we have found it today: “A man who flatters his neighbor spreads a net for his feet.” Prov 29:5.

Hopeful: They also gave us a note of directions about the way, so that we might find it more surely; but we have forgotten to read that too, and have not kept ourselves from the paths of the destroyer. Here David was wiser than we are; for he says, “As for the deeds of men, by the word of Your lips I have kept myself from the paths of the destroyer.” Ps 17:4. So they lay in the net, lamenting their plight. At last they saw a Shining One coming towards them with a whip of small cords in his hand. When he had come to the place where they were, he asked them where they came from, and what they were doing there. They told him that they were poor pilgrims going to Zion, but had been led out of their way by a black man clothed in white, who told us, they said, to follow him, for he was going there too. Then the one with the whip said, It is Flatterer, a false apostle, who has transformed himself into an angel of light. Dan 11:32; 2 Cor 11:13, 14. So he tore the net and let the men out. Then he said to them, Follow me, so that I may set you on your way again. So he led them back to the way they had left to follow the Flatterer. Then he asked them, Where did you sleep last night? They said, With the shepherds on the Delectable Mountains. He then asked them whether the shepherds had not given them a note of directions for the way. They answered, Yes. But when you were at a standstill, he said, did you not take out your note and read it? They answered, No. He asked them, Why? They said they forgot. He asked, moreover, whether the shepherds had not told them to beware of the Flatterer. They answered, Yes; but we did not imagine, they said, that this fine-spoken man was he. Rom 16:17, 18.

Then I saw in my dream that he commanded them to lie down; and when they did, he chastised them severely, to teach them the good way in which they should walk, Deut 25:2; 2 Chr 6:27; and as he chastised them, he said, “Those I love, I rebuke and chasten. Therefore be earnest and repent.” Rev 3:19. When this was done, he told them to go on their way, and to pay close attention to the shepherds’ other directions. So they thanked him for all his kindness, and went quietly along the right way, singing,

““Come here, you+ who walk along the way,

See how the pilgrims fare who go astray:

They have been caught in an entangling net,

Because good counsel they would lightly forget:

It’s true, they were rescued; but yet, you+ see,

They’re scourged to boot; let this your+ caution be.””

Now after a while they saw someone far off, coming quietly and alone along the highway to meet them. Then Christian said to his companion, There is a man over there with his back towards Zion, and he is coming to meet us.

Hopeful: I see him; let us be on our guard now, in case he turns out to be a Flatterer too. So he drew nearer and nearer, and at last came up to them. His name was Atheist, and he asked them where they were going.

Christian: We are going to Mount Zion.

Then Atheist burst into a great fit of laughter.

Christian: Why are you laughing?

Atheist: I laugh to see what ignorant people you are, to take on so tedious a journey, when you are likely to get nothing but your travel for your pains.

Christian: Why, man, do you think we will not be received?

Atheist: Received! There is no such place as you dream of in all this world.

Christian: But there is in the world to come.

Atheist: When I was at home in my own country I heard what you now affirm, and having heard it I went out to see, and I have been looking for this city for twenty years, but I find no more of it than I did the first day I set out. Eccl 10:15; Jer 17:15.

Christian: We have both heard, and we believe, that there is such a place to be found.

Atheist: If I had not believed, when I was at home, I would not have come this far to look; but finding none (and yet I would have found it, had there been such a place to be found, for I have gone farther than you to look for it), I am going back again, and will try to refresh myself with the things that I then threw away in hope of what I now see does not exist.

Christian: Then Christian said to Hopeful his companion, Is what this man has said true?

Hopeful: Be careful; he is one of the Flatterers. Remember what it has already cost us once to listen to fellows of that kind. What! No Mount Zion? Did we not see the gate of the city from the Delectable Mountains? Also, are we not now to walk by faith? 2 Cor 5:7.

Let us go on, in case the man with the whip overtakes us again. You should have taught me the lesson that I will now sound in your ears: “Cease, my son, to hear the instruction that causes you to stray from the words of knowledge.” Prov 19:27. I say, my brother, cease to hear him, and let us believe to the saving of the soul.

Christian: My brother, I did not put the question to you because I doubted the truth of our belief myself, but to test you, and to draw from you a fruit of the honesty of your heart. As for this man, I know that he is blinded by the god of this world. Let us go on, you and I, knowing that we have belief in the truth, and no lie is of the truth. 1 John 2:21.

Hopeful: Now I rejoice in hope of the glory of God. So they turned away from the man; and he, laughing at them, went his way.

I then saw in my dream that they went on until they came into a certain country whose air naturally tended to make one drowsy, if he came into it as a stranger. And here Hopeful began to feel very dull and heavy with sleep; so he said to Christian, I am now growing so drowsy that I can hardly keep my eyes open; let us lie down here and take one nap.

Christian: By no means, the other said; for if we sleep, we may never wake again.

Hopeful: Why, my brother? Sleep is sweet to the laboring man; we may be refreshed if we take a nap.

Christian: Don’t you remember that one of the shepherds told us to beware of the Enchanted Ground? He meant by that that we should beware of sleeping; so “let us not sleep as the others do, but let us remain awake and sober.” 1 Thess 5:6.

Hopeful: I admit I was at fault; and had I been here alone, I would have run the risk of death by sleeping. I see that what the wise man says is true: “Two are better than one.” Eccl 4:9. Until now your company has been a mercy to me; and you will have a good reward for your labor.

Christian: Now, then, Christian said, to keep off drowsiness in this place, let us fall into some good conversation.

Hopeful: With all my heart, the other said.

Christian: Where shall we begin?

Hopeful: Where God began with us. But you begin, if you would.

Christian: First I will sing you this song:

““When saints grow sleepy, let them come and gather,

And hear how these two pilgrims talk together;

Yes, by all means, let them learn from them, likewise

Thus to keep open their drowsy, slumb’ring eyes.

Saints’ fellowship, if it is managed well,

Keeps them awake, and that in spite of hell.””

Then Christian began, and said, I will ask you a question. How did you first come to think of doing what you are doing now?

Hopeful: Do you mean, how did I first come to seek the good of my soul?

Christian: Yes, that is what I mean.

Hopeful: For a long time I went on delighting in the things that were seen and sold at our fair; things which, I now believe, would have drowned me in perdition and destruction, had I gone on in them.

Christian: What things were they?

Hopeful: All the treasures and riches of the world. I also took great delight in carousing, reveling, drinking, swearing, lying, uncleanness, Sabbath-breaking, and everything else that tended to destroy the soul. But at last I found, by hearing and thinking about divine things, which indeed I heard from you, and also from beloved Faithful, who was put to death for his faith and good living in Vanity Fair, that the end of these things is death, Rom 6:21–23; and that because of these things the wrath of God comes on the children of disobedience. Eph 5:6.

Christian: And did you at once fall under the power of this conviction?

Hopeful: No, I was not willing to know at once the evil of sin, or the damnation that follows on committing it; but when my mind first began to be shaken by the word, I tried to shut my eyes against its light.

Christian: But what was the reason you treated the first workings of God’s blessed Spirit on you like this?

Hopeful: The causes were: 1. I did not know that this was the work of God on me. I never thought that God begins the conversion of a sinner by first awakening him to his sin. 2. Sin was still very sweet to my flesh, and I was unwilling to leave it. 3. I did not know how to part with my old companions; their company and doings were so pleasing to me. 4. The hours when convictions of sin were on me were such troubling and such terrifying hours that I could not bear, no, not even the memory of them on my heart.

Christian: Then, as it seems, at times you got rid of your trouble?

Hopeful: Yes, truly, but it would come back into my mind; and then I would be as bad as I was before, indeed worse.

Christian: Why, what was it that brought your sins to mind again?

Hopeful: Many things, such as:

1. If I merely met a good man in the street; or,

2. If I heard anyone read from the Bible; or,

3. If my head began to ache; or,

4. If I was told that some of my neighbors were sick; or,

5. If I heard the bell toll for any who had died; or,

6. If I thought of dying myself; or,

7. If I heard that sudden death had come to others.

8. But especially when I thought of myself, that I must soon come to judgment.

Christian: And could you ever easily get rid of the guilt of sin, when it came on you in any of these ways?

Hopeful: No, not I; for then they got a tighter hold on my conscience; and then, if I so much as thought of going back to sin (though my mind was turned against it), it would be a double torment to me.

Christian: And what did you do then?

Hopeful: I thought I must try to mend my life; for otherwise, I thought, I am sure to be damned.

Christian: And did you try to mend it?

Hopeful: Yes, and I fled not only from my sins but from sinful company too, and took up religious duties, such as praying, reading, weeping for sin, speaking the truth to my neighbors, etc. These things I did, with many others, too many to tell here.

Christian: And did you think all was well with you then?

Hopeful: Yes, for a while; but in the end my trouble came tumbling down on me again, and that in spite of all my reformations.

Christian: How did that come about, since you were now reformed?

Hopeful: There were several things that brought it on me, especially such sayings as these: “All our righteousnesses are like filthy rags.” Isa 64:6. “By the works of the law no flesh will be justified.” Gal 2:16. “When you+ have done all these things, say, ‘We are unprofitable,’” Luke 17:10; with many more like them. From these I began to reason with myself like this: If all my righteousnesses are like filthy rags; if by the deeds of the law no man can be justified; and if, when we have done all, we are still unprofitable, then it is mere folly to think of heaven by the law. I also thought this: If a man runs up a debt of a hundred pounds with the shopkeeper, and after that pays for everything he buys; yet if his old debt still stands in the book, not crossed out, the shopkeeper may sue him for it and throw him into prison until he pays the debt.

Christian: Well, and how did you apply this to yourself?

Hopeful: Why, I thought like this to myself: I have run a long way into God’s book by my sins, and my reforming now will not pay off that debt; so I should still be thinking, for all my present improvements, But how shall I be freed from the damnation I brought myself in danger of by my former transgressions?

Christian: A very good application; but please go on.

Hopeful: Another thing that has troubled me ever since my recent improvements is that if I look closely at the best of what I do now, I still see sin, new sin, mixing itself with the best of what I do. So now I am forced to conclude that, in spite of my former foolish fancies about myself and my duties, I have committed enough sin in one day to send me to hell, even if my former life had been faultless.

Christian: And what did you do then?

Hopeful: Do! I did not know what to do, until I opened my mind to Faithful, for he and I knew each other well. And he told me that unless I could obtain the righteousness of a man who had never sinned, neither my own righteousness nor all the righteousness of the world could save me.

Christian: And did you think he was telling the truth?

Hopeful: If he had told me that when I was pleased and satisfied with my own improvements, I would have called him a fool for his pains; but now, since I see my own weakness, and the sin that clings to my best performance, I have been forced to agree with him.

Christian: But when he first suggested it to you, did you think that such a man could be found, of whom it could rightly be said that he never committed sin?

Hopeful: I must confess the words sounded strange at first; but after a little more talk and time with him, I was fully convinced of it.

Christian: And did you ask him who this man was, and how you must be justified by him?

Hopeful: Yes, and he told me it was the Lord Jesus, who dwells at the right hand of the Most High. Heb 10:12–21. And this, he said, is how you must be justified by him: by trusting in what he has done by himself in the days of his flesh, and suffered when he hung on the tree. Rom 4:5; Col 1:14; 1 Pet 1:19. I asked him further how that man’s righteousness could have such efficacy as to justify another before God. And he told me he was the mighty God, and did what he did, and died the death too, not for himself but for me; and that his doings, and their worthiness, would be imputed to me if I believed in him.

Christian: And what did you do then?

Hopeful: I raised objections against believing, because I thought he was not willing to save me.

Christian: And what did Faithful say to you then?

Hopeful: He told me to go to him and see. Then I said it would be presumption. He said, No, for I was invited to come. Matt 11:28. Then he gave me a book of Jesus’ composing, to encourage me to come more freely; and he said of that book that every jot and tittle of it stood firmer than heaven and earth. Matt 24:35. Then I asked him what I must do when I came; and he told me I must plead on my knees, Ps 95:6; Dan 6:10, with all my heart and soul, Jer 29:12, 13, asking the Father to reveal him to me. Then I asked him further how I must make my prayers to him; and he said, Go, and you will find him on a mercy-seat, where he sits all year round to give pardon and forgiveness to those who come. Exod 25:22; Lev 16:2; Num 7:89; Heb 4:16. I told him that I did not know what to say when I came; and he told me to say something like this: God be merciful to me a sinner, and make me know and believe in Jesus Christ; for I see that if it were not for his righteousness, or if I do not have faith in that righteousness, I am utterly cast away. Lord, I have heard that you are a merciful God, and have ordained that your Son Jesus Christ should be the Savior of the world; and moreover, that you are willing to give him to such a poor sinner as I am—and I am a sinner indeed. Lord, take this opportunity, then, and magnify your grace in the salvation of my soul, through your Son Jesus Christ. Amen.

Christian: And did you do as you were told?

Hopeful: Yes, over, and over, and over.

Christian: And did the Father reveal the Son to you?

Hopeful: Not the first time, nor the second, nor the third, nor the fourth, nor the fifth; no, nor the sixth time either.

Christian: What did you do then?

Hopeful: What? Why, I did not know what to do.

Christian: Did you not think of giving up praying?

Hopeful: Yes; a hundred times twice over.

Christian: And what was the reason you did not?

Hopeful: I believed that what I had been told was true, namely, that without the righteousness of this Christ all the world could not save me; and so I thought to myself, If I give up, I die, and I can only die at the throne of grace. At the same time, this came into my mind: “Though it lingers, wait for it, since it will surely come and will not delay.” Hab 2:3. So I went on praying until the Father showed me his Son.

Christian: And how was he revealed to you?

Hopeful: I did not see him with my bodily eyes, but with the eyes of my understanding, Eph 1:18, 19; and this is how it was. One day I was very sad, sadder, I think, than at any other time in my life; and this sadness came from a fresh sight of the greatness and vileness of my sins. And as I was then expecting nothing but hell, and the everlasting damnation of my soul, suddenly, as I thought, I saw the Lord Jesus looking down on me from heaven, and saying, “Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved.” Acts 16:31.

But I replied, Lord, I am a great, a very great sinner; and he answered, “My grace is sufficient for you.” 2 Cor 12:9. Then I said, But, Lord, what is believing? And then I saw from that saying, “Whoever comes to Me will never hunger, and whoever believes in Me will never thirst,” John 6:35, that believing and coming were one and the same; and that he who came, that is, whose heart and affections ran out after salvation by Christ, did indeed believe in Christ. Then tears stood in my eyes, and I asked further, But, Lord, may such a great sinner as I am really be accepted by you, and be saved by you? And I heard him say, “And him who comes to Me I will by no means cast out.” John 6:37. Then I said, But how, Lord, must I think of you in my coming to you, so that my faith may rest rightly on you? Then he said, “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners.” 1 Tim 1:15. He is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes. Rom 10:4, and ch. 4. He died for our sins, and rose again for our justification. Rom 4:25. He loved us, and washed us from our sins in his own blood. Rev 1:5. He is the Mediator between God and us. 1 Tim 2:5. He always lives to make intercession for us. Heb 7:25. From all this I gathered that I must look for righteousness in his person, and for satisfaction for my sins by his blood; that what he did in obedience to his Father’s law, and in submitting to its penalty, was not for himself, but for him who will accept it for his salvation, and be thankful. And now my heart was full of joy, my eyes full of tears, and my affections running over with love to the name, people, and ways of Jesus Christ.

Christian: This was a revelation of Christ to your soul indeed. But tell me in particular what effect this had on your spirit.

Hopeful: It made me see that all the world, for all its righteousness, is in a state of condemnation. It made me see that God the Father, though he is just, can justly justify the sinner who comes. It made me deeply ashamed of the vileness of my former life, and confounded me with a sense of my own ignorance; for never before had a thought come into my heart that showed me the beauty of Jesus Christ like that. It made me love a holy life, and long to do something for the honor and glory of the name of the Lord Jesus. Yes, I thought that if I now had a thousand gallons of blood in my body, I could spill it all for the sake of the Lord Jesus.

I saw then in my dream that Hopeful looked back and saw Ignorance, whom they had left behind, coming after them. Look, he said to Christian, how far behind that youngster over there is lagging.

Christian: Yes, yes, I see him; he does not care for our company.

Hopeful: But I suppose it would not have hurt him to keep pace with us so far.

Christian: That is true; but I am sure he thinks otherwise.

Hopeful: I think he does; but all the same, let us wait for him. (So they did.)

Then Christian said to him, Come along, man; why do you lag so far behind?

Ignorance: I enjoy walking alone, a great deal more than walking in company, unless I like the company better.

Then Christian said to Hopeful (but quietly), Did I not tell you he did not care for our company? But all the same, he said, come up, and let us talk away the time in this lonely place. Then, turning to Ignorance, he said, Come, how are you? How do things stand between God and your soul now?

Ignorance: Well, I hope; for I am always full of good stirrings that come into my mind to comfort me as I walk.

Christian: What good stirrings? Please tell us.

Ignorance: Why, I think of God and heaven.

Christian: So do the devils and damned souls.

Ignorance: But I think of them, and desire them.

Christian: So do many who are never likely to get there. “The soul of the sluggard desires, and has nothing.” Prov 13:4.

Ignorance: But I think of them, and leave all for them.

Christian: That I doubt; for to leave all is a very hard thing; indeed, a harder thing than many realize. But why, or by what, are you persuaded that you have left all for God and heaven?

Ignorance: My heart tells me so.

Christian: The wise man says, “He who trusts in his own heart is a fool.” Prov 28:26.

Ignorance: That is spoken of an evil heart; but mine is a good one.

Christian: But how do you prove that?

Ignorance: It comforts me with hopes of heaven.

Christian: That may be through its deceitfulness; for a man’s heart may give him comfort in hoping for a thing he has as yet no ground to hope for.

Ignorance: But my heart and life agree; and so my hope is well-grounded.

Christian: Who told you that your heart and life agree?

Ignorance: My heart tells me so.

Christian: “Ask my fellow if I am a thief.” Your heart tells you so! Unless the word of God bears witness in this matter, no other testimony is of any value.

Ignorance: But is it not a good heart that has good thoughts? And is it not a good life that is lived according to God’s commandments?

Christian: Yes, that is a good heart that has good thoughts, and that is a good life that is lived according to God’s commandments; but it is one thing really to have these, and another only to think so.

Ignorance: Tell me, what do you count as good thoughts, and a life according to God’s commandments?

Christian: There are good thoughts of various kinds: some concerning ourselves, some God, some Christ, and some other things.

Ignorance: What are good thoughts concerning ourselves?

Christian: Such as agree with the word of God.

Ignorance: When do our thoughts of ourselves agree with the word of God?

Christian: When we pass the same judgment on ourselves that the word passes. To explain myself: the word of God says of people in their natural condition, “There is no one righteous, there is no one who does good.” It says also that “every inclination of the thoughts of man’s heart is altogether evil all the time.” Gen 6:5; Rom 3. And again, “Every inclination of man’s heart is evil from his youth.” Gen 8:21. Now, then, when we think this of ourselves, and feel it to be so, then our thoughts are good ones, because they agree with the word of God.

Ignorance: I will never believe that my heart is as bad as that.

Christian: Then you have never had one good thought about yourself in your life. But let me go on. As the word passes a judgment on our hearts, so it passes a judgment on our ways; and when the thoughts of our hearts and ways agree with the judgment that the word gives of both, then both are good, because they agree with it.

Ignorance: Explain what you mean.

Christian: Why, the word of God says that man’s ways are crooked ways, not good but perverse; it says that they are by nature out of the good way, that they have not known it. Ps 125:5; Prov 2:15; Rom 3:12. Now, when a man thinks this of his ways, I say, when he thinks it with feeling and with a humbled heart, then he has good thoughts of his own ways, because his thoughts now agree with the judgment of the word of God.

Ignorance: What are good thoughts concerning God?

Christian: Just as I have said concerning ourselves: when our thoughts of God agree with what the word says of him; and that is, when we think of his being and attributes as the word has taught, of which I cannot now speak more fully. But to speak of him in relation to us: we have right thoughts of God when we think that he knows us better than we know ourselves, and can see sin in us when and where we can see none in ourselves; when we think he knows our inmost thoughts, and that our heart, with all its depths, is always open to his eyes; also when we think that all our righteousness stinks in his nostrils, and that therefore he cannot bear to see us stand before him in any confidence, even in all our best performances.

Ignorance: Do you think I am such a fool as to think that God can see no further than I can, or that I would come to God in the best of my performances?

Christian: Why, what do you think in this matter?

Ignorance: Why, to be short, I think I must believe in Christ for justification.

Christian: What! You think you must believe in Christ, when you do not see your need of him! You see neither your original nor your actual infirmities, but have such an opinion of yourself, and of what you do, that it plainly shows you to be one who never saw the necessity of Christ’s personal righteousness to justify you before God. How, then, can you say, I believe in Christ?

Ignorance: I believe well enough, for all that.

Christian: How do you believe?

Ignorance: I believe that Christ died for sinners, and that I will be justified before God from the curse through his gracious acceptance of my obedience to his laws. Or put it this way: Christ makes my religious duties acceptable to his Father by virtue of his merits, and so I will be justified.

Christian: Let me give an answer to this confession of your faith.

1. You believe with a fanciful faith; for this faith is nowhere described in the word.

2. You believe with a false faith; because it takes justification from the personal righteousness of Christ and applies it to your own.

3. This faith makes Christ a justifier not of your person but of your actions, and of your person for your actions’ sake, which is false.

4. So this faith is deceitful, the kind that will leave you under wrath in the day of God Almighty. For true justifying faith, when the soul is made aware of its lost condition by the law, sets it fleeing for refuge to Christ’s righteousness (and this righteousness of his is not an act of grace by which he makes your obedience accepted with God for justification, but his personal obedience to the law, in doing and suffering for us what the law required of us). This righteousness, I say, true faith accepts; and the soul, covered under the fold of its robe, and presented by it as spotless before God, is accepted, and acquitted from condemnation.

Ignorance: What! Would you have us trust in what Christ has done in his own person without us? This notion would loosen the reins of our lust, and let us live as we please; for what does it matter how we live, if we may be justified from all by Christ’s personal righteousness, when we believe it?

Christian: Ignorance is your name, and as your name is, so are you: this very answer of yours proves what I say. You are ignorant of what justifying righteousness is, and just as ignorant of how to secure your soul from the heavy wrath of God through faith in it. Yes, you are also ignorant of the true effects of saving faith in this righteousness of Christ, which are to bow and win over the heart to God in Christ, to love his name, his word, ways, and people, and not as you ignorantly imagine.

Hopeful: Ask him whether he ever had Christ revealed to him from heaven.

Ignorance: What! You are a man for revelations! I do believe that what you and all the rest of you say about that matter is nothing but the fruit of crazed brains.

Hopeful: Why, man, Christ is so hidden in God from the natural understanding of the flesh that he cannot be savingly known by any man, unless God the Father reveals him to him.

Ignorance: That is your faith, but not mine; yet mine, I have no doubt, is as good as yours, though I do not have as many whims in my head as you.

Christian: Allow me to put in a word. You ought not to speak so lightly of this matter; for I will boldly affirm this, as my good companion has done, that no man can know Jesus Christ except by the revelation of the Father; yes, and faith too, by which the soul lays hold of Christ (if it is right), must be worked by the exceeding greatness of his mighty power, Matt 11:27; 1 Cor 12:3; Eph 1:17–19; and of the working of that faith, I see, poor Ignorance, you are ignorant. Wake up, then, see your own wretchedness, and flee to the Lord Jesus; and by his righteousness, which is the righteousness of God (for he himself is God), you will be delivered from condemnation.

Ignorance: You go so fast I cannot keep pace with you; you go on ahead: I must stay behind a while.

Then they said,

““Well, Ignorance, will you still foolish be,

To slight good counsel, ten times given free?

And if you still refuse it, you will know,

Before long, the evil of your doing so.

Remember, man, in time: stoop, do not fear:

Good counsel, taken well, saves; therefore hear.

But if you slight it still, then you will be

The loser, Ignorance, I guarantee.””

THE TENTH STAGE

Then Christian spoke to his companion like this:

Christian: Well, come, my good Hopeful, I see that you and I must walk by ourselves again.

So I saw in my dream that they went on quickly ahead, and Ignorance came hobbling after. Then Christian said to his companion, I pity this poor man very much: it will certainly go badly with him in the end.

Hopeful: Alas! There are a great many in our town in his condition, whole families, yes, whole streets, and pilgrims too; and if there are so many in our parts, how many do you think there must be in the place where he was born?

Christian: Indeed, the word says, “He has blinded their eyes, so that they cannot see,” etc.

But now that we are by ourselves, what do you think of such men? Do you think they never have convictions of sin, and so, as a result, fears that their state is dangerous?

Hopeful: No, you answer that question yourself, for you are the older man.

Christian: Then I say that sometimes (as I think) they may; but since they are ignorant by nature, they do not understand that such convictions work for their good; and so they desperately try to stifle them, and presumptuously go on flattering themselves in the way of their own hearts.

Hopeful: I do believe, as you say, that fear does men much good, and helps to set them right when they first begin to go on pilgrimage.

Christian: Without any doubt it does, if it is right; for that is what the word says, “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.” Job 28:28; Ps 111:10; Prov 1:7; 9:10.

Hopeful: How would you describe right fear?

Christian: True or right fear is shown by three things:

1. By where it comes from: it is caused by saving convictions of sin.

2. It drives the soul to take firm hold of Christ for salvation.

3. It produces and keeps alive in the soul a great reverence for God, his word, and his ways; it keeps the soul tender, and makes it afraid to turn from them, to the right hand or to the left, to anything that may dishonor God, break its peace, grieve the Spirit, or cause the enemy to speak reproachfully.

Hopeful: Well said; I believe you have spoken the truth. Are we nearly past the Enchanted Ground now?

Christian: Why? Are you tired of this talk?

Hopeful: No, truly; I only want to know where we are.

Christian: We have no more than two miles further to go on it now. But let us get back to our subject.

Now, the ignorant do not know that such convictions as tend to make them afraid are for their good, and so they try to stifle them.

Hopeful: How do they try to stifle them?

Christian: 1. They think that those fears are caused by the devil (though in fact they are caused by God), and thinking so, they resist them as things that lead straight to their overthrow. 2. They also think that these fears tend to spoil their faith; when, alas for them, poor men that they are, they have none at all; and so they harden their hearts against them. 3. They assume that they ought not to be afraid, and so, in spite of those fears, they grow presumptuously confident. 4. They see that those fears tend to take away their pitiful old self-holiness, and so they resist them with all their might.

Hopeful: I know something of this myself; for before I knew myself, it was like that with me.

Christian: Well, we will leave our neighbor Ignorance to himself for now, and take up another profitable question.

Hopeful: With all my heart; but you must still be the one to begin.

Christian: Well then, did you not know, about ten years ago, a man named Temporary in your parts, who was zealous in religion at that time?

Hopeful: Know him! Yes; he lived in Graceless, a town about two miles from Honesty, and he lived next door to a man named Turnback.

Christian: Right; he lived under the same roof with him. Well, that man was once greatly awakened: I believe that he then had some sight of his sins, and of the wages that were due for them.

Hopeful: I agree with you, for (since my house was no more than three miles from him) he would often come to me, and with many tears. Truly I pitied the man, and was not altogether without hope for him; but, as one can see, it is not everyone who cries, “Lord, Lord!”

Christian: He told me once that he was determined to go on pilgrimage, as we are going now; but all of a sudden he got to know a man named Save-self, and then he became a stranger to me.

Hopeful: Now, since we are talking about him, let us look a little into the reason for the sudden backsliding of him and others like him.

Christian: It may be very profitable; but you begin.

Hopeful: Well, then, there are, in my judgment, four reasons for it:

1. Though the consciences of such men are awakened, their minds are not changed: so when the power of guilt wears off, what moved them to be religious comes to an end, and they naturally go back to their own course again. It is just as we see with the dog that is sick from what he has eaten: as long as his sickness lasts, he vomits and throws up everything; not that he does this from a free mind (if we may say a dog has a mind), but because it upsets his stomach. But when his sickness is over, and his stomach is eased, his desires are not at all turned away from his vomit, and he turns around and licks it all up; and so what is written is true, “The dog has turned to his own vomit again.” 2 Pet 2:22. So, I say, since they are hot for heaven only because of the sense and fear of the torments of hell, as their sense and fear of damnation chills and cools, their desires for heaven and salvation cool too. So then it comes about that when their guilt and fear are gone, their desires for heaven and happiness die, and they return to their course again.

2. Another reason is that they have slavish fears that overpower them: I mean now the fears they have of men; for “the fear of man is a snare.” Prov 29:25. So then, though they seem to be hot for heaven as long as the flames of hell are about their ears, yet when that terror has passed a little, they have second thoughts, namely, that it is good to be wise, and not to run the risk (for they do not know what) of losing everything, or at least of bringing themselves into unavoidable and unnecessary troubles; and so they fall in with the world again.

3. The shame that goes with religion also lies like a block in their way: they are proud and haughty, and in their eyes religion is low and contemptible; so when they have lost their sense of hell and the wrath to come, they return again to their former course.

4. Guilt, and meditating on terror, are painful to them; they do not like to see their misery before they come into it; though perhaps the sight of it at first, if they loved that sight, might make them flee to where the righteous flee and are safe. But because, as I hinted before, they even shun the thoughts of guilt and terror, once they are rid of their awakenings about the terrors and wrath of God, they gladly harden their hearts, and choose such ways as will harden them more and more.

Christian: You are fairly close to the point, for at the bottom of it all is the lack of a change in their mind and will. And so they are only like the felon who stands before the judge: he quakes and trembles, and seems to repent most heartily, but at the bottom of it all is the fear of the noose; not that he has any hatred of the offense, as is plain; because if you only let this man have his freedom, he will be a thief, and so a rogue, still; whereas, if his mind were changed, he would be different.

Hopeful: Now that I have shown you the reason for their going back, you show me how it happens.

Christian: I will gladly do so.

1. They draw their thoughts away, as much as they can, from remembering God, death, and judgment to come.

2. Then little by little they give up private duties, such as private prayer, curbing their lusts, watchfulness, sorrow for sin, and the like.

3. Then they shun the company of lively and warm Christians.

4. After that, they grow cold toward public duty, such as hearing the word, reading, godly conversation, and the like.

5. Then they begin to pick holes, as we say, in the coats of some of the godly, and that devilishly, so that they may have a plausible excuse to throw religion (because of some weaknesses they have spotted in them) behind their backs.

6. Then they begin to attach themselves to, and keep company with, carnal, loose, and wanton men.

7. Then they give way to carnal and wanton talk in secret; and they are glad if they can see such things in any who are counted upright, so that they may do it more boldly because of their example.

8. After this they begin to play with little sins openly.

9. And then, being hardened, they show themselves for what they are. So, launched again into the gulf of misery, unless a miracle of grace prevents it, they perish forever in their own self-deceptions.

Now I saw in my dream that by this time the pilgrims had got over the Enchanted Ground, and were entering the country of Beulah, whose air was very sweet and pleasant, Isa 62:4–12; Song 2:10–12; and since the way lay directly through it, they took comfort and refreshment there for a time. Indeed, here they heard the singing of birds continually, and every day saw the flowers appear on the earth, and heard the voice of the turtledove in the land. In this country the sun shines night and day; so this was beyond the Valley of the Shadow of Death, and also out of the reach of Giant Despair; nor could they so much as see Doubting Castle from this place. Here they were within sight of the city they were going to; here also some of its inhabitants met them; for in this land the shining ones commonly walked, because it was on the borders of heaven. In this land also the contract between the Bride and the Bridegroom was renewed; yes, here, “as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so does God rejoice over them.” Here they had no lack of grain and wine; for in this place they found plenty of what they had sought in all their pilgrimage. Here they heard voices from the city, loud voices, saying, “Say to the daughter of Zion, Behold, your salvation comes! Behold, His reward is with Him!” Here all the inhabitants of the country called them “the Holy People, the Redeemed of the Lord, Sought Out,” etc.

Now, as they walked in this land, they had more rejoicing than in parts farther from the kingdom they were bound for; and as they drew near to the city, they had a still fuller view of it. It was built of pearls and precious stones, and its streets were paved with gold; so that, because of the natural glory of the city and the reflection of the sunbeams on it, Christian fell sick with desire; Hopeful also had a fit or two of the same sickness; so they were laid up here for a while, crying out because of their pangs, “If you see my Beloved, tell him that I am sick with love.”

But, being a little strengthened, and better able to bear their sickness, they walked on their way, and came still nearer and nearer, where there were orchards, vineyards, and gardens, and their gates opened onto the highway. Now, as they came up to these places, there was the gardener, standing in the way; and the pilgrims said to him, Whose fine vineyards and gardens are these? He answered, They are the King’s, and are planted here for his own delight, and also for the comfort of pilgrims. So the gardener took them into the vineyards, and told them to refresh themselves with the delicacies, Deut 23:24; he also showed them the King’s walks and arbors there, where the King delighted to be; and here they stayed and slept.

Now I saw in my dream that they talked more in their sleep at this time than they ever had in all their journey; and as I wondered about this, the gardener said even to me, Why do you wonder at this? It is the nature of the fruit of the grapes of these vineyards “to go down so sweetly as to cause the lips of those who are asleep to speak.” Song 7:9.

So I saw that when they awoke, they got ready to go up to the city. But, as I said, the reflection of the sun on the city (for the city was pure gold, Rev 21:18) was so extremely glorious that they could not yet look at it with unveiled face, except through an instrument made for that purpose. 2 Cor 3:18. So I saw that as they went on, two men met them in garments that shone like gold; their faces also shone like the light.

These men asked the pilgrims where they came from, and they told them. They also asked them where they had lodged, and what difficulties and dangers, what comforts and pleasures, they had met with on the way; and they told them. Then the men who met them said, You have only two more difficulties to meet with, and then you are in the City.

Then Christian and his companion asked the men to go along with them; and they told them that they would. But, they said, you must obtain it by your own faith. So I saw in my dream that they went on together until they came in sight of the gate.

Now I further saw that between them and the gate was a river; but there was no bridge to go over, and the river was very deep. So at the sight of this river the pilgrims were much stunned; but the men who went with them said, You must go through, or you cannot come to the gate.

The pilgrims then began to ask whether there was no other way to the gate. To which they answered, Yes; but no one except two, that is, Enoch and Elijah, has been allowed to tread that path since the foundation of the world, nor will anyone be until the last trumpet sounds. Then the pilgrims, especially Christian, began to lose heart, and looked this way and that, but they could find no way by which they might escape the river. Then they asked the men whether the waters were all of one depth. They said, No; yet they could not help them in that matter; for, they said, you will find it deeper or shallower as you believe in the King of the place.

Then they took to the water; and as they went in, Christian began to sink, and crying out to his good friend Hopeful, he said, I sink in deep waters; the billows go over my head; all his waves go over me. Selah.

Then the other said, Be of good cheer, my brother: I feel the bottom, and it is good. Then Christian said, Ah! my friend, the sorrows of death have encompassed me; I shall not see the land that flows with milk and honey. And with that a great darkness and horror fell on Christian, so that he could not see ahead of him. Here also he largely lost his senses, so that he could neither remember nor talk in an orderly way about any of those sweet refreshments that he had met with on the way of his pilgrimage. But all the words he spoke kept showing that he had horror of mind, and fears in his heart that he would die in that river and never gain entrance at the gate. Here also, as those who stood by could see, he was much taken up with troubling thoughts of the sins he had committed, both since and before he began to be a pilgrim. It was also noticed that he was troubled with apparitions of hobgoblins and evil spirits; for every now and then he would hint as much in his words.

So Hopeful had a hard time here keeping his brother’s head above water; indeed, sometimes Christian would go quite under, and then, after a while, he would rise up again half dead. Hopeful also tried to comfort him, saying, Brother, I see the gate, and men standing by to receive us; but Christian would answer, It is you, it is you they are waiting for; for you have been hopeful ever since I knew you. And so have you, said Hopeful to Christian. Ah, brother, said Christian, surely if I were right, he would now rise up to help me; but because of my sins he has brought me into the snare, and has left me. Then Hopeful said, My brother, you have quite forgotten the text where it is said of the wicked, “They have no struggle in their death; their bodies are well-fed. They are free of the burdens others carry; they are not afflicted like other men.” Ps 73:4, 5. These afflictions and distresses that you are going through in these waters are no sign that God has forsaken you; they are sent to test you, whether you will call to mind what you have received of his goodness in the past, and live on him in your distresses.

Then I saw in my dream that Christian was lost in thought for a while. To him Hopeful also added these words, Be of good cheer, Jesus Christ makes you whole. And with that Christian broke out with a loud voice, Oh, I see him again; and he tells me, “When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and through the rivers, they will not overwhelm you.” Isa 43:2. Then they both took courage, and after that the enemy was as still as a stone until they had gone over. Christian, therefore, at once found ground to stand on, and so it turned out that the rest of the river was only shallow. And so they got over.

Now on the bank of the river, on the other side, they saw the two shining men again, waiting there for them. So, when the pilgrims had come out of the river, the shining men greeted them, saying, We are ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for those who shall be the heirs of salvation. So they went along toward the gate.

Now you must note that the city stood on a mighty hill; but the pilgrims went up that hill with ease, because they had these two men to lead them up by the arms; they had also left their mortal garments behind them in the river, for though they went in with them, they came out without them. So they went up here with great agility and speed, though the foundation on which the city was built was higher than the clouds. And so they went up through the region of the air, talking sweetly as they went, comforted because they had got safely over the river, and had such glorious companions to attend them.

The talk that they had with the shining ones was about the glory of the place; and the shining ones told them that its beauty and glory were beyond words. There, they said, is “Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, the innumerable company of angels, and the spirits of just men made perfect.” Heb 12:22–24. You are going now, they said, to the paradise of God, where you shall see the tree of life, and eat of its never-fading fruits; and when you come there you shall have white robes given you, and your walk and talk shall be every day with the King, all the days of eternity. Rev 2:7; 3:4, 5; 22:5. There you shall not see again such things as you saw when you were in the lower region on earth, namely, sorrow, sickness, affliction, and death; “For the former things have passed away.” Rev 21:4. You are going now to Abraham, to Isaac, and Jacob, and to the prophets, men whom God has taken away from the evil to come, and who are now “resting upon their beds, each one walking in his righteousness.” The men then asked, What must we do in the holy place? And they were answered, There you must receive the comfort of all your toil, and have joy for all your sorrow; you must reap what you have sown, the fruit of all your prayers and tears and sufferings for the King along the way. Gal 6:7, 8. In that place you must wear crowns of gold, and enjoy the perpetual sight and vision of the Holy One; for “there you will see Him as He is.” 1 John 3:2. There also you shall serve him continually with praise, with shouting and thanksgiving, whom you desired to serve in the world, though with much difficulty, because of the weakness of your flesh. There your eyes shall be delighted with seeing, and your ears with hearing the pleasant voice of the Mighty One. There you shall enjoy your friends again who have gone there before you; and there you shall receive with joy even everyone who follows into the holy place after you. There also you shall be clothed with glory and majesty, and fitted out to ride out with the King of Glory. When he comes with the sound of the trumpet in the clouds, as on the wings of the wind, you shall come with him; and when he sits on the throne of judgment, you shall sit by him; yes, and when he passes sentence on all the workers of iniquity, whether they are angels or men, you also shall have a voice in that judgment, because they were his enemies and yours. Also, when he returns to the city again, you shall go too, with the sound of the trumpet, and be with him forever. 1 Thess 4:14–17; Jude 14, 15; Dan 7:9, 10; 1 Cor 6:2, 3.

Now, while they were drawing near the gate like this, behold, a company of the heavenly host came out to meet them; and the other two shining ones said to them, These are the men who loved our Lord when they were in the world, and who have left all for his holy name; and he has sent us to bring them, and we have brought them this far on their desired journey, so that they may go in and look their Redeemer in the face with joy. Then the heavenly host gave a great shout, saying, “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.” Rev 19:9. At this time also several of the King’s trumpeters came out to meet them, clothed in white and shining garments, who with melodious and loud music made even the heavens echo with their sound. These trumpeters greeted Christian and his companion with ten thousand welcomes from the world; and they did this with shouting and the sound of trumpets.

This done, they surrounded them on every side; some went in front, some behind, and some on the right hand, and some on the left (as if to guard them through the upper regions), sounding continually as they went, with melodious music, in notes on high; so that the very sight was, to those who could see it, as if heaven itself had come down to meet them. So they walked on together; and as they walked, every now and then these trumpeters, with joyful sound, would keep showing Christian and his brother, by mixing their music with looks and gestures, how welcome they were into their company, and with what gladness they had come to meet them. And now these two men were, as it were, in heaven before they came to it, being swallowed up with the sight of angels, and with hearing their melodious notes. Here also they had the city itself in view; and they thought they heard all the bells in it ringing to welcome them there. But above all, the warm and joyful thoughts they had about their own dwelling there with such company, and that for ever and ever; oh, by what tongue or pen can their glorious joy be expressed! And so they came up to the gate.

Now when they had come up to the gate, there was written over it, in letters of gold,

“Blessed are those who do His commandments, that they may have the right to the tree of life, and may enter in through the gates into the city.”

Then I saw in my dream that the shining men told them to call at the gate; and when they did, some looked over the gate from above, namely Enoch, Moses, and Elijah, etc., and they were told, These pilgrims have come from the City of Destruction, for the love that they bear to the King of this place. Then the pilgrims each handed in to them his certificate, which they had received at the beginning; these were therefore carried in to the King, who, when he had read them, said, Where are the men? He was answered, They are standing outside the gate. The King then commanded them to open the gate, “So that the righteous nation (he said) that remains faithful may enter.” Isa 26:2.

Now I saw in my dream that these two men went in at the gate; and look, as they entered, they were transfigured, and they had garments put on them that shone like gold. There were also some who met them with harps and crowns, and gave them to them; the harps to praise with, and the crowns as a token of honor. Then I heard in my dream that all the bells in the city rang again for joy, and that it was said to them,

“Enter into the joy of your+ Lord.”

I also heard the men themselves sing with a loud voice, saying,

“Blessing and honor and glory and power be to Him who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb, forever and ever.”

Now, just as the gates were opened to let the men in, I looked in after them, and behold, the city shone like the sun; the streets also were paved with gold; and in them walked many men, with crowns on their heads, palms in their hands, and golden harps to sing praises with.

There were also some among them who had wings, and they answered one another without ceasing, saying, Holy, holy, holy is the Lord. And after that they shut the gates; and when I had seen that, I wished myself among them.

Now, while I was gazing at all these things, I turned my head to look back, and saw Ignorance come up to the riverside; but he soon got over, and without half the difficulty that the other two men met with. For it happened that there was then in that place a ferryman named Vain-Hope, who helped him over with his boat; so he, as I had seen the other two do, climbed the hill to come up to the gate; only he came alone, and no man met him with the least encouragement. When he had come up to the gate, he looked up at the writing above it, and then began to knock, supposing that he would quickly be let in; but the men who looked over the top of the gate asked him, Where do you come from? And what do you want? He answered, I have eaten and drunk in the presence of the King, and he has taught in our streets. Then they asked him for his certificate, so that they might go in and show it to the King; so he fumbled inside his coat for one, and found none. Then they said, Have you none? But the man did not answer a word. So they told the King, but he would not come down to see him, but commanded the two shining ones who had conducted Christian and Hopeful to the city to go out and take Ignorance, and bind him hand and foot, and take him away. Then they took him up, and carried him through the air to the door that I saw in the side of the hill, and put him in there. Then I saw that there was a way to hell, even from the gate of heaven, as well as from the City of Destruction. So I awoke, and behold it was a dream.

CONCLUSION

Now, reader, I have told my dream; now see

Whether you can interpret it to me,

Or to yourself, or neighbor; but take heed

Of misinterpreting; for that, instead

Of doing good, will only lead you astray:

By misinterpreting, evil comes your way.

Take care, also, that you are not extreme

In playing with the outside of my dream;

Nor let my figure or similitude

Set you to laughing, or into a feud.

Leave that to boys and fools; but you, instead,

Look at the substance of what I have said.

Draw back the curtains, look behind my veil,

Turn up my metaphors, and do not fail.

There, if you look for them, such things you’ll find

As will be helpful to an honest mind.

Whatever dross you find of mine, be bold

To throw away, but still preserve the gold.

What if my gold is wrapped up in ore?

No one throws out the apple for the core:

But if you throw it all away as vain,

It may, for all I know, make me dream again.

PART TWO

In which is set forth the manner of the setting out of Christian’s wife and children; their dangerous journey, and safe arrival at the desired country.

I have used similitudes.—Hos 12:10.

THE AUTHOR’S WAY

OF

SENDING FORTH HIS SECOND PART

OF

THE PILGRIM

Go, now, my little Book, to every place

Where my first Pilgrim has but shown his face:

Call at their door: if any say, Who’s there?

Then answer them, Christiana is here.

If they invite you in, then enter now,

With all your boys; and then, as you know how,

Tell who they are, and from what place they came;

Perhaps they’ll know them by their looks, or name:

But if they don’t, then ask them once again

If in the past they did not entertain

One Christian, a Pilgrim? If they say

They did, and were delighted with his way;

Then let them know that these are, every one,

His kin: yes, his own wife and every son.

Tell them that they have left their house and home;

Have turned Pilgrims; seek a world to come;

That they have met with hardships on the way;

That they keep meeting troubles night and day;

That they have trod on serpents; fought with devils;

Have also overcome a host of evils;

Yes, tell them also of the next, who have,

For love of pilgrimage, been bold and brave

Defenders of that way; and how they still

Refuse this world to do their Father’s will.

Go, tell them also of the delightful things

That pilgrimage to every Pilgrim brings.

Let them be made aware, too, how they share

Their King’s own love, and live under his care;

What splendid mansions he for them provides;

Though they meet with rough winds and swelling tides,

How fine a calm they will enjoy at last,

Who cling to their Lord, and by his ways hold fast.

Perhaps with heart and hand they will embrace

You, as they did my firstborn; and will grace

You and your fellows with such cheer and fare

As shows how dearly they for Pilgrims care.

Objection i

But what if they will not believe of me

That I am truly yours? For, certainly,

Some counterfeit the Pilgrim and his name,

And seek, disguised, to seem the very same;

And by that means have worked their way into

The hands and houses of I don’t know who.

Answer

It’s true that some, of late, to counterfeit

My Pilgrim, have on their own my title set;

Yes, others half my name, and title too,

Have stitched onto their books, to make them do.

But still their features plainly will declare

They are not mine, whoever’s books they are.

If you meet such, then your only way,

Before them all, is just to have your say

In your own native language, which no man

Now speaks, nor fakes with ease, try as he can.

If, after all, they still about you+ doubt,

Thinking that you+, like gypsies, roam about

In wicked ways the country to defile;

Or that you+ seek good people to beguile

With things not warranted, then send and call

For me; I’ll testify you+ are pilgrims, all;

Yes, I will testify that only you+

Are my Pilgrims, and that alone will do.

Objection ii

But then, perhaps, I may ask after him

Of those who wish him damned, both life and limb.

What shall I do when I, at such a door,

Ask for the Pilgrims, and they rage the more?

Answer

Do not take fright, my Book, for such bugbears

Are nothing more than grounds for groundless fears.

My Pilgrim’s book has traveled sea and land,

Yet I could never come to understand

That it was scorned, or turned out of the door,

By any Kingdom, whether rich or poor.

In France and Flanders, where men kill each other,

My Pilgrim is esteemed a friend, a brother.

In Holland, too, it’s said, as I am told,

My Pilgrim is, to some, worth more than gold.

Highlanders and wild Irish can agree

My Pilgrim should be one they often see.

In New England it’s raised to such a height,

Receives such loving favor in their sight

As to be trimmed, new-clothed, with gems arrayed,

That its features and its limbs might be displayed.

What’s more, my Pilgrim has so fine a walk

That thousands daily of him sing and talk.

If you come nearer home, it will appear

My Pilgrim knows no cause for shame or fear:

City and country gladly take him in

With, Welcome, Pilgrim! yes, they can’t help but grin

If my Pilgrim is only standing by,

Or shows his head in any company.

Fine gentlemen will hug my Pilgrim, love

It, prize it much, yes, value it above

Things of a greater size; yes, with delight

They say, my lark’s leg is better than a kite.

Young ladies, and young gentlewomen too,

Show my Pilgrim kindnesses not a few;

Their cabinets, their bosoms, and their hearts

My Pilgrim has, because to them he imparts

His pretty riddles in such wholesome strains

As pay them double profit for their pains

Of reading; yes, I think I may be bold

To say some prize him far above their gold.

The very children walking in the street,

If they should meet my holy Pilgrim, greet

Him; they will wish him well, and they will say

He is the only youngster of the day.

Those who have never seen him yet admire

What they have heard of him, and much desire

To have his company, and hear him tell

Those Pilgrim stories which he knows so well.

Yes, some who did not love him at the first,

But called him fool and nitwit, say they must,

Now they have seen and heard him, recommend

Him, and they send him on to every friend.

So then, my Second Part, you need not fear

To show your head: no one can hurt you here

Who wishes well to him who went before;

Since you come after with a second store

Of things as good, as rich, as profitable,

For young, for old, for staggering, and for stable.

Objection iii

But there are some who say, He laughs too loud;

And others say, His head is in a cloud.

Some say, His words and stories are so dark

They don’t know how, by them, to find his mark.

Answer

One may, I think, say, Both his laughs and cries

May well be guessed at from his watery eyes.

Some things are of a nature that can make

One’s fancy chuckle while his heart will ache:

When Jacob saw his Rachel, as she kept

The sheep, at the same time he kissed and wept.

Whereas some say, A cloud is in his head;

That only shows his wisdom’s overspread

With its own mantles—and, to stir the mind

To search well after what it longs to find,

Things that seem hidden in words that are obscure

Will draw the godly mind with greater lure

To study what those sayings may contain

That speak to us in such a cloudy strain.

I also know a dark similitude

Will on the curious fancy more intrude,

And will stick faster in the head and heart

Than things in which a simile has no part.

So then, my Book, let no discouragement

Hold back your travels. See, you have been sent

To friends, not foes; to friends who will make space

For you and your pilgrims, and your words embrace.

Besides, what my first Pilgrim left concealed,

You, my fine second Pilgrim, have revealed;

What Christian left locked up, and went his way,

Sweet Christiana opens with her key.

Objection iv

But some don’t like the method of your first:

Romance, they call it; throw it out as dust.

If I meet such as these, what should I say?

Must I slight them, as they slight me? Which way?

Answer

My Christiana, any such you meet,

By all means, with all loving kindness greet;

Do not return reviling for revile,

But if they frown, I beg you, give a smile:

Perhaps it’s nature, or some bad report,

That made them so despise, or so retort.

Some love no fish, some love no cheese, and some

Don’t love their friends, nor their own house or home;

Some balk at pork, scorn chicken, love no fowl

More than they love a cuckoo or an owl.

Leave such, my Christiana, to their choice,

And seek those who, to find you, will rejoice;

By no means quarrel, but, as I advise,

Most humbly show yourself in Pilgrim guise.

Go then, my little Book, and show all who say

Come in! and welcome you, and have you stay,

What you will keep shut close from all the rest;

And wish what you will show them may be blessed

To them for good, and make them choose to be

Pilgrims, far better ones than you or me.

Go, then, I say, and tell all men your name:

Say, I am Christiana; and my aim

Is now, with my four sons, to tell you+ what

It is for men to take a Pilgrim’s lot.

Go, also, tell them what they are, and who,

Who now go on pilgrimage along with you;

Say, Here’s my neighbor Mercy: it is she

Who long has been a fellow pilgrim with me:

Come, see her virgin face, and from it learn

The idle from the pilgrim to discern.

Yes, let young women learn from her to prize

The world to come above all, in their eyes.

When little skipping girls will follow God,

And leave old doddering sinners to his rod,

It’s like those days in which the young ones cried

Hosanna! when the old ones would deride.

Next, tell them of old Honest, whom you+ found

With his white hair treading the Pilgrim’s ground;

Yes, tell them how plain-hearted this man was;

How, after his good Lord, he bore the cross.

Perhaps with some gray head this may prevail

To fall in love with Christ, and sin bewail.

Tell them as well how Master Fearing went

On pilgrimage, and how his time was spent

In solitude, amid his fears and cries;

And how, at last, he won the joyful prize.

He was a good man, though much down in spirit;

He is a good man; life is his to inherit.

Tell them of Master Feeble-mind also,

Who not in front, but always behind, would go.

Show them as well how he was all but slain,

And how one Great-Heart won his life again.

This man was true of heart; though weak in grace,

One might read true godliness in his face.

Then tell them of Master Ready-to-Halt,

A man with crutches, but with little fault.

Tell them how Master Feeble-mind and he

Would love each other, and in views agree.

And let all know, though weak by circumstance,

Still, at times one could sing, the other dance.

Do not forget Master Valiant-for-the-Truth,

That man of courage, though still just a youth:

Tell everyone his heart was so stout,

No man could ever make him turn about;

And how Great-Heart and he just had to tear

Down Doubting-Castle, and kill Despair!

Don’t overlook Master Despondency,

Nor Much-afraid, his daughter, though they lie

Under such mantles as may make them look

(To some) like ones whom their own God forsook.

They went on slow but sure; and, at the end,

Found that the Lord of Pilgrims was their friend.

When you have told the world of all these things,

Then turn around, my Book, and touch these strings,

Which, if you touch them, will such music make

They’ll make a cripple dance, a giant quake.

Those riddles that lie hidden in your breast

Freely set forth, expound; and for the rest

Of your mysterious lines, let them remain

For those with nimble fancies, theirs to gain.

Now may this little Book a blessing be

To those who love this little Book and me;

And may its buyer have no cause to say

His money’s only lost, or thrown away.

Yes, may this second Pilgrim yield such fruit

As will the taste of each good Pilgrim suit;

And may it persuade some who go astray

To turn their feet and heart to the right way,

Is the heartfelt prayer of

The Author,

JOHN BUNYAN.

TO THE READER

courteous companions,

Some time ago, telling you+ the dream I had of Christian the pilgrim, and of his dangerous journey towards the Celestial country, was pleasant to me and profitable to you+. I also told you+ then what I saw concerning his wife and children, and how unwilling they were to go with him on pilgrimage; so unwilling that he was forced to go on his progress without them, for he did not dare to run the risk of the destruction he feared would come from staying with them in the City of Destruction. So, as I showed you+ then, he left them and departed.

Now it has so happened, through a great press of business, that I have been much hindered and kept from my usual travels into the parts he came from, and so could not, until now, find an opportunity to inquire further after those he left behind, so that I might give you+ an account of them. But lately, having had some business that way, I went down there again. Now, having taken up my lodging in a wood about a mile from the place, as I slept, I dreamed again.

And as I was in my dream, behold, an aged gentleman came by where I lay; and because he was going some part of the way I was traveling, I thought I got up and went with him. So as we walked, as travelers usually do, it seemed we fell into conversation; and our talk happened to be about Christian and his travels, for this is how I began with the old man:

Sir, I said, what town is that down there, lying on the left side of our way?

Then Mr. Sagacity (for that was his name) said, It is the City of Destruction, a populous place, but filled with a very ill-natured and idle sort of people.

I thought that was the city, I said; I once went through that town myself, and so I know that this report you give of it is true.

Mr. Sagacity: Too true! I wish I could speak better of those who live there and still speak the truth.

Well, sir, I said, then I see that you are a well-meaning man, and so one who takes pleasure in hearing and telling of what is good. Tell me, did you never hear what happened some time ago to a man of this town (whose name was Christian), who went on a pilgrimage up towards the higher regions?

Mr. Sagacity: Hear of him! Yes, and I also heard of the attacks, troubles, wars, captivities, cries, groans, frights, and fears that he met with and had on his journey. Besides, I must tell you, our whole country rings with his name. There are few houses that have heard of him and his doings without having sought out and got the records of his pilgrimage; indeed, I think I may say that his hazardous journey has won many well-wishers to his ways. For though, when he was here, every man’s mouth called him a fool, now that he is gone he is highly praised by all. For it is said he lives splendidly where he is; indeed, many of those who are determined never to run his risks still have their mouths water at his gains.

They may well think, I said, if they think anything that is true, that he lives well where he is; for he now lives at, and in, the fountain of life, and has what he has without labor and sorrow, for there is no grief mixed with it. But tell me, what do the people say about him?

Mr. Sagacity: Talk! The people talk strangely about him. Some say that he now walks in white, Rev 3:4; that he has a chain of gold about his neck; that he has a crown of gold, set with pearls, on his head. Others say that the shining ones, who sometimes showed themselves to him on his journey, have become his companions, and that he is as familiar with them where he is as one neighbor is with another here. Besides, it is confidently reported of him that the King of the place where he is has already given him a very rich and pleasant dwelling at court, and that every day he eats and drinks, and walks and talks with him, and receives the smiles and favors of him who is Judge of all there. Zech 3:7; Luke 14:14, 15. Moreover, some expect that his Prince, the Lord of that country, will soon come into these parts, and will demand to know the reason, if they can give any, why his neighbors thought so little of him and mocked him so much when they saw that he would be a pilgrim. Jude 14, 15.

For they say that he is now so much in his Prince’s affections that his Sovereign is so concerned about the insults that were heaped on Christian when he became a pilgrim, that he will regard them all as done to himself, Luke 10:16; and no wonder, for it was out of the love he had for his Prince that he ventured as he did.

I dare say, I said; I am glad of it. I am glad for the poor man’s sake, because he now has rest from his labor, and because he now reaps the benefit of his tears with joy, and because he has got beyond the gunshot of his enemies and is out of the reach of those who hate him. Rev 14:13; Ps 126:5, 6. I am also glad that a rumor of these things is spreading through this country; who knows whether it may have some good effect on some who are left behind? But please, sir, while it is fresh in my mind, do you hear anything of his wife and children? Poor hearts! I wonder what they are doing.

Mr. Sagacity: Who? Christiana and her sons? They are likely to do as well as Christian did himself; for though they all played the fool at first, and would not be persuaded at all by either the tears or the pleading of Christian, second thoughts have worked wonderfully with them. So they have packed up and gone after him too.

Better and better, I said; but what! Wife and children and all?

Mr. Sagacity: It is true. I can give you an account of the matter, for I was on the spot at the time, and knew the whole affair thoroughly.

Then, I said, it seems a man may report it as the truth.

Mr. Sagacity: You need not be afraid to say so. I mean that they have all gone on pilgrimage, both the good woman and her four boys. And since we are, as I see, going a good way together, I will give you an account of the whole matter.

As for this Christiana (for that was her name from the day she and her children took up a pilgrim’s life), after her husband had gone over the river and she could hear no more of him, her thoughts began to work in her mind. First, she had lost her husband, and the loving bond between them was utterly broken. For you know, he said to me, nature cannot help but fill the living with many a heavy thought when they remember the loss of those they love. So this loss of her husband cost her many a tear. But that was not all; for Christiana also began to ask herself whether her unbecoming behavior towards her husband was not one reason why she saw him no more, and why he was taken from her in such a way. And at this there came into her mind, in swarms, all her unkind, unnatural, and ungodly conduct towards her dear husband, which also clogged her conscience and loaded her with guilt. She was, moreover, much broken by recalling her husband’s restless groans, salt tears, and laments over himself, and how she had hardened her heart against all his pleading and his loving persuasion of her and her sons to go with him. Indeed, there was nothing that Christian either said to her or did in front of her, all the while his burden hung on his back, but it came back to her like a flash of lightning and tore apart the covering of her heart; especially that bitter outcry of his, “What shall I do to be saved?” rang in her ears most mournfully.

Then she said to her children, Sons, we are all undone. I have sinned away your father, and he is gone. He would have had us with him, but I would not go myself; I have also kept you from life. At that the boys burst into tears and cried out to go after their father. Oh, said Christiana, if only it had been our lot to go with him! Then it would have gone well with us, far better than it is likely to now. For though I once foolishly imagined, about your father’s troubles, that they came from some foolish fancy of his, or because he was overrun with melancholy, yet now I cannot get it out of my mind that they sprang from another cause, namely, that the Light of Light was given him, Jas 1:23–25; and by its help, as I now see, he has escaped the snares of death. Prov 14:27. Then they all wept again, and cried out, Oh, woe to the day!

The next night Christiana had a dream; and behold, she saw what seemed to be a broad parchment opened before her, in which the sum of her ways was recorded; and the crimes, as she thought, looked very black against her. Then she cried out aloud in her sleep, “Lord, have mercy on me, a sinner!” Luke 18:13; and the little children heard her.

After this she thought she saw two very ill-favored ones standing by her bedside and saying, What shall we do with this woman? For she cries out for mercy, waking and sleeping. If she is allowed to go on as she has begun, we will lose her as we have lost her husband. So we must, one way or another, try to draw her mind away from thoughts of what will be hereafter, or else all the world cannot keep her from becoming a pilgrim.

Now she woke in a great sweat, and trembling as well; but after a while she fell asleep again. And then she thought she saw Christian, her husband, in a place of bliss among many immortals, with a harp in his hand, standing and playing it before One who sat on a throne with a rainbow around his head. She also saw him, as it seemed, bow his head with his face to the pavement that was under his Prince’s feet, saying, “I heartily thank my Lord and King for bringing me into this place.” Then a company of those who stood round about shouted and harped with their harps; but no man living could tell what they said except Christian and his companions.

Next morning, when she was up, had prayed to God, and had talked with her children a while, someone knocked hard at the door; and she called out to him, “If you come in God’s name, come in.” So he said, “Amen,” and opened the door, and greeted her with, “Peace be to this house.” When he had done that, he said, “Christiana, do you know why I have come?” Then she blushed and trembled; and her heart began to grow warm with longing to know where he came from, and what his errand to her was. So he said to her, “My name is Secret; I dwell with those that are on high. It is said where I dwell that you seem to have a desire to go there; there is also a report that you are aware of the evil you have done to your husband in the past, in hardening your heart against his way, and in keeping these babes in their ignorance.
