Christiana, the Merciful One has sent me to tell you that he is a God ready to forgive, and that he delights to multiply the pardon of offenses. He also wants you to know that he invites you to come into his presence, to his table, and that he will feed you with the fat of his house, and with the heritage of Jacob your father.

“There is Christian, who was your husband, with legions more, his companions, always looking on that face that gives life to those who look on it; and they will all be glad when they hear the sound of your feet stepping over your Father’s threshold.”

At this Christiana was greatly abashed, and bowed her head to the ground. The visitor went on, and said, “Christiana, here is also a letter for you, which I have brought from your husband’s King.” So she took it and opened it, and it smelled like the best perfume. Song 1:3. It was also written in letters of gold. The contents of the letter were these: that the King wanted her to do as Christian her husband had done; for that was the way to come to his city, and to live in his presence with joy for ever. At this the good woman was quite overcome; so she cried out to her visitor, Sir, will you take me and my children with you, so that we too may go and worship the King?

Then the visitor said, Christiana, the bitter comes before the sweet. You must enter this Celestial City through troubles, as he who went before you did. So I advise you to do as Christian your husband did: go to the Wicket-gate over there, across the plain, for it stands at the head of the way you must go up; and I wish you all good speed. I also advise you to put this letter in your bosom, and to read it to yourself and to your children until you+ have got it by heart; for it is one of the songs that you must sing while you are in this house of your pilgrimage, Ps 119:54; and you must also hand it in at the far gate.

Now I saw in my dream that this old gentleman, as he told me the story, seemed himself to be greatly moved by it. He went on, and said, So Christiana called her sons together, and began to speak to them like this: “My sons, as you may see, I have lately been in much trouble in my soul about the death of your father; not that I doubt his happiness at all, for I am now satisfied that he is well. I have also been much moved by thoughts of my own state and yours, which I truly believe is miserable by nature. My conduct towards your father in his distress is also a great load on my conscience; for I hardened both my own heart and yours against him, and refused to go with him on pilgrimage.

“The thought of these things would kill me outright now, if it were not for a dream I had last night, and for the encouragement this stranger has given me this morning. Come, my children, let us pack up and be off to the gate that leads to the Celestial country, so that we may see your father, and be with him and his companions in peace, according to the laws of that land.”

Then her children burst into tears, for joy that their mother’s heart was so inclined. So their visitor bid them farewell, and they began to get ready to set out on their journey.

But while they were getting ready to go, two of the women who were Christiana’s neighbors came up to her house and knocked at her door. She said to them, as before, If you come in God’s name, come in. At this the women were stunned; for they were not used to hearing this kind of language, or to hearing it fall from Christiana’s lips. Still, they came in; and there they found the good woman getting ready to leave her house.

So they began by saying, Neighbor, please, what do you mean by this?

Christiana answered, saying to the eldest of them, whose name was Mrs. Timorous, I am getting ready for a journey.

This Timorous was the daughter of the man who met Christian on the Hill of Difficulty, and wanted him to go back for fear of the lions.

Timorous: What journey, may I ask?

Christiana: Why, to go after my good husband. And with that she began to weep.

Timorous: I hope not, good neighbor. Please, for your poor children’s sake, do not throw yourself away in so unwomanly a fashion.

Christiana: No, my children will go with me; not one of them is willing to stay behind.

Timorous: I wonder with all my heart what or who has put this into your head!

Christiana: O neighbor, if you only knew as much as I do, I have no doubt that you would go along with me.

Timorous: Tell me, what new knowledge have you got, that draws your mind away from your friends like this, and tempts you to go nobody knows where?

Christiana: Then Christiana replied, I have been deeply afflicted since my husband left me, but especially since he went over the river. But what troubles me most is my churlish conduct towards him when he was in his distress. Besides, I am now as he was then; nothing will do for me but going on pilgrimage. I was dreaming last night that I saw him. Oh, that my soul were with him! He lives in the presence of the King of the country; he sits and eats with him at his table; he has become a companion of immortals, and has now been given a house to live in, compared with which the best palace on earth seems to me no better than a dunghill. 2 Cor 5:1–4. The Prince of the place has also sent for me, with the promise of a welcome if I come to him; his messenger was here just now, and has brought me a letter, which invites me to come. And with that she pulled out her letter, and read it, and said to them, Now what will you say to this?

Timorous: Oh, the madness that has possessed you and your husband, to rush into such difficulties! You have heard, I am sure, what your husband met with almost at the very first step he took on his way, as our neighbor Obstinate can still testify, for he went along with him; yes, and Pliable too, until they, like wise men, were afraid to go any further. We also heard, besides, how he met with the lions, Apollyon, the Shadow of Death, and many other things. Nor should you forget the danger he met with at Vanity Fair. For if he, though a man, was so hard pressed, what can you do, being only a poor woman? Consider also that these four sweet babes are your children, your flesh and your bones. So, though you should be so rash as to throw yourself away, yet for the sake of the fruit of your body, stay at home.

But Christiana said to her, Do not tempt me, my neighbor. I now have the means put into my hands to get gain, and I would be a fool of the greatest size if I had no heart to seize the opportunity. And as for all these troubles you tell me I am likely to meet with on the way, they are so far from discouraging me that they show I am in the right. The bitter must come before the sweet, and that will also make the sweet the sweeter. So, since you did not come to my house in God’s name, as I said, please be gone, and do not disturb me any further.

Then Timorous railed at her, and said to her companion, Come, neighbor Mercy, let us leave her to herself, since she scorns our advice and our company. But Mercy hesitated, and could not so readily go along with her neighbor, and that for a twofold reason. 1. Her heart yearned over Christiana. So she said to herself, If my neighbor must go, I will go a little way with her and help her. 2. Her heart yearned over her own soul; for what Christiana had said had taken some hold on her mind. So she said to herself again, I will have more talk with this Christiana yet; and if I find truth and life in what she says, I myself will go with her too, with all my heart. So Mercy began to answer her neighbor Timorous like this:

Mercy: Neighbor, I did indeed come with you to see Christiana this morning; and since she is, as you see, taking her last farewell of the country, I think I will walk a little way with her this sunny morning, to help her on her way. But she did not tell her about her second reason; she kept it to herself.

Timorous: Well, I see you have a mind to go off fooling too; but take care in time, and be wise: while we are out of danger, we are out; but when we are in, we are in.

So Mrs. Timorous went back to her house, and Christiana set out on her journey. But when Timorous had got home, she sends for some of her neighbors, namely, Mrs. Bat’s-Eyes, Mrs. Inconsiderate, Mrs. Light-Mind, and Mrs. Know-Nothing. So when they had come to her house, she starts telling them the story of Christiana and her intended journey. And this is how she began her tale:

Timorous: Neighbors, having little to do this morning, I went to pay Christiana a visit; and when I came to the door I knocked, as you know is our custom; and she answered, If you come in God’s name, come in. So in I went, thinking all was well; but when I came in, I found her getting ready to leave the town, she and her children too. So I asked her what she meant by that. And she told me, in short, that she now had a mind to go on pilgrimage, as her husband did. She also told me of a dream she had, and how the King of the country where her husband was had sent her a letter inviting her to come there.

Then Mrs. Know-Nothing said, And what! Do you think she will go?

Timorous: Oh yes, go she will, whatever comes of it; and I think I know it by this: what was my great argument to persuade her to stay at home (namely, the troubles she was likely to meet with on the way) is one great argument with her for pressing on with her journey. For she told me in so many words, The bitter goes before the sweet; yes, and since it does, it makes the sweet the sweeter.

Mrs. Bat’s-Eyes: Oh, this blind and foolish woman! she said; and will she not take warning from her husband’s afflictions? For my part, I can see that if he were here again, he would be content to keep his skin whole, and never run so many risks for nothing.

Mrs. Inconsiderate also replied, saying, Away with such fanciful fools from the town! A good riddance of her, I say, for my part. If she stayed where she lives and kept this mind of hers, who could live quietly next to her? For she will either be gloomy, or unneighborly, or talk of such matters as no sensible person can stand. So, for my part, I will never be sorry she has gone; let her go, and let someone better come in her place. It was never a good world since these whimsical fools lived in it.

Then Mrs. Light-Mind added this: Come, enough of this kind of talk. Yesterday I was at Madam Wanton’s, where we were as merry as the maids. For who do you think was there but me and Mrs. Love-the-Flesh, and three or four more, with Mrs. Lechery, Mrs. Filth, and some others; so there we had music and dancing, and whatever else was fitting to fill up the pleasure. And I dare say my lady herself is an admirably well-bred gentlewoman, and Mr. Lechery is as pretty a fellow.

THE FIRST STAGE

By this time Christiana had got on her way, and Mercy went along with her; so as they went, with her children there too, Christiana began to talk. And, Mercy, said Christiana, I take it as an unexpected kindness that you should set out of doors with me to keep me company a little way.

Mercy: Then young Mercy said (for she was only young), If I thought it would do any good to go with you, I would never go near the town again.

Christiana: Well, Mercy, said Christiana, cast in your lot with me. I know well what the end of our pilgrimage will be: my husband is in a place he would not leave for all the gold in the Spanish mines. Nor will you be rejected, though you go only on my invitation. The King, who has sent for me and my children, is one who delights in mercy. Besides, if you like, I will hire you, and you can go along with me as my servant. Yet we will have all things in common between you and me: only go along with me.

Mercy: But how can I be sure that I too would be received? If I had this hope from just one who can tell, I would not hesitate at all, but would go, helped by Him who can help, however tedious the way might be.

Christiana: Well, loving Mercy, I will tell you what to do. Go with me to the Wicket-gate, and there I will inquire further for you; and if you do not meet with encouragement there, I will be content for you to go back to your own place. I will also pay you for the kindness you are showing me and my children in coming with us on the way as you do.

Mercy: Then I will go there, and will take whatever follows; and the Lord grant that my lot may fall there, just as the King of heaven sets his heart on me.

Christiana was glad at heart then, not only that she had a companion, but also because she had persuaded this poor young woman to fall in love with her own salvation. So they went on together, and Mercy began to weep. Then Christiana said, Why is my sister weeping so?

Mercy: Alas! she said, how can anyone help grieving, if he only rightly considers what a state and condition my poor family are in, still living in our sinful town? And what makes my grief heavier is that they have no one to teach them, nor anyone to tell them what is to come.

Christiana: Pity befits pilgrims; and you weep for your family, as my good Christian did for me when he left me. He mourned because I would not heed or regard him; but his Lord and ours gathered up his tears and put them into his bottle; and now both I and you, and these sweet babes of mine, are reaping the fruit and benefit of them. I hope, Mercy, that these tears of yours will not be lost; for the truth has said that “those who sow in tears will reap with shouts of joy.” And “he who goes out weeping, bearing a trail of seed, will surely return with shouts of joy, carrying sheaves of grain.” Ps 126:5, 6.

Then Mercy said,

““Let the Most Blessed be my guide,

If it be his blessed will,

Unto his gate, into his fold,

Up to his holy hill.”

“And let him never suffer me

To swerve, or turn aside

From his free-grace and holy ways,

Whate’er shall me betide.”

“And let him gather them of mine

That I have left behind;

Lord, make them pray they may be thine,

With all their heart and mind.””

Now my old friend went on, and said, But when Christiana came to the Slough of Despond, she began to hold back; for, she said, this is the place where my dear husband was nearly smothered in mud. She also saw that, in spite of the King’s command to make this place good for pilgrims, it was rather worse than before. So I asked if that was true. Yes, said the old gentleman, too true; for there are many who pretend to be the King’s laborers, and say they are for mending the King’s highways, who bring dirt and dung instead of stones, and so mar instead of mend. So here Christiana and her boys came to a stop. But Mercy said, Come, let us venture; only let us be careful. Then they watched their steps closely, and managed to stagger across.

Yet Christiana nearly went in, and that not once or twice. Now they had no sooner got over than they thought they heard words that said to them, “Blessed is she who has believed that the Lord’s word to her will be fulfilled.” Luke 1:45.

Then they went on again; and Mercy said to Christiana, If I had as good ground as you to hope for a loving welcome at the Wicket-gate, I think no Slough of Despond would discourage me.

Well, said the other, you know your sore, and I know mine; and, good friend, we will all have evil enough before we come to our journey’s end. For can it be imagined that people who aim to attain such excellent glories as we do, and whose happiness is as envied as ours is, will not meet with whatever fears and snares, whatever troubles and afflictions, those who hate us can possibly assault us with?

And now Mr. Sagacity left me to dream out my dream by myself. So I thought I saw Christiana, and Mercy, and the boys all go up to the gate; and when they had come to it, they held a short debate about how they should go about calling at the gate, and what should be said to him who opened to them. So it was agreed that, since Christiana was the eldest, she should knock for entrance, and should speak for the rest to him who opened. So Christiana began to knock, and, as her poor husband had done, she knocked and knocked again. But instead of anyone answering, they all thought they heard what seemed to be a dog come barking at them; a dog, and a great one too; and this made the women and children afraid. Nor did they dare for a while to knock any more, for fear the mastiff would fly at them. Now, therefore, they were greatly tumbled up and down in their minds, and did not know what to do. They did not dare to knock, for fear of the dog; they did not dare to go back, for fear the keeper of that gate would see them going and be offended with them. At last they thought of knocking again, and knocked harder than they had at first. Then the keeper of the gate said, Who is there? So the dog stopped barking, and he opened to them.

Then Christiana bowed low, and said, May our Lord not be offended with his handmaidens for having knocked at his princely gate. Then the keeper said, Where do you+ come from? And what is it you+ want?

Christiana answered, We have come from where Christian came from, and on the same errand as he; that is, to be, if you please, graciously admitted by this gate into the way that leads to the Celestial City. And in the second place, my Lord, I answer that I am Christiana, once the wife of Christian, who has now gone above.

At that the keeper of the gate marveled, saying, What, has she now become a pilgrim, who only a little while ago hated that life? Then she bowed her head, and said, Yes; and so have these sweet babes of mine.

Then he took her by the hand and led her in, and also said, Let the little children come to me; and with that he shut the gate. When this was done, he called to a trumpeter who was above, over the gate, to welcome Christiana with shouting and with the sound of the trumpet for joy. So he obeyed, and sounded, and filled the air with his melodious notes.

Now all this while poor Mercy stood outside, trembling and crying, for fear that she had been rejected. But when Christiana had gained entrance for herself and her boys, she began to intercede for Mercy.

Christiana: And she said, My Lord, I have a companion still standing outside, who has come here for the same reason as I have: one who is very downcast in her mind, because she comes, as she thinks, without being sent for; whereas I was sent for by my husband’s King to come.

Now Mercy began to be very impatient, and each minute seemed as long to her as an hour; so, before Christiana could intercede for her more fully, she knocked at the gate herself. And she knocked so loudly then that she made Christiana start. Then the keeper of the gate said, Who is there? And Christiana said, It is my friend.

So he opened the gate and looked out, but Mercy had fallen down outside in a swoon; for she had fainted, afraid that no gate would be opened to her.

Then he took her by the hand and said, Young woman, I tell you, arise.

Oh, sir, she said, I am faint; there is hardly any life left in me. But he answered that one once said, “When my soul fainted within me, I remembered the Lord my prayer went up to You, to Your holy temple.” Jonah 2:7. Do not be afraid, but stand on your feet, and tell me why you have come.

Mercy: I have come for what I was never invited to, as my friend Christiana was. Her invitation came from the King, and mine only from her. So I fear I am presuming.

Keeper: Did she ask you to come with her to this place?

Mercy: Yes; and, as my Lord sees, I have come. And if there is any grace and forgiveness of sins to spare, I beg that your poor handmaid may have a share in it.

Then he took her by the hand again, and led her gently in, and said, I pray for all who believe in me, by whatever means they come to me. Then he said to those who stood by, Fetch something and give it to Mercy to smell, to stop her fainting; so they fetched her a bundle of myrrh, and a little while later she revived.

And now Christiana and her boys, and Mercy, were received by the Lord at the head of the way, and he spoke kindly to them. Then they said to him further, We are sorry for our sins, and beg our Lord’s pardon, and further instruction in what we must do.

I grant pardon, he said, by word and by deed: by word in the promise of forgiveness, by deed in the way I obtained it. Take the first from my lips with a kiss, and the other as it shall be revealed. Song 1:2; John 20:20.

Now I saw in my dream that he spoke many good words to them, which greatly gladdened them. He also took them up to the top of the gate and showed them by what deed they were saved; and told them besides that they would have that sight again as they went along the way, to their comfort.

So he left them a while in a summer parlor below, where they began to talk among themselves; and Christiana began like this: Oh, how glad I am that we have got in here.

Mercy: Well you may be; but I, of all of us, have cause to leap for joy.

Christiana: At one point, as I stood at the gate, because I had knocked and no one answered, I thought all our labor had been lost, especially when that ugly cur made such a heavy barking at us.

Mercy: But my worst fear came after I saw that you were taken into his favor and I was left behind. Now, I thought, what is written is fulfilled: “Two women will be grinding at the mill: one will be taken and the other left.” Matt 24:41. It was all I could do to keep from crying out, Undone! And I was afraid to knock any more; but when I looked up at what was written over the gate, I took courage. I also thought that I must either knock again or die; so I knocked, but I cannot tell how, for my spirit was now struggling between life and death.

Christiana: Can you not tell how you knocked? I am sure your knocks were so earnest that the very sound of them made me start; I thought I had never heard such knocking in all my life. I thought you would come in by force, or take the kingdom by storm. Matt 11:12.

Mercy: Alas! Who, in my case, could have done anything else? You saw that the door was shut on me, and there was a most cruel dog nearby. Who, I say, as faint-hearted as I was, would not have knocked with all their might? But please, what did my Lord say to my rudeness? Was he not angry with me?

Christiana: When he heard your banging, he gave a wonderfully innocent smile; I believe what you did pleased him well, for he showed no sign to the contrary. But I wonder in my heart why he keeps such a dog. If I had known about it before, I would not have had the heart to venture myself like this. But now we are in, we are in, and I am glad with all my heart.

Mercy: If you like, I will ask him next time he comes down why he keeps such a filthy cur in his yard; I hope he will not take it amiss.

Do so, said the children, and persuade him to hang him; for we are afraid he will bite us when we leave here.

So at last he came down to them again, and Mercy fell to the ground on her face before him, and worshiped, and said, “Let my Lord accept the sacrifice of praise which I now offer to him with the fruit of my lips.”

So he said to her, Peace be to you; stand up. But she stayed on her face, and said, “Righteous are You, O Lord, when I plead with You; yet let me talk with You about Your judgments.” Jer 12:1. Why do you keep so cruel a dog in your yard, at the sight of which women and children such as we are ready to flee from your gate in fear?

He answered and said, That dog has another owner. He is also kept shut up in another man’s ground; only my pilgrims hear his barking. He belongs to the castle you see over there in the distance, but he can come up to the walls of this place. He has frightened many an honest pilgrim from worse to better by the great voice of his roaring. Indeed, the one who owns him does not keep him out of any good will to me or mine, but to keep the pilgrims from coming to me, and to make them afraid to come and knock at this gate for entrance. Sometimes too he has broken out and has mauled some that I loved; but for the present I bear it all patiently. I also give my pilgrims timely help, so that they are not handed over to his power, to do with them whatever his doggish nature would prompt him to. But what, my purchased one! I believe that if you had known ever so much beforehand, you would not have been afraid of a dog. The beggars who go from door to door will, rather than lose the alms they hope for, run the risk of the bawling, barking, and biting too of a dog; and should a dog, a dog in another man’s yard, a dog whose barking I turn to the profit of pilgrims, keep anyone from coming to me? I deliver them from the lions, and my darling from the power of the dog. Ps 22:21, 22.

Mercy: Then Mercy said, I confess my ignorance; I spoke of what I did not understand; I acknowledge that you do all things well.

Christiana: Then Christiana began to talk about their journey, and to ask about the way. So he fed them and washed their feet, and set them in the way of his steps, just as he had dealt with her husband before.

THE SECOND STAGE

So I saw in my dream that they walked on their way, and the weather was very pleasant for them.

Then Christiana began to sing, saying,

“Blessed be the day that I began

A pilgrim for to be;

And blessed also be the man

That thereto moved me.”

“’Tis true, ’twas long ere I began

To seek to live for ever;

But now I run fast as I can:

’Tis better late than never.”

“Our tears to joy, our fears to faith,

Are turned, as we see;

Thus our beginning (as one saith)

Shows what our end will be.”

Now on the other side of the wall that fenced in the way up which Christiana and her companions were to go, there was a garden, and that garden belonged to the owner of that barking dog which was mentioned before. And some of the fruit trees that grew in that garden reached their branches over the wall; and as the fruit was ripe, those who found it picked it up and ate it, to their harm. So Christiana’s boys, as boys tend to do, were taken with the trees and with the fruit that hung on them, and they picked it and began to eat. Their mother scolded them for doing so; but the boys kept on all the same.

Well, she said, my sons, you transgress, for that fruit is not ours; but she did not know that it belonged to the enemy: I can tell you, if she had known, she would have been ready to die of fear. But that passed, and they went on their way. Now, when they had gone about two bow-shots from the place that led them into the way, they saw two very ill-favored ones coming down quickly to meet them. At that, Christiana and her friend Mercy covered themselves with their veils, and so kept on their journey; the children also went on ahead; so at last they met. Then the two who came down to meet them came right up to the women, as if they would embrace them; but Christiana said, Stand back, or go on peaceably as you should. Yet these two, like men who are deaf, paid no attention to Christiana’s words, but began to lay hands on them. At that Christiana grew very angry and kicked at them with her feet. Mercy also did what she could to push them off. Christiana again said to them, Stand back, and be gone, for we have no money to lose, since we are pilgrims, as you see, and pilgrims who live on the charity of our friends.

Ill-Favored Ones: Then one of the two men said, We are not attacking you for money; we have come out to tell you that if you will only grant one small request which we will ask, we will make women of you forever.

Christiana: Now Christiana, imagining what they meant, answered them again, We will neither listen to, nor heed, nor give in to anything you ask. We are in a hurry, and cannot stop; our business is a business of life and death. So once more she and her companion made a fresh attempt to get past them; but they blocked their way.

Ill-Favored Ones: And they said, We mean no harm to your lives; it is something else we want.

Christiana: Yes, said Christiana, you want us body and soul, for I know that is what you have come for; but we would rather die on the spot than allow ourselves to be brought into snares that would endanger our well-being hereafter. And with that they both screamed and cried, Murder! murder! and so put themselves under the laws that are provided for the protection of women. Deut 22:25–27. But the men still kept closing in on them, intending to overpower them. So they cried out again.

Now, as I said, they were not far from the gate by which they had come in, and their voices carried from where they were back to the gate; so some of the household came out, and knowing that it was Christiana’s voice, they hurried to help her. But by the time they came within sight of them, the women were in a very great struggle, and the children stood by crying. Then the one who came to their rescue called out to the ruffians, saying, What is this you are doing? Would you make my Lord’s people transgress? He also tried to seize them, but they escaped over the wall into the garden of the man to whom the great dog belonged; so the dog became their protector. This Reliever then came up to the women and asked them how they were. They answered, Thanks to your Prince, we are fairly well, only we have been rather frightened; we thank you also for coming to help us, for otherwise we would have been overcome.

Reliever: So, after a few more words, this Reliever said: I wondered very much, when you+ were received at the gate above, that, knowing you+ were only weak women, you+ did not ask the Lord for a conductor; then you+ might have avoided these troubles and dangers, for he would have granted you+ one.

Christiana: Alas! said Christiana, we were so taken up with our present blessing that we forgot the dangers to come. Besides, who could have thought that such wicked ones could be lurking so near the King’s palace? Indeed, it would have been well for us if we had asked our Lord for one; but since our Lord knew it would be for our good, I wonder that he did not send one along with us.

Reliever: It is not always necessary to grant things that are not asked for, because by doing so they may come to be little valued; but when the lack of a thing is felt, then in the eyes of the one who feels it, it gains the value that is properly its due, and so it will be used accordingly afterward. If my Lord had granted you a conductor, you would not have regretted that oversight of yours, in not asking for one, as much as you now have cause to. So all things work for good, and tend to make you more careful.

Christiana: Shall we go back to my Lord, and confess our folly, and ask for one?

Reliever: I will present your confession of your folly to him. You do not need to go back, for in all the places you will come to, you will find nothing lacking at all; for in every one of my Lord’s lodgings, which he has prepared to receive his pilgrims, there is enough to equip them against every kind of attack. But, as I said, He will be asked by them to do it for them. Ezek 36:37. And it is a poor thing that is not worth asking for. When he had said this, he went back to his place, and the pilgrims went on their way.

Mercy: Then Mercy said, What a sudden disappointment this is! I had counted on our being past all danger, and on never seeing sorrow again.

Christiana: Your innocence, my sister, Christiana said to Mercy, may excuse you a great deal; but as for me, my fault is all the greater, because I saw this danger before I came out of my door, and yet did not provide against it when provision could have been made. I am much to blame.

Mercy: Then Mercy said, How did you know this before you left home? Please explain this riddle to me.

Christiana: Why, I will tell you. Before I set foot out of doors, one night as I lay in my bed I had a dream about this; for I thought I saw two men, as like these as any two in the world could look, standing at the foot of my bed, plotting how they might prevent my salvation. I will tell you their very words. They said (it was when I was in my troubles), What shall we do with this woman? for she cries out, waking and sleeping, for forgiveness: if she is allowed to go on as she has begun, we will lose her as we have lost her husband. This, you know, might have made me take heed, and provide against it when provision could have been made.

Mercy: Well, said Mercy, just as this neglect has given us an occasion to see our own imperfections, so our Lord has taken the occasion to show the riches of his grace; for he, as we see, has followed us with kindness we did not ask for, and has delivered us from the hands of those who were stronger than we, of his sheer good pleasure.

So now, when they had talked a little longer, they drew near to a house which stood by the way, a house built for the relief of pilgrims, as you will find told more fully in the first part of these records of the Pilgrim’s Progress. So they went on toward the house (the house of the Interpreter); and when they came to the door, they heard a great deal of talk inside. Then they listened, and heard, as they thought, Christiana mentioned by name; for you must know that word of her and her children’s going on pilgrimage had gone on even ahead of her. And this pleased the household all the more, because they had heard that she was Christian’s wife, the woman who some time ago had been so unwilling to hear of going on pilgrimage. So they stood still and heard the good people inside praising her, little thinking that she stood at the door. At last Christiana knocked, as she had done at the gate before. Now, when she had knocked, a young woman came to the door, and opened it, and looked, and there were two women.

The Damsel: Then the young woman said to them, Whom do you wish to speak to here?

Christiana: Christiana answered, We understand that this is a privileged place for those who have become pilgrims, and we who are now at this door are pilgrims; so we ask that we may share in what we have now come for; for the day, as you see, is far spent, and we do not want to go any further tonight.

The Damsel: Please, what name may I give, so that I can tell it to my Lord inside?

Christiana: My name is Christiana; I was the wife of the pilgrim who traveled this way some years ago, and these are his four children. This maiden is my companion, and she is going on pilgrimage too.

Innocent: Then Innocent ran in (for that was her name), and said to those inside, Can you guess who is at the door? It is Christiana and her children, and her companion, all waiting to be welcomed here. Then they leaped for joy, and went and told their Master. So he came to the door, and looking at her, he said, Are you that Christiana whom Christian the good man left behind him when he took up a pilgrim’s life?

Christiana: I am the woman who was so hard-hearted as to make light of my husband’s troubles, and who left him to go on his journey alone, and these are his four children; but now I have come too, for I am convinced that no way is right but this.

Interpreter: Then that is fulfilled which is written of the man who said to his son, “Go and work today in my vineyard; and he said to his father, ‘I will not’; but afterward he repented and went.” Matt 21:29.

Christiana: Then Christiana said, So be it: Amen. God make it a true saying of me, and grant that I may be found by him at the last in peace, without spot, and blameless.

Interpreter: But why do you stand like this at the door? Come in, daughter of Abraham; we were talking about you just now, for the news reached us ahead of you that you had become a pilgrim. Come, children, come in; come, maiden, come in. So he brought them all into the house.

So when they were inside, they were invited to sit down and rest; and when they had done so, those who looked after the pilgrims in the house came into the room to see them. And one smiled, and another smiled, and they all smiled for joy that Christiana had become a pilgrim. They also looked at the boys, and stroked their faces with their hands as a sign of their kind welcome to them; they also treated Mercy lovingly, and made them all welcome in their Master’s house.

After a while, because supper was not ready, the Interpreter took them into his Significant Rooms, and showed them what Christian, Christiana’s husband, had seen some time before. So here they saw the man in the cage, the man and his dream, the man who cut his way through his enemies, and the picture of the biggest of them all, together with the rest of the things that had been so profitable to Christian then.

When this was done, and Christiana and her company had somewhat digested those things, the Interpreter takes them aside again, and brings them first into a room where there was a man who could look no way but down, with a muck-rake in his hand. There also stood one over his head with a celestial crown in his hand, offering him that crown for his muck-rake; but the man neither looked up nor paid any attention, but raked to himself the straws, the small sticks, and the dust of the floor.

Then Christiana said, I believe I know something of the meaning of this; for this is a picture of a man of this world: is it not, good sir?

Interpreter: You are right, he said; and his muck-rake shows his carnal mind. And when you see him paying attention to raking up straws and sticks, and the dust of the floor, rather than doing what He says who calls to him from above with the celestial crown in his hand, it is to show that to some people heaven is only a fable, and that the things here are counted the only things of substance. And when you were also shown that the man could look no way but down, it is to let you know that earthly things, when they take hold of men’s minds with power, carry their hearts right away from God.

Christiana: Then Christiana said, O deliver me from this muck-rake. Prov 30:8.

Interpreter: That prayer, said the Interpreter, has been laid aside so long that it is almost rusty: “Do not give me riches,” is hardly the prayer of one in ten thousand. Straws, and sticks, and dust are the great things most people go after now.

With that Christiana and Mercy wept, and said, It is, alas! too true.

When the Interpreter had shown them this, he took them into the very best room in the house; a very fine room it was. So he told them to look all around, and see if they could find anything profitable there. Then they looked round and round; for there was nothing to be seen but a very large spider on the wall, and that they overlooked.

Mercy: Then Mercy said, Sir, I see nothing; but Christiana said nothing.

Interpreter: But, said the Interpreter, look again. So she looked again, and said, There is nothing here but an ugly spider, hanging by her hands on the wall. Then he said, Is there only one spider in all this spacious room? Then the water stood in Christiana’s eyes, for she was a woman quick to understand; and she said, Yes, Lord, there are more here than one; yes, and spiders whose venom is far more deadly than hers. The Interpreter then looked kindly at her, and said, You have spoken the truth. This made Mercy blush, and the boys cover their faces; for they were all beginning now to understand the riddle.

Then the Interpreter said again, “The spider takes hold with her hands,” as you see, “and is in kings’ palaces.” Prov 30:28. And why is this recorded, if not to show you that however full of the venom of sin you may be, you may still, by the hand of Faith, lay hold of and dwell in the best room that belongs to the King’s house above?

Christiana: I did think something of this, said Christiana; but I could not make it out at all. I thought that we were like spiders, and that we looked like ugly creatures, however fine the room we were in; but that by this spider, that venomous and ill-favored creature, we were to learn how to exercise faith, that never came into my thoughts; and yet she has taken hold with her hands, and, as I see, lives in the best room in the house. God has made nothing in vain.

Then they all seemed to be glad; but the water stood in their eyes; yet they looked at one another, and also bowed before the Interpreter.

He took them into another room, where there was a hen with her chickens, and told them to watch for a while. So one of the chickens went to the trough to drink, and every time she drank she lifted up her head and her eyes toward heaven. See, he said, what this little chick does, and learn from her to acknowledge where your mercies come from, by receiving them with looking up. Watch again, he said, and look: so they paid attention, and saw that the hen dealt with her chickens in four ways: 1. She had a common call, and that she has all day long. 2. She had a special call, and that she had only at times. 3. She had a brooding note. Matt 23:37. And, 4. She had an outcry.

Now, he said, compare this hen to your King, and these chickens to his obedient ones; for, matching her, he himself has his ways of dealing with his people. By his common call he gives nothing; by his special call he always has something to give; he also has a brooding voice, for those who are under his wing; and he has an outcry, to give the alarm when he sees the enemy coming. I choose, my darlings, to lead you into the room where such things are, because you are women, and they are easy for you.

Christiana: And, sir, said Christiana, please let us see some more. So he took them into the slaughterhouse, where a butcher was killing a sheep; and look, the sheep was quiet, and took her death patiently. Then the Interpreter said, You must learn from this sheep to suffer and to put up with wrongs without grumbling and complaining. See how quietly she takes her death, and without objecting she lets her skin be pulled over her ears. Your King calls you his sheep.

After this he led them into his garden, where there was a great variety of flowers; and he said, Do you see all these? Christiana said, Yes. Then he said again, See, the flowers differ in height, in quality, and color, and smell, and virtue; and some are better than others; also, where the gardener has set them, there they stand, and they do not quarrel with one another.

Next he took them into his field, which he had sown with wheat and other grain; but when they looked, the tops of all of it were cut off, and only the straw was left. He said again, This ground was manured, and plowed, and sown, but what shall we do with the crop? Then Christiana said, Burn some, and make muck of the rest. Then the Interpreter said again, Fruit, you see, is what you look for; and for lack of it you condemn the crop to the fire, and to be trampled underfoot by men: beware that in this you do not condemn yourselves.

Then, as they were coming in from outside, they spotted a little robin with a great spider in his mouth. So the Interpreter said, Look here. So they looked, and Mercy wondered at it, but Christiana said, What a discredit this is to such a pretty little bird as the robin redbreast, a bird, too, that more than many others loves to keep a kind of friendly company with men! I had thought they lived on crumbs of bread, or on other such harmless things: I like him less than I did.

The Interpreter then replied, This robin is an emblem that pictures some professing Christians very well; for to look at they are, like this robin, pretty in song, color, and bearing. They also seem to have a very great love for sincere professing Christians, and above all others to want to keep company with them and be with them, as if they could live on the good man’s crumbs. They also pretend that this is why they frequent the houses of the godly and the ordinances of the Lord; but when they are by themselves, like the robin, they can catch and gobble up spiders; they can change their diet, drink iniquity, and swallow down sin like water.

So, when they had come back into the house, because supper was still not ready, Christiana again asked the Interpreter to show or tell them some other things that are profitable.

Then the Interpreter began, and said, The fatter the sow is, the more she wants the mire; the fatter the ox is, the more friskily he goes to the slaughter; and the healthier the lustful man is, the more prone he is to evil. There is a desire in women to dress neat and fine; and it is a lovely thing to be adorned with that which in God’s sight is of great price. It is easier to keep watch a night or two than to sit up a whole year together: so it is easier for one to begin to profess well than to hold out as he should to the end. Every shipmaster in a storm will willingly throw overboard what is of least value in the ship; but who will throw the best out first? No one but he who does not fear God. One leak will sink a ship, and one sin will destroy a sinner. He who forgets his friend is ungrateful to him; but he who forgets his Savior is unmerciful to himself. He who lives in sin, and looks for happiness hereafter, is like the man who sows weeds and expects to fill his barn with wheat or barley. If a man would live well, let him bring his last day close to him, and keep it always as his companion. Whispering, and change of thoughts, prove that sin is in the world. If the world, which God thinks little of, is valued so highly by men, what is heaven, which God commends? If we are so unwilling to let go of the life that comes with so many troubles, what is the life above? Everybody will praise the goodness of men; but who is there that is moved as he should be by the goodness of God? We seldom sit down to a meal without eating and leaving some over. So there is in Jesus Christ more merit and righteousness than the whole world needs.

When the Interpreter had finished, he takes them out into his garden again, and brought them to a tree whose inside was all rotten and gone, and yet it grew and had leaves. Then Mercy said, What does this mean? This tree, he said, whose outside is fair and whose inside is rotten, is what many may be compared to who are in the garden of God; who with their mouths speak loftily on God’s behalf, but in fact will do nothing for him; whose leaves are fair, but whose heart is good for nothing but to be tinder for the devil’s tinderbox.

Now supper was ready, the table spread, and everything set on the table; so they sat down and ate, after one of them had given thanks. And the Interpreter usually entertained those who stayed with him with music at meals; so the musicians played. There was also one who sang, and a very fine voice he had. His song was this:

““The Lord is only my support,

And he that doth me feed;

How can I then want any thing

Whereof I stand in need?””

When the song and music were over, the Interpreter asked Christiana what it was that had first moved her to take up a pilgrim’s life like this. Christiana answered, First, the loss of my husband came into my mind, and I grieved over it from my heart; but all that was only natural affection. Then after that my husband’s troubles and pilgrimage came into my mind, and also how churlishly I had treated him over it. So guilt took hold of my mind, and would have drawn me into the pond, but just in time I had a dream of my husband’s well-being, and a letter was sent me by the King of the country where my husband lives, inviting me to come to him. The dream and the letter together so worked on my mind that they drove me to this way.

Interpreter: But did you meet with no opposition before you set out from home?

Christiana: Yes, a neighbor of mine, one Mrs. Timorous: she was related to the man who would have persuaded my husband to go back for fear of the lions. She also called me a fool for what she called my desperate venture; she also used every argument she could to discourage me from it, the hardships and troubles that my husband met with on the way; but I got over all this fairly well. But a dream I had of two ill-looking ones, who I thought were plotting how to make me fail in my journey, has troubled me a great deal: yes, it still runs in my mind, and makes me afraid of everyone I meet, in case they are meeting me to do me harm, and to turn me out of my way. Yes, I may tell my Lord, though I would not want everybody to know of it, that between here and the gate by which we got into the way, we were both so violently assaulted that we were made to cry out murder; and the two who assaulted us were like the two that I saw in my dream.

Then the Interpreter said, Your beginning is good; your latter end shall greatly increase. Then he turned to Mercy, and said to her, And what moved you to come here, sweetheart?

Mercy: Then Mercy blushed and trembled, and for a while said nothing.

Interpreter: Then he said, Do not be afraid; only believe, and speak your mind.

Mercy: So she began, and said, Truly, sir, my lack of experience is what makes me want to keep silent, and it is also what fills me with fears of falling short in the end. I cannot tell of visions and dreams, as my friend Christiana can; nor do I know what it is to mourn for having refused the advice of those of my family who were good.

Interpreter: What was it, then, dear heart, that has persuaded you to do as you have done?

Mercy: Why, when our friend here was packing up to leave our town, another woman and I happened to go to see her. So we knocked at the door and went in. When we were inside, and saw what she was doing, we asked her what she meant by it. She said she had been sent for to go to her husband; and then she up and told us how she had seen him in a dream, living in an exquisite place among immortals, wearing a crown, playing on a harp, eating and drinking at his Prince’s table, and singing praises to him for bringing him there, and so on. Now, I thought, while she was telling us these things, my heart burned within me. And I said in my heart, If this is true, I will leave my father and my mother, and the land of my birth, and will, if I may, go along with Christiana. So I asked her more about the truth of these things, and whether she would let me go with her; for I saw now that there was no living in our town any longer without the danger of ruin. But still I came away with a heavy heart; not because I was unwilling to come away, but because so many of my family were left behind. And I have come with all the desire of my heart, and will go, if I may, with Christiana to her husband and his King.

Interpreter: Your setting out is good, for you have believed the truth; you are a Ruth, who, for the love she bore to Naomi and to the Lord her God, left father and mother and the land of her birth, to come out and go with a people she had not known before. “May the Lord repay your work, and may you receive a rich reward from the Lord, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have taken refuge.” Ruth 2:11, 12.

Now supper was over, and preparations were made for bed; the women were each given a bed to themselves, and the boys slept by themselves. Now when Mercy was in bed, she could not sleep for joy, because her fears of missing at the last were now removed further from her than they had ever been before. So she lay blessing and praising God, who had shown her such favor.

In the morning they rose with the sun, and got ready to leave; but the Interpreter wanted them to stay a while; for, he said, you must go from here in proper order. Then he said to the young woman who had first opened the door to them, Take them into the garden to the bath, and there wash them and make them clean from the dirt they have gathered by traveling. Then the young woman Innocent took them and led them into the garden, and brought them to the bath; and she told them that there they must wash and be clean, for that was what her Master wanted the women to do who called at his house on their way on pilgrimage. Then they went in and washed, yes, they and the boys and all; and they came out of that bath not only sweet and clean, but also much refreshed and strengthened in their joints. So when they came in, they looked a great deal fairer than when they went out to the washing.

When they had come back from the bath in the garden, the Interpreter took them and looked at them, and said to them, “As fair as the moon.” Then he called for the seal with which those who were washed in his bath used to be sealed. So the seal was brought, and he set his mark on them, so that they might be known in the places where they were still to go. Now the seal was the contents and sum of the passover which the children of Israel ate, Exod 13:8–10, when they came out of the land of Egypt; and the mark was set between their eyes. This seal added greatly to their beauty, for it was an ornament to their faces. It also added to their gravity, and made their faces more like the faces of angels.

Then the Interpreter said again to the young woman who waited on these women, Go into the vestry, and bring out garments for these people. So she went and brought out white clothing, and laid it down before him; and he commanded them to put it on: it was fine linen, white and clean. When the women were dressed like this, they seemed to fill one another with awe; for none of them could see in herself the glory which she could see in the others. Now therefore they began to think more highly of each other than of themselves. For, You are fairer than I am, said one; and, You are lovelier than I am, said another. The children also stood amazed to see how they had been transformed.

THE THIRD STAGE

The Interpreter then called for one of his servants, a man named Great-heart, and told him to take a sword, and helmet, and shield; and, Take these daughters of mine, he said, and lead them to the house called Beautiful, where they will rest next. So he took his weapons and went before them; and the Interpreter said, God speed. Those who belonged to the household also sent them off with many a good wish. So they went on their way, and sang,

“This place has been our second stage:

Here we have heard, and seen

Those good things, that from age to age

To others hid have been.”

“The dunghill-raker, spider, hen,

The chicken, too, to me

Have taught a lesson: let me then

Conformed to it be.”

“The butcher, garden, and the field,

The robin and his bait,

Also the rotten tree, all yield

Me argument of weight,”

“To move me, then, to watch and pray,

To strive to be sincere;

To take my cross up day by day,

And serve the Lord with fear.”

Now I saw in my dream that they went on, with Great-Heart in front of them. So they went on, and came to the place where Christian’s burden fell off his back and tumbled into a sepulcher. Here they stopped for a while, and here they also blessed God. Now, said Christiana, I remember what we were told at the gate, namely, that we would have pardon by word and deed: by word, that is, by the promise; by deed, that is, in the way it was obtained. What the promise is, I know something of; but what it is to have pardon by deed, or in the way it was obtained, Mr. Great-Heart, I suppose you know; so, if you please, let us hear you speak about it.

Mr. Great-Heart: Pardon by the deed done is pardon obtained by someone for another who needs it; not by the person pardoned, but in the way, says another, in which I have obtained it. So then, to speak to the question more fully, the pardon that you, and Mercy, and these boys have attained was obtained by another; that is, by him who let you in at the gate. And he has obtained it in this double way: he has performed righteousness to cover you, and shed his blood to wash you in.

Christiana: But if he parts with his righteousness to us, what will he have for himself?

Mr. Great-Heart: He has more righteousness than you need, or than he needs himself.

Christiana: Please show us how that can be.

Mr. Great-Heart: With all my heart: but first I must lay this down, that he of whom we are now about to speak is one who has no equal. He has two natures in one person, plain to be distinguished, impossible to be divided. To each of these natures a righteousness belongs, and each righteousness is essential to that nature; so that one could as easily make that nature cease to exist as separate its justice or righteousness from it. So we are not made partakers of these righteousnesses in such a way that they, or any of them, should be put on us so that we might be made just and live by them. Besides these, there is a righteousness which this person has as these two natures are joined in one. And this is not the righteousness of the Godhead, as distinguished from the manhood, nor the righteousness of the manhood, as distinguished from the Godhead; but a righteousness which lies in the union of both natures, and may properly be called the righteousness that is essential to his being prepared by God and fitted for the mediatory office with which he was to be entrusted. If he parts with his first righteousness, he parts with his Godhead; if he parts with his second righteousness, he parts with the purity of his manhood; if he parts with his third, he parts with the perfection that fits him for the office of mediation. He has therefore another righteousness, which lies in performance, or obedience to a revealed will; and that is what he puts on sinners, and that is what covers their sins. So he says, “Just as through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous.” Rom 5:19.

Christiana: But are the other righteousnesses of no use to us?

Mr. Great-Heart: Yes; for though they are essential to his natures and office, and cannot be imparted to another, yet it is by virtue of them that the righteousness that justifies is efficacious for that purpose. The righteousness of his Godhead gives power to his obedience; the righteousness of his manhood gives his obedience the capacity to justify; and the righteousness that lies in the union of these two natures to his office gives that righteousness authority to do the work for which it was ordained.

So then here is a righteousness that Christ, as God, has no need of, for he is God without it. Here is a righteousness that Christ, as man, has no need of to make him so, for he is perfect man without it. Again, here is a righteousness that Christ, as God-man, has no need of, for he is perfectly so without it. Here then is a righteousness that Christ, as God and as God-man, has no need of with regard to himself, and therefore he can spare it; a justifying righteousness that he does not need for himself, and therefore he gives it away. That is why it is called the gift of righteousness. Since Christ Jesus the Lord has put himself under the law, this righteousness must be given away; for the law binds the one who is under it not only to do justly, but to practice charity. Rom 5:17. So he must, or ought to by the law, if he has two coats, give one to him who has none. Now, our Lord indeed has two coats, one for himself, and one to spare; so he freely gives one to those who have none. And so, Christiana and Mercy, and the rest of you who are here, your pardon comes by deed, or by the work of another man. Your Lord Christ is the one who worked, and he has given away what he worked for to the next poor beggar he meets.

But again, for pardon by deed, something must be paid to God as a price, as well as something prepared to cover us with. Sin has handed us over to the just curse of a righteous law: now from this curse we must be justified by way of redemption, a price being paid for the harm we have done; and this is by the blood of your Lord, who came and stood in your place and stead, and died your death for your transgressions. In this way he has ransomed you from your transgressions by blood, and covered your polluted and deformed souls with righteousness, Rom 8:34; and for the sake of this, God passes over you and will not hurt you when he comes to judge the world. Gal 3:13.

Christiana: This is splendid! Now I see that there was something to be learned from our being pardoned by word and deed. Good Mercy, let us work hard to keep this in mind; and, my children, you remember it too. But, sir, was it not this that made my good Christian’s burden fall from his shoulder, and made him give three leaps for joy?

Mr. Great-Heart: Yes, it was believing this that cut the strings that could not be cut by any other means; and it was to give him proof of the power of this that he was allowed to carry his burden to the cross.

Christiana: I thought so; for though my heart was light and joyful before, it is ten times more light and joyful now. And I am persuaded by what I have felt, though I have felt only a little as yet, that if the most burdened man in the world were here, and saw and believed as I now do, it would make his heart all the more merry and glad.

Mr. Great-Heart: The sight and consideration of these things bring us not only comfort and the easing of a burden, but also a tender affection, born in us by them: for who, if he thinks even once that pardon comes not only by promise but in this way, can help being moved by the way and means of his redemption, and so by the man who has worked it out for him?

Christiana: True; I think it makes my heart bleed to think that he should bleed for me. Oh, you loving One! Oh, you blessed One! You deserve to have me; you have bought me. You deserve to have all of me; you have paid for me ten thousand times more than I am worth. No wonder this made the tears stand in my husband’s eyes, and made him trudge on so nimbly. I am sure he wished I were with him; but, vile wretch that I was, I let him come all alone. Oh, Mercy, if only your father and mother were here; yes, and Mrs. Timorous too: yes, I wish now with all my heart that even Madam Wanton were here too. Surely, surely, their hearts would be moved; and neither the fear of the one nor the powerful lusts of the other could persuade them to go home again and refuse to become good pilgrims.

Mr. Great-Heart: You speak now in the warmth of your feelings; do you think it will always be like this with you? Besides, this is not given to everyone, nor to everyone who saw your Jesus bleed. There were some who stood by and saw the blood run from his heart to the ground, and yet were so far from this that instead of mourning, they laughed at him, and instead of becoming his disciples, they hardened their hearts against him. So all that you have, my daughters, you have by a special impression made by divine meditation on what I have said to you. Remember that you were told that the hen, by her common call, gives no food to her chickens. So you have this by a special grace.

Now I saw in my dream that they went on until they came to the place where Simple, and Sloth, and Presumption lay asleep when Christian went by on pilgrimage; and there they were, hanging in chains a little way off on the other side.

Mercy: Then Mercy said to their guide and conductor, Who are these three men, and why are they hanged there?

Mr. Great-Heart: These three were men of very bad character; they had no wish to be pilgrims themselves, and whoever they could, they hindered. They were sloth and folly themselves, and whoever they could persuade they made like themselves, and also taught them to presume that they would come out well at last. They were asleep when Christian went by; and now, as you go by, they are hanged.

Mercy: But could they persuade anyone to think as they did?

Mr. Great-Heart: Yes, they turned several out of the way. There was Slow-pace, whom they persuaded to do as they did. They also won over one Short-wind, one No-heart, one Linger-after-Lust, and one Sleepy-head, and a young woman whose name was Dull, to turn out of the way and become like them. Besides, they spread a bad report of your Lord, persuading others that he was a hard taskmaster. They also spread an evil report of the good Land, saying it was not half as good as some made out. They also began to slander his servants, and to count the best of them meddling, troublesome busybodies. Further, they would call the bread of God husks; the comforts of his children, fancies; the travel and labor of pilgrims, things to no purpose.

Christiana: Why, said Christiana, if they were like that, they will never be mourned by me: they have only what they deserve; and I think it is good that they hang so near the highway, so that others may see and take warning. But would it not have been good if their crimes had been engraved on some plate of iron or brass, and left here where they did harm, as a warning to other bad men?

Mr. Great-Heart: So they are, as you can see if you go a little way toward the wall.

Mercy: No, no; let them hang, and their names rot, and their crimes live forever against them. I think it a great favor that they were hanged before we came here: otherwise who knows what they might have done to poor women like us? Then she turned it into a song, saying,

““Now then you+ three hang there, and be a sign

To all who will against the truth combine.

And let him who comes after fear this end,

If to the pilgrims he is not a friend.

And you, my soul, of all such men beware,

Who to holiness opponents are.””

So they went on till they came to the foot of the hill Difficulty, where again the good Mr. Great-Heart took the opportunity to tell them what happened there when Christian himself went by. So he took them first to the spring. Look, he said, this is the spring that Christian drank from before he went up this hill; and then it was clear and good, but now it is muddied by the feet of some who do not want pilgrims to quench their thirst here. Ezek 34:18, 19. At this Mercy said, And why so envious, I wonder? But, said their guide, it will do, if it is drawn up and put into a vessel that is clean and good; for then the dirt will sink to the bottom, and the water will come out clearer by itself. So this is what Christiana and her companions had to do. They drew it up, and put it into an earthenware pot, and let it stand till the dirt had sunk to the bottom, and then they drank it.

Next he showed them the two by-ways at the foot of the hill, where Formality and Hypocrisy lost themselves. And, he said, these are dangerous paths. Two were lost here when Christian came by; and although, as you see, these ways have since been blocked with chains, posts, and a ditch, yet there are those who will choose to risk going this way rather than take the trouble to go up this hill.

Christiana: “The way of transgressors is hard.” Prov 13:15. It is a wonder that they can get into these ways without danger of breaking their necks.

Mr. Great-Heart: They will risk it: yes, if at any time any of the King’s servants happen to see them, and call to them, and tell them that they are on the wrong road, and warn them of the danger, then they rail at them in answer, and say, “As for the word you have spoken to us in the name of the King, we will not listen to you! Instead, we will do everything we vowed to do.” Jer 44:16, 17. Indeed, if you look a little further, you will see that these ways have been marked as a warning plainly enough, not only by these posts, and ditch, and chain, but also by being hedged up: yet they will choose to go that way.

Christiana: They are idle; they do not like taking trouble; an uphill road is unpleasant to them. So it is fulfilled in them as it is written, “The way of the slothful is like a hedge of thorns.” Prov 15:19. Yes, they would rather choose to walk on a snare than go up this hill, and the rest of this way to the city.

Then they set off, and began to go up the hill, and up the hill they went. But before they got to the top, Christiana began to pant, and said, I dare say this hill leaves you out of breath; no wonder if those who love their ease more than their souls choose a smoother way for themselves.

Then Mercy said, I must sit down; and the youngest of the children began to cry. Come, come, said Great-Heart, do not sit down here; for a little higher up is the Prince’s arbor. Then he took the little boy by the hand, and led him up to it.

When they had come to the arbor, they were very glad to sit down, for they were all in a sweltering heat. Then Mercy said, “How sweet is rest to those who labor.” Matt 11:28; and how good the Prince of pilgrims is to provide such resting-places for them! I have heard a great deal about this arbor, but I have never seen it before. But here let us beware of sleeping; for, as I have heard, it cost poor Christian dearly.

Then Mr. Great-Heart said to the little ones, Come, my pretty boys, how are you getting on? What do you think of going on pilgrimage now? Sir, said the youngest, I had almost lost heart; but I thank you for lending me a hand when I needed it. And I remember now what my mother has told me, that the way to heaven is like a ladder, and the way to hell is like going down a hill. But I would rather go up the ladder to life than down the hill to death.

Then Mercy said, But the proverb is, “Going down the hill is easy.” But James said (for that was his name), The day is coming when, in my opinion, going down the hill will be the hardest of all. That’s a good boy, said his master; you have given her the right answer. Then Mercy smiled, but the little boy blushed.

Christiana: Come, said Christiana, will you eat a bite to sweeten your mouths, while you sit here to rest your legs? for I have here a piece of pomegranate which Mr. Interpreter put into my hand just as I came out of his door; he also gave me a piece of honeycomb, and a little bottle of spirits. I thought he gave you something, said Mercy, because he called you aside. Yes, so he did, said the other; but, said Christiana, it shall still be as I said it should be when we first left home: you shall share in all the good that I have, because you so willingly became my companion. Then she gave to them, and they ate, both Mercy and the boys. And Christiana said to Mr. Great-Heart, Sir, will you do as we do? But he answered, You are going on pilgrimage, and I will soon go back; may what you have do you much good: at home I eat the same every day.

THE FOURTH STAGE

Now when they had eaten and drunk, and had chatted a little longer, their guide said to them, The day is wearing on; if you think it best, let us get ready to be going. So they got up to go, and the little boys went ahead; but Christiana forgot to take her bottle of spirits with her, so she sent her little boy back to get it. Then Mercy said, I think this is a place for losing things: here Christian lost his roll, and here Christiana left her bottle behind her. Sir, what is the cause of this? Their guide answered, The cause is sleep, or forgetfulness: some sleep when they should keep awake, and some forget when they should remember; and this is the very reason why, at the resting-places, some pilgrims often come off losers in some things. Pilgrims should watch, and remember what they have already received, in the midst of their greatest enjoyments; but because they fail to do so, their rejoicing often ends in tears, and their sunshine in a cloud: witness the story of Christian at this place.

When they had come to the place where Mistrust and Timorous met Christian, to persuade him to go back for fear of the lions, they saw what looked like a stage, and in front of it, towards the road, a broad plaque with some verses written on it, and underneath, the reason why that stage had been put up in that place. The verses were these:

““Let him who sees this stage take care

Of both his heart and tongue;

Lest, if he doesn’t, here he’ll fare

As some, long since, have done.””

The words underneath the verses were, “This stage was built as a place to punish those who, through timidity or mistrust, are afraid to go further on pilgrimage. Also, on this stage both Mistrust and Timorous were burned through the tongue with a hot iron, for trying to hinder Christian on his journey.”

Then Mercy said, This is very like the saying of the Beloved: “What will He do to you, and what will be added to you, O deceitful tongue? Sharp arrows will come from the warrior, with burning coals of the broom tree!” Ps 120:3, 4.

So they went on till they came within sight of the lions. Now Mr. Great-Heart was a strong man, so he was not afraid of a lion; but when they had come up to the place where the lions were, the boys, who had been going in front, were now glad to shrink behind, for they were afraid of the lions; so they stepped back and went behind. At this their guide smiled and said, What is this, my boys? Do you love to go in front when no danger is near, and love to come behind as soon as the lions appear?

Now, as they went on, Mr. Great-heart drew his sword, meaning to make a way for the pilgrims in spite of the lions. Then someone appeared who, it seems, had taken it on himself to back the lions; and he said to the pilgrims’ guide, What has brought you here? Now the name of that man was Grim, or Bloody-man, because he killed pilgrims; and he was of the race of the giants.

Mr. Great-Heart: Then the pilgrims’ guide said, These women and children are going on pilgrimage, and this is the way they must go; and go it they shall, in spite of you and the lions.

Grim: This is not their way, and they shall not go on it. I have come out to stand against them, and to that end I will back the lions.

Now, to tell the truth, because of the fierceness of the lions, and the grim bearing of the man who backed them, this way had lately been little used, and was almost grown over with grass.

Christiana: Then Christiana said, Though the highways have been deserted until now, and though travelers have in times past been made to walk through by-paths, it must not be so now that I have arisen, now that I have arisen a mother in Israel. Judg 5:6, 7.

Grim: Then he swore by the lions that it would be so; and so he told them to turn aside, for they would not be allowed to pass there.

But Great-Heart their guide went at Grim first, and laid on him so heavily with his sword that he forced him to retreat.

Grim: Then the one who was trying to back the lions said, Will you kill me on my own ground?

Mr. Great-Heart: It is the King’s highway that we are on, and it is on this road that you have placed the lions; but these women and these children, though weak, shall keep on their way in spite of your lions. And with that he gave him another downward blow, and brought him to his knees. With this blow he also broke the giant’s helmet, and with the next he cut off an arm. Then the giant roared so hideously that his voice frightened the women, and yet they were glad to see him lie sprawling on the ground. Now the lions were chained, and so could do nothing by themselves. So when old Grim, who had meant to back them, was dead, Mr. Great-Heart said to the pilgrims, Come now, and follow me, and no harm shall come to you from the lions. So they went on, but the women trembled as they passed by them; the boys also looked as if they would die; but they all got by without further harm.

Now, when they came within sight of the Porter’s lodge, they soon reached it; but they hurried all the more after this to get there, because it is dangerous to travel there at night. So when they had come to the gate, the guide knocked, and the Porter called out, Who is there? But as soon as the guide had said, It is I, the Porter knew his voice and came down, for the guide had often come there before as a conductor of pilgrims. When he had come down, he opened the gate; and seeing the guide standing just in front of it (for he did not see the women, because they were behind him), he said to him, Why, Mr. Great-Heart, what is your business here so late at night? I have brought some pilgrims here, he said, where by my Lord’s command they must lodge. I would have been here some time ago, if I had not been opposed by the giant who used to back the lions. But after a long and tedious fight with him, I have cut him down, and have brought the pilgrims here in safety.

The Porter: Won’t you come in, and stay till morning?

Mr. Great-Heart: No, I will go back to my Lord tonight.

Christiana: Oh, sir, I cannot bring myself to be willing for you to leave us in our pilgrimage: you have been so faithful and loving to us, you have fought so bravely for us, you have been so hearty in counseling us, that I shall never forget your kindness to us.

Mercy: Then Mercy said, Oh, if only we could have your company to our journey’s end! How can poor women like us hold out on a road as full of troubles as this one is, without a friend and defender?

James: Then James, the youngest of the boys, said, Please, sir, let us persuade you to go with us and help us, because we are so weak, and the way is so dangerous.

Mr. Great-Heart: I am at my Lord’s command; if he assigns me to be your guide all the way, I will gladly attend you. But here you failed at first; for when he told me to come this far with you, you should then have begged him to let me go all the way with you, and he would have granted your request. However, for now I must leave you; and so, good Christiana, Mercy, and my fine children, farewell.

Then the Porter, Mr. Watchful, asked Christiana about her country and her family. And she said, I came from the city of Destruction. I am a widow, and my husband is dead; his name was Christian, the pilgrim. What! said the Porter, was he your husband? Yes, she said, and these are his children; and this, pointing to Mercy, is one of my townswomen. Then the Porter rang his bell, as he usually does at such times, and one of the young women, whose name was Humble-Mind, came to the door; and the Porter said to her, Go and tell them inside that Christiana, the wife of Christian, and her children have come here on pilgrimage. So she went in and told them. But oh, what a noise of gladness there was inside when the young woman had barely let that drop from her lips!

So they hurried to the Porter, for Christiana was still standing at the door. Then some of the gravest of them said to her, Come in, Christiana, come in, you wife of that good man; come in, you blessed woman, come in, with all who are with you. So she went in, and those who were her children and companions followed her. When they had gone in, they were taken into a large room, where they were asked to sit down; so they sat down, and the heads of the house were called to see and welcome the guests. Then they came in, and when they understood who the guests were, they greeted each other with a kiss, and said, Welcome, you+ vessels of the grace of God; welcome to us, your+ friends.

Now, because it was rather late, and because the pilgrims were weary from their journey, and also faint from the sight of the fight and of the terrible lions, they wanted to get ready for bed as soon as they could. No, said those of the household, first refresh yourselves with a morsel of food; for they had prepared a lamb for them, with the customary sauce that goes with it, Exod 12:21; John 1:29; for the Porter had heard of their coming beforehand, and had told those inside. So when they had eaten supper, and ended their prayer with a psalm, they asked if they might go to bed.

But let us, said Christiana, if we may be so bold as to choose, be in the room that was my husband’s when he was here; so they took them up there, and they all slept in one room. When they had lain down, Christiana and Mercy talked together about things that suited the occasion.

Christiana: Little did I think, back when my husband went on pilgrimage, that I would ever follow him.

Mercy: And you thought just as little of lying in his bed, and resting in his room, as you are doing now.

Christiana: And still less did I ever think of seeing his face with comfort, and of worshiping the Lord the King with him; and yet now I believe I will.
