Mercy: Listen, don’t you hear a noise?

Christiana: Yes, it is, I believe, the sound of music, for joy that we are here.

Mercy: Wonderful! Music in the house, music in the heart, and music also in heaven, for joy that we are here! They talked like this for a while, and then went to sleep.

So in the morning when they were awake, Christiana said to Mercy, What made you laugh in your sleep last night? I suppose you were dreaming.

Mercy: So I was, and a sweet dream it was; but are you sure I laughed?

Christiana: Yes, you laughed heartily; but please, Mercy, tell me your dream.

Mercy: I was dreaming that I sat all alone in a solitary place, bemoaning the hardness of my heart. Now I had not sat there long before, as I thought, many people gathered around me to look at me, and to hear what it was that I said. So they listened, and I went on bemoaning the hardness of my heart. At this, some of them laughed at me, some called me a fool, and some began to push me around. With that, I thought I looked up and saw someone with wings coming towards me. He came straight to me and said, Mercy, what is wrong? Now when he had heard me make my complaint, he said, Peace be to you; he also wiped my eyes with his handkerchief, and clothed me in silver and gold. Ezek 16:8–11. He put a chain around my neck, and earrings in my ears, and a beautiful crown on my head. Then he took me by the hand and said, Mercy, come after me. So he went up, and I followed until we came to a golden gate. Then he knocked; and when those inside had opened it, the man went in, and I followed him up to a throne, on which one sat; and he said to me, Welcome, daughter. The place looked bright and twinkling, like the stars, or rather like the sun, and I thought that I saw your husband there; so I awoke from my dream. But did I laugh?

Christiana: Laugh! Yes, and well you might, to see yourself so well. For you must let me tell you that it was a good dream; and that, as you have begun to find the first part true, so you will find the second true at last. “God speaks in one way and in another, yet no one notices: in a dream, in a vision in the night, when deep sleep falls upon men as they slumber on their beds.” Job 33:14, 15. We do not need to lie awake in bed to talk with God; he can visit us while we sleep, and make us hear his voice then. Our heart often wakes when we sleep, and God can speak to it, by words, by proverbs, by signs and similitudes, as well as if one were awake.

Mercy: Well, I am glad of my dream; for I hope before long to see it come true, and make me laugh again.

Christiana: I think it is now high time to get up, and to find out what we are to do.

Mercy: Please, if they invite us to stay a while, let us gladly accept the offer. I am all the more willing to stay here a while, to get better acquainted with these young women: I think Prudence, Piety, and Charity have very lovely and sober faces.

Christiana: We will see what they do.

So when they were up and dressed, they came down, and asked one another how they had slept, and whether it had been comfortable or not.

Mercy: Very good, said Mercy: it was one of the best nights’ lodging I have ever had in my life.

Then Prudence and Piety said, If you can be persuaded to stay here a while, you shall have whatever the house can provide.

Charity: Yes, and very gladly, said Charity. So they agreed, and stayed there about a month or more, and did one another much good. And because Prudence wanted to see how Christiana had brought up her children, she asked her permission to catechize them. So she gave her consent freely. Then Prudence began with the youngest, whose name was James.

Prudence: And she said, Come, James, can you tell me who made you?

James: God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit.

Prudence: Good boy. And can you tell me who saved you?

James: God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit.

Prudence: Good boy again. But how does God the Father save you?

James: By his grace.

Prudence: How does God the Son save you?

James: By his righteousness, death and blood, and life.

Prudence: And how does God the Holy Spirit save you?

James: By his illumination, by his renovation, and by his preservation.

Then Prudence said to Christiana, You are to be commended for bringing up your children like this. I suppose I need not ask the others these questions, since the youngest of them can answer them so well. So I will now turn to the next youngest.

Prudence: Then she said, Come, Joseph (for his name was Joseph), will you let me catechize you?

Joseph: With all my heart.

Prudence: What is man?

Joseph: A reasonable creature, made so by God, as my brother said.

Prudence: What does this word, saved, imply?

Joseph: That man, by sin, has brought himself into a state of captivity and misery.

Prudence: What is implied by his being saved by the Trinity?

Joseph: That sin is so great and mighty a tyrant that no one can pull us out of its clutches but God; and that God is so good and loving to man as actually to pull him out of this miserable state.

Prudence: What is God’s purpose in saving poor men?

Joseph: The glorifying of his name, of his grace and justice, etc., and the everlasting happiness of his creature.

Prudence: Who are those who will be saved?

Joseph: Those who accept his salvation.

Prudence: Good boy, Joseph; your mother has taught you well, and you have listened to what she has told you.

Then Prudence said to Samuel, who was the second eldest,

Prudence: Come, Samuel, are you willing for me to catechize you?

Samuel: Yes, indeed, if you please.

Prudence: What is heaven?

Samuel: A place and state most blessed, because God dwells there.

Prudence: What is hell?

Samuel: A place and state most wretched, because it is the dwelling-place of sin, the devil, and death.

Prudence: Why do you want to go to heaven?

Samuel: So that I may see God, and serve him without growing weary; that I may see Christ, and love him forever; that I may have that fullness of the Holy Spirit in me which I can by no means enjoy here.

Prudence: A very good boy, and one who has learned well.

Then she turned to the eldest, whose name was Matthew; and she said to him, Come, Matthew, shall I catechize you too?

Matthew: Very gladly.

Prudence: I ask, then: was there ever anything that existed prior to, or before, God?

Matthew: No, for God is eternal; nor was there anything, except himself, that existed until the beginning of the first day. For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them.

Prudence: What do you think of the Bible?

Matthew: It is the holy word of God.

Prudence: Is there anything written in it that you do not understand?

Matthew: Yes, a great deal.

Prudence: What do you do when you come across passages in it that you do not understand?

Matthew: I think God is wiser than I. I also pray that he will be pleased to let me know everything in it that he knows will be for my good.

Prudence: What do you believe about the resurrection of the dead?

Matthew: I believe they will rise the very same that were buried; the same in nature, though not in corruption. And I believe this for two reasons: first, because God has promised it; secondly, because he is able to do it.

Then Prudence said to the boys, You must keep listening to your mother; for she can teach you more. You must also listen carefully to whatever good talk you hear from others: for it is for your sakes that they speak good things. Notice also, and carefully, what the heavens and the earth teach you; but above all, meditate much on that book which caused your father to become a pilgrim. I, for my part, my children, will teach you what I can while you are here, and will be glad if you ask me questions that lead to godly edification.

Now when these pilgrims had been at this place for a week, Mercy had a visitor who professed some affection for her, and his name was Mr. Brisk; a man of some breeding, who professed religion, but a man who clung very close to the world. So he came once or twice, or more, to Mercy, and offered her his love. Now Mercy was fair of face, and so all the more attractive.

Her mind, too, was set on always keeping herself busy doing things; for when she had nothing to do for herself, she would be making stockings and clothes for others, and would give them to those who were in need. And Mr. Brisk, not knowing where or how she disposed of what she made, seemed to be greatly taken with her, because he never found her idle. I am sure she is a good housewife, he said to himself.

Mercy then told the young women of the house about the matter, and asked them about him, for they knew him better than she did. So they told her that he was a very busy young man, and one who professed religion, but was, they feared, a stranger to the power of what is good.

Well then, said Mercy, I will look at him no more; for I mean never to have a drag on my soul.

Prudence then answered that there was no need to discourage him much; if Mercy only kept on as she had begun, doing for the poor, that would soon cool his ardor.

So the next time he comes, he finds her at her old work, making things for the poor. Then he said, What, always at it? Yes, she said, either for myself or for others. And how much can you earn a day? he said. I do these things, she said, that I may be rich in good works, laying up in store for myself a good foundation for the time to come, that I may lay hold on eternal life. 1 Tim 6:17–19. Why, tell me, what do you do with them? he said. Clothe the naked, she said. With that his face fell. So he stopped coming to her. And when he was asked why, he said that Mercy was a pretty lass, but troubled with bad ways.

When he had left her, Prudence said, Did I not tell you that Mr. Brisk would soon abandon you? Yes, and he will spread a bad report about you; for, in spite of his profession of religion, and his seeming love for Mercy, Mercy and he are of dispositions so different that I believe they will never come together.

Mercy: I might have had husbands before now, though I did not speak of it to anyone; but they were men who did not like my ways, though none of them ever found fault with my looks. So they and I could not agree.

Prudence: Mercy in our days is valued very little except in name: as for the practice of it, which your ways show, there are only a few who can bear it.

Mercy: Well, said Mercy, if nobody will have me, I will die unmarried, or my ways will be a husband to me: for I cannot change my nature; and to have a husband who crosses me in this is something I mean never to allow as long as I live. I had a sister named Bountiful, who was married to one of these misers, but he and she could never agree; and because my sister was resolved to go on as she had begun, that is, to show kindness to the poor, her husband first denounced her at the market cross, and then turned her out of his house.

Prudence: And yet he was a professing Christian, no doubt?

Mercy: Yes, such a one as he was, and the world is now full of men like him: but I will have none of them, not one.

Now Matthew, the eldest son of Christiana, fell sick, and his sickness was severe, for he had great pains in his bowels, so that at times the pain doubled him up, pulling, as it were, both ends of him together. There also lived, not far from there, a Mr. Skill, an old and well-tried physician. Christiana asked for him, so they sent for him, and he came. When he had come into the room, and had watched the boy a little, he concluded that he was sick with colic. Then he said to his mother, What has Matthew’s diet been lately? Diet! said Christiana, nothing but what is wholesome. The physician answered, This boy has been meddling with something that lies undigested in his stomach, and that will not go away without treatment. And I tell you, he must be purged, or else he will die.

Samuel: Then Samuel said, Mother, what was it that my brother picked up and ate as soon as we had come from the gate at the head of this way? You know that there was an orchard on the left, on the other side of the wall, and some of the trees hung over the wall, and my brother picked the fruit and ate it.

Christiana: True, my child, said Christiana, he did take some, and ate it: naughty boy that he was, I scolded him, and still he would eat it.

Mr. Skill: I knew he had eaten something that was not wholesome food; and that food, that is, that fruit, is in fact the most harmful of all. It is the fruit of Beelzebub’s orchard. I am amazed that no one warned you of it; many have died of it.

Christiana: Then Christiana began to cry, and she said, Oh, naughty boy! and oh, careless mother! What shall I do for my son?

Mr. Skill: Come, do not be too downcast; the boy may get well again, but he must purge and vomit.

Christiana: Please, sir, use all your skill on him, whatever it costs.

Mr. Skill: Well, I hope I will be reasonable. So he made him a purge, but it was too weak; it was said to be made of the blood of a goat, the ashes of a heifer, and some of the juice of hyssop. Heb 9:13, 19; 10:1–4. When Mr. Skill saw that that purge was too weak, he made one strong enough to do its work. It was made ex carne et sanguine Christi,4 John 6:54–57; Heb 9:14. (You know that physicians give their patients strange medicines.) And it was made into pills, with a promise or two, and a proportionate amount of salt. Mark 9:49. Now, he was to take them three at a time, on an empty stomach, in half a quarter of a pint of the tears of repentance. Zech 12:10.

When this medicine was prepared, and brought to the boy, he was unwilling to take it, though he was so torn with colic that it seemed he would be pulled to pieces. Come, come, said the physician, you must take it. It turns my stomach, said the boy. I insist that you take it, said his mother. I will vomit it up again, said the boy. Please, sir, said Christiana to Mr. Skill, how does it taste? It has no bad taste, said the doctor; and with that she touched one of the pills with the tip of her tongue. Oh, Matthew, she said, this medicine is sweeter than honey. If you love your mother, if you love your brothers, if you love Mercy, if you love your life, take it. So after much fuss, and a short prayer for God’s blessing on it, he took it, and it worked well in him. It made him purge; it made him sleep, and rest quietly; it put him into a fine warmth and a light sweat, and rid him of his colic completely. So in a little while he got up, and walked about with a staff, and would go from room to room and talk with Prudence, Piety, and Charity about his illness, and how he was healed.

So when the boy was healed, Christiana asked Mr. Skill, Sir, what will repay you for your trouble and care over my child? And he said, You must pay the master of the College of Physicians, Heb 13:11–15, according to the rules laid down for such cases.

Christiana: But, sir, she said, what else is this pill good for?

Mr. Skill: It is a universal pill; it is good against all the diseases that pilgrims are prone to; and when it is well prepared, it will keep good indefinitely.

Christiana: Please, sir, make me up twelve boxes of them; for if I can get these, I will never take any other medicine.

Mr. Skill: These pills are good to prevent diseases, as well as to cure them when one is sick. Yes, I dare say it, and will stand by it, that if a man will only use this medicine as he should, it will make him live forever. John 6:51. But, good Christiana, you must give these pills in no other way than as I have prescribed; for if you do, they will do no good. So he gave Christiana medicine for herself, and her boys, and for Mercy; and told Matthew to beware of eating any more green plums; and kissed them, and went his way.

You were told earlier that Prudence had told the boys that if at any time they wished, they should ask her questions that might do them good, and she would say something to them.

Matthew: Then Matthew, who had been sick, asked her why medicine is, for the most part, bitter to our taste.

Prudence: To show how unwelcome the word of God and its effects are to a carnal heart.

Matthew: Why does medicine, if it does good, purge, and make one vomit?

Prudence: To show that the word, when it works effectually, cleanses the heart and mind. For you see, what the one does to the body, the other does to the soul.

Matthew: What should we learn from seeing the flame of our fire go upwards, and from seeing the beams and sweet influences of the sun strike downwards?

Prudence: From the fire going up, we are taught to rise to heaven by fervent and burning desires. And from the sun sending its heat, beams, and sweet influences downwards, we are taught that the Savior of the world, though high, reaches down with his grace and love to us below.

Matthew: Where do the clouds get their water?

Prudence: Out of the sea.

Matthew: What may we learn from that?

Prudence: That ministers should draw their doctrine from God.

Matthew: Why do they empty themselves on the earth?

Prudence: To show that ministers should give out to the world what they know of God.

Matthew: Why is the rainbow caused by the sun?

Prudence: To show that the covenant of God’s grace is confirmed to us in Christ.

Matthew: Why do the springs come from the sea to us through the earth?

Prudence: To show that the grace of God comes to us through the body of Christ.

Matthew: Why do some of the springs rise out of the tops of high hills?

Prudence: To show that the Spirit of grace will spring up in some who are great and mighty, as well as in many who are poor and low.

Matthew: Why does the fire take hold of the candle-wick?

Prudence: To show that unless grace kindles in the heart, there will be no true light of life in us.

Matthew: Why are the wick and tallow and all used up to keep the candle alight?

Prudence: To show that body and soul, and all, should be at the service of that grace of God that is in us, and spend themselves to keep it in good condition.

Matthew: Why does the pelican pierce her own breast with her beak?

Prudence: To nourish her young with her blood, and so to show that Christ the blessed so loved his young (his people) as to save them from death by his blood.

Matthew: What may one learn from hearing the cock crow?

Prudence: Learn to remember Peter’s sin, and Peter’s repentance. The cock’s crowing also shows that day is coming: so let the crowing of the cock remind you of that last and terrible day of judgment.

Now about this time their month was up; so they told those of the house that it was time for them to be up and going. Then Joseph said to his mother, You should not forget to send to the house of Mr. Interpreter, to ask him to let Mr. Great-Heart be sent to us, so that he may be our conductor for the rest of the way. Good boy, she said, I had almost forgotten. So she drew up a petition, and asked Mr. Watchful the porter to send it by some suitable man to her good friend Mr. Interpreter; and when it had come, and he had seen what the petition said, he said to the messenger, Go, tell them that I will send him.

When the household where Christiana was staying saw that they meant to go on, they called the whole house together to give thanks to their King for sending them such edifying guests as these. When that was done, they said to Christiana, And may we not show you something, as our custom is with pilgrims, for you to meditate on when you are on the way? So they took Christiana, her children, and Mercy into the private room, and showed them one of the apples that Eve ate, and that she also gave to her husband, and for the eating of which they were both turned out of paradise, and asked her what she thought it was. Then Christiana said, It is food or poison, I do not know which. So they explained the matter to her, and she held up her hands and wondered. Gen 3:6; Rom 7:24.

Then they took her to a place, and showed her Jacob’s ladder. Gen 28:12. Now at that time there were some angels ascending on it. So Christiana looked and looked to see the angels go up; so did the rest of the company. Then they were about to go into another place, to show them something else; but James said to his mother, Please, ask them to stay here a little longer, for this is a rare sight. So they turned back, and stood feasting their eyes on so pleasant a view.

After this, they took them into a place where a golden anchor hung. They told Christiana to take it down; for, they said, You shall have it with you, for it is absolutely necessary that you should, so that you may lay hold of that within the veil, Heb 6:19, and stand steadfast if you meet with stormy weather, Joel 3:16: so they were glad of it.

Then they took them to the mount on which Abraham our father offered up Isaac his son, and showed them the altar, the wood, the fire, and the knife, for they remain there to be seen to this very day. Gen 22:9. When they had seen it, they held up their hands, and marveled, and said, Oh, what a man Abraham was, for love to his Master and for denial of himself!

After they had shown them all these things, Prudence took them into a dining room, where there stood a pair of excellent virginals;5 so she played on them, and turned what she had shown them into this excellent song, singing,

““Eve’s apple we have shown you+;

Of that, you+ must beware:

You+ have seen Jacob’s ladder too,

Upon which angels are.

An anchor, too, you+ have;

But let these not suffice,

Until with Abra’m you+ give

Your+ best, a sacrifice.””

Now, about this time, someone knocked at the door; so the Porter opened it, and there was Mr. Great-Heart. But when he had come in, what joy there was! For it now came fresh into their minds how only a little while ago he had killed old Grim Bloody-man the giant, and had delivered them from the lions.

Then Mr. Great-Heart said to Christiana and to Mercy, My Lord has sent each of you a bottle of wine, and also some parched corn, together with a couple of pomegranates; he has also sent the boys some figs and raisins, to refresh you on your way.

Then they set out on their journey, and Prudence and Piety went along with them. When they came to the gate, Christiana asked the Porter if anyone had gone by lately. He said, No; only one, some time ago, who also told me that there had lately been a great robbery committed on the King’s highway, the way you are going. But, he said, the thieves have been caught, and will soon be tried for their lives. Then Christiana and Mercy were afraid; but Matthew said, Mother, there is nothing to fear, as long as Mr. Great-Heart is to go with us, and to be our conductor.

Then Christiana said to the Porter, Sir, I am much obliged to you for all the kindnesses that you have shown me since I came here; and also because you have been so loving and kind to my children. I do not know how to repay your kindness; so please, as a token of my respect for you, accept this small mite. So she put a gold angel6 in his hand; and he bowed low to her, and said, “Let your garments always be white, and let your head never lack oil.” Eccl 9:8. Let Mercy live and not die, and let not her works be few. Deut 33:6. And to the boys he said, Flee youthful lusts, and follow after godliness with those who are grave and wise, 2 Tim 2:22: so you will put gladness into your mother’s heart, and win praise from all who are sober-minded. So they thanked the Porter, and departed.

4. Of the flesh and blood of Christ.

5. A musical instrument.

6. A gold coin worth ten shillings.

THE FIFTH STAGE

Now I saw in my dream that they went on until they had come to the brow of the Hill. There Piety suddenly remembered something and cried out, Alas, I have forgotten what I meant to give Christiana and her companions: I will go back and get it. So she ran and got it. While she was gone, Christiana thought she heard, in a grove a little way off on the right, a most exquisite, melodious singing, with words much like these:

““Through all my life thy favor is

So frankly showed to me,

That in thy House for evermore

My dwelling-place shall be.””

As she kept listening, she thought she heard another answer it, saying,

““For why? The Lord our God is good;

His mercy is forever sure;

His truth at all times firmly stood,

And shall from age to age endure.””

So Christiana asked Prudence who it was that made those exquisite notes. Song 2:11, 12. They are, she answered, our country birds: they sing these notes only rarely, except in the spring, when the flowers appear and the sun shines warm, and then you may hear them all day long. I often go out to hear them, she said; we also often keep them tame in our house. They are very fine company for us when we are melancholy; they also make the woods, and groves, and solitary places, places that one longs to be in.

By this time Piety had come back. So she said to Christiana, Look here, I have brought you a sketch of all the things that you have seen at our house. You can look at it whenever you find yourself forgetting, and call those things to mind again for your edification and comfort.

Now they began to go down the hill into the Valley of Humiliation. It was a steep hill, and the way was slippery; but they were very careful, so they got down fairly well. When they were down in the valley, Piety said to Christiana, This is the place where Christian your husband met the foul fiend Apollyon, and where they had that dreadful fight of theirs: I know you must have heard of it. But take courage; as long as you have Mr. Great-Heart here to be your guide and conductor, we hope you will fare all the better. So when these two had committed the pilgrims to the care of their guide, he went on ahead, and they followed.

Mr. Great-Heart: Then Mr. Great-Heart said, We need not be so afraid of this valley, for there is nothing here to hurt us, unless we bring it on ourselves. It is true that Christian met Apollyon here, and had a hard fight with him too; but that fight was the fruit of the slips he made coming down the hill, for those who slip there must expect fights here. And that is why this valley has such a bad name. For when ordinary people hear that some frightful thing has happened to someone in some place, they think that place is haunted by some foul fiend or evil spirit; when, alas! it is the fruit of their own doing that such things happen to them there. This Valley of Humiliation is in itself as fruitful a place as any the crow flies over; and I am sure that, if we could hit upon it, we might find somewhere around here something that would explain why Christian was so hard pressed in this place.

Then James said to his mother, Look, over there stands a pillar, and it looks as if something is written on it; let us go and see what it is. So they went, and found written there, “Let Christian’s slips, before he came here, and the battles that he met with in this place, be a warning to those who come after.” See, said their guide, did I not tell you that there was something around here that would hint at the reason why Christian was so hard pressed in this place? Then, turning to Christiana, he said, This is no more a discredit to Christian than to any others whose lot and fortune it has been. For it is easier going up this hill than down it, and that can be said of only a few hills in all these parts of the world. But we will leave the good man; he is at rest; he also won a fine victory over his enemy. May He who dwells above grant that we fare no worse than he did, when we come to be tried.

But let us come back to this Valley of Humiliation. It is the best and most fruitful piece of ground in all those parts. It is rich ground and, as you see, is mostly meadows; and if a man were to come here in the summertime, as we do now, knowing nothing about it beforehand, and if he also took delight in what his eyes saw, he might see what would delight him. Look how green this valley is, and how beautiful with lilies. Song 2:1. I have known many laboring men who have gained good estates in this Valley of Humiliation; for God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. Jas 4:6; 1 Pet 5:5. Indeed it is a very fruitful soil, and yields its crops by handfuls. Some also have wished that the nearest way to their Father’s house were here, so that they might be troubled no more with hills or mountains to go over; but the way is the way, and that is the end of it.

Now, as they were going along and talking, they saw a boy feeding his father’s sheep. The boy was in very poor clothes, but had a very fresh and pleasant face; and as he sat by himself, he sang. Listen, said Mr. Great-Heart, to what the shepherd’s boy is saying. So they listened, and he said,

““He that is down, needs fear no fall;

He that is low, no pride:

He that is humble, ever shall

Have God to be his guide.”

“I am content with what I have,

Little be it or much;

And, Lord, contentment still I crave,

Because thou savest such.”

“Fulness to such, a burden is,

That go on pilgrimage;

Here little, and hereafter bliss,

Is best from Age to Age.””

Then the guide said, Do you hear him? I dare say that this boy lives a merrier life, and wears more of that herb called heart’s-ease in his bosom, than the man who is dressed in silk and velvet. But let us go on with our talk.

In this valley our Lord used to have his country house: he loved very much to be here. He also loved to walk these meadows, for he found the air pleasant. Besides, here a man is free from the noise and from the hurry of this life: all states of life are full of noise and confusion; only the Valley of Humiliation is that empty and solitary place. Here a man is not so hindered and interrupted in his contemplation as he tends to be in other places. This is a valley that nobody walks in but those who love a pilgrim’s life. And though Christian had the hard luck to meet Apollyon here, and to get into a sharp fight with him, yet I must tell you that in former times men have met angels here, Hos 12:4, 5, have found pearls here, Matt 13:46, and have found the words of life in this place. Prov 8:35.

Did I say that our Lord had his country house here in former days, and that he loved to walk here? I will add this: in this place, to the people who love and tread these grounds, he has left a yearly income, to be faithfully paid them at set times, for their upkeep along the way, and to encourage them further to go on in their pilgrimage.

Samuel: Now, as they went on, Samuel said to Mr. Great-Heart, Sir, I understand that it was in this valley that my father and Apollyon had their battle; but whereabouts was the fight? For I can see that this valley is large.

Mr. Great-Heart: Your father had the battle with Apollyon at a place over there ahead of us, in a narrow passage just beyond Forgetful Green. And indeed that place is the most dangerous place in all these parts. For if pilgrims ever meet with any hard assault, it is when they forget what favors they have received, and how unworthy they are of them. This is also the place where others have been hard pressed. But more about the place when we come to it; for I am sure that to this day there remains either some sign of the battle, or some monument to testify that such a battle was fought there.

Mercy: Then Mercy said, I think I am as well in this valley as I have been anywhere else in all our journey: the place seems to suit my spirit. I love to be in places like this, where there is no rattling of coaches or rumbling of wheels. It seems to me that here one may, without much disturbance, think about what he is, where he came from, what he has done, and to what the King has called him. Here one may think, and break at heart, and melt in spirit, until one’s eyes become like the fish-pools in Heshbon. Song 7:4. Those who go rightly through this valley of Baca make it a well; the rain that God sends down from heaven on those who are here also fills the pools. This valley is also the one from which the King will give his own their vineyards; and those who go through it will sing, as Christian did, even though he met Apollyon here. Ps 84:5–7; Hos 2:15.

Mr. Great-Heart: That is true, said their guide; I have gone through this valley many a time, and was never better than when I was here. I have also been a guide to several pilgrims, and they have said the same. “This is the one I will esteem,” says the King, “he who is humble and contrite in spirit, who trembles at My word.” Isa 66:2.

Now they had come to the place where the battle mentioned before was fought. Then the guide said to Christiana, her children, and Mercy, This is the place; on this ground Christian stood, and up there Apollyon came against him. And look, did I not tell you? here is some of your husband’s blood on these stones to this day. See, too, how here and there some of the splinters of Apollyon’s broken darts can still be seen on the place. See also how they beat the ground with their feet as they fought, to hold their places against each other; and how with their stray blows they split the very stones in pieces. Truly, Christian played the man here, and showed himself as valiant as Hercules could have done, had he been there, even Hercules himself. When Apollyon was beaten, he retreated to the next valley, which is called the Valley of the Shadow of Death, and which we will come to soon. Look, over there also stands a monument, on which this battle is engraved, and Christian’s victory, to his fame through all ages. So, because it stood right by the wayside in front of them, they stepped up to it and read the writing, which word for word was this:

““Near here there was a battle fought,

Most strange, and yet most true;

Christian and Apollyon fought

Each other to subdue.”

“The man so bravely played the man,

He forced the fiend to fly;

Of which a monument I stand,

The same to testify.””

When they had passed this place, they came to the borders of the Shadow of Death. This Valley was longer than the other, and also a place most strangely haunted by evil things, as many are able to testify; but these women and children got through it the better, because they had daylight, and because Mr. Great-Heart was their conductor.

As they were entering this valley, they thought they heard a groaning, as of dying men; a very great groaning. They also thought they heard words of lamentation, as if spoken by some in extreme torment. These things made the boys quake; the women also looked pale and wan; but their guide told them to take comfort.

So they went on a little further, and they thought they felt the ground begin to shake under them, as if there were some hollow place beneath: they also heard a kind of hissing, as of serpents, but nothing had appeared yet. Then the boys said, Are we not at the end of this dismal place yet? But the guide also told them to take courage, and to watch their feet carefully; or else, he said, you may be caught in some snare.

Now James began to be sick; but I think the cause of it was fear. So his mother gave him some of that glass of spirits that had been given her at the Interpreter’s house, and three of the pills that Mr. Skill had prepared, and the boy began to revive. So they went on till they came to about the middle of the valley; and then Christiana said, I think I see something over there on the road ahead of us, a thing of a shape that I have never seen. Then Joseph said, Mother, what is it? An ugly thing, child; an ugly thing, she said. But, mother, what is it like? he said. It’s like I don’t know what, she said; and now it is only a little way off. Then she said, It is close.

Well, said Mr. Great-Heart, let those who are most afraid keep close to me. So the fiend came on, and the conductor met it; but when it reached him, it vanished from the sight of them all. Then they remembered what had been said some time before: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” Jas 4:7.

So they went on, a little refreshed. But they had not gone far before Mercy, looking behind her, saw, as she thought, something very like a lion, and it came after them at a great padding pace; it had a hollow, roaring voice, and at every roar it gave it made the valley echo, and all their hearts ache, except the heart of him who was their guide. So it came up, and Mr. Great-Heart went to the rear, and put the pilgrims all in front of him. The lion also came on fast, and Mr. Great-Heart made ready to give him battle. 1 Pet 5:8, 9. But when the lion saw that they were resolved to resist him, he also drew back, and came no further.

Then they went on again, with their conductor going before them, till they came to a place where a pit had been dug across the whole breadth of the way; and before they could get ready to cross it, a great mist and a darkness fell on them, so that they could not see. Then the pilgrims said, Alas! what shall we do now? But their guide answered, Do not be afraid; stand still, and see what end will be put to this also. So they stayed there, because their path was ruined. Then they also thought that they heard more plainly the noise and rushing of the enemies; and the fire and the smoke of the pit were much easier to make out. Then Christiana said to Mercy, Now I see what my poor husband went through. I have heard much of this place, but I was never here before now. Poor man! he went through here all alone in the night; he had night almost the whole way through; and these fiends were busy about him, as if they would have torn him to pieces. Many have spoken of it; but none can tell what the Valley of the Shadow of Death means until they come into it themselves. The heart knows its own bitterness; and no stranger shares in its joy. Prov 14:10. To be here is a fearful thing.

Mr. Great-Heart: This is like doing business in great waters, or like going down into the deep. This is like being in the heart of the sea, and like going down to the bottoms of the mountains. Now it seems as if the earth, with its bars, were around us forever. But let those who walk in darkness, and have no light, trust in the name of the Lord, and lean upon their God. Isa 50:10. For my part, as I have told you already, I have often gone through this valley, and have been much harder pressed than I am now; and yet you see I am alive. I would not boast, for I am not my own savior; but I trust we will have a good deliverance. Come, let us pray for light to Him who can lighten our darkness, and who can rebuke not only these, but all the Satans in hell.

So they cried out and prayed, and God sent light and deliverance, for now nothing blocked their way; no, not even there, where just now they had been stopped by a pit. Yet they had not got through the valley. So they went on, and met with great stinks and loathsome smells, which troubled them greatly. Then Mercy said to Christiana, It is not so pleasant being here as at the gate, or at the Interpreter’s, or at the house where we stayed last.

Oh, but, said one of the boys, it is not as bad to go through here as it would be to stay here always; and for all I know, one reason why we must go this way to the house prepared for us is so that our home may be all the sweeter to us.

Well said, Samuel, said the guide; you have spoken like a man now. Why, if I ever get out of here, said the boy, I think I will value light and a good road more than I ever did in all my life. Then the guide said, We will be out soon.

So on they went, and Joseph said, Can we not see the end of this valley yet? Then the guide said, Watch your feet, for we will soon be among the snares. So they watched their feet and went on; but they were much troubled by the snares. Now, when they had come among the snares, they saw a man thrown into the ditch on the left, with his flesh all ripped and torn. Then the guide said, That is one Heedless, who was going this way: he has lain there a long time. There was one Take-Heed with him when he was taken and killed, but he escaped their hands. You cannot imagine how many are killed around here, and yet men are so foolishly reckless as to set out lightly on pilgrimage, and to come without a guide. Poor Christian! it was a wonder that he escaped here; but he was loved by his God, and he also had a good heart of his own, or else he could never have done it.

Now they drew near the end of this way; and just where Christian had seen the cave when he went by, out of it came Maul, a giant. This Maul used to prey on young pilgrims with sophistry; and he called Great-Heart by his name, and said to him, How many times have you been forbidden to do these things? Then Mr. Great-Heart said, What things? What things! said the giant; you know what things: but I will put an end to your trade.

But please, said Mr. Great-Heart, before we go at it, let us understand why we must fight. Now the women and children stood trembling, and did not know what to do. The giant said, You rob the country, and rob it with the worst of thefts. Those are only generalities, said Mr. Great-Heart; come down to particulars, man.

Then the giant said, You practice the craft of a kidnapper; you gather up women and children, and take them away into a strange country, to the weakening of my master’s kingdom. But now Great-Heart replied, I am a servant of the God of heaven; my business is to persuade sinners to repentance. I am commanded to do my best to turn men, women, and children from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan to God; and if this is really the ground of your quarrel, let us go at it as soon as you like.

Then the giant came up, and Mr. Great-Heart went to meet him; and as he went he drew his sword, but the giant had a club. So without more ado they went at it, and at the first blow the giant struck Mr. Great-Heart down on one of his knees. At that the women and children cried out. So Mr. Great-Heart, recovering himself, struck out on every side with full vigor, and gave the giant a wound in his arm. So he fought for a full hour, until it grew so hot that the breath came out of the giant’s nostrils as the heat comes out of a boiling cauldron.

Then they sat down to rest; but Mr. Great-Heart turned to prayer. And the women and children did nothing but sigh and cry the whole time the battle lasted.

When they had rested and got their breath, they both went at it again; and Mr. Great-Heart, with one blow, brought the giant down to the ground. No, wait, let me get up, said the giant; so Mr. Great-Heart, playing fair, let him get up. So they went at it again, and the giant came very close to breaking Mr. Great-Heart’s skull with his club.

Mr. Great-Heart, seeing that, runs at him in the full heat of his spirit, and pierces him under the fifth rib. At that the giant began to faint, and could hold up his club no longer. Then Mr. Great-Heart followed up his blow, and struck the giant’s head from his shoulders. Then the women and children rejoiced, and Mr. Great-Heart also praised God for the deliverance he had worked.

When this was done, they together set up a pillar, fastened the giant’s head on it, and wrote underneath, in letters that passers-by might read,

““He who once wore this head was one

Who pilgrims would misuse;

He stopped their way, he spared none,

But all he would abuse;

Until I, Great-Heart, arose,

The pilgrims’ guide to be;

Until I rose up to oppose

Him who was their enemy.””

THE SIXTH STAGE

Now I saw that they went on to the rise a little way off, which had been raised up as a lookout for pilgrims. That was the place from which Christian had his first sight of Faithful his brother. So here they sat down and rested. Here they also ate and drank and made merry, because they had been delivered from so dangerous an enemy. As they sat eating, Christiana asked the guide whether he had been hurt at all in the battle. Then Mr. Great-Heart said, No, only a little in my flesh; yet even that will be so far from doing me harm that it is a proof, here and now, of my love to my master and to you, and will be a means, by grace, to increase my reward at last.

Christiana: But were you not afraid, good sir, when you saw him coming with his club?

Mr. Great-Heart: It is my duty, he said, to distrust my own ability, so that I may rely on Him who is stronger than all.

Christiana: But what did you think when he knocked you to the ground at the first blow?

Mr. Great-Heart: Why, I thought, he said, that my Master himself was treated the same way, and yet it was he who conquered in the end. 2 Cor 4:10, 11; Rom 8:37.

Matthew: Whatever the rest of you may think, I think God has been wonderfully good to us, both in bringing us out of this valley and in delivering us out of the hand of this enemy. For my part, I see no reason why we should distrust our God any more, since he has now, and in such a place as this, given us such proof of his love. Then they got up and went on.

Now a little ahead of them stood an oak; and under it, when they reached it, they found an old pilgrim fast asleep. They knew that he was a pilgrim by his clothes, his staff, and his belt.

So the guide, Mr. Great-Heart, woke him; and the old gentleman, as he looked up, cried out, What’s the matter? Who are you, and what is your business here?

Mr. Great-Heart: Come, man, do not get so heated; there is no one here but friends. Yet the old man gets up, and stands on his guard, and demands to know who they are. Then the guide said, My name is Great-Heart: I am the guide of these pilgrims who are going to the Celestial country.

Mr. Honest: Then Mr. Honest said, I beg your pardon: I was afraid you were some of that company who robbed Little-Faith of his money a while ago; but now that I look about me more carefully, I see you are more honest people.

Mr. Great-Heart: Why, what would or could you have done to help yourself, if we really had been some of that company?

Mr. Honest: Done! Why, I would have fought as long as there was breath in me; and if I had done so, I am sure you could never have got the better of me; for a Christian can never be overcome unless he gives in of his own accord.

Mr. Great-Heart: Well said, father Honest, the guide answered; for by this I know you are a cock of the right kind, for you have spoken the truth.

Mr. Honest: And by this I also know that you know what true pilgrimage is; for everyone else thinks that we are the easiest of all to overcome.

Mr. Great-Heart: Well, now that we have met so happily, please let me ask your name, and the name of the place you came from.

Mr. Honest: I cannot tell you my name, but I came from the town of Stupidity: it lies about four degrees beyond the city of Destruction.

Mr. Great-Heart: Oh, are you from that country? Then I think I can half guess who you are: your name is Old Honesty, is it not?

Mr. Honest: So the old gentleman blushed and said, Not honesty in the abstract, but Honest is my name; and I hope that my nature may agree with what I am called. But, sir, the old gentleman said, how could you guess that I am such a man, since I came from such a place?

Mr. Great-Heart: I had heard of you before from my Master; for he knows all things that are done on the earth. But I have often wondered that anyone should come from your place; for your town is worse than the city of Destruction itself.

Mr. Honest: Yes, we lie farther from the sun, and so we are colder and more numb. But if a man were in a mountain of ice, yet if the Sun of righteousness arises on him, his frozen heart will feel a thaw; and so it has been with me.

Mr. Great-Heart: I believe it, father Honest, I believe it; for I know it is true.

Then the old gentleman greeted all the pilgrims with a holy kiss of love, and asked them their names, and how they had fared since they set out on their pilgrimage.

Christiana: Then Christiana said, I suppose you have heard my name; good Christian was my husband, and these four are his children. But can you imagine how the old gentleman was moved when she told him who she was? He skipped, he smiled, he blessed them with a thousand good wishes, saying,

Mr. Honest: I have heard much of your husband, and of the travels and wars he went through in his day. Let it be said for your comfort, the name of your husband rings through all these parts of the world: his faith, his courage, his endurance, and his sincerity through it all had made his name famous. Then he turned to the boys and asked them their names, which they told him. Then he said to them, Matthew, be like Matthew the tax collector, not in vice, but in virtue. Matt 10:3. Samuel, he said, be like Samuel the prophet, a man of faith and prayer. Ps 99:6. Joseph, he said, be like Joseph in Potiphar’s house, chaste, and one who flees from temptation. Gen 39. And James, be like James the just, and like James the brother of our Lord. Acts 1:13. Then they told him about Mercy, and how she had left her town and her relatives to come along with Christiana and her sons. At that the honest old man said, Mercy is your name: by mercy you shall be sustained and carried through all the difficulties that will attack you on your way, till you come to the place where you shall look the Fountain of mercy in the face with comfort. All this while the guide, Mr. Great-Heart, was very well pleased, and smiled on his companions.

Now, as they walked along together, the guide asked the old gentleman whether he knew a Mr. Fearing, who came on pilgrimage from his part of the country.

Mr. Honest: Yes, very well, he said. He was a man who had the root of the matter in him; but he was one of the most troublesome pilgrims I ever met in all my days.

Mr. Great-Heart: I see you knew him, for you have given a very true description of him.

Mr. Honest: Knew him! I was a close companion of his; I was with him almost all the time; when he first began to think about what would come upon us hereafter, I was with him.

Mr. Great-Heart: I was his guide from my Master’s house to the gates of the Celestial City.

Mr. Honest: Then you found him a troublesome one.

Mr. Great-Heart: I did; but I could bear it very well; for men of my calling are often entrusted with the charge of men like him.

Mr. Honest: Well then, please let us hear a little about him, and how he conducted himself under your guidance.

Mr. Great-Heart: Why, he was always afraid that he would fall short of the place he wanted to reach. Everything he heard anyone speak of frightened him, if it had even the least appearance of opposition in it. I heard that he lay roaring at the Slough of Despond for more than a month on end; nor did he dare venture across, though he saw several go over before him, and many of them offered to lend him a hand. He would not go back again, either. The Celestial City—he said he would die if he did not come to it; and yet he was downcast at every difficulty, and stumbled at every straw that anyone threw in his way. Well, after he had lain at the Slough of Despond a great while, as I have told you, one sunny morning, I do not know how, he ventured, and so got over; but when he was over, he could hardly believe it. He had, I think, a Slough of Despond in his mind, a slough that he carried everywhere with him, or else he could never have been as he was. So he came up to the gate, you know what I mean, that stands at the head of this way, and there too he stood a good while before he would venture to knock. When the gate was opened, he would step back and make way for others, and say that he was not worthy. For though he got to the gate before some, yet many of them went in before him. There the poor man would stand shaking and shrinking; I dare say it would have moved anyone’s heart to pity to see him. Yet he would not go back again. At last he took the knocker that hung on the gate in his hand, and gave a small rap or two; then someone opened to him, but he shrank back as before. The one who opened stepped out after him and said, You trembling one, what do you want? At that he fell down to the ground. The one who spoke to him marveled to see him so faint, so he said to him, Peace be to you; get up, for I have set the door open for you; come in, for you are blessed. With that he got up and went in trembling; and when he was in, he was ashamed to show his face. Well, after he had been received there a while, as you know the custom is, he was told to go on his way, and was also told the way he should take. So he went on till he came to our house; but as he behaved at the gate, so he did at my Master the Interpreter’s door. He lay about there in the cold a good while before he would venture to call; yet he would not go back: and the nights were long and cold then. In fact, he had a note of necessity in his bosom to my master, asking him to receive him and grant him the comfort of his house, and also to allow him a strong and valiant conductor, because he was himself such a chicken-hearted man; and yet for all that he was afraid to call at the door. So he hung about, up and down near there, till, poor man, he had almost perished with cold; indeed, so great was his dejection that, though he saw several others get in by knocking, he was still afraid to venture. At last, I think, I looked out of the window, and seeing a man going up and down about the door, I went out to him and asked who he was; but, poor man, the water stood in his eyes; so I saw what he needed. So I went in and told it in the house, and we made it known to our Lord: so he sent me out again to beg him to come in; but I dare say I had hard work to do it. At last he came in; and I will say this for my Lord, he was wonderfully loving to him. There were only a few good bits on the table, but some of them were laid on his plate. Then he presented the note; and my Lord looked at it and said his request should be granted. So when he had been there a good while, he seemed to take some heart, and to be a little more comforted. For my Master, you must know, is one of a very tender heart, especially to those who are afraid; so he behaved toward him in whatever way would most encourage him. Well, when he had seen the things of the place, and was ready to set out on his journey to the city, my Lord, as he did for Christian before, gave him a bottle of spirits and some comforting things to eat. So we set out, and I went ahead of him; but the man was a man of few words, only he would sigh aloud.

When we came to where the three fellows were hanged, he said that he feared that would be his end too. Only he seemed glad when he saw the cross and the sepulcher. There, I confess, he wanted to stay a little to look; and for a while afterward he seemed a little more cheerful. When he came to the Hill Difficulty, he did not balk at that, nor did he much fear the lions: for you must know that his troubles were not about things like these; his fear was about being accepted at last.

I got him into the house Beautiful, I think, before he was willing. Also, when he was in, I introduced him to the young women of the place; but he was ashamed to put himself forward much in company. He wanted very much to be alone; yet he always loved good talk, and would often get behind the screen to hear it. He also loved very much to see ancient things, and to ponder them in his mind. He told me afterward that he loved being in those two houses he had last come from, that is, at the gate and at the Interpreter’s, but that he did not dare be so bold as to ask.

When we went on from the house Beautiful, down the hill into the Valley of Humiliation, he went down as well as I ever saw a man go in my life; for he did not care how lowly he was, so long as he might be happy at last. Indeed, I think there was a kind of sympathy between that Valley and him; for I never saw him better in all his pilgrimage than he was in that Valley.

Here he would lie down, embrace the ground, and kiss the very flowers that grew in this valley. Lam 3:27–29. He would now be up every morning at daybreak, pacing and walking back and forth in the valley.

But when he came to the entrance of the Valley of the Shadow of Death, I thought I would lose my man: not that he had any inclination to go back—that he always abhorred—but he was ready to die of fear. Oh, the hobgoblins will get me! the hobgoblins will get me! he cried; and I could not talk him out of it. He made such a noise and such an outcry here that, had they only heard him, it would have been enough to encourage them to come and fall on us.

But I took very careful note of this: this valley was as quiet when we went through it as I ever knew it before or since. I suppose those enemies here had been given a special restraint by our Lord just then, and a command not to meddle until Mr. Fearing had passed through.

It would be too tedious to tell you everything; so we will mention only a passage or two more. When he came to Vanity Fair, I thought he would have fought with all the men in the fair. I was afraid we would both be knocked on the head there, so hot was he against their follies. On the Enchanted Ground he was very wakeful. But when he came to the river where there was no bridge, he was again in great distress. Now, now, he said, he would be drowned forever, and so never see with comfort that face he had come so many miles to behold.

And here also I noticed something very remarkable: the water of that river was lower at this time than I ever saw it in all my life; so at last he went over hardly wetting more than his feet. When he was going up to the gate, I began to take leave of him and to wish him a good welcome above. So he said, I shall, I shall. Then we parted, and I saw him no more.

Mr. Honest: Then it seems all was well with him at last?

Mr. Great-Heart: Yes, yes, I never had any doubt about him. He was a man of a fine spirit, only he was always kept very low, and that made his life so burdensome to himself and so troublesome to others. Ps 88. He was, more than many, tender about sin: he was so afraid of wronging others that he would often deny himself what was lawful, because he would not cause others to stumble. Rom 14:21; 1 Cor 8:13.

Mr. Honest: But what could be the reason that such a good man should spend all his days so much in the dark?

Mr. Great-Heart: There are two sorts of reasons for it. One is, the wise God will have it so: some must pipe, and some must weep. Matt 11:16. Now Mr. Fearing was one who played the bass. He and his fellows sound the sackbut, whose notes are more mournful than the notes of other music: though indeed, some say, the bass is the foundation of music. And for my part, I care nothing at all for a profession of religion that does not begin in heaviness of mind. The first string the musician usually touches is the bass, when he means to put everything in tune. God also plays on this string first, when he sets the soul in tune for himself. Only here was Mr. Fearing’s imperfection: he could play no other music but this until near the end of his life.

[I venture to talk metaphorically like this to ripen the wits of young readers, and because, in the book of Revelation, the saved are compared to a company of musicians who play on their trumpets and harps and sing their songs before the throne. Rev 5:8; 14:2, 3.]

Mr. Honest: He was a very zealous man, as one can see from the account you have given of him. Difficulties, lions, or Vanity Fair—he did not fear them at all; it was only sin, death, and hell that were a terror to him, because he had some doubts about his share in that celestial country.

Mr. Great-Heart: You are right; those were the things that troubled him; and they, as you have well observed, arose from the weakness of his mind on that point, not from weakness of spirit in the practical part of a pilgrim’s life. I truly believe that, as the proverb goes, he could have bitten a firebrand had it stood in his way; but the things that weighed him down, no man has ever yet been able to shake off with ease.

Christiana: Then Christiana said, This account of Mr. Fearing has done me good; I thought nobody had ever been like me. But I see there was some likeness between this good man and me; only we differed in two things. His troubles were so great that they broke out; but mine I kept within. His also lay so heavy on him that they kept him from knocking at the houses provided for hospitality; but my trouble was always such as made me knock the louder.

Mercy: If I may also speak my heart, I must say that something of him has also dwelt in me. For I have always been more afraid of the lake, and of losing a place in paradise, than I have been of losing other things. Oh, I thought, if only I may have the happiness of a dwelling there! It is enough, though I part with all the world to win it.

Matthew: Then Matthew said, Fear was one thing that made me think I was far from having within me that which accompanies salvation. But if it was so with such a good man as he, why should it not also go well with me?

James: No fears, no grace, James said. Though there is not always grace where there is the fear of hell, yet, to be sure, there is no grace where there is no fear of God.

Mr. Great-Heart: Well said, James; you have hit the mark. For the fear of God is the beginning of wisdom; and to be sure, those who lack the beginning have neither middle nor end. But we will close our talk about Mr. Fearing here, after we have sent this farewell after him.

““Well, Master Fearing, you did fear

Your God, and were afraid

Of doing anything, while here,

That would have you betrayed.

And did you fear the lake and pit?

If only others did too!

For, as for those who lack your wit,

Themselves they will undo.””

Now I saw that they still went on talking. For after Mr. Great-Heart had finished with Mr. Fearing, Mr. Honest began to tell them about another, whose name was Mr. Self-will. He made himself out to be a pilgrim, Mr. Honest said; but I am sure he never came in at the gate that stands at the head of the way.

Mr. Great-Heart: Did you ever talk with him about it?

Mr. Honest: Yes, more than once or twice; but he would always be like himself: self-willed. He cared nothing for man, or reasoning, or even example; whatever his mind prompted him to do, that he would do, and nothing else could anyone get him to do.

Mr. Great-Heart: Tell me, what principles did he hold? For I suppose you can say.

Mr. Honest: He held that a man might follow the vices as well as the virtues of pilgrims; and that if he did both, he would certainly be saved.

Mr. Great-Heart: What? If he had said that it is possible for the best to be guilty of the vices, as well as to share in the virtues, of pilgrims, he could not have been much blamed; for indeed we are not absolutely exempt from any vice, but only on condition that we watch and strive. But this, I see, is not the point; if I understand you right, you mean that he was of the opinion that it was allowable to be so.

Mr. Honest: Yes, yes, that is what I mean, and so he believed and practiced.

Mr. Great-Heart: But what grounds did he have for saying so?

Mr. Honest: Why, he said he had the Scripture as his warrant.

Mr. Great-Heart: Please, Mr. Honest, give us a few examples.

Mr. Honest: That I will. He said that having to do with other men’s wives had been practiced by David, God’s beloved; and therefore he could do it. He said that having more women than one was a thing that Solomon practiced, and therefore he could do it. He said that Sarah and the godly midwives of Egypt lied, and so did Rahab, who was saved, and therefore he could do it. He said that the disciples went at their Master’s bidding and took away the owner’s donkey, and therefore he could do so too. He said that Jacob got his father’s inheritance by guile and deceit, and therefore he could do so too.

Mr. Great-Heart: Vile indeed! And are you sure he held this opinion?

Mr. Honest: I heard him plead for it, bring Scripture for it, bring arguments for it, and so on.

Mr. Great-Heart: An opinion not fit to be allowed anywhere in the world!

Mr. Honest: You must understand me rightly: he did not say that any man might do this; but that those who had the virtues of those who did such things might also do the same.

Mr. Great-Heart: But what could be more false than such a conclusion? For this is as much as to say that, because good men in the past have sinned out of weakness, therefore he had leave to do it out of a presumptuous mind; or that, because a child, blown by the wind, or because it stumbled on a stone, fell down and dirtied itself in the mire, therefore he might willfully lie down and wallow in it like a boar. Who could have thought that anyone could be so blinded by the power of lust? But what is written must be true: they “stumble at the word, being disobedient—and to this they were appointed.” 1 Pet 2:8. His supposing that those who give themselves up to the vices of godly men may have the godly men’s virtues is also a delusion as strong as the other. To eat up the sin of God’s people, Hos 4:8, as a dog licks up filth, is no sign that one possesses their virtues. Nor can I believe that one who holds this opinion can at present have faith or love in him. But I know you have made strong objections to him; tell me, what can he say for himself?

Mr. Honest: Why, he says that to do this and hold it as one’s opinion seems far more honest than to do it and yet hold the opposite opinion.

Mr. Great-Heart: A very wicked answer. For though to give our lusts free rein while our opinions are against such things is bad, yet to sin and plead that we are allowed to do so is worse: the one makes onlookers stumble by accident, the other leads them into the snare.

Mr. Honest: There are many of this man’s mind who do not have this man’s mouth; and that is why going on pilgrimage is held in such low esteem.

Mr. Great-Heart: You have spoken the truth, and it is to be lamented: but he who fears the King of paradise shall come out of them all.

Christiana: There are strange opinions in the world. I know of one who said it was time enough to repent when we come to die.

Mr. Great-Heart: Such people are not very wise; if that man had had a week to run twenty miles for his life, he would have been unwilling to put off his journey to the last hour of that week.

Mr. Honest: You are right; and yet most of those who count themselves pilgrims really do just this. I am, as you see, an old man, and have been a traveler on this road many a day; and I have noticed many things.

I have seen some who set out as if they would drive the whole world before them, who yet in a few days died as those in the wilderness did, and so never got sight of the promised land. I have seen some who promised nothing when they first set out to be pilgrims, and who one would have thought could not live a day, who have yet proved very good pilgrims. I have seen some who ran hastily forward, who again, after a little while, ran just as fast back again. I have seen some who spoke very well of a pilgrim’s life at first, who after a while spoke just as much against it. I have heard some, when they first set out for paradise, say positively that there is such a place, who, when they were almost there, came back again and said there is none. I have heard some boast what they would do if they were opposed, who, even at a false alarm, have run from faith, the pilgrim’s way, and all.

Now, as they were going on their way like this, someone came running to meet them and said, Gentlemen, and you of the weaker sort, if you love life, save yourselves, for the robbers are ahead of you.

Mr. Great-Heart: Then Mr. Great-Heart said, They are the three who attacked Little-Faith some time ago. Well, he said, we are ready for them: so they went on their way. Now at every turn they expected to meet the villains; but whether they had heard of Mr. Great-Heart, or whether they had some other prey in view, they did not come up to the pilgrims.

Christiana then wished for an inn where she and her children could refresh themselves, because they were weary. Then Mr. Honest said, There is one a little way ahead, where a very honorable disciple named Gaius lives. Rom 16:23. So they all decided to turn in there; and all the more because the old gentleman gave him such a good report. When they came to the door they went in without knocking, for folks do not usually knock at the door of an inn. Then they called for the master of the house, and he came to them. So they asked if they might stay there that night.

Gaius: Yes, gentlemen, if you are true men; for my house is for no one but pilgrims. Then Christiana, Mercy, and the boys were all the more glad, because the innkeeper was a lover of pilgrims. So they asked for rooms, and he showed them one for Christiana and her children and Mercy, and another for Mr. Great-Heart and the old gentleman.

Mr. Great-Heart: Then Mr. Great-Heart said, Good Gaius, what do you have for supper? For these pilgrims have come far today and are weary.

Gaius: It is late, Gaius said, so we cannot conveniently go out to look for food; but you shall be welcome to such as we have, if that will satisfy you.

Mr. Great-Heart: We will be content with what you have in the house; for since I have tested you, I know you are never without what is fitting.

Then he went down and spoke to the cook, whose name was Taste-that-which-is-good, to get supper ready for so many pilgrims. This done, he comes up again, saying, Come, my good friends, you are welcome here, and I am glad that I have a house to lodge you in; and while supper is being made ready, if you please, let us entertain one another with some good talk: so they all said, Agreed.

Gaius: Then Gaius said, Whose wife is this elderly lady? And whose daughter is this young woman?

Mr. Great-Heart: This woman is the wife of a man called Christian, a pilgrim of former times; and these are his four children. The young woman is an acquaintance of hers, whom she has persuaded to come with her on pilgrimage. The boys take after their father in everything, and long to tread in his steps; indeed, if they only see any place where the old pilgrim has lain, or any print of his foot, it brings joy to their hearts, and they long to lie or tread in the same place.

Gaius: Then Gaius said, Is this Christian’s wife, and are these Christian’s children? I knew your husband’s father, and his father’s father too. Many of this stock have been good; their ancestors lived first at Antioch. Acts 11:26. Christian’s forefathers (I suppose you have heard your husband talk of them) were very worthy men. They have, more than any I know, shown themselves men of great virtue and courage for the Lord of the pilgrims, his ways, and those who loved him. I have heard of many of your husband’s relatives who have stood every trial for the sake of the truth. Stephen, who was one of the first of the family from which your husband sprang, was knocked on the head with stones. Acts 7:59, 60. James, another of this family, was killed with the edge of the sword. Acts 12:2. To say nothing of Paul and Peter, men of old of the family your husband came from, there was Ignatius, who was thrown to the lions; Romanus, whose flesh was cut in pieces from his bones; and Polycarp, who played the man in the fire. There was the man who was hung up in a basket in the sun for the wasps to eat; and the one they put into a sack and threw into the sea to be drowned. It would be utterly impossible to count up all of that family who have suffered injuries and death for the love of a pilgrim’s life. And I cannot help being glad to see that your husband has left behind him four such boys as these. I hope they will uphold their father’s name, and tread in their father’s steps, and come to their father’s end.

Mr. Great-Heart: Indeed, sir, they are promising lads: they seem to choose their father’s ways with all their hearts.

Gaius: That is what I said. So Christian’s family is likely to go on spreading far and wide over the face of the ground, and to be numerous upon the face of the earth; let Christiana seek out some young women for her sons, to whom they may be betrothed, and so on, so that the name of their father and the house of his forefathers may never be forgotten in the world.

Mr. Honest: It is a pity that his family should fall and die out.

Gaius: It cannot fall, but it may be diminished; but let Christiana take my advice, and that is the way to keep it up. And, Christiana, the innkeeper said, I am glad to see you and your friend Mercy here together, a lovely pair. And if I may advise, take Mercy into a closer relationship with you: if she is willing, let her be given to Matthew, your eldest son. It is the way to preserve descendants on the earth. So this match was agreed, and in due time they were married: but more of that later.

Gaius went on and said, I will now speak on behalf of women, to take away their reproach. For as death and the curse came into the world by a woman, Gen 3, so also did life and health: God sent forth his Son, born of a woman. Gal 4:4. Indeed, to show how much those who came after abhorred the act of their mother, the women of the Old Testament longed for children, in the hope that this or that woman might be the mother of the Savior of the world. I will say again that when the Savior had come, women rejoiced in him before either man or angel did. Luke 1:42–46. I do not read that any man ever gave Christ so much as one groat; but the women followed him, and ministered to him from their own means. Luke 8:2, 3. It was a woman who washed his feet with tears, Luke 7:37–50, and a woman who anointed his body at the burial. John 11:2; 12:3. It was women who wept when he was going to the cross, Luke 23:27, and women who followed him from the cross, Matt 27:55, 56; Luke 23:55, and sat opposite his tomb when he was buried. Matt 27:61. It was women who were first with him on the morning of his resurrection, Luke 24:1, and women who first brought word to his disciples that he had risen from the dead. Luke 24:22, 23. Women therefore are highly favored, and show by these things that they are sharers with us in the grace of life.

Now the cook sent up word that supper was almost ready, and sent someone to lay the cloth and the plates, and to set out the salt and bread.

Then Matthew said, The sight of this cloth, and of this forerunner of the supper, awakens in me a greater appetite for my food than I had before.

Gaius: So let all the doctrines ministered to you in this life awaken in you a greater desire to sit at the supper of the great King in his kingdom; for all preaching, books, and ordinances here are only like the laying of the plates and the setting of salt on the table, compared with the feast that our Lord will make for us when we come to his house.

So supper came up. And first a heave-shoulder and a wave-breast were set on the table before them, to show that they must begin their meal with prayer and praise to God. With the heave-shoulder David lifted up his heart to God; and with the wave-breast, where his heart lay, he used to lean on his harp when he played. Lev 7:32–34; 10:14, 15; Ps 25:1; Heb 13:15. These two dishes were very fresh and good, and they all ate heartily of them.

The next thing they brought up was a bottle of wine, as red as blood. Deut 32:14; Judg 9:13; John 15:5. So Gaius said to them, Drink freely; this is the true juice of the vine, which gladdens the heart of God and man. So they drank and were merry.

The next was a dish of milk with bread crumbled well into it; Gaius said, Let the boys have that, so that they may grow by it. 1 Pet 2:1, 2.

Then in due course they brought up a dish of butter and honey. Then Gaius said, Eat freely of this, for it is good to cheer and strengthen your judgments and understandings. This was our Lord’s dish when he was a child: “Butter and honey He shall eat, that He may know to refuse the evil and choose the good.” Isa 7:15.

Then they brought them a dish of apples, and they were very good-tasting fruit. Then Matthew said, May we eat apples, since it was with such fruit that the serpent beguiled our first mother?

Then Gaius said,

““Apples they were with which we were beguiled,

Yet sin, not apples, has our souls defiled:

Forbidden apples, eaten, corrupt the blood;

To eat such, when commanded, does us good:

Drink of his flagons then, you church, his dove,

And eat his apples, you who are sick with love.””

Then Matthew said, I raised that concern because a while ago I was sick from eating fruit.

Gaius: Forbidden fruit will make you sick; but not what our Lord has permitted.

While they were talking like this, they were served another dish, and it was a dish of nuts. Song 6:11. Then some at the table said, Nuts spoil tender teeth, especially children’s teeth: and when Gaius heard this, he said,

““Hard texts are nuts, (I will not call them cheaters,)

Whose shells keep back the kernel from the eaters:

Open the shells, and you will have the meat;

They’re brought here for you to crack and eat.””

Then they were very merry, and sat at the table a long time, talking of many things. Then the old gentleman said, My good landlord, while we are cracking your nuts, if you please, solve this riddle:

““A man there was, though some thought him mad,

The more he cast away, the more he had.””

Then they all listened closely, wondering what good Gaius would say; so he sat still a while, and then replied like this:

““He who bestows his goods upon the poor,

Will have as much again, and ten times more.””

Then Joseph said, I must say, sir, I did not think you could have worked it out.

Oh, Gaius said, I have been trained in this way a great while: nothing teaches like experience. I have learned from my Lord to be kind, and have found by experience that I have gained by it. There is one who scatters, and yet increases; and there is one who withholds more than is right, but it tends to poverty: there is one who makes himself rich, yet has nothing; there is one who makes himself poor, yet has great riches. Prov 11:24; 13:7.

Then Samuel whispered to Christiana, his mother, and said, Mother, this is a very good man’s house: let us stay here a good while, and let my brother Matthew be married here to Mercy before we go any further. Gaius the host overheard this and said, With all my heart, my child.

So they stayed there more than a month, and Mercy was given to Matthew as his wife.

While they stayed here, Mercy, as her custom was, kept making coats and garments to give to the poor, and by this she won a very good name for the pilgrims.

But to return to our story: after supper the lads wanted a bed, for they were weary with traveling. Then Gaius called for someone to show them their room; but Mercy said, I will put them to bed. So she put them to bed, and they slept well; but the rest sat up all night; for Gaius and they were such congenial company that they did not know how to part. After much talk about their Lord, themselves, and their journey, old Mr. Honest, the one who had put the riddle to Gaius, began to nod. Then Great-Heart said, What, sir, you are getting drowsy; come, rouse yourself, here is a riddle for you. Then Mr. Honest said, Let us hear it. Then Mr. Great-heart replied,

““He that would kill, must first be overcome:

Who would live abroad, must first die at home.””

Ha, said Mr. Honest, it is a hard one; hard to explain, and harder to practice. But come, landlord, he said, if you please, I will leave my part to you: you explain it, and I will hear what you say.

No, said Gaius, it was put to you, and you are expected to answer it. Then the old gentleman said,

““He first by grace must conquered be,

Who sin would mortify;

Who would prove that he lives to me,

Unto himself must die.””
