That is right, said Gaius; good doctrine and experience teach this. For, first, until grace shows itself and overcomes the soul with its glory, the soul has no heart at all to oppose sin. Besides, if sin is Satan’s cords, by which the soul lies bound, how could it resist before it is freed from that weakness? Secondly, no one who knows either reason or grace will believe that a man who is a slave to his own corruptions can be a living monument of grace. And now that it comes to mind, I will tell you a story worth hearing. There were two men who went on pilgrimage; one began when he was young, the other when he was old. The young man had strong corruptions to grapple with; the old man’s were weak with the decay of nature. The young man kept his steps as even as the old one did, and was in every way as light as he. Now which of them had his graces shining the clearest, since both seemed to be alike?

Mr. Honest: The young man’s, without doubt. For what makes headway against the greatest opposition gives the best proof that it is strongest; especially when it also keeps pace with what meets with not half so much, as old age certainly does not. Besides, I have observed that old men have flattered themselves with this mistake: they take the decay of nature for a gracious conquest over corruptions, and so they have been apt to deceive themselves. Indeed, old men who are gracious are best able to advise those who are young, because they have seen the most of the emptiness of things; but still, when an old man and a young man set out together, the young one has the advantage of the clearest showing of a work of grace within him, though the old man’s corruptions are naturally the weakest. So they sat talking till daybreak.

Now, when the household was up, Christiana told her son James to read a chapter; so he read the 53rd of Isaiah. When he had finished, Mr. Honest asked why it was said that the Savior was to come “out of dry ground,” and also that “He had no form or comeliness.”

Mr. Great-Heart: Then Mr. Great-Heart said, To the first I answer: because the church of the Jews, from which Christ came, had by then lost almost all the sap and spirit of religion. To the second I say: the words are spoken in the voice of unbelievers, who, because they lack the eye that can see into our Prince’s heart, judge him by the lowliness of his outside; just like those who, not knowing that precious stones are covered with a homely crust, when they have found one, because they do not know what they have found, throw it away again, as men do a common stone.

Well, Gaius said, now that you are here, and since, as I know, Mr. Great-Heart is good with his weapons, if you please, after we have refreshed ourselves, we will walk out into the fields to see if we can do any good. About a mile from here there is a giant called Slay-good, who causes much trouble on the King’s highway in these parts; and I know where his haunt is. He is master of a band of thieves: it would be good if we could rid these parts of him. So they agreed and went: Mr. Great-Heart with his sword, helmet, and shield; and the rest with spears and staffs.

When they came to the place where he was, they found him with a man called Feeble-mind in his hand, whom his servants had brought to him, having caught him on the way. Now the giant was robbing him, intending afterward to pick his bones; for he was by nature a flesh-eater.

Well, as soon as he saw Mr. Great-Heart and his friends at the mouth of his cave with their weapons, he demanded to know what they wanted.

Mr. Great-Heart: We want you; for we have come to avenge the wrongs of the many pilgrims you have killed when you dragged them out of the King’s highway: so come out of your cave. So he armed himself and came out, and they went into battle and fought for over an hour, and then stood still to catch their breath.

Slay-Good: Then the giant said, Why are you here on my ground?

Mr. Great-Heart: To avenge the blood of pilgrims, as I told you before. So they went at it again, and the giant made Mr. Great-Heart give ground; but he came on again, and in the greatness of his spirit he let fly with such force at the giant’s head and sides that he made him let his weapon fall out of his hand. So he struck him, and killed him, and cut off his head, and brought it away to the inn. He also took Feeble-mind the pilgrim and brought him along to his lodgings. When they had come home, they showed the head to the family, and set it up, as they had done with others before, as a terror to any who might try to do as the giant had done in time to come.

Then they asked Mr. Feeble-Mind how he had fallen into the giant’s hands.

Mr. Feeble-Mind: Then the poor man said, I am a sickly man, as you see; and because death used to knock at my door once a day, I thought I would never be well at home. So I took up a pilgrim’s life, and have traveled here from the town of Uncertain, where my father and I were born. I am a man with no strength at all, either of body or of mind; but I would, if I could, spend my life in the pilgrim’s way, though I can only crawl. When I came to the gate at the head of the way, the Lord of that place welcomed me freely; he made no objection to my sickly looks or to my feeble mind, but gave me what I needed for my journey, and told me to hope to the end. When I came to the house of the Interpreter, I received much kindness there; and because the hill of Difficulty was judged too hard for me, one of his servants carried me up it. Indeed, I have had much help from pilgrims, though none were willing to go as slowly as I am forced to go; yet whenever they came up with me, they told me to take heart, and said that it was the will of their Lord that comfort should be given to the feeble-minded, 1 Thess 5:14; and then they went on at their own pace. When I had got as far as Assault-lane, this giant met me there and told me to get ready for a fight. But, alas, feeble one that I was, I had more need of a restorative; so he came up and took me. I imagined he would not kill me. Also, when he had got me into his den, since I had not gone with him willingly, I believed I would come out alive again; for I have heard that no pilgrim who is taken captive by violent hands, if he keeps his heart whole toward his Master, is, by the laws of providence, to die by the hand of the enemy. I expected to be robbed, and robbed I certainly am; but, as you see, I have escaped with my life, for which I thank my King as the author and you as the means. I expect other blows as well; but this I have resolved on: to run when I can, to walk when I cannot run, and to creep when I cannot walk. As for the main thing, I thank him who loved me, I am settled; my way is before me, my mind is beyond the river that has no bridge, though, as you see, I have only a feeble mind.

Mr. Honest: Then old Mr. Honest said, Were you not acquainted, some time ago, with a Mr. Fearing, a pilgrim?

Mr. Feeble-Mind: Acquainted with him! Yes. He came from the town of Stupidity, which lies four degrees north of the city of Destruction, and as many away from where I was born; yet we knew each other well, for indeed he was my uncle, my father’s brother. He and I have been much of the same disposition; he was a little shorter than I, but even so we were much alike in make.

Mr. Honest: I can see you knew him, and I am inclined to believe also that you were related to each other; for you have his pale look, a cast like his in your eye, and your speech is much alike.

Mr. Feeble-Mind: Most who have known us both have said so; and besides, what I have read in him I have for the most part found in myself.

Gaius: Come, sir, said good Gaius, take heart; you are welcome to me and to my house. Whatever you want, ask for it freely; and whatever you would like my servants to do for you, they will do it willingly.

Then Mr. Feeble-mind said, This is an unexpected favor, like the sun shining out of a very dark cloud. Did giant Slay-good mean me this favor when he stopped me and resolved to let me go no further? Did he mean that after he had rifled my pockets I should go to Gaius my host? Yet so it is.

Now, just as Mr. Feeble-mind and Gaius were talking like this, someone came running and called at the door, and said that about a mile and a half away a pilgrim named Mr. Not-right had been struck dead on the spot by a thunderbolt.

Mr. Feeble-Mind: Alas! said Mr. Feeble-mind, has he been killed? He overtook me some days before I got this far, and wanted to keep me company. He was also with me when Slay-good the giant took me, but he was quick on his feet, and escaped; but it seems he escaped to die, and I was taken to live.

““What one would think intends to slay outright,

Often delivers from the saddest plight.

That very Providence whose face is death,

Will often to the lowly life bequeath.

I was taken; he escaped and went free;

Hands crossed gave death to him and life to me.””

Now about this time Matthew and Mercy were married; Gaius also gave his daughter Phebe to James, Matthew’s brother, as his wife; after which they stayed about ten days longer at Gaius’ house, spending their time and the seasons as pilgrims usually do.

When they were about to leave, Gaius made them a feast, and they ate and drank and were merry. Now the hour had come when they must be gone; so Mr. Great-heart asked for the bill. But Gaius told him that at his house it was not the custom for pilgrims to pay for their lodging. He boarded them by the year, but expected his pay from the good Samaritan, who had promised him that at his return he would faithfully repay him whatever expense he had been put to for them. Luke 10:34, 35. Then Mr. Great-heart said to him,

Mr. Great-Heart: Beloved, you are faithful in what you are doing for the brothers, and for strangers, who have testified to the church about your love. You will do well to send them on their way in a manner worthy of God. 3 John 5, 6. Then Gaius said farewell to them all and to his children, and especially to Mr. Feeble-mind. He also gave him something to drink on the way.

Now Mr. Feeble-mind, as they were going out of the door, acted as if he meant to stay behind. When Mr. Great-Heart noticed this, he said, Come, Mr. Feeble-mind, please come along with us; I will be your conductor, and you will fare as the rest do.

Mr. Feeble-Mind: Alas! I lack a suitable companion. You are all hearty and strong, but I, as you see, am weak; so I would rather come behind, so that my many infirmities do not make me a burden both to myself and to you. I am, as I said, a man of a weak and feeble mind, and I will be made to stumble and made weak by what others can bear. I will not like laughing; I will not like showy clothes; I will not like unprofitable questions. Indeed, I am so weak a man as to stumble at what others are free to do. I do not yet know all the truth; I am a very ignorant Christian man. Sometimes, if I hear others rejoice in the Lord, it troubles me because I cannot do so too. It is with me as it is with a weak man among the strong, or with a sick man among the healthy, or as with a lamp despised; so that I do not know what to do. “He who is ready to slip with his feet is like a lamp despised in the thought of him who is at ease.” Job 12:5.

Mr. Great-Heart: But, brother, said Mr. Great-Heart, it is part of my commission to comfort the feeble-minded and to support the weak. You must come along with us; we will wait for you; we will lend you our help; we will deny ourselves some things, both of opinion and of practice, for your sake; we will not get into doubtful disputes in front of you; we will be made all things to you, rather than have you left behind. 1 Thess 5:14; Rom 14; 1 Cor 8:9–13; 9:22.

Now all this while they were at Gaius’ door; and just then, as they were in the heat of their talk, Mr. Ready-to-halt came by with his crutches in his hand, and he too was going on pilgrimage.

Mr. Feeble-Mind: Then Mr. Feeble-mind said to him, Man, how did you get here? I was just now complaining that I had no suitable companion, but you are just what I wished for. Welcome, welcome, good Mr. Ready-to-halt; I hope you and I may be some help to each other.

Mr. Ready-to-Halt: I will be glad of your company, said the other; and, good Mr. Feeble-mind, rather than part, since we have had the good fortune to meet, I will lend you one of my crutches.

Mr. Feeble-Mind: No, he said, though I thank you for your good will, I have no wish to limp before I am lame. Still, I think that when the occasion comes, it may help me against a dog.

Mr. Ready-to-Halt: If either I or my crutches can do you a kindness, we are both at your service, good Mr. Feeble-mind.

So they went on. Mr. Great-Heart and Mr. Honest went in front, Christiana and her children went next, and Mr. Feeble-mind came behind, and Mr. Ready-to-halt with his crutches. Then Mr. Honest said,

Mr. Honest: Please, sir, now that we are on the road, tell us some edifying things about some who have gone on pilgrimage before us.

Mr. Great-Heart: Gladly. I suppose you have heard how Christian, in his day, met Apollyon in the Valley of Humiliation, and also what hard work he had to get through the Valley of the Shadow of Death. I think, too, you must have heard how Faithful was hard pressed by Madam Wanton, by Adam the First, by one called Discontent, and by Shame: four villains as deceitful as a man can meet on the road.

Mr. Honest: Yes, I have heard of all this; but indeed good Faithful was hardest pressed by Shame: Shame never tired.

Mr. Great-Heart: Yes; for, as the pilgrim rightly said, he of all men had the wrong name.

Mr. Honest: But please, sir, where was it that Christian and Faithful met Talkative? He was another notable one.

Mr. Great-Heart: He was a confident fool; yet many follow his ways.

Mr. Honest: He nearly deceived Faithful.

Mr. Great-Heart: Yes, but Christian quickly showed Faithful a way to find him out.

So they went on until they came to the place where Evangelist met Christian and Faithful and prophesied what would happen to them at Vanity Fair. Then their guide said, It was about here that Christian and Faithful met Evangelist, who prophesied to them the troubles they would meet with at Vanity Fair.

Mr. Honest: Is that so? I dare say it was a hard chapter that he read to them then.

Mr. Great-Heart: It was, but he gave them encouragement along with it. But why are we talking about them? They were a pair of lion-like men; they had set their faces like a flint. Don’t you remember how undaunted they were when they stood before the judge?

Mr. Honest: Well, Faithful suffered bravely.

Mr. Great-Heart: So he did, and things just as splendid came of it; for Hopeful and some others, as the story tells, were converted by his death.

Mr. Honest: Well, but please go on; for you know these things well.

Mr. Great-Heart: Of all that Christian met with after he had passed through Vanity Fair, a man called By-ends was the chief of them.

Mr. Honest: By-ends! What sort of man was he?

Mr. Great-Heart: A very crafty fellow, a downright hypocrite; one who would be religious whichever way the world went, but so cunning that he made sure never to lose or suffer for it. He had his own form of religion for every new occasion, and his wife was as good at it as he was. He would turn from opinion to opinion; yes, and argue for doing so, too. But as far as I could learn, he came to a bad end with his by-ends; nor did I ever hear that any of his children were ever thought well of by anyone who truly feared God.

Now by this time they had come within sight of the town of Vanity, where Vanity Fair is held. So when they saw how near the town they were, they discussed with one another how they should pass through it; and some said one thing, and some another. At last Mr. Great-Heart said, As you may know, I have often been a conductor of pilgrims through this town. Now, I know a Mr. Mnason, Acts 21:16, a Cypriot by birth, an old disciple, at whose house we may lodge. If you agree, we will turn in there.

Agreed, said old Honest; Agreed, said Christiana; Agreed, said Mr. Feeble-mind; and so they all said. Now you must understand that it was evening by the time they got to the outskirts of the town; but Mr. Great-Heart knew the way to the old man’s house. So they came there; and he called at the door, and the old man inside knew his voice as soon as he heard it; so he opened the door, and they all came in. Then Mnason, their host, said, How far have you+ come today? They said, From the house of Gaius our friend. I tell you+, he said, you+ have come a good long way. You+ may well be tired; sit down. So they sat down.

Mr. Great-Heart: Then their guide said, Come, good sirs, how are you feeling now? I am sure you are welcome to my friend.

Mr. Mnason: I welcome you too, said Mr. Mnason; and whatever you need, just say so, and we will do what we can to get it for you.

Mr. Honest: Our great need, a while ago, was shelter and good company, and now I hope we have both.

Mr. Mnason: As for shelter, you see what it is; but as for good company, that will be seen when it is put to the test.

Mr. Great-Heart: Well, said Mr. Great-Heart, will you take the pilgrims up to their rooms?

Mr. Mnason: I will, said Mr. Mnason. So he took each of them to his own room; and he also showed them a very fine dining room, where they might be together and eat supper until it was time to go to bed.

Now when they were settled in their places, and a little cheered after their journey, Mr. Honest asked his landlord if there were many good people in the town.

Mr. Mnason: We have a few; for indeed they are only a few compared with those on the other side.

Mr. Honest: But how can we manage to see some of them? For the sight of good men, to those who are going on pilgrimage, is like the moon and stars appearing to those who are sailing on the seas.

Mr. Mnason: Then Mr. Mnason stamped his foot, and his daughter Grace came up. So he said to her, Grace, go and tell my friends, Mr. Contrite, Mr. Holy-man, Mr. Love-saints, Mr. Dare-not-lie, and Mr. Penitent, that I have a friend or two at my house who would like to see them this evening. So Grace went to call them, and they came; and after greeting one another, they sat down together at the table.

Then Mr. Mnason their landlord said, My neighbors, as you+ see, I have a company of strangers come to my house; they are pilgrims; they come from far away, and are going to Mount Zion. But who, he said, do you+ think this is? pointing his finger at Christiana. It is Christiana, the wife of Christian, the famous pilgrim who, with Faithful his brother, was so shamefully treated in our town. At that they were astonished, and said, We little thought we would see Christiana when Grace came to call us; so this is a very heartening surprise. They then asked how she was, and if these young men were her husband’s sons. And when she had told them they were, they said, May the King whom you+ love and serve make you+ like your+ father, and bring you+ where he is in peace.

Mr. Honest: Then Mr. Honest (when they had all sat down) asked Mr. Contrite and the rest how things stood in their town at present.

Mr. Contrite: You may be sure we are all hurry and bustle at fair-time. It’s hard to keep our hearts and spirits in good order when we are so encumbered. He who lives in such a place as this, and has to deal with such people as we have, needs a reminder to warn him to take care every moment of the day.

Mr. Honest: But how peaceable are your neighbors now?

Mr. Contrite: They are much more moderate now than they used to be. You know how Christian and Faithful were treated in our town; but lately, I say, they have been far more moderate. I think the blood of Faithful lies on them like a load to this day; for since they burned him, they have been ashamed to burn any more. In those days we were afraid to walk the street; but now we can show our faces. Then the name of a professing Christian was hated; now, especially in some parts of our town (for you know our town is large), religion is thought honorable. Then Mr. Contrite said to them, Tell me, how are you getting on in your pilgrimage? How does the country treat you?

Mr. Honest: It goes with us as it goes with men on a journey: sometimes our way is clean, sometimes foul; sometimes uphill, sometimes downhill; we are seldom sure of anything. The wind is not always at our backs, nor is everyone we meet on the way a friend. We have met with some notable obstacles already, and what are still ahead we do not know; but for the most part we find true what was said long ago, A good man must suffer trouble.

Mr. Contrite: You talk of obstacles; what obstacles have you met with?

Mr. Honest: No, ask Mr. Great-Heart, our guide; he can give the best account of that.

Mr. Great-Heart: We have been attacked three or four times already. First, Christiana and her children were attacked by two ruffians, who they feared would take their lives. We were attacked by Giant Bloody-man, Giant Maul, and Giant Slay-good. Indeed, we attacked the last rather than he attacked us. And this is how it was: after we had been some time at the house of Gaius, my host and the host of the whole church, we decided one day to take our weapons with us and go and see if we could come upon any of those who are enemies to pilgrims; for we had heard that there was a notable one in those parts. Now Gaius knew his haunt better than I did, because he lived around there. So we looked and looked, until at last we spotted the mouth of his cave; then we were glad, and plucked up our spirits. So we went up to his den; and look, when we got there, he had dragged this poor man, Mr. Feeble-mind, into his net by sheer force, and was about to put an end to him. But when he saw us, supposing, as we thought, that he had another prey, he left the poor man in his hole and came out. So we fell to it hard, and he laid about him with all his strength; but in the end he was brought down to the ground, and his head was cut off and set up by the wayside as a terror to any who should practice such ungodliness afterward. That I am telling you the truth, here is the man himself to confirm it, who was like a lamb taken out of the mouth of the lion.

Mr. Feeble-Mind: Then Mr. Feeble-mind said, I found this true, to my cost and to my comfort: to my cost, when he threatened every moment to pick my bones; and to my comfort, when I saw Mr. Great-Heart and his friends come so near with their weapons to deliver me.

Mr. Holy-Man: Then Mr. Holy-man said, There are two things that those who go on pilgrimage need to have: courage, and a spotless life. If they do not have courage, they can never keep on their way; and if their lives are loose, they will make the very name of a pilgrim stink.

Mr. Love-Saints: Then Mr. Love-saints said, I hope this warning is not needed among you; but truly there are many on the road who show themselves strangers to pilgrimage rather than strangers and pilgrims on the earth.

Mr. Dare-Not-Lie: Then Mr. Dare-not-lie said, It’s true. They have neither the pilgrim’s clothing nor the pilgrim’s courage; they do not walk uprightly, but all awry with their feet; one shoe turns in, the other out; and their stockings are worn through at the back: here a rag, and there a tear, to the discredit of their Lord.

Mr. Penitent: These things, said Mr. Penitent, they ought to be troubled about; nor are the pilgrims likely to have the honor they desire put upon them and their Pilgrim’s Progress until the way is cleared of such spots and blemishes. So they sat talking and passing the time until supper was put on the table; they went to it and refreshed their weary bodies, and then they went to bed.

Now they stayed in the fair a long while, at the house of Mr. Mnason, who in the course of time gave his daughter Grace to Samuel, Christian’s son, as his wife, and his daughter Martha to Joseph.

The time they stayed here, as I said, was long, for it was not now as in former times. So the pilgrims got to know many of the good people of the town, and did them what service they could. Mercy, as she always did, worked hard for the poor; so their bellies and backs blessed her, and she was an ornament to her profession of faith there. And to tell the truth about Grace, Phebe, and Martha, they were all of a very good nature, and each did much good in her own place. They were also all of them very fruitful; so that Christian’s name, as was said before, was likely to live on in the world.

While they were staying here, a monster came out of the woods and killed many of the people of the town. It would also carry away their children and teach them to suck its whelps. Now, no man in the town dared so much as face this monster; but all fled when they heard the noise of his coming.

The monster was like no single beast on the earth. Its body was like a dragon, and it had seven heads and ten horns. It made great havoc among children, and yet it was ruled by a woman. Rev 17:3. This monster offered terms to men; and the men who loved their lives more than their souls accepted those terms. So they came under its rule.

Now Mr. Great-Heart, together with those who came to visit the pilgrims at Mr. Mnason’s house, made a covenant to go and fight this beast, in the hope that they might deliver the people of this town from the paws and mouth of so devouring a serpent.

Then Mr. Great-Heart, Mr. Contrite, Mr. Holy-man, Mr. Dare-not-lie, and Mr. Penitent went out with their weapons to meet him. Now at first the monster was very fierce, and looked on these enemies with great scorn; but they beat him so soundly, being sturdy men at arms, that they made him retreat; so they came home to Mr. Mnason’s house again.

The monster, you must know, had certain seasons when he came out and made his attempts on the children of the people of the town. At these seasons these valiant champions watched for him and attacked him again and again, so much so that in the course of time he became not only wounded but lame. Also, he has not made such havoc among the townsmen’s children as he did before; and some firmly believe that this beast will die of his wounds.

This, then, made Mr. Great-Heart and his fellows very famous in this town; so that many of the people who did not share their taste for these things still had a reverent esteem and respect for them. It was on this account, then, that these pilgrims did not come to much harm here. True, there were some of the baser sort, who could see no more than a mole, nor understand any more than a beast; these had no reverence for these men, and took no notice of their valor and adventures.

THE SEVENTH STAGE

Well, the time drew near when the pilgrims must go on their way; so they got ready for their journey. They sent for their friends; they talked things over with them; they set some time apart to commit each other to the protection of their Prince. Again there were some who brought them such things as they had, fit for the weak and the strong, for the women and the men, and so loaded them with what they needed. Acts 28:10. Then they set out on their way; and with their friends going with them as far as was fitting, they again committed each other to the protection of their King, and parted.

So those who were of the pilgrims’ company went on, and Mr. Great-Heart went ahead of them. Now, since the women and children were weak, they had to go at a pace they could bear; and so Mr. Ready-to-halt and Mr. Feeble-mind had more company who shared their condition.

When they had left the townsmen, and their friends had said farewell to them, they soon came to the place where Faithful was put to death. So they stopped there, and thanked him who had enabled Faithful to bear his cross so well; and all the more because they now found that they themselves had benefited from such a manly suffering as his.

After this they went on a good way further, talking of Christian and Faithful, and how Hopeful joined Christian after Faithful was dead.

Now they had come up to the hill Lucre, where the silver mine was that drew Demas away from his pilgrimage, and into which, as some think, By-ends fell and perished; so they thought about that. But when they had come to the old monument that stood opposite the hill Lucre, that is, the pillar of salt, which also stood within sight of Sodom and its stinking lake, they marveled, as Christian had before, that men of such knowledge and maturity of mind as they were should be so blinded as to turn aside here. But then they considered again that nature is not moved by the harm that others have come to, especially if the thing it looks at has an attracting power over the foolish eye.

I saw now that they went on until they came to the river that was on this side of the Delectable Mountains; the river where the fine trees grow on both banks, whose leaves, if taken inwardly, are good against overindulgence; where the meadows are green all year round, and where they might lie down safely. Ps 23:2.

By this river, in the meadows, there were pens and folds for sheep, and a house built for the nourishing and bringing up of those lambs, the babies of the women who go on pilgrimage. There was also one here who was entrusted with them, who could have compassion, and who could gather these lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and gently lead those that were with young. Heb 5:2; Isa 40:11. Now Christiana urged her four daughters to commit their little ones to this man’s care, so that by these waters they might be housed, sheltered, cared for, and nourished, and that none of them might be missing in time to come. If any of them go astray or are lost, this man will bring them back; he will also bind up what was broken, and strengthen those who are sick. Jer 23:4; Ezek 34:11–16. Here they will never lack food, drink, and clothing; here they will be kept from thieves and robbers; for this man will die before one of those committed to his trust is lost. Besides, here they will be sure to have good nurture and admonition, and will be taught to walk in right paths, and that, you know, is a favor of no small account. Also here, as you see, are delightful waters, pleasant meadows, lovely flowers, a variety of trees, and trees that bear wholesome fruit: not fruit like the fruit Matthew ate, which fell over the wall out of Beelzebub’s garden, but fruit that brings health where there is none, and keeps it and increases it where it is. So they were content to commit their little ones to him; and what also encouraged them to do so was that all this was to be at the King’s expense, and so was like a charitable home for young children and orphans.

Now they went on. And when they had come to By-path Meadow, to the stile over which Christian went with his companion Hopeful when they were taken by Giant Despair and put into Doubting Castle, they sat down and discussed what was best to do: that is, whether, now that they were so strong and had such a man as Mr. Great-Heart for their conductor, it would not be best to make an attempt on the giant, demolish his castle, and, if there were any pilgrims in it, set them free before they went any further. So one said one thing, and another the opposite. One questioned whether it was lawful to go on unconsecrated ground; another said they might, provided their purpose was good; but Mr. Great-Heart said, Though that last claim cannot be true in every case, yet I have a commandment to resist sin, to overcome evil, to fight the good fight of faith; and tell me, with whom should I fight this good fight, if not with Giant Despair? So I will try to take away his life and to demolish Doubting Castle. Then he said, Who will go with me? Then old Honest said, I will. And so will we, said Christiana’s four sons, Matthew, Samuel, Joseph, and James; for they were young men and strong. 1 John 2:13, 14. So they left the women in the road, and with them Mr. Feeble-mind, and Mr. Ready-to-halt with his crutches, to guard them until they came back; for in that place, though Giant Despair lived so near, as long as they kept to the road a little child might lead them. Isa 11:6.

So Mr. Great-Heart, old Honest, and the four young men went up to Doubting Castle to look for Giant Despair. When they came to the castle gate, they knocked to be let in, with an unusual noise. At that the old Giant comes to the gate, and Diffidence his wife follows. Then he said, Who and what is he who is so bold as to disturb the Giant Despair like this? Mr. Great-Heart replied, It is I, Great-Heart, one of the King of the Celestial country’s conductors of pilgrims to their place; and I demand that you open your gates to let me in. Get ready also to fight, for I have come to take off your head, and to demolish Doubting Castle.

Now Giant Despair, because he was a giant, thought no man could overcome him; and again he thought, Since I have conquered angels before now, should Great-Heart make me afraid? So he armed himself and went out. He had a steel cap on his head and a breastplate of fire fastened about him, and he came out in iron shoes, with a great club in his hand. Then these six men closed in on him, and attacked him from behind and in front; also, when Diffidence the giantess came up to help him, old Mr. Honest cut her down with one blow. Then they fought for their lives, and Giant Despair was brought down to the ground, but was very unwilling to die. He struggled hard, and had, as they say, as many lives as a cat; but Great-Heart was his death, for he did not leave him until he had severed his head from his shoulders.

Then they set about demolishing Doubting Castle, and that, you know, could easily be done, since Giant Despair was dead. They spent seven days in destroying it; and of pilgrims in it they found one Mr. Despondency, almost starved to death, and one Much-afraid, his daughter: these two they rescued alive. But it would have astonished you to see the dead bodies that lay here and there in the castle yard, and how full of dead men’s bones the dungeon was.

When Mr. Great-Heart and his companions had carried out this exploit, they took Mr. Despondency and his daughter Much-afraid under their protection; for they were upright people, though they had been prisoners in Doubting Castle to that tyrant Giant Despair. So, I say, they took the giant’s head with them (for they had buried his body under a heap of stones), and came down to the road and to their companions, and showed them what they had done. Now when Feeble-mind and Ready-to-halt saw that it really was the head of Giant Despair, they were very glad and merry. Now Christiana, when there was need, could play the viol, and her daughter Mercy the lute; so, since they were in such a merry mood, she played them a tune, and Ready-to-halt wanted to dance. So he took Despondency’s daughter, Much-afraid, by the hand, and they began dancing in the road. True, he could not dance without one crutch in his hand, but I promise you he stepped it out well; and the girl was to be praised too, for she kept time with the music beautifully.

As for Mr. Despondency, the music was not much to his taste; he was for eating rather than dancing, because he was almost starved. So Christiana gave him some of her bottle of spirits for immediate relief, and then made him something to eat; and in a little while the old gentleman came to himself and began to revive nicely.

Now I saw in my dream that, when all these things were finished, Mr. Great-Heart took the head of Giant Despair and set it on a pole by the side of the highway, right opposite the pillar that Christian set up as a warning to the pilgrims who came after him, to beware of entering the giant’s grounds.

Then he wrote under it, on a marble stone, the following verses:

““This is the head of him whose name only

In former times would pilgrims terrify.

His castle’s down, and Diffidence his wife

Brave Mr. Great-Heart has bereft of life.

Despondency, his daughter Much-afraid,

Great-Heart for them as well the man has played.

Who doubts this, if he’ll only cast his eye

Up here, may his misgivings satisfy.

This head also, when doubting cripples dance,

Shows that from fears they have deliverance.””

When these men had shown themselves so brave against Doubting Castle, and had killed Giant Despair, they went forward, and went on until they came to the Delectable Mountains, where Christian and Hopeful had refreshed themselves with the many good things of the place. They also got to know the shepherds there, who welcomed them to the Delectable Mountains, as they had welcomed Christian before.

Now the shepherds, seeing so large a party following Mr. Great-Heart (for they knew him well), said to him, Good sir, you have a fine company here; please, where did you find all these?

Then Mr. Great-Heart replied,

““First, here is Christiana, in whose care

Are her sons and their wives, who, like the Great Bear,

Keep by the pole, and by the compass steer

From sin to grace, or they would not be here.

Next here’s old Honest come on pilgrimage,

Ready-to-halt too, who, I dare to pledge,

Is true-hearted, and so is Feeble-mind,

Who was not willing to be left behind.

Despondency, good man, is coming after,

And so also is Much-afraid, his daughter.

May we be given lodging here, or must

We go on farther? Tell us what to trust.””

Then the shepherds said, This is a heartening company. You are welcome here; for we provide for the feeble as well as for the strong. Our Prince takes note of what is done to the least of these; so Infirmity must not be an obstacle to our welcome. Matt 25:40. So they took them to the palace door, and then said to them, Come in, Mr. Feeble-Mind; come in, Mr. Ready-to-halt; come in, Mr. Despondency, and Mrs. Much-afraid his daughter. These, Mr. Great-Heart, said the shepherds to the guide, we call in by name, because they are the most apt to draw back; but as for you and the rest who are strong, we leave you to your usual liberty. Then Mr. Great-Heart said, Today I see that grace shines in your faces, and that you are my Lord’s shepherds indeed; for you have not pushed these sick ones with either side or shoulder, but have rather strewn their way into the palace with flowers, as you should. Ezek 34:21.

So the feeble and weak went in, and Mr. Great-Heart and the rest followed. When they too had sat down, the shepherds said to those of the weaker sort, What would you like? For, they said, everything here must be managed to support the weak as well as to warn the unruly. So they made them a feast of things easy to digest, pleasant to the taste, and nourishing; and when they had eaten it, they went to their rest, each one to his own place.

When morning came, because the mountains were high and the day clear, and because it was the shepherds’ custom to show the pilgrims some rare sights before they left, after they were ready and had refreshed themselves the shepherds took them out into the fields, and showed them first what they had shown Christian before.

Then they took them to some new places. The first was Mount Marvel, where they looked and saw a man in the distance who tumbled the hills about with words. Then they asked the shepherds what that meant. So they told them that that man was the son of one Mr. Great-grace, of whom you read in the first part of the records of the Pilgrim’s Progress; and he is set there to teach pilgrims how to believe down, or to tumble out of their way, whatever difficulties they meet with, by faith. Mark 11:23, 24. Then Mr. Great-Heart said, I know him; he is a man above many.

Then they took them to another place, called Mount Innocence. And there they saw a man clothed all in white, and two men, Prejudice and Ill-will, continually throwing dirt at him. Now look: whatever dirt they threw at him would in a little while fall off again, and his garment would look as clean as if no dirt had been thrown at it. Then the pilgrims said, What does this mean? The shepherds answered, This man is named Godlyman, and this garment is to show the innocence of his life. Now, those who throw dirt at him are such as hate his doing good; but as you see the dirt will not stick to his clothes, so it shall be with him who lives innocently in the world. Whoever they are who would make such men dirty, they labor all in vain; for God, when a little time has passed, will make their innocence break forth like the light, and their righteousness like the noonday.

Then they took them to Mount Charity, where they showed them a man who had a bundle of cloth lying in front of him, out of which he cut coats and garments for the poor who stood around him; yet his bundle or roll of cloth never grew any smaller. Then they said, What does this mean? This is, said the shepherds, to show you that he who has a heart to give of his labor to the poor shall never lack the means to do it. He who waters shall be watered himself. And the cake that the widow gave to the prophet did not leave her with any less in her barrel.

They also took them to the place where they saw Fool and Want-wit washing an Ethiopian, intending to make him white; but the more they washed him, the blacker he was. Then they asked the shepherds what that meant. So they told them, Thus it is with the vile person; all the means used to get such a one a good name will in the end only make him more abominable. Thus it was with the pharisees; and so it shall be with all hypocrites.

Then Mercy, the wife of Matthew, said to Christiana her mother, Mother, if it may be, I would like to see the hole in the hill, or what is commonly called the By-way to hell. So her mother told the shepherds her wish. Then they went to the door; it was in the side of a hill; and they opened it, and told Mercy to listen a while. So she listened, and heard one saying, Cursed be my father for holding my feet back from the way of peace and life. Another said, Oh, that I had been torn in pieces before I lost my soul to save my life! And another said, If I were to live again, how I would deny myself rather than come to this place! Then it was as if the very earth groaned and shook under the feet of this young woman for fear; so she turned white, and came away trembling, saying, Blessed are he and she who are delivered from this place!

Now when the shepherds had shown them all these things, they took them back to the palace and gave them the best the house could provide. But Mercy, being a young married woman, longed for something she saw there, but was ashamed to ask. Her mother-in-law then asked her what was wrong, for she looked as if she was not well. Then Mercy said, There is a mirror hanging in the dining room that I cannot take my mind off; so if I do not have it, I think I will miscarry. Then her mother said, I will tell the shepherds what you want, and they will not refuse you. But she said, I am ashamed that these men should know that I longed for it. No, my daughter, she said, it is no shame, but a virtue, to long for such a thing as that. So Mercy said, Then, mother, if you please, ask the shepherds if they are willing to sell it.

Now the mirror was one in a thousand. Held one way, it would show a man his own features exactly; turn it just another way, and it would show the very face and likeness of the Prince of pilgrims himself. Yes, I have talked with those who know, and they have said that they have seen the very crown of thorns on his head by looking in that mirror; they have also seen in it the holes in his hands, his feet, and his side. Indeed, there is such excellence in this mirror that it will show him to anyone in whatever way they wish to see him, whether living or dead; whether on earth or in heaven; whether in his state of humiliation or in his exaltation; whether coming to suffer or coming to reign. Jas 1:23; 1 Cor 13:12; 2 Cor 3:18.

So Christiana went to the shepherds privately (now the names of the shepherds were Knowledge, Experience, Watchful, and Sincere), and said to them, One of my daughters, who is expecting a child, longs, I think, for something she has seen in this house; and she thinks she will miscarry if you refuse her.

Experience: Call her, call her; she shall certainly have whatever we can give her. So they called her, and said to her, Mercy, what is it that you would like? Then she blushed and said, The great mirror that hangs in the dining room. So Sincere ran and fetched it, and it was given to her with joyful consent. Then she bowed her head and gave thanks, and said, By this I know that I have found favor in your eyes.

They also gave the other young women such things as they desired, and gave their husbands high praise, because they had joined with Mr. Great-Heart in killing Giant Despair and demolishing Doubting Castle.

Around Christiana’s neck the shepherds put a necklace, and so they did around the necks of her four daughters; they also put earrings in their ears, and jewels on their foreheads.

When they were ready to go on from there, the shepherds let them go in peace, but did not give them the particular warnings that had been given before to Christian and his companion. The reason was that these had Great-Heart for their guide, who knew these things well, and so could give them their warnings at a more fitting time, that is, just when the danger was drawing near. Whatever warnings Christian and his companion had received from the shepherds, they had also lost by the time they needed to put them into practice. So here was the advantage that this company had over the other.

From there they went on singing, and they said,

““Behold how fitly are the stages set

For their relief who pilgrims have become,

And how they take us in, no hindrance met,

Who make the other life our mark and home!”

“What new things they have, to us they give,

So we, though pilgrims, joyful lives may live;

They also upon us such things bestow

That show we’re pilgrims, wherever we go.””

THE EIGHTH STAGE

When they had left the shepherds, they quickly came to the place where Christian met one Turn-away, who lived in the town of Apostasy. So Mr. Great-Heart their guide now reminded them of him, saying, This is the place where Christian met one Turn-away, who carried the mark of his rebellion on his back. And this I have to say about this man: he would listen to no advice, but once he began to fall, no persuasion could stop him. When he came to the place where the cross and the sepulcher were, he met someone who told him to look there; but he gnashed his teeth, and stamped, and said he was determined to go back to his own town. Before he came to the gate, he met Evangelist, who offered to lay hands on him, to turn him back into the way; but this Turn-away resisted him, and after treating him with great contempt, he got away over the wall, and so escaped his hand.

Then they went on; and just at the place where Little-Faith was once robbed, there stood a man with his sword drawn, and his face all covered with blood. Then Mr. Great-Heart said, Who are you? The man answered, I am one whose name is Valiant-for-truth. I am a pilgrim, and I am going to the Celestial City. Now, as I was on my way, three men surrounded me, and put these three things to me: 1. Whether I would become one of them. 2. Or go back to where I came from. 3. Or die on the spot. Prov 1:11–14. To the first I answered that I had been an honest man for a long time, and so they could not expect me to cast in my lot with thieves now. Then they demanded what I would say to the second. So I told them that, as for the place I came from, if I had not found it a hardship to me, I would not have left it at all; but since I found it altogether unsuited to me, and very unprofitable for me, I left it for this way. Then they asked me what I said to the third. And I told them my life had cost far too dear for me to give it away lightly. Besides, you have no business putting things to my choice like this; so if you meddle, it is at your own peril. Then these three, namely Wild-head, Inconsiderate, and Pragmatic, drew on me, and I also drew on them. So we fell to it, one against three, for more than three hours. They have left on me, as you see, some of the marks of their valor, and they have also carried away with them some of mine. They have only just now gone; I suppose they may, as the saying is, have heard your horse dash, and so they took to flight.

Mr. Great-Heart: But those were great odds, three against one.

Valiant-for-Truth: It is true; but few and many are nothing to him who has the truth on his side. “Though an army encamps around me,” said one, Ps 27:3, “my heart will not fear; though a war breaks out against me, I will keep my trust,” etc. Besides, he said, I have read in some records that one man has fought an army: and how many did Samson kill with the jawbone of an ass!

Mr. Great-Heart: Then the guide said, Why did you not cry out, so that someone might have come to help you?

Valiant-for-Truth: I did, to my King, who I knew could hear me and give me unseen help, and that was enough for me.

Mr. Great-Heart: Then Great-Heart said to Mr. Valiant-for-truth, You have behaved worthily; let me see your sword. So he showed it to him.

When he had taken it in his hand and looked at it for a while, he said, Ha, it is a true Jerusalem blade.

Valiant-for-Truth: It is. Let a man have one of these blades, with a hand to wield it and skill to use it, and he may take on an angel with it. He need not fear that it will not hold, if only he knows how to lay on. Its edge will never grow blunt. It will cut flesh and bones, and soul, and spirit, and all. Heb 4:12.

Mr. Great-Heart: But you fought a long while; I wonder you were not worn out.

Valiant-for-Truth: I fought until my sword stuck to my hand; and then they were joined together as if a sword grew out of my arm; and when the blood ran through my fingers, then I fought with the most courage.

Mr. Great-Heart: You have done well; you have resisted to the point of shedding your blood, striving against sin. You shall stay with us, and come in and go out with us; for we are your companions. Then they took him and washed his wounds, and gave him some of what they had, to refresh him; and so they went on together.

Now, as they went on, because Mr. Great-Heart was delighted with him (for he greatly loved anyone he found to be a man of valor), and because there were some in the company who were feeble and weak, he asked him about many things; first, where he was from.

Valiant-for-Truth: I am from Dark-land; for I was born there, and my father and mother are still there.

Mr. Great-Heart: Dark-land! said the guide; does that not lie on the same coast as the City of Destruction?

Valiant-for-Truth: Yes, it does. Now what made me come on pilgrimage was this. A man called Mr. Tell-true came into our parts, and he spread the word about what Christian had done, who went from the City of Destruction; namely, how he had forsaken his wife and children, and taken up a pilgrim’s life. It was also confidently reported how he had killed a serpent that came out to resist him on his journey, and how he got through to where he meant to go. It was also told what welcome he had at all his Lord’s lodgings, especially when he came to the gates of the Celestial City; for there, the man said, he was received with the sound of trumpets by a company of shining ones. He told also how all the bells in the city rang for joy at his reception, and what golden garments he was clothed with; with many other things that I will not stop to tell now. In a word, that man told the story of Christian and his travels in such a way that my heart fell into a burning haste to go after him; and neither father nor mother could hold me back. So I got away from them, and have come this far on my way.

Mr. Great-Heart: You came in at the gate, did you not?

Valiant-for-Truth: Yes, yes; for the same man also told us that it would all count for nothing unless we began this way by entering at the gate.

Mr. Great-Heart: Look, said the guide to Christiana, the pilgrimage of your husband, and what he has gained by it, is talked of far and near.

Valiant-for-Truth: Why, is this Christian’s wife?

Mr. Great-Heart: Yes, it is indeed; and these are his four sons too.

Valiant-for-Truth: What, and going on pilgrimage too?

Mr. Great-Heart: Yes, indeed, they are following after him.

Valiant-for-Truth: It makes my heart glad. Good man, how joyful he will be when he sees those who would not go with him entering after him all the same, in at the gates into the Celestial City!

Mr. Great-Heart: No doubt it will be a comfort to him; for, next to the joy of seeing himself there, it will be a joy to meet his wife and children there.

Valiant-for-Truth: But now that you have touched on that, please let me hear your opinion about it. Some wonder whether we will know one another when we are there.

Mr. Great-Heart: Do you think they will know themselves then, or that they will rejoice to see themselves in that bliss? And if they think they will know themselves and do this, why not know others, and rejoice in their welfare also? Again, since our families are our second selves, though those ties will be dissolved there, why may we not reasonably conclude that we will be more glad to see them there than to find them missing?

Valiant-for-Truth: Well, I see where you stand on this. Do you have anything more to ask me about how I began to come on pilgrimage?

Mr. Great-Heart: Yes; were your father and mother willing for you to become a pilgrim?

Valiant-for-Truth: Oh no; they used every means imaginable to persuade me to stay at home.

Mr. Great-Heart: Why, what could they say against it?

Valiant-for-Truth: They said it was an idle life; and that if I were not inclined to sloth and laziness myself, I would never think well of a pilgrim’s life.

Mr. Great-Heart: And what else did they say?

Valiant-for-Truth: Why, they told me that it was a dangerous way; in fact, the most dangerous way in the world, they said, is the one the pilgrims take.

Mr. Great-Heart: Did they show you what makes this way so dangerous?

Valiant-for-Truth: Yes; and on many points.

Mr. Great-Heart: Name some of them.

Valiant-for-Truth: They told me of the Slough of Despond, where Christian was nearly smothered. They told me that there were archers standing ready in Beelzebub-castle to shoot anyone who knocked at the Wicket-gate to get in. They also told me of the wood and the dark mountains; of the hill Difficulty; of the lions; and also of the three giants, Bloody-man, Maul, and Slay-good. They said, moreover, that a foul fiend haunted the Valley of Humiliation, and that Christian was almost robbed of his life by him. Besides, they said, you must go through the Valley of the Shadow of Death, where the hobgoblins are, where the light is darkness, where the way is full of snares, pits, traps, and nooses. They told me also of Giant Despair, of Doubting Castle, and of the ruin that the pilgrims met with there. Further, they said I must go over the Enchanted Ground, which was dangerous; and that after all this I would find a river with no bridge over it; and that this river lay between me and the Celestial country.

Mr. Great-Heart: And was this all?

Valiant-for-Truth: No. They also told me that this way was full of deceivers, and of people who lay in wait there to turn good men out of the path.

Mr. Great-Heart: But how did they show that?

Valiant-for-Truth: They told me that Mr. Worldly Wiseman lay in wait there to deceive. They also said that Formality and Hypocrisy were always on the road. They said too that By-ends, Talkative, or Demas would very likely pick me up; that the Flatterer would catch me in his net; or that, with green-headed Ignorance, I would presume to go on to the gate, from which he was sent back to the hole in the side of the hill, and made to go the by-way to hell.

Mr. Great-Heart: I assure you, this was enough to discourage you; but did they stop there?

Valiant-for-Truth: No, wait. They also told me of many who had tried that way long ago, and had gone a long way on it, to see if they could find something of the glory there that so many had talked so much about from time to time; and how they came back again, and called themselves fools for ever setting foot out of doors on that path, to the satisfaction of the whole country. And they named several who did so, such as Obstinate and Pliable, Mistrust and Timorous, Turn-away and old Atheist, and several more; some of whom, they said, had gone far to see what they could find, but not one of them had gained so much as a feather’s weight by going.

Mr. Great-Heart: Did they say anything more to discourage you?

Valiant-for-Truth: Yes. They told me of one Mr. Fearing, who was a pilgrim, and how he found the way so lonely that he never had an hour’s comfort on it; also that Mr. Despondency had nearly starved on it; yes, and also (which I had almost forgotten) that Christian himself, about whom there has been such a noise, after all his adventures for a celestial crown, was certainly drowned in the Black River and never went a foot further, however it was hushed up.

Mr. Great-Heart: And did none of these things discourage you?

Valiant-for-Truth: No; they seemed like so many nothings to me.

Mr. Great-Heart: How was that?

Valiant-for-Truth: Why, I went on believing what Mr. Tell-true had said; and that carried me past them all.

Mr. Great-Heart: Then this was your victory, even your faith.

Valiant-for-Truth: It was. I believed, and so came out, got into the way, fought all who set themselves against me, and by believing have come to this place.

““Who would true valor see,

Let him come hither;

One here will constant be,

Come wind, come weather;

There’s no discouragement

Shall make him once relent

His first avow’d intent

To be a pilgrim.”

“Whoso beset him round

With dismal stories,

Do but themselves confound;

His strength the more is.

No lion can him fright,

He’ll with a giant fight,

But he will have a right

To be a pilgrim.”

“Hobgoblin nor foul fiend

Can daunt his spirit;

He knows he at the end

Shall life inherit.

Then fancies fly away,

He’ll not fear what men say;

He’ll labor night and day

To be a pilgrim.””

By this time they had reached the Enchanted Ground, where the air naturally tended to make one drowsy. And that place was all overgrown with briars and thorns, except here and there, where there was an enchanted arbor; and if a man sits in one, or sleeps in one, it is a question, some say, whether he will ever rise or wake again in this world. So they went over this forest, one and all, and Mr. Great-Heart went in front, because he was the guide; and Mr. Valiant-for-truth came behind as rear-guard, for fear that some fiend, or dragon, or giant, or thief might perhaps fall upon their rear and do them harm. They went on here, each man with his sword drawn in his hand; for they knew it was a dangerous place. They also cheered one another up as well as they could. Mr. Great-Heart ordered Feeble-mind to come up after him; and Mr. Despondency was under the eye of Mr. Valiant.

Now they had not gone far when a great mist and darkness fell on them all, so that for a long while they could hardly see one another. So for some time they had to feel for one another by words; for they were not walking by sight. Anyone can see that this was nothing but hard going even for the best of them; but how much worse for the women and children, who were tender both in feet and in heart! Yet so it was that, through the encouraging words of the one who led in front and the one who brought them up behind, they managed pretty well to jog along.

The way here was also very wearisome, through dirt and sludge. Nor was there, in all this ground, so much as one inn or eating-house in which to refresh the weaker ones. So here there was grunting, and puffing, and sighing, while one tumbles over a bush, another sticks fast in the dirt, and some of the children lost their shoes in the mire; while one cries out, I am down; and another, Hello, where are you? and a third, The bushes have got such a hold on me, I do not think I can get away from them.

Then they came to an arbor, warm, and promising much refreshment to the pilgrims; for it was finely made overhead, decorated with greenery, and furnished with benches and seats. It also had a soft couch in it on which the weary might lean. This, as you can imagine, all things considered, was tempting; for the pilgrims were already beginning to be worn down by the badness of the way: but not one of them made so much as a move to stop there. Indeed, as far as I could see, they paid such constant heed to the advice of their guide, and he told them so faithfully of the dangers, and of the nature of the dangers when they were at them, that usually, when they were nearest to them, they plucked up their spirits most, and encouraged one another to deny the flesh. This arbor was called The Slothful’s Friend, and was made on purpose to lure some of the pilgrims, if it could, to take up their rest there when weary.

I saw then in my dream that they went on in this lonely ground of theirs, till they came to a place where a man is apt to lose his way. Now, though in the light their guide could tell well enough how to avoid the ways that led wrong, in the dark he was brought to a standstill. But he had in his pocket a map of all the ways leading to or from the Celestial City; so he struck a light (for he never goes without his tinder-box either), and takes a look at his book or map, which tells him to be careful in that place to turn to the right. And had he not been careful here to look at his map, they would in all probability have all been smothered in the mud; for just a little ahead of them, and that at the end of the cleanest way too, was a pit, no one knows how deep, full of nothing but mud, made there on purpose to destroy the pilgrims in.

Then I thought to myself, Who, going on pilgrimage, would not want one of these maps with him, so that when he is at a standstill he may look to see which way he must take?

Then they went on in this Enchanted Ground till they came to another arbor, built by the side of the highway. And in that arbor lay two men, whose names were Heedless and Too-bold. These two had gone this far on pilgrimage; but here, being wearied with their journey, they sat down to rest, and so fell fast asleep. When the pilgrims saw them, they stood still and shook their heads; for they knew that the sleepers were in a pitiful state. Then they discussed what to do, whether to go on and leave them sleeping, or to step over to them and try to wake them; and they decided to go to them and wake them, that is, if they could; but with this caution, namely, to take care that they themselves did not sit down or accept the comfort that arbor offered.

So they went in and spoke to the men, and called each by his name, for the guide, it seems, knew them; but there was neither voice nor answer. Then the guide shook them, and did what he could to rouse them. Then one of them said, I will pay you when I get my money. At which the guide shook his head. I will fight as long as I can hold my sword in my hand, said the other. At that, one of the children laughed.

Then Christiana said, What does this mean? The guide said, They are talking in their sleep. If you strike them, beat them, or do whatever else you like to them, they will answer you in this way; or, as one of them said long ago, when the waves of the sea beat upon him, and he slept like one lying on the mast of a ship, Prov 23:34, 35, When I awake, I will seek it yet again. You know that when men talk in their sleep they say anything; their words are not governed by either faith or reason. Their words do not hang together now, just as their going on pilgrimage and their sitting down here did not hang together before. This, then, is the harm of it: when heedless people go on pilgrimage, it is twenty to one that this is what happens to them. For this Enchanted Ground is one of the last refuges that the enemy of pilgrims has; so it is, as you see, placed almost at the end of the way, and so it stands against us with all the more advantage. For when, the enemy thinks, will these fools be so eager to sit down as when they are weary? and when so likely to be weary as when they are almost at their journey’s end? That is why, I say, the Enchanted Ground is placed so near to the land Beulah, and so near the end of their race. So let pilgrims look to themselves, so that it does not happen to them as it has to these, who, as you see, have fallen asleep, and no one can wake them.

Then the pilgrims, trembling, longed to go forward; only they begged their guide to strike a light, so that they might go the rest of their way by the help of the light of a lantern. So he struck a light, and by its help they went through the rest of this way, though the darkness was very great. 2 Pet 1:19. But the children began to be very weary, and they cried out to him who loves pilgrims to make their way more comfortable. So by the time they had gone a little further, a wind arose that drove away the fog, and the air became clearer. Yet they were not off the Enchanted Ground (far from it); only now they could see one another better, and the way in which they should walk.

Now when they were almost at the end of this ground, they noticed that a little ahead of them there was a solemn noise, as of someone deeply concerned. So they went on and looked ahead: and there, as they thought, they saw a man on his knees, with hands and eyes lifted up, speaking, as they thought, earnestly to one who was above. They drew near, but could not make out what he said; so they went softly till he had finished. When he had finished, he got up and began to run toward the Celestial City. Then Mr. Great-Heart called after him, saying, Hello there, friend, let us have your company, if you are going, as I suppose you are, to the Celestial City. So the man stopped, and they came up to him. But as soon as Mr. Honest saw him, he said, I know this man. Then Mr. Valiant-for-truth said, Please tell us, who is it? It is one, he said, who comes from near where I lived. His name is Standfast; he is certainly a truly good pilgrim.

So they came up to one another; and at once Standfast said to old Honest, Why, father Honest, are you there? Yes, he said, that I am, as sure as you are there. I am truly glad, said Mr. Standfast, that I have found you on this road. And I am just as glad, said the other, that I caught sight of you on your knees. Then Mr. Standfast blushed, and said, But why, did you see me? Yes, that I did, said the other, and my heart was glad at the sight. Why, what did you think? said Standfast. Think! said old Honest; what could I think? I thought we had an honest man on the road, and so would soon have his company. If you thought rightly, said Standfast, how happy I am! But if I am not as I should be, I alone must bear it. That is true, said the other; but your fear makes me all the more sure that things are right between the Prince of pilgrims and your soul. For he says, “Blessed is the man who fears always.” Prov 28:14.

Valiant-for-Truth: Well, but, brother, please tell us what it was that brought you to your knees just now: was it because some special mercy had laid obligations on you, or what was it?

Standfast: Why, we are, as you see, on the Enchanted Ground; and as I was coming along, I was thinking to myself how dangerous the road in this place was, and how many who had come even this far on pilgrimage had been stopped and destroyed here. I thought also of the kind of death by which this place destroys men. Those who die here die of no violent disease: the death they die is not painful to them. For he who goes off in his sleep begins that journey with desire and pleasure. Indeed, such men give themselves up willingly to the will of that disease.

Mr. Honest: Then Mr. Honest, interrupting him, said, Did you see the two men asleep in the arbor?

Standfast: Yes, yes, I saw Heedless and Too-bold there; and for all I know, there they will lie till they rot. Prov 10:7. But let me go on with my story. As I was thinking like this, as I said, someone in very fine clothes, but old, came and presented herself to me, and offered me three things, namely, her body, her purse, and her bed. Now the truth is, I was both weary and sleepy. I am also as poor as an owlet, and perhaps the witch knew that. Well, I rebuffed her again and again, but she brushed my refusals aside and smiled. Then I began to be angry; but she did not care about that at all. Then she made her offers again, and said that if I would let her rule me, she would make me great and happy; for, she said, I am the mistress of the world, and men are made happy by me. Then I asked her name, and she told me it was Madam Bubble. This drove me further from her; but she still followed me with enticements. Then I went, as you saw, to my knees, and with hands lifted up, and cries, I prayed to Him who had said he would help. So, just as you came up, the gentlewoman went her way. Then I went on giving thanks for this great deliverance of mine; for I truly believe she meant no good, but rather was trying to stop me on my journey.

Mr. Honest: No doubt her designs were bad. But wait, now that you talk of her, I think I have either seen her or read some story about her.

Standfast: Perhaps you have done both.

Mr. Honest: Madam Bubble! Is she not a tall, handsome lady, with a rather dark complexion?

Standfast: Right, you have hit it: she is just like that.

Mr. Honest: Does she not speak very smoothly, and give you a smile at the end of a sentence?

Standfast: You have hit on it again, for that is just how she behaves.

Mr. Honest: Does she not wear a great purse at her side, and is her hand not often in it, fingering her money, as if that were her heart’s delight?

Standfast: That is just it; if she had stood here all this while, you could not have described her to me more fully, nor have pictured her features better.

Mr. Honest: Then he who drew her picture was a good painter, and he who wrote of her told the truth.

Mr. Great-Heart: This woman is a witch, and it is by the power of her sorceries that this ground is enchanted. Whoever lays his head down in her lap might as well lay it on the block over which the axe hangs; and whoever sets eyes on her beauty is counted an enemy of God. It is she who keeps in their splendor all those who are the enemies of pilgrims. Jas 4:4. Indeed, it is she who has bought many a man off from a pilgrim’s life. She is a great gossip; she is always, she and her daughters, at one pilgrim’s heels or another’s, now commending, and then promoting the excellences of this life. She is a bold and impudent hussy: she will talk with any man. She always laughs poor pilgrims to scorn, but highly praises the rich. If there is someone clever at getting money in a place, she will speak well of him from house to house. She is extremely fond of banqueting and feasting; she is always at one full table or another. She has put it about in some places that she is a goddess, and so some worship her. She has her times and open places of cheating; and she will say and swear that no one can show a good to compare with hers. She promises to live with children’s children, if only they will love her and make much of her. In some places and to some persons she will throw gold out of her purse like dust. She loves to be sought after, spoken well of, and to lie in the bosoms of men. She is never tired of praising her goods, and she loves those most who think best of her. She will promise crowns and kingdoms to some, if only they will take her advice; yet she has brought many to the noose, and ten thousand times more to hell.

Standfast: Oh, said Standfast, what a mercy it is that I resisted her; for where might she have drawn me!

Mr. Great-Heart: Where? Indeed, none but God knows where. But in general, to be sure, she would have drawn you into many foolish and harmful lusts, which drown men in ruin and destruction. 1 Tim 6:9. It was she who set Absalom against his father, and Jeroboam against his master. It was she who persuaded Judas to sell his Lord, and who won Demas over to forsake the godly pilgrim’s life. No one can tell the harm she does. She stirs up strife between rulers and subjects, between parents and children, between neighbor and neighbor, between a man and his wife, between a man and himself, between the flesh and the spirit. So, good Mr. Standfast, be as your name is, and when you have done all, stand.

At this talk there was a mixture of joy and trembling among the pilgrims; but at length they broke out and sang,

““What danger is the Pilgrim in!

How many are his foes!

How many ways there are to sin

No living mortal knows.”

“Some in the ditch are ruined, yes, can

Lie tumbling in the mire:

Some, though they shun the frying-pan

Will leap into the fire.””

After this, I watched until they had come into the land of Beulah, where the sun shines night and day. Here, because they were weary, they gave themselves up to rest for a while. And because this country was open to pilgrims, and because the orchards and vineyards here belonged to the King of the Celestial country, they were free to help themselves to any of his things. But a little while soon refreshed them here; for the bells rang so, and the trumpets sounded so continually and so melodiously, that they could not sleep; and yet they were as refreshed as if they had slept ever so soundly. Here also the cry of all who walked the streets was, More pilgrims have come to town! And another would answer, And so many went over the water, and were let in at the golden gates today! They would cry again, There is now a legion of shining ones just come to town, by which we know that there are more pilgrims on the road; for they come here to wait for them, and to comfort them after all their sorrow. Then the pilgrims got up and walked to and fro. But how their ears were now filled with heavenly sounds, and their eyes delighted with celestial visions! In this land they heard nothing, saw nothing, felt nothing, smelled nothing, tasted nothing that was offensive to their stomach or mind; only when they tasted the water of the river they were to go over, they thought it tasted a little bitter to the palate; but it proved sweeter when it was down.

In this place a record was kept of the names of those who had been pilgrims long ago, and a history of all the famous deeds they had done. There was also much talk here of how the river had been in flood for some, and how it had ebbed while others went over. It has been almost dry for some, while it has overflowed its banks for others.

In this place the children of the town would go into the King’s gardens and gather posies for the pilgrims, and bring them to them with much affection. Here also grew henna, with spikenard and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, with all the trees of frankincense, myrrh, and aloes, with all the chief spices. With these the pilgrims’ rooms were perfumed while they stayed here; and with these their bodies were anointed, to prepare them to go over the river when the appointed time had come.

Now, while they lay here waiting for the good hour, word went round the town that a messenger had come from the Celestial City, with a matter of great importance for one Christiana, the wife of Christian the pilgrim. So inquiries were made for her, and the house where she was staying was found. So the messenger handed her a letter. It read: Hail, good woman; I bring you news that the Master calls for you, and expects you to stand in his presence in clothes of immortality within these ten days.

When he had read this letter to her, he gave her with it a sure token that he was a true messenger, and had come to tell her to make haste to be gone. The token was an arrow with a point sharpened with love, let gently into her heart, which by degrees worked so effectually in her that at the appointed time she must be gone.

When Christiana saw that her time had come, and that she was the first of this company to go over, she called for Mr. Great-Heart her guide, and told him how matters stood. So he told her he was heartily glad of the news, and would have been glad if the messenger had come for him. Then she asked him to advise her how everything should be prepared for her journey. So he told her, saying, Such and such must be done, and we who survive will go with you to the river-side.

Then she called for her children and gave them her blessing, and told them that she had read with comfort the mark that was set on their foreheads, and was glad to see them there with her, and that they had kept their garments so white. Lastly, she left to the poor the little she had, and charged her sons and daughters to be ready for when the messenger should come for them.

When she had spoken these words to her guide and to her children, she called for Mr. Valiant-for-truth, and said to him, Sir, you have shown yourself true-hearted in every place; be faithful unto death, and my King will give you a crown of life. Rev 2:10. I would also ask you to keep an eye on my children; and if at any time you see them faint, speak comforting words to them. As for my daughters, my sons’ wives, they have been faithful, and the fulfilling of the promise to them will be their end. But she gave Mr. Standfast a ring.

Then she called for old Mr. Honest, and said of him, “Here is a true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit!” John 1:47. Then he said, I wish you a fair day when you set out for Mount Zion, and I will be glad to see you go over the river dry-shod. But she answered, Come wet, come dry, I long to be gone; for however the weather is on my journey, I will have time enough when I get there to sit down and rest and dry myself.

Then that good man Mr. Ready-to-halt came in to see her. So she said to him, Your journey so far has been hard; but that will make your rest all the sweeter. Watch, and be ready; for the messenger may come at an hour when you do not expect him.

After him came Mr. Despondency and his daughter Much-afraid, to whom she said, You+ ought to remember forever, with thankfulness, your+ deliverance from the hands of Giant Despair and out of Doubting Castle. The fruit of that mercy is that you+ have been brought here in safety. You+ be watchful, and cast away fear; be sober, and hope to the end.

Then she said to Mr. Feeble-mind, You were delivered from the mouth of Giant Slay-good so that you might live in the light of the living and see your King with comfort. Only I advise you to repent of your readiness to fear and doubt his goodness before he sends for you; so that you will not be forced, when he comes, to stand before him blushing for that fault.

Now the day drew near when Christiana must go. So the road was full of people come to see her set out on her journey. But behold, all the banks beyond the river were full of horses and chariots, which had come down from above to go with her to the city gate. So she came out and entered the river, with a wave of farewell to those who followed her. The last words she was heard to say were, I come, Lord, to be with you and bless you! So her children and friends went back to their place, for those who waited for Christiana had carried her out of their sight. So she went and called, and entered in at the gate with all the ceremonies of joy with which her husband Christian had entered before her. At her departure, the children wept.
