But Mr. Great-Heart and Mr. Valiant played on the well-tuned cymbal and harp for joy. So all went off to their own places.

In the course of time a messenger came to the town again, and his business was with Mr. Ready-to-halt. So he sought him out and said, I have come from Him whom you have loved and followed, though on crutches; and my message is to tell you that he expects you at his table to eat supper with him in his kingdom, the day after Easter; so prepare yourself for this journey. Then he also gave him a token that he was a true messenger, saying, “I have broken your golden bowl, and loosed your silver cord.” Eccl 12:6.

After this, Mr. Ready-to-halt called for his fellow-pilgrims and told them, I am sent for, and God will surely visit you too. So he asked Mr. Valiant to make his will. And because he had nothing to bequeath to those who would survive him but his crutches and his good wishes, he said this: These crutches I bequeath to my son who will tread in my steps, with a hundred warm wishes that he may prove better than I have been.

Then he thanked Mr. Great-Heart for his guidance and kindness, and so made ready for his journey. When he came to the brink of the river, he said, Now I will have no more need of these crutches, since there are chariots and horses over there for me to ride on. The last words he was heard to say were, Welcome life! So he went his way.

After this, word was brought to Mr. Feeble-mind that the messenger had sounded his horn at the door of his room. Then he came in and told him, I have come to tell you that your Master has need of you, and that in a very little while you must behold his face in brightness. And take this as a token of the truth of my message: “Those watching through windows are darkened.” Eccl 12:3. Then Mr. Feeble-mind called for his friends, and told them what message had been brought to him, and what token he had received of the truth of it. Then he said, Since I have nothing to leave to anyone, what is the point of my making a will? As for my feeble mind, I will leave that behind me, for I will have no need of it in the place where I am going, nor is it worth giving to the poorest pilgrims: so, when I am gone, I want you, Mr. Valiant, to bury it in a dunghill. When this was done, and the day had come on which he was to depart, he entered the river like the rest. His last words were, Hold out, faith and patience! So he went over to the other side.

When many days had passed, Mr. Despondency was sent for; for a messenger had come, and brought him this message: Trembling man! this is to summon you to be ready with the King by next Lord’s day, to shout for joy for your deliverance from all your doubtings. And, said the messenger, to prove that my message is true, take this: so he gave him a grasshopper to be a burden to him. Eccl 12:5.

Now Mr. Despondency’s daughter, whose name was Much-afraid, said, when she heard what had happened, that she would go with her father. Then Mr. Despondency said to his friends, My daughter and I, you know what we have been, and how troublesome we have been in every company. My will and my daughter’s is that our desponds and slavish fears be received by no man, from the day of our departure, forever; for I know that after my death they will offer themselves to others. For, to be plain with you, they are ghosts which we took in when we first began to be pilgrims, and could never shake off afterward; and they will walk about and look for a welcome from the pilgrims: but for our sakes, shut the doors on them. When the time came for them to depart, they went up to the brink of the river. The last words of Mr. Despondency were, Farewell, night; welcome, day! His daughter went through the river singing, but no one could understand what she said.

Then a while later a messenger came to the town and asked for Mr. Honest. So he came to the house where he was, and put these lines into his hand: You are commanded to be ready a week from this day, to present yourself before your Lord at his Father’s house. And for a token that my message is true, “All the daughters of song grow faint.” Eccl 12:4. Then Mr. Honest called for his friends, and said to them, I die, but I will make no will. As for my honesty, it shall go with me; let him who comes after be told of this. When the day came for him to go, he made ready to go over the river. Now the river at that time overflowed its banks in some places; but Mr. Honest, in his lifetime, had arranged with one Good-conscience to meet him there, which he did, and gave him his hand, and so helped him over. The last words of Mr. Honest were, Grace reigns! So he left the world.

After this the news went round that Mr. Valiant-for-truth had received a summons by the same messenger as the other, and had this as a token that the summons was true, “That his pitcher was broken at the fountain.” Eccl 12:6. When he understood it, he called for his friends and told them of it. Then he said, I am going to my Father’s; and though I have got here with great difficulty, yet now I do not regret all the trouble I have gone through to arrive where I am. My sword I give to him who shall succeed me in my pilgrimage, and my courage and skill to him who can get it. My marks and scars I carry with me, to be a witness for me that I have fought His battles who will now be my rewarder. When the day came that he must go from here, many went with him to the river-side, and as he went into it he said, “Death, where is your sting?” And as he went down deeper, he said, “Grave, where is your victory?” 1 Cor 15:55. So he passed over, and all the trumpets sounded for him on the other side.

Then a summons came for Mr. Standfast. This Mr. Standfast was the one whom the rest of the pilgrims found on his knees in the Enchanted Ground. And the messenger brought it to him open in his hands; it said that he must prepare for a change of life, for his Master was not willing for him to be so far from him any longer. At this Mr. Standfast fell into deep thought. No, said the messenger, you need not doubt the truth of my message; for here is a token of its truth, “Your wheel is broken at the cistern.” Eccl 12:6. Then he called Mr. Great-Heart, who was their guide, to him and said to him, Sir, although it was not my lot to be much in your good company during the days of my pilgrimage, yet since the time I have known you, you have done me good. When I came from home, I left behind me a wife and five small children; let me ask you, when you return (for I know that you go and return to your Master’s house, in the hope that you may yet be a conductor to more of the holy pilgrims), to send to my family, and let them know all that has happened and shall happen to me. Tell them moreover of my happy arrival at this place, and of the blessed condition I am in now and have been in of late. Tell them also of Christian and Christiana his wife, and how she and her children came after her husband. Tell them also what a happy end she made, and where she has gone. I have little or nothing to send to my family, unless it is prayers and tears for them; it will be enough for you to tell them of these, if perhaps they may prevail. When Mr. Standfast had set things in order like this, and the time had come for him to hurry away, he too went down to the river. Now there was a great calm in the river at that time; so Mr. Standfast, when he was about half-way in, stood a while and talked with his companions who had gone with him there. And he said, This river has been a terror to many; yes, the thought of it has often frightened me too; but now I think I stand at ease; my foot is fixed on that on which the feet of the priests who bore the ark of the covenant stood while Israel went over Jordan. Josh 3:17. The waters indeed are bitter to the palate, and cold to the stomach; yet the thought of what I am going to, and of the convoy that waits for me on the other side, lies like a glowing coal at my heart. I see myself now at the end of my journey; my toilsome days are ended. I am going to see that head which was crowned with thorns, and that face which was spit upon for me. Until now I have lived by hearsay and faith; but now I am going where I shall live by sight, and shall be with him in whose company I delight. I have loved to hear my Lord spoken of; and wherever I have seen the print of his shoe in the earth, there I have longed to set my foot too. His name has been to me like a civet-box; yes, sweeter than all perfumes. His voice has been most sweet to me, and I have desired his face more than those who have most desired the light of the sun. I used to gather his words for my food, and as antidotes against my faintings. He has held me, and has kept me from my iniquities; yes, my steps he has strengthened in his way.

Now, while he was speaking like this, his face changed; his strong man bowed under him; and after he had said, Take me, for I come to you, they saw him no more.

But it was glorious to see how the open region was filled with horses and chariots, with trumpeters and pipers, with singers and players on stringed instruments, to welcome the pilgrims as they went up and followed one another in at the beautiful gate of the city.

As for Christiana’s children, the four boys Christiana brought with her, with their wives and children, I did not stay where I was until they had gone over. Also, since I came away, I have heard someone say that they were still alive, and would remain so for the increase of the church in the place where they were, for a time.

Should it be my lot to go that way again, I may give those who wish it an account of what I am silent about here: meanwhile I bid my reader

FAREWELL.

THE END.
